News.title: Hilarious moment hungry vulture repeatedly rolls croc in water as it desperately tries balance & feast on carcass
News.content:
Next

THIS is the hilarious moment a ravenous vulture is sent on a bizarre log-rolling ride as it desperately tries to feast on a dead caiman.

Wild footage shows the hungry scavenger furiously flapping its enormous black wings as the reptile carcass spins beneath its feet in the water.



The slippery caiman becomes a makeshift treadmill as the determined bird frantically tries to stay upright while eyeing up its grisly meal.

But every attempt to grab a bite sends the carcass rolling again – forcing the vulture into an extraordinary balancing act.



The baffled bird spreads its wings wide and desperately treads across the rotating reptile like a hamster racing on a wheel.

At one point, the famished creature appears tantalisingly close to finally tucking in before its floating feast shifts beneath it once again.

The comical wildlife battle was spotted by photographer Sandesh Kadur while on safari in the Pantanal.

He initially noticed the lone black vulture stranded in the middle of the water and had no idea what had caught its attention.



But after his boat moved closer, the bizarre scene became clear.

Kadur said: “I wasn’t sure what was going on, so our amazing Boat Guide, Branco, veered towards the vulture. That’s when I saw a dead caiman floating on the water’s surface.

“The single vulture that had landed on it was trying in desperation to feed on the carcass, but the log-rolling caiman proved to be quite the challenge-like trying to eat while on a treadmill.”

The remarkable encounter comes after another hilarious animal showdown saw a knife-wielding crab square up to a terrified pooch.

Bizarre footage showed the feisty crustacean scuttling through a Florida garden armed with what appeared to be a pocket knife.



The pint-sized menace then appeared to take a swipe at adorable dog Summer as she cautiously sniffed around the blade-brandishing intruder.

Her stunned owner Eduardo Alvarez spotted the bizarre danger and raced over – only to find himself locked in an extraordinary stand-off with the armed crab.

A baffled Alvarez asked: “Summer, where the heck did you find a crab with a freaking shank?”

Footage showed the fearless Florida resident desperately trying to snatch the creature while dodging its snapping claws and unlikely weapon.

After a tense tussle, he finally managed to seize the nippy beast and carry it further into the yard.

“Summer, I don’t recommend messing with this,” he warns.

“This is a gangster-ass crab,” Alvarez quips.

News.title: Charles Spencer’s Diana book is HIS ‘swan song’ with a litany of bizarre attacks & he leaves King question unanswered
News.content:
Next

IF you’re thinking Swan Song is a book on Diana you’ll be disappointed because it’s a classic tale of an author displaying main character energy.

Finishing Earl Spencer‘s account of his sister’s life leaves you’re crying out for more. Not for more of his meandering prose but more about the life of the former Princess of Wales.



Because just like Harry’s similar hatchet-job Spare, Spencer’s attempt is billed as an inside tell-all account but is instead written to settle the author’s personal grudges by deliberately attempting to embarrass the Royals with salacious and selected stories.

Spencer confessed in his BBC interview the book is also his own ‘swan song’ and he is right; because it’s all about him.

There are hundreds of royal books about Diana’s life over the years and you would have hoped her own brother could usurp them all.



Instead, it’s a quick romp through Spencer family history and Diana’s childhood, sprinkled with disputed attacks against Charles, which have all been heavily trailed before its release.

It also veers into the bizarre, with accounts of one of Charles’s ‘retinue’ at Diana’s burial trying to hide while saying, ‘Please ignore me – I am a tree,’ and an overly-described tale of a ‘shaggy’ man with a ‘generous belly’ stopping him in the street to say, ‘Top speech,’ following his eulogy at Di’s funeral.

Just like Spare the hero of the book – Charles Spencer in this case – is painted as a caring rebel struggling against a Royal Family incapable of expressing love.



While King Charles, the story’s villain, is painted as a gruff, aged, heartless relic who not only claims he never loved Diana but, heaven forbid, once asked her to turn down her loud music.

Naturally, there are pages and pages of criticism of the media, even though Charles Spencer also openly states in his book the many times he had given interviews about Diana to the press and how he colluded with author Andrew Morton and Daily Mail reporter Richard Kay.

These contradictions and one-sided accounts are very much like Harry’s Spare but at least the Duke of Sussex was lucky enough to employ an excellent ghostwriter to create a gripping read.



Spencer prides himself on being a historian or note and author of seven non-fiction books but his recollections were disputed by Buckingham Palace before it was even published.

Now, Piers Morgan is threatening to sue over what he says are “demonstrable lies” about him in the book.

Dare I say it, Swan Song feels rushed and reads like it was hastily crafted and incomplete.

Running just 367 pages Spencer’s book falls far short of being a compelling read and adds little to the Diana books already on your shelf.

At an eye-watering £28 (which is 8p a page) you reach the end feeling rather short-changed.



And we still don’t have an answer to The Sun’s front page last week, ‘Why is he doing this to the King now?’

One star out of five.

News.title: Film star faces bulldozers tearing up £9k garden at £900k home after making it 5ft too high in council row
News.content:
Next

A BOLLYWOOD actor and singer faces having the garden at his £900,000 home torn apart by bulldozers for building it 1.6m too high without planning permission.

Sumeet Singh Sarao, 39, is embroiled in a bitter six year planning dispute with his local council after he raised the ground levels of his £9,000 garden at his property in Telford, Shropshire.



Telford & Wrekin Council now claims neighbouring residents are suffering an “unacceptable” loss of privacy because of the height of the garden close to the rear boundary.

Mr Sarao says he raised a lower section of his garden to match the level of the rest of the plot during the landscaping works in 2020 without it overlooking any other properties.



But planning bosses have now launched enforcement action to make him dig out a huge part of his raised back garden or face having it bulldozed by them.

Mr Sarao insists he has repeatedly offered compromises such as putting up more trees and plantation to protect his neighbours‘ privacy but says planners have rejected every suggestion.





The commercial singer, who has lived at the house for 14 years with his mum and dad, said: “I’m being made out to be a criminal just for raising my garden.

“I’m just a normal human and don’t cause any harm to anybody. It feels really unfair.

“The issue relates to a section of my garden that I raised to match the level of the existing higher ground.

“The council argues that the raised garden affects neighbouring privacy but you can look at the garden and see there’s no privacy issues,

“There is already a thick hedge along the boundary that prevents overlooking which is much taller than me – it just doesn’t make sense.



“Also both my neighbour and I would need a step-ladder to be able to see over the fence anyway.

“I offered to replace the existing planting with a continuous row of conifers to create an even stronger privacy screen.

“But the council rejected that proposal, saying it would appear too bulky regardless of me trying to co-operate.

“I don’t understand that argument when there are already mature trees and conifers along the same boundary.

“The council wants me to lower the garden by around 1.6 metres.



“That would make the ground level lower than it was originally before the works were carried out.

“I’ve spent around £8,000 to £9,000 on the garden and put a lot of work into it.

“If I don’t comply, they could carry out the work themselves and charge me for the cost.

“It’s not sensible because they would have to take out walls to get the bulldozers in.

“These would be unnecessary and potentially disruptive works. It just doesn’t make sense to me.



“I’ve tried repeatedly to find a constructive solution, but the council insists the garden must be dug out and returned to its previous level.”

Mr Sarao says the six year dispute has caused “significant stress” for his family.

He added: “The whole family has been affected by the uncertainty and the threat of enforcement action.

“I feel as though I’m up against a brick wall because the council is unwilling to consider my proposals.

“It feels like I’ve been pushed into a corner.”



After carrying out the work himself during Covid, council planners got in touch to say he must apply for retrospective planning permission.

Telford & Wrekin Council says that neighbour amenity is “unacceptably harmed” by overlooking and loss of privacy and it must act “to uphold the planning system and protect the amenity of neighbouring residents”.

Mr Sarao has been told he must dig out down to 1,600mm (5.2 ft) at the end of the garden nearest a boundary and make it slope to a depth of 900mm nearest the house (2.9 ft).

He said he is not ignoring a recent enforcement notice but has proposed to remove the retaining wall, introduce a sloping transition near the boundary and add substantial landscaping and screening to protect the neighbours’ privacy and amenity.

He added: “The council has now contacted me to arrange a meeting, although they have not indicated whether they are willing to consider any alternatives.



“We are simply asking for fair treatment, proper engagement and a reasonable opportunity to agree a solution that protects neighbouring amenity while taking account of the practical circumstances at the property.”

A council spokesperson said the issue has been the subject of ongoing planning and enforcement investigations for a number of years.

An enforcement notice was supported by an independent planning inspector following an appeal in September 2025.

The council spokesperson said: “Since that time we have engaged with the land owner, and most recently considered a pre-application submission to explore a revised scheme for the site but were unable to support that proposal in its proposed form and that the planning harm could not be satisfactorily addressed.

“The Enforcement Notice was upheld by the Planning Inspectorate in September 2025, with a further period provided for compliance.



“Despite this, the required remedial works have still not been carried out and the site remains in breach of planning control. The Council has therefore advised that it is now considering further formal action to secure compliance.

“This could include prosecution proceedings and/or works in default with costs recovered from the landowner.

“Whilst our preference remains to secure voluntary compliance, there comes a point where the Council must act to uphold the planning system and protect the amenity of neighbouring residents.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The Council has therefore asked for a timetable for implementation of the required remedial work.

“We have also offered to meet with the landowner in person to work with him to resolve this matter as soon as possible.”

News.title: How Oxford grooming gang forced girls as young as 12 to have sex with hundreds- & police labelled them ‘prostitutes’
News.content:
STOLEN INNOCENCE How Oxford grooming gang forced girls as young as 12 to have sex with hundreds- & police labelled them ‘prostitutes’







Next

A WOMAN who was sexually abused as a child by an Oxford grooming gang has said she still sees men she was forced to sleep with roaming the streets freely.

“A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant – everywhere you can imagine – you’ll see a man that’s done something,” the victim said in a BBC Panorama documentary, Grooming Gangs: Why Were We Ignored?, which aired this week.



Rachel, not her real name, estimated that she was abused by “hundreds” of men in Oxford from the age of 12, but claimed her attempts to tell the police about the abuse at first fell on deaf ears.

Despite its reputation as being one of the world’s most beautiful cities, Oxford was home to a prolific grooming gang, mostly operated by older men of Pakistani heritage, between the 90s and late 2010s, according the the BBC.



The Oxford Bullfinch trial, which took place in 2013, revealed the systematic grooming, trafficking, and rape of six young girls in the city over an eight year period, and led to a series of follow up investigations in other parts of the country.

The 2011 investigation which led to the trial exposed a web of abusers, mostly of Pakistani heritage, who were targeting and exploiting young, predominately white girls throughout Oxford.

Rotherham, Rochdale, Oldham and Bradford are among several sites with prominent sexual abuse scandals, many dating back decades.

Police investigated from between 1998 and 2011, though it’s now thought that some victims’ abuse started even before then.

Rachel was just 12 when she was befriended by gangs in Oxford.

“They gave me cigarettes, showed an interest in my life,” she recalled during an interview with BBC journalist Ellie Flynn.



What started off as a friendly interaction in the street became three years of horrendous physical and sexual abuse spanning three years between 2004 and 2006.

“We were mostly taken to these bedsit type places. [They were] horrible, dingy, nasty,” she recalled.

By the time she was 13, she was trapped in a cycle of sexual abuse and drug addiction.



At the time, she had been referred to social services and was living between her family home and in care.

During this time, Rachel said she was trafficked to other cities around the UK, where more men paid the gang for sex with her.

Rachel reported the abuse to her social worker but said she was not taken seriously. “It was written down that I was manipulative and that I was enjoying the attention that I was getting,” she said.

“There are literal sentences in my files that say I was fantasising. Even though you’ve got a child covered in cigarette burns that have gone septic.”

On one occasion, she described going to the police with her mum.



“I was actually bleeding through my bottoms. My mum came. She was very clear with the police that the blood had to be the result of something pretty horrendous.”

However, the police did not respond as she hoped. Rachel was just 13 at the time she claimed the police accused her of being a prostitute.

“They said, ‘if you’re going to carry on prostituting yourself, then this is going to be the outcome isn’t it?’”

“A 13-year-old can’t consent to sex and they certainly can’t make a decision to prostitute themselves,” Rachel said.



She even claimed a police officer asked her for oral sex while in the car with them, which she refused, the incident further deteriorating her faith in social and police services.

Her records show dozens of occasions when she reported instances of abuse, including giving the names of offenders.

She said she was even discovered with her abusers by the police on some occasions. One time they were arrested but Rachel dropped the case in fear.

“I thought that would be where it ended for me because no one was doing anything to help me or the other girls,” she said.



Thames Valley police were informed about the gang’s operation in 2006, but victims accounts show the men were still abusing girls three years later, the documentary said.

One of those was Chloe, not her real name, who, prior to the documentary, had only told “a handful of people” her abuse.

She claimed she was assaulted by a man at an after school club aged 13.

Chloe, now in her 30s, was later drawn in by grooming gangs and went on to suffer years of abuse.

After meeting gang members who initially appeared to be her friends, they started asking her to return their generosity with favours.



“They’d try and give you money or they’d pay for things and then it would quickly turn into, ‘you owe us something’,” she said.

“They’d pick us up and they’d be this random old man in the car and we’d go to this flat, for example.”

There, Chloe would be plied with alcohol and raped. “I think, to be honest, they preferred it when you were paralytic,” she said.

She believes her abusers were aged between 20 and 60. “It was people I’d have never had anything to do with,” she said.

“There were a few times I’d say, I don’t want to do it, and that’s when they would just be really scary.”



Chloe never told the police about what had happened to her.

She said: “I didn’t understand what was happening completely… How I felt about myself was so low that I kind of just accepted that situation.”

In 2011, Thames Valley police launched an investigation. Using surveillance, they soon uncovered the extent of the gangs evil operation.

Speaking in the documentary, Simon Morton, former acting detective inspector at Thames Valley Police, called the gang’s scheme a “money-making business.”

Chloe was 15 and still involved with the abusers when police identified her as a potential victim during their investigation in 2011.



She told officers that the men would have sex with, physically abuse, and threaten her and other victims.

However, she still felt some officers didn’t see her as a victim.

She said: “They were saying we were all prostitutes… How can a kid be a prostitute? But if the police are saying it you start to believe it about yourself.

“You’re a kid, but you’re being treated like an adult because of the adult things that have happened to you.”

Chloe chose not to go through a police investigation or give evidence against her abusers



Meanwhile, it wasn’t until she was 15 that Rachel broke free from her abusers, and it was in 2011 that police approached her to help.

She agreed and gave evidence in the Bullfinch trial at the age of 21, including having to face nine defence barristers of the accused men, who “scrutinised” and “shamed” her “whole life”.

Seven men were found guilty. Akhtar Dogar, Anjum Dogar and Kamar Jamil were found guilty of rape, conspiracy to rape and arranging child prostitution for the crimes against Rachel.

A third woman, called Sarah, not her real name, spoke about how she was targeted by grooming gangs in the 1990s at the age of 11.

In the years that followed her abuse, Sarah suffered heavily with drug addiction, which she claims is the result of being introduced to drugs at an early age by groomers.



She said: “At first, it’s ‘do you want a cigarette?’ but you don’t know what you’re heading for. Some of the cigarettes they were giving us had brown stuff coming out of it. It was laced with heroin.

“My addiction, through my whole life now, has resulted from them giving us those cigarettes,” she said. “I was addicted very highly from the age of 11.”

Sarah said her abusers would then tell her she owed them money and have to repay it.

“They’d lock us in. Then, before you know it, there’s six, seven people turning up. You’re just outnumbered basically.”

It took much longer for Sarah’s abusers to face up to the crimes they had committed. She spent years battling addiction which had led to a criminal record.



“I was that horrified by what I’d been through that I was not gonna disclose it to anyone. I was actually going to take it to my grave,” she said.

Sarah was in prison when police approached her suspecting she could be a victim.

At first, still struggling with the shame of her abuse, she denied everything.

But with more evidence pouring in, she eventually gave in and told them what happened to her.

“My whole family was devastated,” she recalled.



In 2020, she gave evidence against three men who were found guilty of 35 offences committed against her from the age of 13.

Naim Kahn was sentenced to 24 years, Mohammed Nazir to 20 years and Raheem Ahmed to five years, although Sarah said she hoped these would be higher.

Steps to Keep Your Child Safe From Grooming By Emma Kenny, true crime psychologist and parenting expert Encourage your child to share their day-to-day experiences. Ask who they talked to on the way home, what happened at the bus stop, and if anything made them feel uncomfortable. The more openly you talk, the more confident they’ll be to speak up if something feels off. If possible, arrange for your child to walk or travel with friends. Identify safe spaces along the route, trusted neighbours or shops where they can go if they feel threatened. Groomers often switch to online contact once they’ve made initial in-person connections. Monitor your child’s digital devices in a respectful but proactive way. Agree on ground rules for social media use, and encourage them to show you anything that makes them feel uneasy. If your parental alarm bells are going off, do not dismiss those feelings. Challenge unusual behaviour or new relationships gently but firmly. Seek professional advice if you suspect your child is at risk. If you have any evidence or strong suspicions that someone is grooming your child, contact the police immediately. Support and guidance from organisations like the NSPCC or Barnardo’s can also be invaluable in helping you navigate this distressing situation.

“I may not be in prison now, but it feels like a prison sentence, day in and day out,” she said.

In total, 21 men have been convicted in Oxford.

When asked how many abusers are still free, ex police officer Simon Morton said there were “hundreds”.



“The amount of people who are still out there… It was nationwide,” he said. “We got the core group, that doesn’t mean there isn’t more.”

According to the BBC, reports into grooming nationally have asked why these crimes weren’t acted on sooner.

In some parts of the country, such as Rotherham, police and councils were accused of failing to act for fear of being accused of being racist.

However, a serious 2015 case review into the Oxford grooming gang found there was no evidence of that this was a factor.

The review discovered numerous failings by Oxfordshire County Council and Thames Valley Police.



Rachel brought a civil case against the council and received an out-of-court settlement, as well as an apology from the chief-constable of Thames Valley Police.

Thames Valley Police told the BBC: “The impact of child sexual exploitation is lifelong… [It] works tirelessly to investigate these horrific crimes and bring offenders to justice.”

It added: “It is never too late to come forward… [It] will listen… and do everything it can to support victims, survivors and their families.”

Oxfordshire County Council said: “Protecting children remains [its] highest priority.”

It accepted the findings of the serious case review and apologised for failings identified.



It also said it has strengthened “safeguarding arrangements” and “improved multi-agency working” to ensure young people are heard.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It has also enhanced “the identification and response to child sexual exploitation”, and said its children’s services had been rated good by Ofsted over the last 12 years.

News.title: Shameless ‘Oliver Twist’ kids as young as 5 are being ‘trained to steal’ from our shops – we MUST ban balaclava masks
News.content:
Next

STORE owners in a town where two children in balaclavas were filmed shoplifting have called for a ban on masks.

The tiny thieves – who are thought to be as young as five – were captured wearing balaclavas as they snatched watermelon and other fruit before fleeing.



The disturbing footage was captured by shopkeeper Erdogan Yigitoglu, who says the incident is just one example of the enormous shoplifting problem facing his business on Charminster Road, Bournemouth.

And now other traders have told The Sun they want the wearing of masks inside shops banned.



Mr Yigitoglu, 52 – who has run his store for 19 years – said he was stunned to see such young children involved during the incident, understood to have taken place last year.

He claims one mum even smiled and patted a boy on the head, as if congratulating him on the theft.

The scene has drawn comparisons to Charles Dickens’ Oliver Twist, in which criminal Fagin employs children to steal on his behalf.

Mr Yigitoglu said: “It seemed like they were training the kids to steal. I’m a father myself and I just thought that is such a bad way to raise kids.”



He says he has further CCTV of other brazen thefts – with fellow traders also up in arms.

Johnnie and Lorna Lovell, who run BH Vape, told The Sun this week people should be banned from wearing face coverings in shops – but encouraged storekeepers to be alert.



Johnnie, 61, said: “We are an established venue here for 15 years, we don’t have any problems with shoplifters but that’s because we don’t give them the opportunity.

“We have CCTV and we don’t really leave anything out they can take without us seeing.

“But it is a problem in the area. I think the shops are allowing it, everybody is scared to take action.”

He continued: “All we can do as shopkeepers is keep eyes out and minimise the opportunity – don’t put your stock out the front. Owners have got to be more alert.



“You also have to look at the parents of these young kids letting them go out and do this in balaclavas. I think any head covering should be banned in shops.

“And I think we need some stronger rules and government because it is really prevalent.”

Alex Shenker, 35, who works with them, added: “I saw the footage of the kids in balaclavas, it was pretty shocking.

“Even though you couldn’t see their faces, they looked really little.



“I don’t think anyone has ever got a good intention if they’re wearing a balaclava.”

A worker at the Taj Supermarket said shoplifting used to involve only alcoholics or drug users, but now it seems like everyone is doing it.

They said: “I think shoplifting is a real problem at the moment because of the rise in prices. We do have to keep watch and we have CCTV through the shop.

“It used to just be people with alcohol or drugs problems, now it seems to be anyone.



“You get smartly-dressed people and kids shoplifting so you don’t know who is a shoplifter and who’s not.”

Another shopkeeper, who didn’t want to be named, said: “We don’t have an issue because we have a bit of a reputation, we don’t allow it.

“But I think it’s more of an issue for other shops, it might be the way they have their shop set up, it’s easier for people to steal.

“Times are hard and it happens to every business, the number of incidents is definitely going up.

“I think shoplifters think they can get away with it because they know police won’t come out for less than £200 value so they’re saying ‘you can’t touch me’.”



Erdogan – who said he shared the footage on social media in a bid to identify the youngsters – said nobody has come forward and he has not seen them again.

In one alarming raid at his store, a man allegedly stole £120 worth of disposable barbecues in a matter of seconds.

Another incident showed an elderly woman using a walking frame allegedly pilfering chocolate.

Erdogan also described a man who threw tomatoes at passersby before allegedly mooning people.

He recalled another case involving a girl aged around 11 or 12 who stole a toothbrush, before her mum returned to pay and apologise.



He said: “Of course these incidents make us fearful. They affect us much more than people might realise.

“Sometimes we feel that we cannot even breathe properly because we are so worried about what might happen next.

“Even when we leave the shop, our minds are still here.

“We are always thinking, ‘has anything gone missing? Has someone stolen something?’

“You cannot properly switch off from it!”



The dad-of-three said his biggest concern is the effect such behaviour could have on children who grow up seeing theft as normal.

He said: “What concerns me most is the effect this can have on the next generation.

“If young people grow up seeing this behaviour as normal or something to copy, I really worry about where we will be in the future if nothing changes.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He added: “My message is simple: we need to stop treating shoplifting as something normal or harmless.

“We want to see action so that small businesses can feel safe again.”

News.title: Woman among four injured in ‘machete attack’ – as cops swoop on street next to woodland & four people arrested
News.content:
Next

A WOMAN is among four people injured in an alleged machete attack – as cops make four arrests.

Officers swooped on a quiet street in Halifax, West Yorkshire, shortly after 2pm on Monday following reports a group of people were fighting.



Cops said a group of adults were reportedly seen emerging from a nearby woodland on Maltings Road.

Upon arrival, cops found four people with non-life threatening injuries believed to have been caused by “bladed weapons”.



According to reports, the weapon in question was a machete.

West Yorkshire Police said three men – aged 30, 53 and 56 – and a woman, aged 26, have now been arrested.

The three injured men were raced to hospital for treatment.

Forensic officers could be spotted combing the street for several hours following the incident as the force appeals for witnesses.

A police spokesperson said: “Police have made arrests and are appealing for witnesses after an affray incident in Halifax.

“Detectives at Calderdale CID would like to speak to anyone who has footage or information about the incident in which a group of people were fighting near Maltings Road in Halifax on Monday afternoon.



“Officers were called to Maltings Road at a just after 2pm to a report a group of adults had been seen coming out of woodland there with injuries.

“Attending officers located four people with non-life threatening injuries believed to have been caused by bladed weapons.

“Three men aged 30, 53 and 56, and a 26-year-old woman were arrested.

“The three injured men needed hospital treatment.

“Enquires remain ongoing into the circumstances of the affray, and Halifax Neighbourhood Policing Team officers have been conducting reassurance patrols in the area.”



Anyone with information about the incident is urged to get in touch with the force quoting reference number 13260537619.

News.title: Exact time the Autumn Equinox falls tonight and how to follow
News.content:
Next

ASTRONOMICAL summer comes to an end tonight as the autumn equinox arrives in the UK.

The annual event marks the point when the Sun crosses the celestial equator, signalling the start of autumn in the Northern Hemisphere.



What time is the autumn equinox 2026?

The autumn equinox takes place at exactly 1.06am on Wednesday, September 23.

That means the astronomical event falls during the night of Tuesday, September 22, into Wednesday morning.



It comes just over three weeks after meteorological autumn began on Tuesday, September 1, with the two systems using different ways to divide up the seasons.

From today, Britain loses roughly four minutes of daylight every day as we head towards winter.



It also means the next big seasonal milestone isn’t far off, with the clocks going back an hour at 2am on Sunday, October 25, giving you an extra hour in bed but darker evenings.

What does the autumn equinox mean?

Instead of the Northern Hemisphere – where the UK sits – tilting towards the Sun as it does at the height of summer, Earth hits a tipping point today where the Sun sits directly over the equator.

That leaves the Northern and Southern hemispheres getting a 50/50 split of sunlight for a brief moment before the UK starts tilting away from the Sun as we head into the winter months.

The autumn equinox marks the beginning of astronomical autumn in the UK, which continues until the winter solstice on Monday, December 21.



But its name can be slightly misleading. Although “equinox” comes from Latin words meaning “equal night”, day and night are not exactly the same length on September 23.

The point when daylight and darkness are closest to equal is known as the equilux, which falls shortly after the equinox in the UK this year on September 25.

This happens because Earth’s atmosphere acts like a giant lens, bending light over the horizon and giving us a sneaky extra few minutes of daylight even after the Sun has technically set.

From around this point in the year, the nights continue getting longer and the days get shorter until the winter solstice.

How can you follow the autumn equinox?

There will be no sudden spectacle in the sky at exactly 1.06am, as an equinox is a precise astronomical moment rather than a visible event such as an eclipse.



But people will gather at Stonehenge on Wednesday morning to watch the sunrise and mark the changing of the seasons.

English Heritage is providing free Managed Open Access, with the car park opening at 5.15am and the monument field opening as soon as there is enough light.

Sunrise is expected at approximately 6.54am, with open access ending at 8.30am.

You can follow the changing sky above Stonehenge using English Heritage’s Stonehenge Skyscape.

The website provides a live view from within the stone circle, allowing viewers around the world to watch the Sun, Moon and stars above the monument at any time of day or night.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you’re stepping outside to mark the seasonal shift yourself, look to the skies in the early evening.

Sunsets will start creeping earlier each day, with darkness arriving before 7pm across most of the UK this week.

News.title: Maker of celeb anti-ageing potion made from fish scales loses £3.6m tax fight after claiming £50 drink is ‘food’
News.content:
WRINKLE IN THE PLAN Maker of celeb anti-ageing potion made from fish scales loses £3.6m tax fight after claiming £50 drink is ‘food’







Next

THE maker of a celebrity-endorsed anti-ageing potion using fish scales has lost a £3.6million fight with the taxman after claiming the £50 drink was “food”.

London-based entrepreneur Tony Sanguinetti, 59, founded beauty company Minerva Research Labs Ltd in 2009 to produce collagen supplements made from waste sardine scales and cow hides after becoming “obsessed with finding a way to reverse the signs of ageing”.



The company now has a yearly turnover of around £16million and makes the best-selling collagen drink in the UK, Gold Collagen Pure.

Its products are advertised and endorsed by stars including Yasmin Le Bon, TV presenter Charlotte Hawkins and former Olympic champion Dame Denise Lewis.



In 2022, however, the company asked the taxman to hand back around £3.6m it had paid out since 2018, claiming that it had been classified in the wrong tax bracket and ought to have been “zero rated” for VAT.

After HMRC refused the refund, the company took the case to a tax tribunal, arguing that the supplements ought to be regarded as a “food” providing “healthy nutrition” for tax purposes, rather than being more akin to a “medicine.”



It argued the beauty drink provides customers with “the perfect blend of nutritional ingredients to act as a building block for great skin, great hair, functional joints and muscles”.

But Judge Anne Redston, sitting in the tax chamber of the First-tier Tribunal, has now rejected Minerva’s bid to avoid the massive tax bill.



Giving judgment, she said the products are not marketed to be taken as a meal or snack and that just because they “taste nice doesn’t mean that purchasers are buying them as a food.”

“The sole issue for determination was whether the products were ‘food of a kind used for human consumption’ and so zero-rated,” she said.

“Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, found in connective tissue, muscle and skin.

“As we age, the amount of collagen reduces, so skin becomes thinner and less elastic, joints become less supple and hair becomes thinner.

“All of the products contain either hydrolysed marine collagen or hydrolysed bovine collagen.



“The marine collagen is produced from waste fish scales by a French company…The bovine collagen is produced from cow skin or hides by a German company.

“The products are consistently held out as providing nourishment for bones, cartilage, muscles, joints, hair and skin.

“Since the purpose of food is to provide nourishment for the body, we have found this to be a weighty factor supporting the appellant’s case.

“There are however many factors on the other side of the scales.

“Minerva usually refers to the quantity a person should consume every day as a ‘dose’, with occasional references to it as a ‘treatment’ and a ‘serving’.



“The products are also held out for sale as liquid beauty supplements…and the reviews and social media posts concerning the products demonstrate that consumers purchase the products for their cosmetic and anti-ageing benefits.

“The products are not marketed to be eaten instead of a meal, or even as a snack. Although they are sold via some outlets which also sell food, they are not positioned alongside food products.

“A number of factors are indicative of a medicine rather than a food. In our judgment… the products are not ‘food for human consumption’.”

The tribunal heard that Mr Sanguinetti, who grew up in Italy, founded Minerva in 2009 and “became slightly obsessed with finding a way to reverse the signs of ageing”.

In the same year he travelled to Japan, where collagen drinks were on sale and began to research and test how to produce collagen-based drinks in Europe.



Minerva’s first products were created in 2011, with the help of Japanese partners, and Gold Collagen Pure launched in the UK in June of that year.

He told the tribunal that, anxious about getting his goods through customs and with no equivalent product in the UK, he accepted the customs code given to him and Minerva paid VAT at the standard rate.

“Since then, Minerva has developed a range of products, all based on collagen,” said the judge.

“Mr Sanguinetti described them as ‘perfect blend of nutritional ingredients to act as a building block for great skin, great hair, functional joints and muscles’. Gold Collagen Pure is now the best-selling collagen drink in the UK.”

The case ended up before the tribunal after an HMRC inspector refused Minerva’s request to reclassify the products as food.



The inspector had found the products were “predominately held out for sale as a health and beauty supplement” and that, despite having nutritional benefits, “are primarily taken by the consumer for their anti-ageing properties”.

Backing HMRC’s stance, the judge said the products are sold as a “liquid beauty supplement,” adding, “We find as a fact, having considered all the evidence, that consumers purchase the products for their cosmetic and anti-ageing benefits.

“Some of the outlets sell food as well as beauty products, but…we find that the outlets which also sell foods do not sell the products as part of the food sections of their stores or their websites.

“The fact that the products are ‘food supplements’ indicates no more than that they are edible, have been added to food and must meet various regulatory requirements.

“That does not help us answer the statutory question, namely whether what has been added to the food is itself ‘food of a kind used for human consumption’.



“It is clear from our findings of fact that the products provide nourishment: they supply between 8 percent and 23 percent of a man’s daily protein requirement, and between 6 percent and 13 percent of a woman’s requirement, the source of protein being the collagen which forms the key ingredient of all the products.

“The products also contain some carbohydrate, which gives energy, and… the vitamins and minerals supplied by the additional ingredients also have nutritional value.”

She said the nourishment provided by the products is a key part of Minerva’s marketing and that its first products were born out of Mr Sanguinetti’s interest in “healthy nutrition.”

“There is no dispute that collagen in the form of bone broth has been consumed for centuries and was thus ‘food of a kind used for human consumption’,” she continued.

“However, that is not this case: the products are not the same as bone broth, but instead a condensed, processed form of hydrolysed collagen from fish scales and hides.



“The fact that the products taste nice doesn’t mean that purchasers are buying them as a food.

“The products are also held out for sale as liquid beauty supplements… Minerva was the official supplier of beauty supplements to London Fashion Week, and the reviews and social media posts concerning the products demonstrate that consumers purchase the products for their cosmetic and anti-ageing benefits.

“The products are not marketed to be eaten instead of a meal, or even as a snack. Although they are sold via some outlets which also sell food, they are not positioned alongside food products.

“A number of factors are indicative of a medicine rather than a food.

“The amount which should be consumed is almost always described as a ‘dose’, and there are some references to ‘treatment’; both these terms are suggestive of medicine.



“Some of the products are sold as ‘specially formulated’ for particular age groups, and all are marketed as ‘not suitable for under the age of 18’.

“Although some foods, notably alcohol, are subject to age restrictions on sale, it is generally atypical for the sale of foods to be restricted in this way.

“All the products are labelled with ‘precautions’ or ‘warnings’ so that customers are warned to consult their doctor if they are pregnant, breastfeeding or on medication. That too is not characteristic of foods.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We considered that the factors in the appellant’s favour were outweighed by those on the other side of the scales.

“In our judgment, the outcome of the multi-factorial test is that the products are not ‘food for human consumption,’” the judge concluded.

News.title: PM to warn EU chief of 'damage' posed by Made in Europe scheme
News.content:
Andy Burnham has warned of the "collateral damage" posed by the EU's Made In Europe rules, ahead of a meeting later with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen during a UN summit in New York.

The proposals aim to curb the presence of Chinese companies in the EU by giving manufacturers inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his "immediate priority" was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach "practical agreement that will further boost the British economy".

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the UK government is concerned that plans to favour EU companies could harm British manufacturing.

Burnham said it could "affect British industry and supply chains" and that he would raise his concerns with von der Leyen during a meeting that is expected to take place on Tuesday at the UN's annual summit.

"We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us," he added.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies hereâ¦ we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

Tensions over the Made in Europe policy have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

News.title: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
News.content:
Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives.

Prof Fowler told the BBC that a Martha's Rule call would mean a patient receives an "appropriate response", for example, a senior nurse or member of the critical care outreach team could conduct a review of the case.

Staff can themselves also ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken.

During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care.

Prof Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further "is on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings".

This included in-patient wards, where Prof Fowler said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls"; three quarters of which came from families.

Prof Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions."

Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Prof Fowler told the BBC this had not played out in the recent tests.

"There was a concern we would receive an overwhelming number of calls, and that would be a distraction and actually divert staff from the important work they're doing," he said.

"But that hasn't been the case, actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls."

Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS."

Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's rule "is making a difference on the wards".

"It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, and urged parents: "if you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion."

Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'".

The phased rollout in England will be completed by March 2028.

Patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff.

News.title: Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor
News.content:
An unexpected surge in government borrowing in August, driven by persistently higher inflation, has added to pressure on Chancellor John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first Budget at the end of October.

Borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was Â£18.3bn in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

That figure was Â£3.5bn more than official forecasters expected.

Inflation rose to its highest rate in five months in August in the UK, driven up by higher petrol and diesel prices.

Although tax receipts were higher in August compared with a year ago, spending on public services, benefits, and other costs grew more as the pace of price rises increased.

The interest the government is paying on its debt rose to Â£8.8bn, its highest August level since records began in 1997.

The cost of servicing that debt comes as the government is under pressure to spend more on defence and cost-of-living support to households, said Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy.

He said it was important not to "overinterpret a single month given the volatility in the numbers", but added that there were some "concerning elements".

He said the cost of paying the interest on government debt is likely to rise in the coming months.

News.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe suspends production at key UK plants blaming high gas prices
News.content:
Billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe's industrial giant Ineos is pausing production at its three plants in Hull, blaming high UK gas prices.

The firm said gas prices in the UK are twelve times higher than in the US, and eight times more expensive than the coal-based processes used by Chinese competitors.

Sir Jim said: "We are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe, but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete."

The facilities produce raw materials used to make pharmaceuticals, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction materials and military explosives in the UK and Europe. Gas is a key ingredient in production.

Ineos said the move will affect up to 1,000 of its staff, of whom 245 work directly at the site.

But the BBC understands workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from the US at lower prices - which could take up to a year - or waits for gas prices to go down.

Ineos is asking governments in the UK and the EU â where most of its products are exported to â to put in tariff protections against Chinese products.

One plant makes acetic acid, which is used in vinegar, paint and glue. Another makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin, and the third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and for decaffeinating tea and coffee.

He said the current government's energy policy was "economic vandalism on an industrial scale".

The wholesale price of natural gas â used for heating homes and generating electricity â has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

The disruption of supplies of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran has pushed up prices around the world.

Ineos says that its plants in Humberside are "among the most efficient in the world", producing materials with half the carbon footprint of US rivals, and only one eighth the footprint of Chinese equivalents.

Two plants are already shut and a third will stop production in the coming days, the company said.

It's the second time in less than a week that Sir Jim, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, has heavily criticised government policy.

He told BBC News last week that he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide", which he blamed on high taxes and high immigration.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be a "concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families".

A spokesperson said: "We've taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including Â£350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

"We've also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive."

News.title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
News.content:
Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-in appointments too, external.

Two doses offer the best protection. First doses are available until 31 December 2026, with second doses available until 31 March 2027.

Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA, said: "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change.

"The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.

Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before.

These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added.

Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.

Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.

The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.

It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening.

Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.

Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread.

People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others.

Prof Robert Heyderman, an expert in infectious diseases at University College London, said the outbreak strain could have been carried by healthy people for some time before the conditions were right for the outbreak to occur.

Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.

Advisers, are asking the government to consider introducing MenB jabs routinely for secondary school-aged people at around the age of 15 to better protect them against a disease that can be deadly.

Anyone concerned about symptoms of meningitis or sepsis, which can include fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, a rash that does not fade under pressure, difficulty breathing and muscle pain should seek medical help immediately.

News.title: Watch: Six-year-old girl from China sets new Rubik's Cube world record
News.content:
A young girl has broken the women's world record for the 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube twice in three days at the World Cube Association.

At age six, Lian Yunzhi has become the only female cuber in the world to have an average time under 4.5 seconds. She first broke the record with an average of 4.52 seconds and then 4.27 seconds at competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, China.

The young competitor from Sichuan Province has mastered more than 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms after vigorous training that involved spending two to three hours a day on the cube over the past year.

News.title: Father admits causing death of his son in hotel fall
News.content:
A British man has pleaded guilty to causing the death of his two-year-old son who fell from a hotel window in Cyprus.

The father, from Essex, admitted a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act at a court in Paphos on Tuesday.

The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the Times had previously reported.

A further hearing will take place on 5 October when the prosecutor will set out the facts of the case and the defence will present mitigation, a court official confirmed.

The defendant's name was not given during the hearing.

News.title: How Trump's media ban sparked a broadcaster boycott
News.content:
It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday.

There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category.

The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it's not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around.

Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media.

The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation.

This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC.

It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team.

A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled.

On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events.

That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House.

With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks.

But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there.

News.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.

The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".

"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."

Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."

The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".

He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.

His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

News.title: No regular contact with pair held in Iran, family say
News.content:
A British couple who have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months have not had regular contact restored with their family, despite assurances, their family say.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman, who were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges which they deny, were promised family contact after they ended hunger strikes, but there had not been regular calls since, they said.

The family of the couple, who are from East Sussex, is calling for an urgent meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to discuss what action can be taken.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said the couple's welfare was its "top priority" and officials had been working to provide assistance.

It said this included the ambassador visiting the pair in prison and facilitating calls with their family back in the UK.

The couple began hunger strikes earlier this year, after claiming that prison authorities had began to prevent them from speaking to their families. The hunger strikes lasted 93 and 84 days respectively.

The family is now calling for the government to provide regular consular visits and implement a focused strategy to secure the couple's release.

A spokesperson for the family says a British consular visit is planned for 5 October, which they say will be just the second visit of 2026.

They said the length of time it took to arrange the meeting, particularly following the hunger strikes, was "extremely concerning".

The FCDO said the family met with Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty and the UK's envoy for complex consular detentions Alistair Burt in August.

A spokesperson for the office said Doughty "set out how unjustified and appalling we consider Lindsay and Craig's incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try and secure their release".

News.title: Council's 'Lego-type blocks' anger fenced-in woman
News.content:
A council has placed two "concrete Lego-type" blocks at the rear access to the home of an 81-year-old just one week after she won a legal wrangle over access.

Retired teacher Helene Ball won a three-year battle against Derbyshire County Council after it fenced off a 98cm gated gap between her garden and a council car park in April 2023.

As well as being fenced in, dozens of concrete blocks were laid on the access road leading to the car park, off Cavendish Road in Matlock, after it was put on the market.

After a first-tier tribunal ruled in Ball's favour on 27 August, external, she said the council was "a law unto themselves" after two new concrete blocks were laid at the rear of her home.

The BBC understands the two additional blocks were to protect the grassed area and trees from unauthorised parking and damage once the car park entrance is opened.

The council has acknowledged it was "unreasonable" to erect the original green fence at the heart of the dispute, adding it had "apologised for any distress caused".

A right of way has now been established, while the council has been ordered by the courts to pay Â£50,000 costs and to ensure Ball's access is not impeded again.

News.title: Record number of homeless people in temporary housing in Scotland
News.content:
The number of people living in temporary homeless housing in Scotland has risen to another record high, according to the latest figures, external.

More than 19,000 homeless households were being accommodated by local authorities by March - a 10% increase on the previous year.

The number of children living in temporary accommodation also reached a record high, rising by 5% to 10,715.

And the number of open cases - people stuck in the system waiting to be housed - also increased by 10% to nearly 35,000.

The total number of homeless applications rose slightly, by 197 to 41,443, and a total of 35,002 households were assessed as homeless or threatened with homelessness - an increase of 346 from 2024-25.

News.title: Vet prescription fees capped under rule changes
News.content:
Written prescription fees from vets will be capped at Â£21 as part of a raft of changes that practices will be legally required to bring in over the coming months.

Vets must also tell clients if cheaper medicine is available online, write price estimates ahead of treatment, and publish price lists for services as part of the rule updates.

The official competition watchdog has brought the measures into force after its investigation into the sector found prices had been rising at nearly twice the rate of inflation.

However, critics say the measures will hit independent vets hardest and will benefit the six firms that own more than two-thirds of practices.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) made its remedies for the sector legally binding as of Tuesday and vets have up to 12 months to bring all the changes in.

As well as capping prescription fees, other changes include:

Vet practices must publish a "comprehensive" price list for standard services â including consultations, common procedures, and cremation options

A written estimate must be provided in advance for any treatment expected to cost Â£500 or more, including aftercare costs, plus an itemised bill. Emergencies are the only exception to this

Vet businesses must make clear whether they are part of a group or an independent business

To help pet owners compare local practices, price and ownership information will be made available through the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons' "Find a Vet" service, which will share the data with third-party comparison sites.

The timelines for when vets need to bring in the fixes depends on the exact regulation and the group's size. The CMA sets it out here., external

"The changes that are being required are changes that will help inform pet owners about prices," said CMA panel chair Martin Coleman.

News.title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
News.content:
Italian authorities are searching for a British man who went missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager.

The local coastguard said the man, in his late thirties, had been attempting to rescue two people - a father and his 16-year-old son - who were in distress in the water near the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, local officials said.

The man, who was friends with the family, had been on a boating trip with them at the time, the coastguard said. The father and son were later rescued by a passing boat, but the man has not been seen again.

The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities."

A helicopter, divers and boat units from the fire department, coastguard and state police have been drafted into the search.

As the lake's depth can reach more than 250m in the search area, rescuers were also preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, the Italian Coast Guard said in a statement.

The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (12:30 BST) on Monday, when the man noticed his friend and the boy experiencing difficulty swimming and jumped in to help them.

The teenager's mother, who had remained on the boat with her younger son, called the emergency services when she saw the man sinking beneath the surface.

The father and son were transferred to a coastguard boat that had responded to the call and were given medical treatment after suffering from the onset of hypothermia, officials said.

The mother and younger son, who were at this point adrift around 600m from shore, were then brought back to land.

The coastguard earlier said that it had been the father who had jumped in to save the boy and the 37-year-old man, before revising its statement of events.

Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows.

However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

News.title: NHS trust blames 'human error' for new baby data loss
News.content:
A trust at the centre of the largest maternity scandal in NHS history has revealed it lost historical data during routine IT work, with police now assessing its impact.

Maternity records of women and babies who received care between September 2011 and November 2022 were overwritten during work at Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust.

Information has been restored since the "human error" on 18 August, but the trust has not been able to restore the history showing who viewed maternity records during this period.

A police probe last year into a missing data file containing the details of hundreds of maternity cases found it was most likely deleted "intentionally or maliciously".

Nottinghamshire Police has been notified of the data incident and is assessing whether there has been any impact on Operation Perth - the investigation into deaths and injuries related to maternity care at Nottingham City Hospital and Queen's Medical Centre, the main two hospitals run by the trust.

The force said it was told of the data loss on 4 September, and added officers attended NUH on 7 September to establish what happened and how, to consider any potential criminal offences and to find out if the lost data could be recovered.

Deputy Chief Constable Rob Griffin, gold commander for Operation Perth, said: "At present, no crime has been identified. We have received a report from the individual concerned and have spoken with them.

"Further assessment is ongoing, and we are awaiting analysis of the digital process that was used.

"In relation to recovery, we are awaiting a copy of the database, before any further attempts can be made. We anticipate receiving this during the course of the week.

"The overall impact on Operation Perth remains under assessment and we will be in a better position to provide a fuller update once the outstanding analysis and recovery work has been completed.

"I appreciate that this update may cause concern for families, and I would encourage anyone with questions or concerns to contact Operation Perth, where the team will be happy to provide support and, where possible, further information."

News.title: Schools not ready for AI and 'crying out' for government guidance, report warns
News.content:
Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned.

Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic".

His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year.

The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation.

Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival.

Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely.

His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine.

Laura Anne Jones, a Tory defector who was suspended for a racial slur less than a year ago, has been named the deputy leader of Reform UK in Wales.

It comes after former deputy Helen Jenner was named leader on Monday.

Ms Jenner replaced Dan Thomas, who stepped down last week after being arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Mr Thomas said that he had done “nothing wrong”, but did not want the case to be a “distraction” from the party’s work.

Ms Jones defected to Reform from the Welsh Conservatives last summer.

open image in gallery Laura Anne Jones delivers a speech at Trago Mills ( Getty )

At the time, she said: “I've just suddenly felt that the Conservative Party was unrecognisable to me. It wasn't the party that I joined over three decades ago.”

She is a Member of the Senedd for Sir Fynwy Torfaen.

She said in a post on Facebook on Tuesday: “I am honoured to have been elected Deputy Leader of Reform UK Wales and hugely grateful to my colleagues for their trust and support.

“We have made a fantastic start in the Senedd, giving a voice to the voiceless, holding the Welsh Government to account and standing up for communities that have been ignored for too long.”

She said that Ms Jenner would be a “strong, effective leader” and added “I will do everything I can to support her”.

open image in gallery Laura Anne Jones announces her defection to Reform UK at the 2025 Royal Welsh Show, alongside Reform leader Nigel Farage ( Getty )

In November, Ms Jones was suspended from the Siambr (Senedd debating chamber) for 14 days after using a racial slur about Chinese people in a WhatsApp group during a discussion of the Chinese-owned app TikTok in August 2023.

She said in the Senedd in November: “I never meant to cause any offence and would never have that intention of doing so.

“It is deeply regrettable that the message and others in which I had aired my frustrations in private, which I’ve also apologised for and do again, were leaked to the press and made public where they had the potential of being misconstrued and hurt someone unnecessarily.

“My staff and I have all completed Senedd respect and conduct training, and I have actively been in contact and helped the community that is being referred to.

“I have reflected deeply on this, and I wholly accept the need to take greater care with my language at all times.”

open image in gallery Helen Jenner was named the new leader of Reform Wales on Monday ( PA )

In a statement last week, Mr Thomas said: “It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

“With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons.

“Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge.

“I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this Government to account.

“I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader.”

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage visited Cardiff on Monday to announce Ms Jenner as the new head of the party in Wales, describing recent events as a “bump in the road”.

He said: “I’ve known Helen for many, many years.

“She’s a determined campaigner, someone that I trust, and I think’s going to do a very, very good job.”

News.title: This No7 advent calendar includes 22 full-size products – and I put it to the test
News.content:
Presented in a solid pink box, the No7 ultimate beauty advent calendar is quite heavy to carry, but robust, with a red, pink and gold finish that makes it look more premium. Each item is presented in a festive-looking cardboard box of varying sizes. To explore the goodies, I’ll talk you through the calendar’s contents. So as a fair warning, there are spoilers ahead.

To start with, I opened up some staple skincare essentials, with the No7 future renew serum and day cream in the first two days’ boxes. The lightweight serum is a brilliant option for dry skin like mine, and I find it offers an even base underneath make-up while helping to improve the look of fine lines.

Meanwhile, the day cream is hydrating, smoothing and soothing, plus it’s suitable for sensitive skin. Later on in the month, you’ll also open the No7 future renew night serum and night creams, making for a full morning and evening routine.

The calendar contains a mix of No7 skincare and make-up (Helen Wilson-Beevers)

Opening up No7 pro artist liquid blush in taupe on day three kickstarts the make-up goodies, and it’s followed by a glittery pro artist lipstick, and creamy pro artist eyeshadow pot. Standouts for me are the luxe-looking palette, No7 pro artist eye quad, and the classic No7 pro artist 12hr eyeliner. Wearing both, paired with the No7 pro artist instant impact black mascara makes for a party-ready make-up look. Or, I’ve also dabbed a little bit of the eyeshadow on with eyeliner for a more neutral, timeless look.

The contents are perfect for creating a party-ready make-up look (Helen Wilson-Beevers)

I think the No7 pro artist glow lip shine in diamond pink is a worthy gloss alternative to brands like Charlotte Tilbury. Also on the make-up front, the calendar includes a No7 free pro artist weightless silk sheer foundation voucher, so you can be shade-matched in-store. Unfortunately the highlight and bronzer palette had shattered when I opened it up, so I would liked to have seen more durable packaging.

There’s a full wind-down routine included too, from No7 eye make-up remover (which effectively budges both shadow and mascara) and No7 prime forever gel cleanser (a gel to oil to milk formula), to soothing multiple-use No7 prime forever ender eye patches in a handy tin. A favourite of mine is also day 23’s No7 hydraluminous mask. Containing hyaluronic acid and niacinamide, the rich formula feels comforting on skin and leaves a softened, moisturised finish.
