“The season has started well individually and as a team. England’s got unbelievable talent and players all over the pitch. I believe I am good enough to be in the England squad so hopefully I can show that.”

Sports.title: Édouard Mendy: ‘Winning Afcon was 10 times better than the Champions League’
Sports.content:
“I had to stay patient and try to have a cool head because everywhere else there was fire,” Édouard Mendy remembers. In the cauldron of the Stade Prince Moulay Abdellah in Rabat, the Senegal goalkeeper was about to face a penalty against the hosts, Morocco, in stoppage time of the Africa Cup of Nations final.

Mendy had just been shown a yellow card after a 17-minute delay where he and most of his teammates had controversially headed to their dressing room in protest at the referee’s decision to penalise El Hadji Malick Diouf after a Morocco corner.

Senegal had also had a goal disallowed minutes earlier, while Mendy’s complaints to the Congolese referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, about having his towel stolen by Ismael Saibari – a misdemeanour for which the Bayern Munich forward later apologised – and lasers being directed in his eyes from the crowd seemed to fall on deaf ears. Now the goalkeeper who won the Champions League with Chelsea in 2021 tried to maintain his focus as Real Madrid’s Brahim Díaz stood over the ball.

“I realised two steps before he shot … usually when a player does a Panenka they slow down for the last step, but I noticed he did it early,” says Mendy, who is widely regarded as one of the best African goalkeepers having played a central role in the most successful period in Senegal’s history. “I know his preferred side is on the right. But when I saw him slow down way before, I just stood up and managed to catch the ball.”

View image in fullscreen In a chaotic Africa Cup of Nations final, Édouard Mendy kept his head to read Brahim Díaz’s Panenka. Photograph: Youssef Loulidi/AP

Four minutes into extra time, Pape Gueye’s goal meant Senegal and Mendy crowned African champions for the second time in four years. Or so it seemed. More than seven months after Morocco were awarded a 3-0 victory in March when the Confederation of African Football ruled Senegal had forfeited the final by leaving the pitch, a preliminary hearing for their appeal is finally set to be heard at the court of arbitration for sport in Switzerland next month.

“The only thing we have to remember is that the game went to the end. We went off the pitch but the game restarted,” Mendy said. “For me there is no issue because the final was completed – we were given the trophy and celebrated in our country. That was it. When you speak to me about the Afcon, I just simply tell you that: ‘Yes, we have won it twice.’ That’s nothing against the Moroccan people or anyone else. It’s just how we feel. I’m not a lawyer but it’s just common sense. You can’t change something that has already been decided.”

In the meantime, Mendy has added to his bulging trophy cabinet by winning a second successive Asian Champions League with Al-Ahli, faced World Cup heartache after sustaining a knee injury against Norway and, at the age of 34, announced his international retirement last week. Even a phone call from Senegal’s new manager, Patrick Vieira, could not persuade him to change his mind and potentially add to his 59 caps.

“He [Vieira] is a legend so to have the chance to work with him was really something that came into my mind,” Mendy says. “But at the end of the call I asked for some time to really think about everything. A couple of days later I called him and explained that I wanted to stick to my decision. I started thinking about it after the Afcon and I just came to the conclusion that it was my time to say stop.”

View image in fullscreen Despite being stripped of the title, Senegal still paraded the trophy in Paris before playing a friendly against France. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters

Mendy has high hopes that Senegal’s next generation, which includes Monaco’s Lamine Camara – the midfielder who almost joined Chelsea in the summer – and Aston Villa’s Ibrahim Mbaye can emulate the achievements of his. The Teranga Lions were crowned African champions for the first time in 2022, around eight months after Mendy kept a clean sheet in the 2021 Champions League final. But he says there is no comparison between the two when he looks back now. “[Winning Afcon] was the best moment of my football career: it was 10 times better [than the Champions League]. I can compare now because I’ve also won the Asian Champions League twice.

“To win for your club is something really incredible. But you cannot compare with winning for your country, especially when they have never won anything before. It happens only once in your life so being part of the team that made history was amazing.”

View image in fullscreen Édouard Mendy kept nine clean sheets, a joint record for one tournament, on Chelsea’s run to winning the Champions League in 2021. Photograph: Pierre Philippe Marcou/AP

Mendy’s exploits in 2021 led to him being named best goalkeeper at Fifa’s now defunct The Best awards, but he missed out on the Yashin trophy awarded by the organisers of the Ballon d’Or to Gianluigi Donnarumma. Both have been nominated again for this year’s award and Mendy says he is proud to be in the conversation again after what he describes as “my best year since I became a professional” after a season in which no other goalkeeper won as many major honours.

He says: “To be nominated for the Yashin trophy while I play in Saudi Arabia means a lot to me. My journey has not been easy – everything is about working hard and being resilient. When I see goalkeepers in Senegal wearing the No 16 jersey it makes me so proud. It means that at some point I gave them some inspiration and this is very powerful.”

Mendy was born in Normandy, and started his professional career at Cherbourg but found himself unemployed for a year after enduring successive relegations. He was eventually given another chance by Marseille and is now helping to fund a school in his parents’ hometown of Keur Massar that has recently expanded to 200 students. Mendy is also behind a scheme that supports budding entrepreneurs in the country.

“There is so much talent in Senegal and we have a young population that is very dynamic. That’s why it’s important to give them the opportunity to have a better life,” he says. “When my mum sees the school she is so proud and that is the biggest gift anyone can have.”

Sports.title: ‘It’s bordering on exploitation’: how pseudoscience is duping football
Sports.content:
Dr Claire-Marie Roberts was working at Coventry City when she received a call from someone asking whether she knew how much oxygen was in the atmosphere. As the performance director, responsible for optimising players’ potential, she was accustomed to being pitched the latest gimmick promising miraculous gains. At times, she could receive up to 50 LinkedIn messages a week offering a device, supplement or technology that claimed to produce magical results.

“It is only 21%,” the caller told her. That’s GCSE chemistry, she thought. Then came the sales pitch: “So what we’ve done is put oxygen in a can and we think you might want to use it.”

“Right … oxygen in a can,” Roberts says, laughing at the memory. Suffice to say, she did not take the caller up on his offer to buy oxygen in a can for Coventry’s players.

Roberts has spent decades working in elite athlete performance and professional football, including nine years at the Premier League and two at Coventry, where she played a key role in their promotion as Championship champions before joining the Formula One team McLaren as director of human performance in the summer. She is shocked by how professional football is being duped by pseudoscience: from coaches and performance staff misled by snake-oil sellers, to players desperate for a shortcut and with money to burn.

“It’s the science-practice gap, which is widening in my experience,” Roberts says. “I think it’s getting much worse. There’s so much sparkly marketing behind all these things. It’s bordering on exploitation.

“They’re taking a population that is very susceptible to: ‘How can I hack my performance advantage? How can I shortcut my preparation and recovery?’ Which I don’t think is a great starting point.”

Roberts says some of the practices commonplace in elite football have little evidence behind them. She includes cryotherapy chambers – a common feature at elite training grounds. If unavailable, ice baths are a fallback. Players enjoy them so much that Harry Kane was photographed standing in a wheelie bin full of ice after a Bayern Munich match at last year’s Club World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Claire-Marie Roberts was part of Frank Lampard’s staff during Coventry’s Championship-winning season. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

“Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them, because there’s no evidence for them apart from a very slim piece of work that says it might help prevent dementia,” Roberts says. “There’s very sketchy evidence on cryotherapy.”

They could even be detrimental to recovery, Roberts says. “There’s a recent suggestion that cryotherapy might blunt muscular adaptation. When are you using it and why are you using it? If you’re using it for recovery, sleep and nutrition are your best recovery modalities. No amount of putting anybody in a whole-body cryotherapy chamber is going to help them recover more if those two things aren’t taken care of.”

But players are constantly attempting to shortcut nutrition, too. Supplements are a multibillion-pound industry that has its claws in the game. But beyond vitamin D, in which it is “evidence-based” that people in the northern hemisphere are commonly deficient owing to a lack of sunlight, and vitamin C, which is usually short in our diets, supplementation should, Roberts says, be targeted to deficiencies.

“You’ve got people popping pills not really asking what they’re for. It should always be needs-based. If you don’t eat fish and fish oil is important to you, you might supplement it. It should all be based on need.

“Your athletic performance and recovery is based on sleep quality and nutritional quality and amounts. No amount of supplementation will improve a bad diet, but people think it will. We don’t do enough of the basics and think we can shortcut and hack everything.”

View image in fullscreen Claire-Marie Roberts: ‘Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them.’ Photograph: Eddie Keogh for The FA/Rex/Shutterstock

Roberts says she used an evidence-based, scientific approach to support Frank Lampard’s squad and that many clubs follow practices from the top of the game when often they are flawed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“People passively suck these things up,” she says. “Because England or Manchester City or Chelsea who have all the resources under the sun have got this, there’s a misappropriation of confidence and understanding of the scientific basis or evidence. It’s powerful in driving behaviour, but it’s driving the wrong behaviour.”

Roberts, a former swimmer who missed the 1996 Atlanta Olympics owing to injury, says: “Football is more susceptible to it than any other sport I’ve experienced first-hand. I think because the stakes are higher.”

Kinesiology tape – or k-tape, as it is commonly known – is another trend that baffles Roberts. Players from Cristiano Ronaldo to Gareth Bale and David Beckham have been spotted wearing it over the years, often resembling strips of gaffer tape stuck to limbs.

“There’s no evidence kinesiology tape has any impact on injury prevention or performance-related outcomes. It gives you a bit of proprioception – maybe you feel like someone has done something – but in any environment I’ve worked in you’d never see anyone wearing k-tape. It’s a big white elephant.

“If an athlete has dislocated their shoulder, you should strap it – strapping is different. It provides an element of external support that can provide minimal protection to the joint and reminds the person they’ve got a problem. It’s a risk-mitigation strategy. It’s not hugely successful, but you’d do it rather than not do it. K-tape is a placebo.”

Often, managers who have been in the game for decades insist on practices they have adopted for years, or because another coach, with no scientific background, has heard about a revolutionary new product. Roberts believes that until football puts science at the centre of decision-making and employs qualified staff to scrutinise claims, the problem will worsen.

“We think we can accelerate to an outcome without putting the hard yards in – the basic things: diet and sleep and the quality of your training,” she says.

“Football in general is very anti-intellectual and it has been for a long time. There are a few clubs that do it well, but the majority don’t. The game is definitely anti-science. There’s a reason for that. There isn’t a critical mass of people that are applying critical thought to situations.”

Sports.title: ‘Have some humanity’: Diogo Jota chants at Rúben Neves a wake-up call for Saudi Arabia
Sports.content:
The good thing about Cristiano Ronaldo playing in your league is that he is one of the most famous footballers ever and when he scores a great goal or reaches 1,000 (just 21 to go), many people watch. The bad thing about Cristiano Ronaldo playing in your league is that when something negative happens and he is involved, just as many people will watch and listen. Global attention is something that the big European leagues have had for years but it is something the Saudi Pro League, which has spent billions in search of achieving a similar stature, needs to get used to.

On Sunday 13 September, Ronaldo wrote to his 680 million Instagram followers to discuss the events of Saturday evening. That was when Al-Taawoun supporters were coming to terms with a 6-0 home thrashing by Al-Hilal, whose £150m-plus forward line, Ollie Watkins and Gabriel Martinelli, got five between them. Fair to say that some handled it better than others as what followed was in the worst possible taste.

At the end, what seemed to be a small number of fans saw Al-Hilal’s Rúben Neves in the centre circle and started chanting the name of his former Portugal and Wolves teammate Diogo Jota, who tragically died in a car accident in July 2025. Neves, who has a tattoo of the Liverpool star, was visibly upset and made a gesture which clearly said to those supporters that “God is watching you”. He also said to Saudi reporters after the game: “I hope they don’t go to pray afterwards.”

Ronaldo then weighed in. “The league must take ⁠action and punish this kind of fan behaviour,” he wrote. “This is no longer football, and there have to be limits. People who behave ‌like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again.” Al-Hilal made an official complaint. This was a big story.

Ayman al-Hotami, one of Al-Hilal’s best-known fans, says: “I found the chants hard to believe but those responsible were few in number and very young. Al-Hilal’s fanbase completely condemn the chants and demanded an apology regarding the actions of individuals in their stands. We appreciate the club’s response in condemning this isolated incident, which represents neither the club nor our society.”

Away from home in small stadiums with low attendances, often the case when the big teams play outside Jeddah and Riyadh, the chants of a few can carry far. More than once, Ronaldo has heard the name of a certain Argentinian star coming his way and reacted badly. This, though, was on a completely different level.

View image in fullscreen Rúben Neves (centre) and Diogo Jota (left) played together at club and international level. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

The well-known Saudi broadcaster Waleed al-Faraj says: “To shout ‘Messi’ at Ronaldo is acceptable within the context of the rivalry between them, but to chant the name of his deceased teammate Jota at Neves is an inappropriate act. How can you play on people’s grief like this? You should have some humanity.”

The Saudi legend Sami al-Jaber, who played at four World Cups and had a short spell in England with Wolves, sent a message to Neves: “Rúben, your presence in Saudi football means a great deal to us. As Saudis, we take pride in our values of respect and hospitality … they transcend any sporting rivalry. This behaviour does not reflect those values. I hope you know how warmly you are regarded here, and how much you belong.”

Ronaldo’s call for action was met four days later. “The Saudi Arabian Football Federation (Saff) and the Saudi Pro League (SPL) condemn the unacceptable conduct by some supporters in attendance,” a statement said, adding that the chants were inconsistent with the values of Saudi football and sportsmanship in general. Al-Taawoun have been handed a ban of around £20,000 and ordered to play two matches behind closed doors. An earlier statement said that “exploiting personal tragedies for the purpose of abuse or provocation is unacceptable behaviour that has no place in Saudi football”.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo spoke out after fans of Al-Taawoun chanted the name of Diogo Jota to taunt Rúben Neves. Photograph: Reuters

Some felt that more could have been made of an opportunity to send a message to the rest of the league, one of zero tolerance and harsh punishments for those individuals responsible. Nobody would have complained – Al Taawoun had condemned what happened and said it was “not representative of their supporters”. Here was a clearcut case of fans behaving badly as you are going to get.

European football has worked hard to try and stamp out offensive chants. “Stadiums in places such as Portugal and England are nowadays heavily controlled spaces,” says Simon Chadwick, professor of Afro-Eurasian Sport at Emlyon Business School in Paris. “Hence, when someone like Ronaldo encounters [verbal abuse] he will inevitably respond, thereby attracting attention from the media and others. Saudi Arabian fans need to get used to such a reaction fast.”



It is not just the international media that get involved. “Organisations such as the AFC and Fifa may even implement codes of conduct and penalties for situations like the Jota episode,” Chadwick says. “In other words, if Saudi fans and/or the Pro League can’t regulate or control the situation, then someone else will.”

With the Asian Cup coming to the country in January for the first time – and preparation for the 2034 World Cup on the way – Saudi Arabia will be hoping that such action will not be necessary.

Sports.title: Lions and Irons: the Dockers derby – a photo essay
Sports.content:
When Millwall hosted West Ham at the Den on Saturday, it was the 100th competitive meeting between the clubs, and the first in 14 years.

The pair are separated and connected by the Thames. They were formed around the heavy industries of east London’s docklands in the late 19th century and were geographically much closer then – Millwall on the Isle of Dogs and Thames Ironworks, from which West Ham emerged, around Canning Town. Before Millwall relocated south of the Thames to New Cross in 1910, both were north of the river and only a little over two miles apart.

Now the Lions, Millwall were known as the Dockers during their formative years. West Ham’s nickname, the Irons, refers to their origins among workers at the Thames Ironworks and Shipbuilding Company. Dock work was precarious and physically demanding. Men could turn up each morning with no guarantee of being chosen for work, and competition for a day’s labour could be fierce. That world fostered ideas of toughness, loyalty and hard work which still form part of how both clubs understand and present themselves.

View image in fullscreen Straight to the point: graffiti on a wall near the Den.

With histories stretching back so far, it can be difficult to separate fact from folklore. One enduring story places the origins of the rivalry in the General Strike of 1926, when West Ham dock workers supposedly supported the strike while those at Millwall did not. Historians David Sullivan and Brian Belton dispute that version. Belton says the strike was solid in the Millwall docks, while only a handful of workers broke ranks around Canning Town. Yet the story has survived for a century and become part of the mythology surrounding the fixture.

View image in fullscreen Millwall fans in the vicinity of, and outside, the Den.

The clubs’ histories first crossed in the 1890s, when Millwall Athletic played Thames Ironworks. Belton cautions against treating Thames simply as an earlier West Ham as the company team was dissolved before the new club was formed in 1900. Sullivan and Belton both question the idea of an ancient Dockers Derby. Much of the hostility associated with the fixture today developed later, particularly during the 1970s. There was serious disorder at Harry Cripps’s testimonial in 1972, despite Cripps being well-loved at both clubs, and in 1976 a Millwall supporter died after falling from a train, with some believing West Ham supporters were involved. When the clubs met competitively again in 1978 after a long absence, violence accompanied the fixture.

View image in fullscreen Mounted police keep fans at bay outside the Den and move across the car park; a Millwall fan shouts at the West Ham team bus as it arrives at the ground; a West Ham fan gesticulates towards Millwall supporters across a barrier blockaded by police.

It is perhaps more than coincidence that the rivalry intensified during the same period in which the industrial world from which both clubs had emerged was disappearing. London’s docks were closing, traditional industries were shedding tens of thousands of jobs and many surrounding communities were experiencing unemployment and economic decline. It would be too simplistic to draw a direct line between industrial decline and football hooliganism, but the two occurred concurrently. Football offered a place in which territory, masculinity, belonging and local pride could still be asserted at a time when some of the institutions that had previously provided those identities were disappearing.

Through the 1980s, 90s and early 2000s, the reputation of the rivalry was reinforced by occasional but memorable flashpoints. The most notorious came at Upton Park in 2009, when a League Cup tie was overshadowed by fighting outside the stadium, a stabbing and pitch invasions. Their two Championship meetings in 2011-12 passed without anything approaching the disorder of 2009, and after that they did not meet competitively again until this season.

Both clubs carry reputations for violence, reinforced by films such as ID and Green Street, and the Dockers Derby amplifies that mythology further. Despite predictable heated posts and banter on social media, there was a general feeling before Saturday that the day would pass without serious trouble, which it mostly did.

There is suspicion towards journalists, including photographers, among both fanbases, and people on both sides warned me to be careful. I had a few choice words thrown at me during the day, but they came from a minority. What was far more visible was the strength of community around the clubs and the friendliness and warmth of the majority of supporters I spoke to and photographed.

View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen West Ham fans making their way to the ground, at the fan zone and inside the Den.

The game was broadcast live on ITV. Kick-off was moved to 12.30pm, limiting the time available for drinking beforehand, and an extensive police operation involving about 400 officers was put in place. West Ham received just 1,774 tickets in a crowd of about 20,000 and most of their supporters avoided wearing club colours. They were instructed to travel via London Bridge to South Bermondsey, from where they were escorted to the away end.

West Ham arrived at the Den top of the table and having recently beaten Wrexham 6-0, but Millwall, despite dealing with a number of injuries, dominated much of the first half and went into the interval two goals ahead. West Ham found their way back into the game and equalised with 10 minutes remaining. Each goal produced an explosive reaction from the stands, but the equaliser was the only point when the crowd appeared in danger of spilling over, with additional police support called in. In the 89th minute, as Kyrell Lisbie broke through on goal, Mohamadou Kanté pulled him down, earning a straight red card and possibly denying Millwall a winner. It finished 2-2, a result both clubs could find reasons to be disappointed and satisfied with.

View image in fullscreen The Lions dominated the first half and the home side went in at the break two goals to the good, courtesy of Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli.

View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen A West Ham fan sings in the stands; Jake Cooper of Millwall and Morato of West Ham square off as their teammates try to separate them (below).

View image in fullscreen Mohamadou Kanté got West Ham back in the game in the 74th minute and six minutes later Konstantinos Mavropanos restored parity.

Afterwards there were a few brief scuffles between Millwall supporters and police outside the ground, but they quickly petered out. Within minutes, young fans were waiting by the stadium for autographs while others stood around discussing the match.

To an outsider, the similarities between Millwall and West Ham can appear greater than their differences. Many supporters I have met have friends or relatives on the other side, and both clubs draw heavily on values of working-class London such as toughness, loyalty and authenticity. Yet when they meet there remains real animosity among sections of both fanbases. Perhaps that is part of what gives the rivalry its intensity – both clubs are competing, in different ways, to represent a similar place, culture and identity, and to claim themselves as the more authentic expression of it.

Millwall and West Ham have now played one another across three centuries. The docks that gave the fixture its name have largely disappeared, the clubs have moved further apart and competitive meetings have become increasingly rare. But the competition over what each club represents, and the need to distinguish one side from the other, has survived.

Sports.title: Liverpool’s Aurélie Csillag on making women’s football more diverse: ‘Visibility starts at the top’
Sports.content:
“When I was young I never had a role model. I only watched men’s football, but when women’s football got bigger there were no really good black players. I also want to be a role model for the next generation,” says the Liverpool forward Aurélie Csillag about why she is involved in an initiative being launched by the club in October.

Beyond the Goalposts aims to give black and marginalised girls and women pathways and opportunities in football on and off the pitch. It is being carried out by the club’s foundation and wants to “create a safe, inclusive and empowering environment” by providing sessions, including educational and mentoring help, in Liverpool’s community. Sessions begin on 1 October, but people can register their interest at any time.

There will be experts, as well as players, who will assist with on-pitch sessions and provide support to those who sign up. “I heard about the programme and I reached out to the foundation,” the 23-year-old Switzerland international says. “I wanted to support it because it is an important topic for me in football.

“I was really surprised, I was so happy that such a big club thinks about things like this. We can improve women’s football for black people. I was very excited Liverpool were doing this and I was proud I am a part of a club that is aware of this issue.”

The sessions are concentrated on leadership, mentoring, health and wellbeing, community engagement and advocacy. There will be on-pitch sessions and a focus on how careers can progress in the sport off the pitch. There will also be activities at Anfield on match days and a football festival. Premier League funding is helping run the programme.

The club says it is “the start that is needed in women’s sport, and the legacy of the project will extend beyond the delivery of sessions, creating sustainable change for participants, the foundation, the club, and the wider community. Through leadership development, peer support and meaningful engagement with the LFC Foundation, participants will build the confidence, skills and networks needed to influence positive change.”

View image in fullscreen Aurélie Csillag says ‘Everyone should feel that football is a place for them.’ Photograph: Nick Taylor/LFC/Getty Images

Research provided by Liverpool found that girls as young as five feel they do not belong in sport and only 30% of parents believe playing sport is important. The research also found that despite 60% of black girls wanting to be an elite athlete, they are the least active group of girls in England. It also found that one in two black girls feel they need to play down their cultural identity.

When asked why she believed black and marginalised girls and women may be deterred from playing football, Csillag said: “The most important part is a lack of role models. Maybe also not being able to access it.

“They [also might be] struggling with their confidence. For example, I was so different when I started to play football and my body was so different. I played in a team where the whole team were white girls and our body structure was so different and I lost some confidence.

“I said: ‘Why am I so tall? Why are my thighs so big? Why is this different?’ I just started to compare myself with them and maybe a lot of other girls may have lost their confidence. They may not keep going because of a lack of support or awareness.

“If I had one [other black person on the team] they would know what I was talking about. That is why I am so happy that in the national team we have four black girls and five years ago it was only one or two. It is so nice to see that we are competing on such a high level to show girls and women it is possible and they have role models and people like this exist in this sport.

“Everyone should feel that football is a place for them and programmes like Beyond the Goalposts help move us closer to that reality by creating opportunities, building confidence and showcasing the diversity that makes the game stronger.”

The club says for now the programme is just for people in Liverpool, but is something they would like to expand. They are also encouraging other sports organisations to adopt similar types of programmes.

View image in fullscreen Beyond the Goalposts will start on 1 October. Photograph: Peter Powell

For Csillag, it starts at the top. “The most important thing is that you have black people in the staff, higher up, because I barely see this,” she says. “Every time I see it I think: ‘Woah, I could one day maybe reach what she is reaching.’

“When you have never seen it, how can a little girl think she can do it? It will go automatically that young girls will follow that dream or path. Visibility starts at the top.”

Sports.title: Women’s Champions League: will OL Lyonnes or English trio topple a weakened Barcelona?
Sports.content:
This competition is wide open. “But, wait, you say that every year!” No, honestly, this time it is wide open. The league phase of a new Women’s Champions League campaign begins on Tuesday with genuine elements of unpredictability, intrigue and a competitive feel after Barcelona, the holders, and winners of four titles in six years, underwent significant changes this summer.

The Spanish champions, who have reached six European finals in a row, have had four players who started the victory in the final last season leave the club. Ona Batlle joined Arsenal, Salma Paralluelo signed for OL Lyonnes – against whom she scored twice in that 4-0 victory to clinch the title in May – and Alexia Putellas and Mapi León moved to London City Lionesses. They have a very different look and feel to the formidable aura they demonstrated in Oslo.

They are still the team to beat, though, and retain an excellent squad, including the winner of the last three Ballons d’Or in Aitana Bonmatí – although she is doubtful for their opener against Paris FC on Wednesday with injury – as well as the top scorer in the competition last season, Ewa Pajor, and their captain, the Spain midfielder Patri Guijarro.

It will still take a world-class team to topple them, but there is perhaps no longer that same air of invincibility accompanying them this time.

Hoping to capitalise and reclaim a title they have not won since 2022 – a relatively long wait given they are the record eight-time winners – are OL Lyonnes. They had a comparatively good transfer window, adding Paralluelo, who scored her first goal for the club on Friday during an 8-1 demolition of Le Havre, and the Scotland midfielder Caroline Weir, who joined after four years at Real Madrid.

Lifting the European Cup would be a defining achievement for their owner, Michele Kang, who also owns Washington Spirit and London City Lionesses, and for their head coach, Jonatan Giráldez, if he could win the competition with a second team after his back-to-back successes with Barcelona in 2023 and 2024.

View image in fullscreen Ewa Pajor scored 11 Champions League goals last season, including two in the final. Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP

Bayern Munich should be in contention along with a trio of English sides – Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City – all of whom have the squads and resources to mount significant challenges. Arsenal, winners in 2025 – and 2007 when the competition was known as the Women’s Cup – remain the only English club to have won major European silverware, which feels at odds with the modern-day big spending in the WSL and the division’s frequent jostling with the NWSL for the unofficial title of the “best league in the world”.

The WSL’s three most successful sides, for all their financial investments, are yet to dominate in Europe, and that could begin to change this season. Arsenal strengthened the depth in their squad this summer, not least with the arrivals of Georgia Stanway from Bayern and Batlle from Barcelona. Their ability to bring top-level internationals on from the bench in almost every position should make them a real force.

Manchester City, the English domestic champions, reached the quarter‑finals in 2025, but missed out last season, and have something of a point to prove and a desire to make up for lost time. They were absent from Europe in 2023-24 as well and failed to make it past the qualifying rounds in the 2021-22 and 2022-23 seasons, when they were knocked out by Real Madrid on both occasions.

They were also eliminated relatively early by another side from the Spanish capital, Atlético Madrid, in 2018-19 and 2019-20, so they have not reached the semi-finals since 2017-18, a barren run which felt unlikely at the time.

They were delighted to retain the services of the WSL’s top scorer, Khadija Shaw, and it will be fascinating to watch the Jamaica striker unleashed on Europe’s biggest club competition. City’s campaign begins with a tricky looking test away to Bayern.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Chelsea went out in the quarter-finals last season in a bad-tempered tie with Arsenal. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Action Images/Reuters

Chelsea, finalists only once when they were beaten by Barcelona in 2021, would love to return to the top stage again at this season’s final, which is being held at Poland’s national stadium in Warsaw, in May.

Real Madrid boosted their attacking ranks with the signing of Felicia Schröder, the breakthrough player of last season’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup, from the Swedish champions, Häcken. They open their campaign at home against Paris Saint-Germain.

For many, it may feel a little strange for the WCL to begin on Tuesday and for Putellas not taking part after so many years of the Spain midfielder being one of the competition’s biggest names. Similarly, the absence of Wolfsburg is jarring, with the two-time champions’ run of 14 successive years – which at one point included 11 quarter-finals in a row – ended in shock fashion when they lost to Inter on penalties in qualifying. Inter are one of three Italian sides in the league phase, the first time so many from Serie A have made it this far. Austria Wien, along with Inter, are debutants at this stage.

The 18-team league phase runs until 16 December. The top four progress directly to the quarter‑finals in March, while the teams ranked between fifth and 12th will contest a knockout-phase playoff in February.

Sports.title: Come back soon Premier League, the endlessly moreish mega-product | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Get ready for the dopamine crash. And this one really is a proper autumn nosedive. The past 17 days up to and including Sunday’s cut-off gave us 30 Premier League games and 79 goals. Which, if you take Spurs out of it – and this is fair because Spurs are now post‑goal, an entertainment concept unrelated to goals or even football itself – is really quite a lot.

Are your pathways stimulated? Are the neural connectors flickering? Well get ready for cold turkey, for 19 blank days of shivers and shakes until the Premier League show resumes in October. Maybe it really is time to buy one of those powders off the internet.

The international break will provide its own intrigue. There will be discussions about whether Thomas Tuchel is or isn’t responsible for the inherited cultural weaknesses of English football. There will be rage at Tuchel’s inability to coach the players to keep the ball as never before via his few short hours on the training pitch. And yet more rage at the real issues, basically the fact he continues to be German and looks like a scurvy-ridden Napoleonic naval commander powered solely by ship’s biscuits and morphine.

This is unlikely to fill the hole. There will be an unavoidable “contrast effect”, the rush of adrenaline that only serves to deepen the low when it is gone. But there are also some familiar autumn rituals to help us through. One of these is the state‑of‑the‑nation Premier League address, pegged out around key questions such as “where are we?”, “what are we?” and “where is it all going?”. This time around these are relatively easy to answer.

Five rounds into the Premier League season this is pretty much a cut-and-paste job. The big news: there is no big news. Events continue to happen at great volume. But in terms of teams, style, stars, energies and potential outcomes, not much has changed. Roll back one year and this was the broad situation. A powerful team with a bald, irascible manager had won all five games, but also looked defensively fragile. The team that would win the league was second. That team was also Arsenal.

View image in fullscreen Are Tottenham doomed? Probably not. They have enough semi-interested players to retain a solid hold on 17th place. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

The middle classes were the most interesting story, those functional, well-run teams beginning with B, an entity you might call Brightonmouth. Erling Haaland was scoring goals. Bruno Fernandes was generating hair‑tearing anguish, like a young Elvis, but based more around shithousery and risky attacking passes.

As ever there are still some key questions doing the rounds, but luckily these can all be answered easily. Is Michael Carrick the man to take Manchester United to the next level? No. Is Michael Carrick the reason United are not at that level, but in a state where they must now employ Michael Carrick? Also no.

The reality for United is that there are no other levels. This is the level, a club that instead acts as a grand, angst-ridden but very accurate metaphor for modern‑day Britain, furiously retailing its own heritage, run by fill-ins and opportunists, a mobile waxwork museum living on tourism and memories.

Are Tottenham doomed? Probably not. They have enough semi-interested players to retain a solid hold on 17th place. Although frustratingly for Premier League content addicts, even this has been degraded by repetition. Spurs could get relegated now and you would just keep scrolling.

Are Liverpool on the verge of a renaissance? Probably not. The Jürgen Klopp golden era is beginning to look quite distant, surrounded on all sides by something a bit like the present. And, yes, Florian Wirtz is a very good footballer. He just can’t resist contact very well, which is non‑negotiable in the Premier League. He is going to be really good at Paris Saint-Germain/Bayern Munich/Inter.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United have had a difficult start to the season under Michael Carrick. Photograph: Dennis Goodwin/ProSports/Shutterstock

Otherwise, it is a case of stasis and a reliable, entertaining, homogenised product. Tactically, we can still get excited about small changes. If you analyse it deeply you may find a little more counterattack, Anthony Elanga running fast, an inverted winger discovering almost by accident he can also cross with his strong foot.

It is a mark of how standardised the game has become that these are deemed things worth getting excited about. There is still only one elite level style, the Omniball template of the Cruyff-Michels-Guardiola-Gegenpressing school.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

This is skewed towards physicality over control in England, but it still produces football that can feel at times a bit like driving a brand new electric car: fun, high‑grade, but also endlessly repeatable. It seems possible some time soon that a robotic bait‑the‑press system will meet a robotic bait-averse system and in that moment football will just cease to exist, reduced to two banks of human units staring at each other across a strip of empty grass.

There are two things the Premier League could really do with in the remaining 87% of its season. The nudge into greater physicality is exciting and distinct. It is notable how many games have been decided by duels, collisions, a sense of greater wanting-it. Or perhaps not so surprising when the players are at roughly the same technical level, where the only real point of difference is sustained physical power and competitive will.

This is one reason why Brighton’s defeat of Arsenal on Saturday seemed so interesting. It is rare to see any reigning champions not just beaten, but outskilled and outmuscled. For 90 minutes, only one of these teams looked like genuine contenders for every trophy on offer.

This is the second thing the league could really do with. Is it possible for one of the well-run middle class to sustain this level over a season and give us another Leicester or something close? Can Brighton just play like that every week?

There are obvious answers why not. One very good game against an ambushed Arsenal is not a 38-game slog. Brighton have a good squad, but also regular midweek football. Other teams will react and nullify your strengths. Also, and this is not a throwaway detail, Fabian Hürzeler is going to be on TalkSport for an hour on Tuesday just chatting football, which will now include how did you beat the champs and why are you third in the league.

Nothing wrong with this. But it is an indicator of where we are. Hürzeler is 33. The entire job is essentially reinventing himself, just as all of the very good players at those middleweight clubs are auditioning for bigger clubs rather than dreaming of hauling them in, playing for the life-changing money a Champions League-level club will throw at them, motivated by a breezy and entirely logical collective individualism.

Perhaps this is why one of the themes of the season has been a suspicion among fans of bigger clubs that their players don’t want it enough, that being outrun or outworked is a sign of soul sickness or debauched management. But it is also what keeps the league brutally strong, state of the art, and endlessly moreish for all its repeated story arcs. Come back soon Premier League mega-product. The comedown is already hitting.

Sports.title: Fabian Hurzeler reveals Brighton blueprint for huge Arsenal win but denies ‘perfect’ performance
Sports.content:
Fabian Hurzeler has detailed the game plan that saw his Brighton side crush champions Arsenal 3-0 in the Premier League.

Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas fired the Seagulls into a two-goal lead by half-time, with Chema Andres grabbing the third against the holders before the hour mark on a memorable afternoon.

3 Brighton boss Hurzeler has explained how he masterminded the huge weekend win against champions Arsenal Credit: AFP

Arsenal, whose midfielder Declan Rice was lucky to avoid a red card, had the lion's share of possession but failed to make the most of it.

Brighton ended the champions' four-match win streak and extended their own unbeaten run in the league to five this season as they sit third on ten points, earning them an A in our top flight grades.

They are also the fourth side after Manchester United, Bournemouth and Manchester City to beat Arsenal in the Premier League in 2026.

Hurzeler produced a hugely impressive result that has rightly earned plaudits across the division, and he was on hand to tell talkSPORT just how he went about doing it.

Speaking on Brighton's approach against Arsenal when appearing on White and Jordan, he said: "We focused on us, really. We wanted to win the small battles first, what I mean is win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.

"It sounds a little bit old school but it really was our approach because when you win these small battles, then you grow into the game.

"Then you can maybe create a bigger chance, then you can create a bigger win of scoring a goal. But first of all, it's getting into this game, having this commitment to our style of play, to our principles, and then winning the small battles.

"When you win the small battles, the players gain confidence, the players create self-belief, the players really trust each other. We grew into this game, and we also had the right moments on our side."

Brighton were 'exceptional', but not 'perfect'

None of Coventry City, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Sunderland, as well as Napoli in the Champions League and Ipswich Town in the Carabao Cup, could beat Arsenal in their clashes - Brighton are an exception.

They showed intensity right from kick-off and managed to exploit a sense of nervousness from the Gunners, who played like anything but title defenders.

3 Hurzeler believes much of their success in the three-goal display came from winning 'the small battles' Credit: Getty

Host Jim White even went as far as to suggest that Brighton may well have delivered a perfect performance, but a humble Hurzeler was not one to agree.

"Our philosophy is we want to play intense football, having a good balance between defensive ability and controlling the game in possession.

"Therefore, if you want to control the game in possession, you need to have this intensity to win the ball back as quickly as possible.

"You need players who have this commitment to our pressing and I think that was definitely key - they played, we scored, and that was our commitment from the first second.

"Was it a perfect game? I'm a perfectionist, I wouldn't say it was a perfect game.

"There's still things to improve. But, overall, our challenge now will be to make these kind of exceptional performances normal. This is the challenge we have now.

3 Hurzeler has insisted that, whilst the performance was strong, it wasn't perfect and there is still room for improvement Credit: AFP

"We have this phrase, 'We want to challenge the establishment'. Challenging the establishment doesn't mean to challenge them in one-to-one games, you have to challenge them when you're not playing against them.

"So, we have to be consistent in performances and these kind of performances, they have to get normal for us and that, I think, is the biggest challenge we can set ourselves."

Sports.title: Roberto De Zerbi given sack warning with Tottenham fan favourite tipped to replace him
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi given sack warning with Tottenham fan favourite tipped to replace him

Tottenham have been urged to bring back former manager Mauricio Pochettino to the club this season.

Spurs have endured a nightmare start to the campaign under Roberto De Zerbi and sit bottom of the Premier League after their first five matches.



5 Mauricio Pochettino has managed the USA national team since 2024, and last managed in England with Chelsea Credit: Getty

Defeat to Aston Villa on Saturday extended the club's winless start to the new season, who have just two points on the board.

They remain one of just three sides yet to taste victory this term alongside Bournemouth and Fulham.

That's despite a huge summer overhaul at Tottenham with more than £300m being spent on new recruits, as they look to kick on after back-to-back 17th place league finishes.



De Zerbi future questioned

Tottenham's dire start to the season has sparked early speculation over De Zerbi's future, with former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy recently giving him until after the international break to turn things around.

And after Spurs' woes went from bad to worse against Villa, journalist Darren Lewis has now tipped the club to bring back former boss Pochettino to transform their fortunes.



Pochettino endeared himself to Spurs fans during his five-year tenure between 2014 and 2019, the highlight seeing them reach the 2019 Champions League final.

The Argentine is currently in charge of the USA national team having agreed a contract extension until 2030 weeks after the World Cup.



Murphy and Lewis appeared on talkSPORT's Kick Off, where the former said: “My bold prediction. It's not that bold actually. I think we'll see Poch back in the Premier League before the end of it.”

While Murphy claimed he could see Manchester United turning to Pochettino with Michael Carrick currently struggling, Lewis backed him for a homecoming of sorts.

"If Spurs are smart, they'll get him," insisted the Daily Mirror journalist.

5 De Zerbi's Spurs are yet to win a league fixture this term Credit: AFP



5 Pochettino oversaw three successive top three finishes and a run to the Champions League final with Spurs Credit: Getty

Pochettino spent five years in charge of Spurs, where he achieved five successive top five finishes including two third places and a runner-up spot in the Premier League.

Their second place finish in 2017 remains the club's highest league position for 63 years.

In the same show, Lewis tipped current boss De Zerbi to be sacked before the end of the season, and criticised him for his recent comments where he labelled his Spurs side mentally 'fragile'.



The Italian insisted a lack of resilience among his players is to blame for their poor start, but Lewis disagreed and insisted he is at fault.

He argued: “It's deflected a little bit, this whole mentality thing, from the fact that De Zerbi has to be held accountable for where they are right now.

“And listen, I'm experienced enough to say, I don't think he lasts a season.”

5 De Zerbi is yet to put his stamp on Tottenham, despite being backed heavily in the transfer market Credit: Getty



Continuing to slate De Zerbi, Lewis added: “In terms of where Tottenham are, their inability to defend is on you. Their inability to score goals, to win games is on you.

“Their inability, as you were saying, to come back when you go down, when you fall behind, it's on you. What are you gonna do about it?

What has Pochettino said about returning to Spurs?

This isn't the first time Pochettino has been tipped for a return to north London, who revealed the opportunity arose earlier this year.

With Spurs in the midst of a relegation battle in March, the 54-year-old was ultimately denied a second chance at the club last season due to his existing commitments with the USA.



Having been appointed in 2024, he was preparing for their World Cup campaign when Spurs approached him to come back to.

Speaking earlier this month, Pochettino explained: "If I were free, I would have gone back to Tottenham.

5 Pochettino has revealed timing has prevented him from returning to Spurs Credit: Getty

"Even in the Championship. Whatever the division. Another club, no, but Tottenham, yes, of course. It’s the only club I’m always open to help."



While De Zerbi was instead appointed and guided Spurs to safety with a final-day victory over Everton, Pochettino could have been tasked with this instead.

The Argentinian added: "The problem was the timings were never the best.

"When I was free, I never received a contact and then when I was working, I received a contact and then I couldn’t make the decision to come back.

"It was a little bit unlucky. Maybe one day the stars will align and it will happen."

Sports.content:
Nations League outright betting tips and predictions: Selections for the 2026/27 campaign

The 2026-27 Nations League kicks off this week and Thomas Tuchel's England are one of the favourites to lift the trophy.

They face a daunting opening fixture against World Cup winners Spain, who beat the Three Lions in the final of Euro 2024.



Zinedine Zidane's France and Jurgen Klopp's Germany are rated serious contenders while Nations League holders Portugal also have a new manager, replacing Roberto Martinez with former Benfica boss Jorge Jesus.

Nations League Tips

Portugal can enhance strong Nations League record

Spain, France and England dominated the World Cup outright betting and all three reached the semi-finals of this summer's tournament.

Spain outclassed France in the last four before an extra-time victory in the final against Argentina, who stunned England with a late comeback in the semis.



There is serious strength in depth in Europe. The continent provided six of the eight World Cup quarter-finalists despite early exits for Germany and the Netherlands.

Italy, who failed to qualify for the World Cup, are also prominent in the Nations League market but holders Portugal look a decent bet to retain the trophy.



They were the inaugural winners of the tournament in 2018-19 and claimed their second title in June 2025, beating Spain on penalties after a 2-2 draw in the final.

Portugal defeated Croatia 2-1 in the round of 32 at the World Cup and Spain needed a late Mikel Merino winner to edge past them in the last 16.



Roberto Martinez struggled to get the best out of a supremely talented squad but new manager Jorge Jesus is a respected figure in Portuguese football.

Jesus won three Primeira Liga titles with Benfica, also reaching two Europa League finals, and he inherits an exciting group of players.

Nuno Mendes, Joao Neves and Vitinha played key roles in Paris Saint-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs while Bruno Fernandes is the reigning PFA Player of the Year.

Cristiano Ronaldo is still on the international scene and striker Goncalo Ramos should benefit from playing more regularly after his move from PSG to Milan.



Back Norway to build on World Cup heroics

One of Portugal's main threats could come from their Group A4 rivals Norway, who had a memorable World Cup campaign in North America.

Stale Solbakken's men qualified for the tournament in style, scoring 37 goals in eight qualifying wins including a couple of handsome victories over Italy.

They beat Iraq 4-1 and Senegal 3-2 in their first two group games and lost 4-1 to France with a second-string side.

Solbakken's strategy paid off with 2-1 knockout-stage wins over Ivory Coast and Brazil before Norway's run ended with a 2-1 quarter-final defeat to England.



They gave the Three Lions a massive scare in that game and, with captain Martin Odegaard recapturing his best form at Arsenal this season, the Vikings could prove formidable foes in the Nations League.

Sports.title: Transfer Notebook: Harry Kane’s Bayern Munich weigh up blockbuster raid for England teammate
Sports.content:
Nottingham Forest are bracing themselves for serious interest in captain Morgan Gibbs-White next summer, talkSPORT understands.

The 26-year-old has been one of the standout players in the Premier League since the start of last season, and tops the charts for the most goal involvements by any English player in 2026 with 18.



3 Gibbs-White could become a club teammate for Kane amid interest from Bayern Credit: Getty

talkSPORT understands German giants Bayern Munich are one of the leading contenders to sign Gibbs-White, where he would play alongside his England co-star Harry Kane.

Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis will drive a hard bargain with any interested club, after putting the stop to a move to Tottenham Hotspur last summer and even issuing a legal complaint.

Rice reward for Arsenal excellence

Declan Rice is ready to commit his long-term future to Arsenal.

The Gunners are prepared to hand the midfielder a new contract that will keep him at the Emirates until at least the summer of 2031.



Talks over extending the England star's deal, which is due to expire in 2028, have already begun.

He signed a five-year deal when he joined from West Ham in a club record deal worth up to £105m.



Those negotiations, which are set to give Rice parity with Bukayo Saka as Arsenal's top earner, are expected to ramp up once manager Mikel Arteta has finalised his own future.

As previously reported by talkSPORT, Arteta could agree his contract as early as this international break.



United recruitment plans as Gabriel exit looms

Manchester United are scouring Europe for potential replacements for wonder-kid JJ Gabriel.

Club chiefs are now resigned to the fact that Gabriel is leaving Old Trafford, with a move to Barcelona or Real Madrid most likely.

3 Gabriel has asked to leave United, who are already looking to sign a replacement Credit: Getty

One option to replace the 15-year-old sensation in their pool of young players is 16-year-old RC Lens talent Mezian Mesloub.



Attacking midfielder Mesloub, who has already made his first team and Champions League debuts, has been scouted extensively by the recruitment department at Old Trafford.

United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe has made the development of youngsters a priority, which is why Gabriel's decision to quit the club has come as such a blow.

Experienced interest in Peterborough vacancy

Karl Robinson is keen on the vacant manager's job at Peterborough United.

The Posh are looking for a new appointment amid the sacking of Luke Williams following a run of one win in seven games at the start of the season that has left them second from bottom in League One.



Robinson has been out of work since his harsh axing by Salford City in June after their League Two play-off final defeat to Notts County.

3 Robinson is interested in taking the job at League One strugglers Peterborough Credit: Getty

The ex-MK Dons, Charlton Athletic and Oxford United boss is held in high regard by Peterborough owner Darragh MacAnthony.

Sports.title: Premier League grades: Two clubs get an F, Hull shine as every team ranked for start to season
Sports.content:
Premier League grades: Two clubs get an F, Hull shine as every team ranked for start to season

Time flies when you're having fun, right? Well, not all Premier League clubs would agree...

We have made it through the first five games of the 2026/27 season and, already, there has been plenty to dissect as the table begins to take shape.

10 City have been almost flawless at the start of the season with five wins from five, bagging them the only A* rating in talkSPORT's early grades Credit: Getty

As clubs pause their league campaigns for the international break, Manchester City sit top with a 100 per cent record whilst the reigning champions Arsenal are three points behind them following their 3-0 loss at Brighton.

Top flight returnees Hull City have been the surprise package as they find themselves eighth and already dreaming of a potential European push.

Premier League titans Chelsea and Manchester United are in a spot of bother as they linger in tenth and 12th respectively.

However, it's Tottenham Hotspur who have been the laughing stock as they are winless and have scored just two goals - with both coming in the 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa - despite spending more than £300million on new players.

And now that we have had our first impressions of this season's 20 competing clubs, talkSPORT.com has graded each one based on how they have performed so far...

Arsenal

Position: 2nd

Grade: A

It's been 22 years since Arsenal entered a Premier League season as reigning champions and, as it stands, you wouldn't put it past them to go out and win it again.

Wins over Coventry City, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Sunderland handed them a strong start, but they strayed away from perfection during the weekend visit to Brighton.

A lack of cutting edge in the final third mixed with apparent fatigue meant Arsenal, who were fortunate to not have Declan Rice sent off late on, were deservedly beaten - but they're still in title contention.

Aston Villa

Position: 16th

Grade: D

The summer of 2026 is not one that Villa will look back on fondly as past-season heroes such as Morgan Rogers, Emi Martinez and Ollie Watkins all left for pastures new.

However, they still spent in excess of £250m on new signings and 4-0 thumping by Brighton on the opening weekend was a warning shot for the Europa League champions.

10 Arsenal were heading straight for an A*, but the 3-0 defeat to Brighton has bumped them down by a grade Credit: Getty

A 0-0 draw with Hull, on reflection, is a solid point, and they finally picked up their first win to go out of the bottom three by beating Spurs on Saturday, saving them from an even lower grade.

Bournemouth

Position: 7th

Grade: E

Marco Rose was always going to have big shoes to fill as the successor to Andoni Iraola, and he's had an underwhelming start to life on the south coast.

The Cherries are without a win and clean sheet in their opening five, although they have already come up against City and Liverpool.

Bournemouth have led and failed to win on four occasions and this inability to see out a result when in front has put them in a worrying position just above the relegation zone on goal difference.

Brentford

Position: 4th

Grade: A

Now in their sixth consecutive Premier League season, Brentford are thriving under Keith Andrews and boast an unbeaten record.

10 Brentford are one of the Premier League's current top dogs and worthy of an A with their five-game unbeaten run Credit: Getty

They have smashed Spurs 3-0 and entered the international break off the back of an excellent home win over Chelsea by the same scoreline, with Mamadou Sangare one of the signings of the summer.

Brentford were unlucky to miss out on European at the end of last season, but now they are already looking like a side who will be on a continental tour during the 2027/28 campaign.

Brighton

Position: 3rd

Grade: A

Forget Arsenal, City or Chelsea, it's Brighton who are this season's top scorers with 16 goals and with a goal difference off 11 thanks to what has been an excellent start.

Fabian Hurzeler and co. have picked up 4-0, 5-0 and 3-0 victories over Villa, Coventry and, most impressively, Arsenal, with the 4-3 defeat at Chelsea being an anomaly of a result.

With a frontline full of goals and defence that have kept three clean sheets, the Seagulls are soaring in the Premier League top four and could be in for a historic season.

Chelsea

Position: 10th

Grade: D

Attacking excitement, leaky defending and unpredictability - that's how you could describe Chelsea across their opening five matches.

Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer are a front three who look set to score plenty of goals this season - they already have 14 combined goals and assists.

However, Chelsea have been held back by an abundance of frailties in a defence that have shipped a league-high of 12 goals, with Xabi Alonso yet to see his side concede less than two goals per match.

10 Not only are Brighton the Premier League top scorers, but they convincingly beat the reigning champions, so thoroughly deserve an A Credit: Getty

Coventry City

Position: 18th

Grade: E

Before the start of the season, there was confidence in Championship winners Coventry being able to secure their top flight status, but this has now dissipated.

They scored zero goals and conceded ten across their first four, and have gone into the international break as one of numerous sides who already look destined for a relegation battle.

Had it not been for the 1-0 weekend win at Nottingham Forest, who had a late equaliser disallowed after a VAR review, they would have remained winless and goalless, as well as highly likely to go down.

Crystal Palace

Position: 15th

Grade: E

Similar to Rose at Bournemouth, manager Pierre Sage arrived at Palace in the summer as the replacement for a hugely successful manager in Oliver Glasner, who won the FA Cup and Conference League at Selhurst Park.

Defeats to Everton and City were followed by a 3-2 victory at Fulham, but they have gone winless since then and, with 11 goals conceded, have the joint-second worst defence alongside Ipswich Town.

Now that Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Munoz have left the club, the Palace defence is a concern and has not been supplemented by their attack, with left-back Tyrick Mitchell their top scorer on two goals.

Everton

Position: 7th

Grade: B

Only five sides have started the campaign unbeaten, and you could argue that Everton being among those is one of the league's biggest surprises thus far.

Three clean sheets have been kept against Palace, Spurs and Ipswich, whilst a last-minute rocket from Ainsley Maitland-Niles ensured they earned a deserved point at home to United.

10 Coventry have had a rude awakening on their top flight return with four defeats but, thanks to the win over Forest, they have avoided a dreaded F Credit: Getty

Everton also have the joint-best defence with Leeds on three goals conceded, and head into the three-week break full of optimism as only the 15th-biggest summer spenders.

Fulham

Position: 19th

Grade: F

Yes, it's early days, but Fulham are already looking like a side who will be well in the relegation mix this season.

Back-to-back-to-back defeats in their opening three, combined with a transfer window that seemingly lacked desire, means the Cottagers have left themselves with plenty of work to avoid going down.

Alvaro Arbeloa has managed to secure draws against Liverpool and United in their last two, but remains unconvincing at Craven Cottage as the club sit second from bottom.

Hull City

Position: 8th

Grade: A

As a newly-promoted side, Hull mightily impressed when it took three matches to concede their first goal back in the Premier League.

They couldn't have wished for a better start when they beat United 2-0 on the opening weekend, picked up a crucial win at Coventry and held Chelsea to a 2-2 draw on the road.

Although they faltered in a 2-1 defeat to Newcastle on Saturday, Hull have shown that, even with the embedding of 18 new signings, you don't need to biggest and best names to compete near the top.

Ipswich Town

Position: 11th

Grade: B

Promotion back to the Premier League at the first time of asking was a huge success for Ipswich, who were then rocked by Kieran McKenna's resignation as he opted for a break from management.

10 From being tipped for relegation, to beating United and winning eight points - Hull have shone and earned an A Credit: Getty

But in came Gary O'Neil and, despite suffering three defeats, it's been a mostly-positive start for the Tractor Boys in their bid to avoid the drop for a second time in three seasons.

Newbie Emersonn has already impressed with two league goals, and Zian Flemming was their recent hero at Selhurst Park as his late goal delivered three more crucial points in a 3-2 win.

Leeds United

Position: 5th

Grade: B

Months after being tipped for the sack at Leeds, Daniel Farke has got his side sitting pretty in fifth and unbeaten, with less than £100m spent in the summer.

James Trafford and Tarik Muharemovic have been two top signings at the back, and Dominic Calvert-Lewin has been awarded for his three league goals with another England call-up.

The 4-1 home victory over Newcastle United demonstrated just how good they can be going forward, whilst their tally of three goals conceded is a testament to their resilience in defence.

Liverpool

Position: 6th

Grade: B

Gone are the days of Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson being the ever-reliable stars at Anfield, and it's Iraola who has taken the reins at a club whose title defence last season was nothing short of dismal.

Consecutive 2-2 draws with Newcastle and Forest, as well as a stalemate at home to Fulham, mean Liverpool are far from the full package, whilst £123m signing Bradley Barcola is yet to score or assist.

However, Alexander Isak has four league goals - which is already one more than his total from last season - and three clean sheets in as many past fixtures has left them in a strong and unbeaten position.

10 Liverpool are unbeaten and starting to see the best of Isak but, with three draws from five, they have to settle for a B Credit: Getty

Manchester City

Position: 1st

Grade: A*

A disciple of the legendary former City boss Pep Guardiola, Enzo Maresca had made a strong impression during the start of what he hopes to be a long-term dynasty in Manchester.

With five wins from five, which includes their controversial 1-0 victory at rivals United and 5-3 smashing of Sunderland, they have a maximum of 15 points and deserve the highest grade possible.

Erling Haaland is already the league's top scorer on five goals, Rayan Cherki remains a dazzling talent in attack, and a midfield partnership of Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez has early signs of blossoming.

Manchester United

Position: 12th

Grade: E

Michael Carrick was deserving of the long-term head coach job at United after guiding them to third last season, but alarm bells are already ringing with just five games played.

A midfield overhaul that saw Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos sign for a combined £85m just hasn't worked out, although £70m man Carlos Baleba is yet to play as he has just returned from injury.

Barring a hat-trick and assist against Ipswich, club captain Bruno Fernandes has underperformed and United have just one win, with draws against Everton and Fulham coming after they led.

Newcastle United

Position: 9th

Grade: B

Matthias Jaissle became the Newcastle head coach just 18 days before their league opener, but will be pleased with how well has started the post-Eddie Howe reign at St. James' Park.

Victory away at Spurs and a hard-fought home win over Hull are two results that have delivered encouragement - so have the signings of Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez, and improved form of Yoane Wissa.

10 Newcastle boss Jaissle has taken a club in upheaval to a B rating within weeks - it would have been higher if it wasn't for the thumping at Leeds Credit: Getty

The 4-1 thumping to Leeds and goal difference of zero - nine scored, nine conceded - has denied them an excellent start that followed the big sales Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes.

Nottingham Forest

Position: 13th

Grade: C

Picking up just one win before the international break is by no means a poor start for Forest, but there is still a lot to improve on.

Glasner has earned success with draws against Liverpool and Spurs, as well as a 2-1 away win at Villa, though a home defeat against Coventry is one that they will rue over the next three weeks.

On the positive side of things, Morgan Gibbs-White has returned to his very best with a goal and two assists, and £50m arrival Liam Delap has already found the target at the City Ground.

Sunderland

Position: 14th

Grade: C

It was always going to be tough for Sunderland to match their start to what turned out to be a stunning season last time out, where they picked up eight points from their opening five.

Their tally so far is half of that, they have already conceded ten times and 50 per cent of their goals came in the 5-3 loss at City on Sunday.

Sunderland also have just one win but as the Premier League's lowest spenders on £60m, they remain above the relegation zone and, as it stands, unlikely to be drawn into a fight for top flight survival.

Tottenham Hotspur

Position: 20th

Grade: F

With two goals scored, a rock-bottom standing, no wins and a squad that Roberto De Zerbi told talkSPORT is the most 'fragile' of his career, Spurs have been an absolute embarrassment this season.

10 Only one club has performed poorly enough to earn an F, and that's Spurs - a woefully embarrassing start to the season for the big spenders Credit: Getty

10 It has been a tough start to the season for De Zerbi, whose opposite number at Arsenal, Arteta, is flying

The £185m midfield pair of Tonali and Mateus Fernandes have been poor, Savio has not scored or assisted since his £85m move from City, and £52m signing Jan Paul van Hecke left Stuart Pearce stunned.

De Zerbi could already be in line to become the third Spurs boss in the past three seasons - after Ange Postecoglou and Thomas Frank - to steer them towards a mortifying relegation scrap.

Meanwhile, rivals are laughing as a stat emerged revealing that, since November 2024, popstar Beyoncé has had more gigs at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, with six than, Spurs' five league wins there.

Sports.title: Supercomputer tips Tottenham to be relegated as Premier League title prediction made
Sports.content:
Supercomputer tips Tottenham to be relegated as Premier League title prediction made

Tottenham fans, look away now.

Amid a historically poor start to the 2026/27 campaign, it appears that circling the drain for two straight seasons will finally catch up with Spurs.

2 Roberto De Zerbi's side are yet to win a league fixture this term Credit: AFP



According to Opta's supercomputer, Tottenham, who sit last after five games, are predicted to end the season in 18th.

Opta Supercomputer predicts the relegation battle

The prediction model has Spurs picking up 43.12 points, giving them a 29.39 per cent chance of being relegated.

Annoyingly for Spurs, Ipswich Town were tipped to accrue 43.68 points, which has them with a 28.42 per cent chance of going down.

Fulham and Coventry City complete the predicted bottom three in Opta's model.



The Cottagers, who are one of three teams yet to win a league game this term, are expected to finish with 39.84 points.

Unfortunately for Coventry, Opta has tipped them to finish last having given them an expected points haul of 39.60.



Even though there isn't much between the predicted points margin among those four clubs, the relegation percentage difference is significant.

Opta's model has Fulham with a 42.40 per cent chance of going down while Coventry are a 43.82 per cent chance.



Opta Supercomputer predicts the Premier League title race

Moving away from the bottom end of the table, Arsenal are predicted to win back-to-back league titles.

It is a feat the Gunners have never managed in the Premier League era.

2 The Gunners ended their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last term Credit: Getty

In fact, Arsenal have not won consecutive league titles in the English top flight since the 1930s, underlining the significance of their mooted achievement.



However, Arsenal are not tipped to be runaway winners.

According to Opta, the Gunners have been predicted to finish with 75.91 points, which is ever-so-slightly ahead of Manchester City's predicted points tally of 75.33.

Despite the closeness in the predicted points, there is a large difference when it comes to the predicted title percentage.

Opta has the Gunners with a 43.63 per cent chance of retaining their title while City have a 39.71 per cent chance.

But with 33 games to go this season, there's still plenty of twists and turns left to come.



Spurs supporters will hope those same twists and turns don't end with them finishing in the bottom three, something they have not experienced in the Premier League era.
