World.title: FM commends outstanding bilateral relations between Egypt, Latvia
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptians Abroad Badr Abdelatty, praised the distinguished bilateral relations between Egypt and Latvia during his meeting on Monday, September 21, 2026, with Baiba Braže, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Latvia.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the high-level segment of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Abdelatty emphasized Egypt’s keenness to strengthen and advance these relations through the exchange of high-level visits and continued coordination and consultation between both sides, expressing looking forward to expanding bilateral ties to broader horizons, particularly in trade and economic fields, through the regular holding of bilateral cooperation mechanisms.

In this context, Abdelatty highlighted the importance of strengthening trilateral cooperation with Latvia on the African continent, allowing for the utilization of Egypt’s strategic geographic location as a gateway for European exports into African nations.

The two ministers exchanged views on regional and international issues of mutual interest, chief among them the Iranian file, ways to de-escalate tensions in the region, developments in the Palestinian cause, and the Ukrainian crisis.

Both sides stressed the importance of intensifying efforts to give political pathways and negotiations room to reach peaceful solutions to these crises, thereby contributing to the enhancement of security and stability at both regional and international levels.

World.title: Investment Minister stresses boosting exports, production
World.content:
Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid stressed the importance of supporting existing investments and maximizing the use of available production capacities to increase output, expand local manufacturing and create jobs.

He also underscored the importance of boosting exports by existing companies and opening new markets for Egyptian products, affirming the government’s commitment to facilitating investors’ operations, coordinating among relevant authorities to address challenges, and supporting export procedures and access to foreign markets.

Farid made the remarks on Monday, September 21, 2026, during a tour, accompanied by Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem, Sharqia Governor Hazem al-Ashmouni and French Ambassador to Egypt Eric Chevallier, of two factories producing prestressed concrete and cosmetics in the industrial zone of 10th of Ramadan City.

For his part, Hashem said his visit to factories operating in the building materials sector highlighted one of the key sectors supporting the national economy, given its broad industrial base and diverse range of activities and products.

The sector contributes to meeting domestic market needs and supporting construction and development projects, while also offering potential to increase its contribution to exports and open new markets for Egyptian products, he added.

Hashem also noted that the pharmaceutical and cosmetics industries are among the most promising sectors, with a significant opportunity to boost Egypt’s exports to markets across the region.

World.title: Liberia: How a Dutch Fugitive Found His Way Through West Africa’s Porous Ports, Borders, Stashing Drugs
World.content:
Ghana and Liberia sit on the same stretch of West African coast, share the same colonial-era port infrastructure, and now, investigators say, share the same weakness: officials willing to sell access to it. In Ghana, prosecutors say a container flagged by port scanners for “clear structural irregularities” was cleared anyway, allegedly by Ghana Revenue Authority officers now facing charges alongside associates of fugitive Dutch trafficker Jos Leijdekkers. In Liberia, the police chief himself says officers ran marked cruisers as paid escorts for a cocaine landing, pocketing roughly $5,000 each. No one has yet tied the Liberian case to Leijdekkers directly — but the two countries’ parallel scandals expose the same regional vulnerability: ports and patrols for sale to the highest bidder.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — Two countries, an ocean apart in almost everything except geography and a shared coastline of vulnerability, are now telling versions of the same story. In Ghana, prosecutors say a port scanner flagged a shipment’s “clear structural irregularities” — and someone cleared it anyway. In Liberia, the country’s own police chief says officers ran marked cruisers as paid escorts for a coastal cocaine landing, pocketing roughly $5,000 apiece from a $10,000 envelope. Different currencies, different officers, same failure: the men who were supposed to stand between West Africa’s ports and its traffickers instead opened the gate.

Nothing yet on the public record ties the Liberian case to Jos Leijdekkers, the fugitive Dutch trafficker reportedly sheltering in Sierra Leone. But the pattern emerging on both sides of the Ghana-Liberia corridor — officials allegedly paid to look away — is precisely the kind of institutional crack that lets a network like his keep moving even as the walls close in elsewhere in the region. Leijdekkers, it now appears, isn’t just passing through West Africa’s ports. He’s paying his way through them.

The Dunkirk Shipment

It started, as these things often do, with a routine scan that wasn’t routine at all. On September 10, French customs officers at the port of Dunkirk pulled apart four containers that had sailed out of Ghana’s Tema Port and found roughly 3.9 tonnes of cocaine packed inside — a haul worth an estimated €225 million, or $261 million. Leijdekkers’ lawyers, Jan-Hein Kuijpers and Guy Weski, told the Dutch outlet NU.nl that their client denies any involvement.

Ghana’s Narcotics Control Commission moved quickly, arraigning four Ghanaians it says “represented and facilitated” Leijdekkers’ activities: Desmond Koranteng Curiel — who has also gone by “Paul Kweku Yeboah” and “Biggs” — along with Musah Attah (“Kromo”), Kweku Otchere, and Jessica Hartog. Dutch reporting fills in the backstory on Curiel, describing him as one of Leijdekkers’ “most important accomplices” and noting the two once shared a Dutch prison, where Curiel was serving time for a string of violent jewelry-store robberies. All four were remanded at the High Court in Accra on September 16 and return to court October 13.

The Officers Who Cleared It

But four tonnes of cocaine don’t leave a working port on its own — and this is where the case turns from a trafficking story into something closer to a story about the port itself. Separately from the four accused of fronting for Leijdekkers, Ghanaian prosecutors have charged three Ghana Revenue Authority officers — Frank Adu-Boahen, Andrews Tetteh Amponsah, and Togbe Agbeti — plus freight-forwarding director Francis Narh Amanor, over how the shipment made it out of Tema at all. The scan had already raised the alarm, according to the charges; the secondary inspection those red flags were supposed to trigger simply never happened. Adu-Boahen, prosecutors say, went further still — handing his own system login, the credentials used to sign off on scan results, to his co-defendants — and he’s now named as a beneficial owner of the shipment itself. Amanor was arrested September 15, Adu-Boahen the next day; all appeared in court September 17 and are due back September 24.

No filing has drawn a straight line from these three officers to Leijdekkers personally. The charges concern the shipment, not the man alleged to be behind it. But laid side by side, Ghana’s two cases sketch the same failure from opposite ends: a network with a documented personal tie to Leijdekkers on one side, a screening system allegedly hollowed out from within on the other. A scan overridden. A login shared. A shipment waved through.

Accra has noticed. MP Ntim Fordjour has publicly called for a parliamentary probe into what he’s calling Ghana’s emergence as a “cocaine coast,” and the presidency has since ordered inter-agency investigations and restored NACOC’s mandatory role in screening port cargo — the kind of response that suggests officials themselves see Dunkirk as a systemic breach, not a bad afternoon at customs.

A Familiar Pattern, Still Unconfirmed, in Liberia

Liberia’s own reckoning is unfolding on a parallel track. Inspector General Gregory Coleman has told reporters that Liberian National Police officers actively helped move roughly four tons of cocaine — “We have identified key state actors who played a role in transporting, escorting the movement of this narcotic substance,” he said. Two names have surfaced: Wadell W. Kwarbo, chief of the Highway Patrol Section, and Anthony T. Blaye, chief of the Financial Crime Division, both accused of escorting a shipment from a coastal landing site in marked police cruisers for roughly $5,000 each.

It’s a near-mirror image of what’s now public in Ghana — officials allegedly easing a shipment’s path for cash. What’s missing, so far, is the Leijdekkers connection. Coleman’s account doesn’t name him or link the seizure to a Dutch buyer or supplier, and no other source has made that connection either. Until someone does, the Liberia case stands on its own: proof of the same vulnerability across the region, not proof of the same hand behind it.

The Ghana-Liberia thread runs deeper than the two escort allegations, though. Liberian officials tell FrontPageAfrica that one of the foreign nationals now in Liberian custody carries a Ghanaian passport — one Ghanaian authority have since called fake — and a residence permit issued under two different names: Mihovil Vrhovac, also known as Michael. It’s not an isolated detail. Liberian authorities say most of the Eastern Europeans moving through these networks — Serbian, Croatian, Ukrainian, Georgian — are based in Accra and carry Ghanaian passports, some of them, FrontPageAfrica has learned, using those documents to enter Liberia as far back as 2021.

Liberia’s own case has produced two arrests so far tied to July’s $318 million bust: Spanish Colombian national Johann David Garces Grajales and Serbian former kickboxer Srđan Seleš. Prosecutors have charged five European nationals in total in the wider investigation, including Croatian nationals Nikolai Ivancic (also spelled Nicolad Avancik) and Mihovil Vrovac (Mio Vuvak), and Ukrainian national Tara Zaderieko (Taras Zargo) — the latter three indicted and now pursued in absentia through Interpol. Investigators have since traced four of them — Mihovil, Tara, David, and Seleš — to multiple visits to Freetown, with what officials describe as strong indications of ties to Leijdekkers. Mihovil, notably, was arrested in Accra at Liberia’s request — and then reportedly vanished.

A Region Under Siege

Dunkirk didn’t happen in isolation. A regional drug threat assessment obtained by FrontPageAfrica on Sunday describes an intensifying run of seizures across nearly every country on the West and Central African coast between June and September — a stretch that raises an uncomfortable question: how many of those cases, like Ghana’s, involved not just traffickers but the officials meant to be stopping them?

In Ghana alone, the Dunkirk arrests landed a week after NACOC shut down the Amsterdam Pub in Accra’s Laboma neighborhood on September 9, arresting three suspects while the principal target got away. Days before that, a joint NACOC-National Security raid in Weija caught a couple, Jibreel Hardi, 51, and his wife, Abiba Fatawu, 42, with cannabis, Tramadol, a firearm, and 50 rounds of ammunition. In August, police in the Upper East Region seized 500 cartons of Tramadol from a network allegedly running through Mali, Togo, Burkina Faso, and Senegal via the town of Widana — and earlier that month, 866 parcels of cocaine worth an estimated $6.9 million turned up hidden in sacks of gari at Tema Harbor.

Sierra Leone, where Leijdekkers is believed to be hiding, has had its own exposure: a September 10 tramadol seizure in Freetown that turned violent and left one person dead, and weeks before that, 51 kilograms of cocaine found in suitcases aboard a Brussels Airlines flight out of Freetown — leading to the arrest of a 22-year-old Belgian woman who wasn’t even on the flight’s passenger list.

Nigeria’s drug enforcement agency had one of its busiest stretches anywhere in the region — synthetic cannabis, opioids and other drugs found hidden in cargo, speakers and bread across eight states in mid-September, more than 2 million opioid pills and over 2,000 kilograms of cannabis seized in a nine-state sweep on September 6, and 329,865 kilograms of drugs destroyed in Lagos. Cabo Verde’s two main airports were hit within 24 hours of each other, couriers arrested arriving from Dakar and Bissau — one had swallowed 73 capsules of cocaine — while Brazilian authorities separately intercepted more than 100 kilograms bound for the islands hidden in drills, shock absorbers, a dental chair, and chocolate powder tins.

Liberia, for its part, has posted two of the region’s largest seizures in the same window: 3,971 kilograms in Duazon, Margibi County, on July 21 — worth roughly $317.68 million — and 237.6 kilograms at Roberts International Airport on June 8, hidden in six cargo boxes bound for Europe and valued near $19.2 million. Whether either shipment is the same one referenced in Coleman’s police-escort account remains unclear.

The wave has touched Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, The Gambia, Guinea, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, and Senegal as well — networks dismantled, drug dens destroyed, everything from tramadol to captagon seized across a sub-region where the trade has clearly stopped respecting borders.

Ghana as the Hub

Liberian authorities, watching two major busts of their own unfold in a matter of months, believe — based on FrontPageAfrica’s reporting — that Ghana has become the operational center of drug smuggling in West Africa. The pattern keeps repeating: a Ghanaian passport later called fake, a residence permit under two names, a community of Eastern European operatives based in Accra who’ve been slipping into Liberia on those same documents since at least 2021.

“Thank God our joint security forces have intercepted or made arrests in Liberia, and not shipped [drugs] out like Ghana, Sierra Leone, and others,” a senior member of Liberia’s joint security drug force told FrontPageAfrica on Monday.

Whether that holds — whether Liberia catches what Ghana’s port let through — may be the question the rest of this story is still being written to answer.

World.title: Liberia: Police Reject VP’s Plea, Charges Wrato on Four Cybercrime Counts
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Liberia National Police (LNP) has concluded its investigation into Jerry Nyantee Wrato and will forward him to court on four cybercrime charges, rebuffing a public appeal from Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung for the young man’s release.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

In a letter dated September 21 to Koung, Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman said Wrato will face charges of Misuse of Devices, Cyberstalking, Distribution of Data Messages That Incite Damage to Property or Violence, and Distribution of Harmful Data Messages — alleged violations of Sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Cybercrime Act of 2025. The suspect is to be forwarded to a court of competent jurisdiction “tomorrow morning,” Coleman wrote.

The letter was a direct response to a phone call Koung placed to Coleman, and to the Vice President’s subsequent public statement asking for Wrato’s release. Coleman thanked Koung for his “tolerance and restraint” but made clear the police would proceed regardless: “Once conduct potentially constituting a criminal offense comes to the attention of law enforcement, the matter is no longer determined solely by the personal wishes of the individual affected.”

He said the LNP has a “statutory responsibility to investigate the allegations objectively,” and stressed that referring the case to court “does not constitute a determination of guilt” — Wrato retains the presumption of innocence and all constitutional protections pending trial.

Wrato’s arrest followed AI-generated images and videos, circulated on Facebook, that appeared to depict Koung in a derogatory manner — content tied to earlier controversy over reports of the Vice President’s security screening at Brussels Airport, which Koung has denied. Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye defended applying the Cybercrime Act to manipulated political content.

The law itself is barely a month old: the Senate passed it in November 2025, and President Boakai signed it on August 19, 2026 — a fact made awkward by Koung’s role as President of the Senate, the body that passed it, while he is also the case’s alleged victim.

Former Finance Minister Samuel D. Tweah Jr. has called the law “draconian” and argued Koung should never have had to request Wrato’s release in the first place. Legal commentators have also raised a narrower question: whether a complainant can end a prosecution simply by declining to pursue it, given that criminal cases are ordinarily controlled by the state.

World.title: Liberia: Jewel Starfish Foundation Beneficiaries Share Life-Changing Stories After 25 Years of Humanitarian Service
World.content:
Monrovia – The Jewel Starfish Foundation celebrated its silver jubilee in December 2025 and continues to provide educational and other opportunities to young Liberian women from across the country.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Foundation is a leading Liberian non-governmental organization dedicated to empowering underprivileged girls through education, leadership mentoring, and social protection.

Beneficiaries are glad, happy, and feel loved as they recounted how the former Vice President, Madam Jewel Howard Taylor, transformed their lives from uncertainty to university.

They spoke out to defend what they believe is a “life-changing” intervention in their educational journey.

In exclusive video interviews conducted on September 20, 2026, several beneficiaries from across Liberia shared emotional testimonies of how the Foundation rescued their education when all hope was lost.

From Potato Seller to Biology Major, A Story of Nancy

Narrating her story, Nancy Fayiah from Bomi County, a proud beneficiary of the Foundation, recounted how she was selling potatoes just to pay her school fees before meeting “Mama Jewel.”

“I met her in Bomi County when she gave us forms to be part of the family. Education, feeding, transportation – these are some of the things I receive from Mama Jewel,” she explained.

Nancy, who was then a student at C.H. Dewey Central High School, said she has been on the scholarship for seven years. She is now a junior student at the faith-based African Methodist Episcopal University, majoring in Biology and minoring in Chemistry.

“Imagine a girl selling potatoes just to pay her fees to be among her colleagues. That privilege was given by me and since then she started paying my fees. I never stayed out of class, even up to university level,” Nancy indicated

Reacting to her link to the drugs saga, Nancy indicated: “She is a good woman. She has inspired a lot of people. She is my mentor. She is a God-fearing woman. I feel inspired, I feel motivated, I feel important in society.”

“She Is An Angel In My Life” – Pearline Narrates

Pearline Campbell from Sinoe County, in southeastern Liberia, described Madam Taylor as “an angel in my life.”

Pearline explained with the former Vice President through her grandmother when her educational journey was uncertain.

“I was at the point where my educational journey was uncertain, and continuing my education was something difficult. Meeting her and her offering me a scholarship changed my entire life,” she narrated.

Pearline revealed she first got on the Jewel Starfish scholarship when she was in the 8th grade and has been sponsored through her first three semesters in college, where she is now studying Criminal Justice at the university.

To Liberians and fellow beneficiaries, she had this message: “She has served as a mother and mentor for so many young women.”

“Resilient Woman Who Lifts Every Girl” – Cecelia From Cape Mount

For Cecelia Bendu Freeman from Grand Cape Mount County, now a Sociology major at the University of Liberia, the Foundation came at a time when her entire class at the More Than Me Academy in West Point thought their education had ended due to “confusion” surrounding the school.

“When they took over the program, she visited the school and we explained our situation to her. We invited her as guest speaker for our 9th grade graduation. When she came, she awarded every single graduate a scholarship to attend Wells-Hairston and CWA,” Cecelia explained.

“It is such an honor, such a privilege that no matter how far I go in life, I will always appreciate that.”

Apart from educational support, Cecelia said “Mama Jewel” mentors her personally.

On the current saga facing the former Vice President, Cecelia “prayed God to be the one to take control and speak,” adding: “I know the kind of sponsor I have.”

“In a direct message to her sponsor, she said: “You are that strong woman that lifts up every young woman that comes across you. I believe in you, I believe in your work, I believe in your impact. It is a test of time, be strong and trust that God is in control.”

She described the former Vice President as a “resilient” and a “very powerful woman” who continues to impact lives.

Several other beneficiaries maintained that the Jewel Starfish Foundation is more than a scholarship scheme, stating that it is a family and a breeding ground for female leadership that has touched lives in Liberia, Ghana, Malawi and Sierra Leone.

World.title: Liberia: Three Videos Put Saudi Rice Distribution Under Fresh Scrutiny as Defense Witness Continues Testimony
World.content:
MONROVIA — Three video recordings depicting the distribution of Saudi-donated rice were presented by the defense Monday as its first witness continued testifying in the closely watched trial involving former government officials and other defendants accused of the alleged mismanagement of the humanitarian donation.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Archievo Doe, a former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) communications official, presented the footage before Criminal Court “C” as part of the defense’s effort to challenge the prosecution’s account of how the rice was distributed.

Doe testified that one video was recorded in 2023, during the tenure of former NDMA Executive Director Henry O. Williams, while the other two were recorded in 2024, after Williams had left the position.

The defense is seeking to use the footage, alongside media reports, community witnesses and distribution records, to challenge aspects of the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce’s investigation.

However, the recordings’ dates, locations and the identities of those involved remain important considerations in determining whether the distributions shown relate to the specific transactions at issue in the case.

The footage alone does not establish who authorized each distribution, the quantities involved or whether the transactions complied with established procedures.

The defendants, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, have pleaded not guilty and remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Doe Cites Media Reports, Community Beneficiaries

Doe also referenced media coverage that he said documented the distribution of the Saudi-donated rice.

He specifically mentioned Joseph Daniel, a former mainstream journalist now associated with the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, who Doe said had previously reported on the distribution.

He also cited State Radio as another source of coverage.

Doe further told the court that the mother of the late Angel Togbah could testify that she and others received portions of the rice.

The defense maintains that such accounts could help establish that the distribution exercise was conducted openly and involved identifiable beneficiaries.

150 Bags Delivered to Caldwell Family

Testifying about the Caldwell distribution, Doe said the project’s concept note provided for two bags of rice per disaster-affected family.

However, he told the court that the Togbah family received 150 bags.

Doe testified that he signed the waybill associated with the movement of the consignment from the General Services Agency warehouse.

According to him, the rice was loaded onto an NDMA truck operated under the supervision of the Armed Forces of Liberia, with an AFL driver transporting it to Caldwell.

Doe said Williams and a team that included him followed the truck in another vehicle.

His testimony sought to place the delivery within an NDMA disaster-response operation, although the legality and significance of the transaction remain for the court to determine.

50 Bags Delivered to Flood-Affected School

Doe also testified that on October 2, 2023, Williams instructed him to deliver 50 bags of rice to Faith Caring Daycare and Elementary School in Chicken Soup Factory because the executive director was occupied with other responsibilities.

He said the school had been affected by flooding that disrupted academic activities.

Doe testified that information collected in the community identified 157 affected persons or infrastructure-related cases, including 46 infrastructure cases.

He said the rice was delivered in the presence of Staff Sergeant Zubah Blama, members of the Togbah family and community residents.

According to Doe, the consignment was transported in an NDMA Toyota Land Cruiser double-cabin pickup bearing license plate RL4704.

Explaining his broader role in the project, Doe said his responsibilities extended beyond the two distributions under scrutiny.

“My role in the Saudi rice project was not only about leading the team to deliver the 50 bags of rice to the Faith Caring Daycare Elementary School, but the Division of Communication I headed covered all the activities of the Saudi rice project,” he testified.

He added that either he or a member of his communications team was present at distribution sites.

Doe Challenges ARREPT Investigation

Doe also challenged the manner in which investigators handled his case, testifying that the two waybills associated with the Caldwell and Chicken Soup Factory distributions were not presented to him during questioning.

He said ARREPT sent him questions concerning his alleged involvement, but he considered some insufficiently specific. He testified that he requested clarification and eventually responded to approximately 18 questions.

Doe said he heard nothing further from investigators until June 27, when he was served with an indictment.

He maintained that he first saw the two waybills after his indictment, when his lawyer-wife showed them to him.

“At no time were the two willbills from Caldwell and Chicken Soup Factory presented to me,” Doe told the court.

He said he would have explained his role and the instructions he received from Williams had the documents been presented during the investigation.

Disputes Prosecution Witness’s Community Account

Doe also disputed testimony from Isaac K. Weede, General Chairman of Lakpazee Community, who previously told the court that he knew of no Saudi rice distribution in the community.

Doe referenced the death of a handicapped resident identified as Tamba and his wife in a fire incident in Lakpazee, challenging Weede’s account of events in the community.

He also cited the deaths of five children in Five-Forty Community, saying they occurred around the period of the rice distribution.

The competing accounts raise questions about the extent of individual witnesses’ knowledge of distributions across communities during the broader relief operation.

Judge Fines Defense Lawyer US$200

Monday’s proceedings also featured a tense exchange between Trial Judge Ousman Feika and defense lawyer Cllr. Jimmy Saah Bombo.

Judge Feika fined Bombo US$200 after the lawyer attempted to object to a question posed by the judge. The court ordered the fine paid within 24 hours and warned that failure to comply could result in imprisonment.

Two additional attempts by the defense to object to questions from the judge were rejected, prompting further disagreement.

The prosecution rested its case after 31 days of jury sitting, and the defense has now begun presenting its evidence.

The indictment reportedly alleges that 25,054 of the 29,412 bags of donated rice were unlawfully handled, diverted or misapplied.

As the defense continues its presentation, the jury will have to weigh the competing testimony, documentary records and video evidence to determine whether the prosecution has established the charges against each defendant beyond a reasonable doubt.

World.title: Liberia: Broken Roofs, Empty Classrooms: Beletanla and Blemeyea Schools Struggle in Bong County
World.content:
The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them

BONG COUNTY – In the villages of District Two, the school day does not always end with the bell. At one school, it can end with the rain. At another, it can end when the only available teacher has to leave for Gbarnga. These are the daily realities at Beletanla Public School and Blemeyea Public School, two institutions that residents and staff say are being asked to educate children with far too little.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Learning at the Mercy of the Weather

Ask residents of Beletanla about their school, and the conversation quickly turns to the roof. According to those who spoke to journalist Exodus Weah of Super Bongese, a local radio station in Gbarnga, during a visit to the campus, the damaged roof and the lack of chairs have left the school in a condition that is not conducive to teaching and learning.

The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them.

In a country where the rainy season stretches across many months, that means learning at Beletanla can stop at a moment’s notice. Residents fear the pattern will repeat if nothing is done, and they worry that the missing chairs and the failing roof will keep disrupting academic activities.

The Parents Who Pay

The pressure on Beletanla does not end with the building. The school currently has two teachers assigned by the government and two volunteers. The volunteers are not on any official payroll. Instead, residents say, members of the Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) make small financial contributions to pay them.

Kpontah explained that he dismissed the students before 1:00 PM so that he could travel to Gbarnga. The second teacher, reportedly ill, was not actively teaching on campus. With no one else to take over, the school day came to an early close

The arrangement keeps the school running, but it rests on a fragile foundation. Half of the school’s teaching staff depends on the generosity of parents rather than on a government commitment, and every contribution is a reminder that the state has not fully met its responsibility to the school.

A School with One Teacher to Spare

A short distance away, Blemeyea Public School, also known as Barsee Kpangbai Public School, faces a different but equally serious challenge. Its acting Principal, James Kollie Kpontah, says the school is operating with only two teachers, and one of them is currently unwell.

With one colleague out of action, Kpontah has taken on the teaching of students from the ABC class through the fifth grade. It is a demanding load for one person, since the range spans the youngest beginners and pupils several years ahead of them. Every child receives a smaller share of a single teacher’s attention.

The strain was visible during a news-gathering visit by journalist Weah on Monday. Kpontah explained that he dismissed the students before 1:00 PM so that he could travel to Gbarnga. The second teacher, reportedly ill, was not actively teaching on campus. With no one else to take over, the school day came to an early close.

Kpontah also disclosed that Blemeyea lacks sufficient instructional materials, a shortage he says is affecting the learning environment. For a teacher already stretched across six levels, the absence of teaching resources makes an uphill task steeper.

The Same Story, Told Twice

The damage has had a direct effect on attendance in the classroom. Residents said that last year, students were sent home whenever it rained because the building could not shelter them

The details differ from one school to the other, but the outline is the same. Beletanla has a broken roof and no chairs, while Blemeyea has a shortage of books and materials. Both rely on very small teaching teams, and both depend on individuals, whether volunteers, parents, or an acting principal doing the work of several teachers, to keep classes going.

Children bear the cost. A pupil who is sent home because of rain, or who spends the day in a crowded multigrade class, loses more than a few hours. Over time, those lost hours add up, and rural pupils risk falling behind their peers in better-equipped schools.

A Phone That Rang Without Answer

FrontPage Africa sought comment from the Bong County Education Officer, David Boakai, on the conditions at both schools and on any plans to address them. Those efforts did not materialize. The Education Officer’s phone rang endlessly without response, and no comment was available at the time of publication.

The silence leaves important questions unanswered. Is the county education office aware of the conditions at Beletanla and Blemeyea? Will more government-assigned teachers be posted to the schools? Are repairs to the roof, the supply of chairs, and the delivery of instructional materials under consideration? Residents and school officials are waiting for answers, and this newspaper remains open to hearing from the county education office.

For the people of Beletanla and Blemeyea, the requests are straightforward. They want a repaired roof, chairs for the students, additional teachers, and materials to support learning. For PTA members who have quietly carried the cost of volunteer teachers, a lasting government solution would bring long-awaited relief.

Until that support arrives, the children of District Two will keep coming to class, and their teachers will keep doing what they can with what they have.

World.title: West Africa Cannot Afford to Fight Jos Leijdekkers One Border at a Time
World.content:
Jos Leijdekkers’ fingerprints are turning up in port after port, patrol after patrol, from Freetown to Tema to a beach in Liberia — not because one fugitive is unusually clever, but because West Africa keeps fighting him one border at a time. Ghana has charged its own customs officers. Liberia’s police chief has named his own officers. Each response has been national, quiet, and separate. None has yet matched the scale of a network that treats the whole coastline as a single market. This editorial argues that unless ECOWAS states build real, shared instruments — intelligence-sharing with teeth, vetted port personnel, extradition that actually works, a joint task force built around networks rather than individual shipments — the region will keep discovering Leijdekkers-style operations one country at a time, always a step behind. The stakes go beyond narcotics: a coastline that cannot secure its ports against traffickers will struggle to secure them against anything else.

ONE MAN’S SHADOW now falls across an entire coastline. From Freetown, where Jos Leijdekkers is reported to be sheltering, to Tema, where his associates allegedly bought their way past a customs scanner, to a Liberian beach where police officers allegedly stood watch over a cocaine landing for $5,000 apiece — the footprints of a single fugitive trafficker keep turning up wherever West Africa’s ports and patrols prove for sale. That is not a coincidence. It is a diagnosis.

WHAT THE DUNKIRK CASE EXPOSED in Ghana, and what Inspector General Gregory Coleman has alleged in Liberia, are not isolated failures of two governments. They are the same failure, wearing two flags. A network built around one man has been able to move tonnes of cocaine through this region not because West African security services lack the will to stop him, but because he has found, again and again, the one official in the one office willing to look away for a price. Every country that has now stumbled onto a piece of his operation — Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone — has treated it as a national embarrassment to be managed quietly, prosecuted separately, and closed. None has yet treated it as what it actually is: evidence of a single, regional criminal architecture that respects no border, because the men running it long ago stopped respecting ours.

THAT HAS TO CHANGE, and it has to change now.

A Threat That Does Not Recognize Borders

LEIJDEKKERS’ NETWORK did not need a visa to move between Sierra Leone, Ghana, and Liberia. It needed a bent scanner operator in one port and a police escort in another. Eastern European operatives tied to his associates have reportedly been slipping into Liberia on Ghanaian passports since at least 2021; one suspect now in Liberian custody was arrested in Accra at Liberia’s own request — and then simply vanished. That single episode is the whole regional problem in miniature: a request for cooperation was honored on paper and defeated in practice, because no mechanism exists to make an arrest in one West African capital actually stick by the time it matters in another.

MEANWHILE THE SEIZURE numbers, taken country by country, look like separate stories: Ghana’s cocaine hidden in gari sacks and container irregularities, Liberia’s $317 million bust in Duazon and its $19 million interception at Roberts International, Sierra Leone’s cocaine-stuffed suitcases out of Freetown, Nigeria’s opioids in bread and speakers, Cabo Verde’s swallowed capsules. Read individually, each is a national success story — an arrest made, a shipment stopped. Read together, across a single June-to-September stretch, they describe a trafficking corridor running the length of the West African coast, probing every port and every patrol for the weakest link. Traffickers already treat this region as one market. It is well past time our governments did too.

What Cooperation Actually Requires

GHANA’S PRESIDENCY has ordered inter-agency investigations and restored its narcotics agency’s mandatory role in screening port cargo. Liberia’s Inspector General has named officers he says took bribes to escort a shipment. These are necessary steps, and each government deserves credit for taking them. But a scanner fixed in Tema and an internal police probe in Monrovia will not stop a network that simply moves its business to the next weak port down the coast. What this moment calls for is not two governments cleaning house separately. It is ECOWAS states finally building the shared instruments they have spent years discussing and never finishing:

A REGIONAL INTELLIGENCE-SHARING arrangement with teeth — not another memorandum of understanding, but a standing mechanism through which a customs flag in Tema, a police tip in Monrovia, and an airport seizure in Praia are treated as one file, not three.

VETTING AND ROTATION of port and customs personnel with regional oversight, so that a scanner operator’s login cannot become, as prosecutors allege happened in Ghana, a key that a trafficking network simply buys.

EXTRADITION AND MUTUAL legal assistance agreements that actually function under pressure — so that an arrest made at a neighbor’s request, as Ghana made of a suspect wanted in Liberia, does not end in a suspect who “reportedly vanished” before he can be handed over.

A JOINT TASK FORCE tracking networks, not just shipments — built to follow people like Leijdekkers and his associates across the borders they cross freely, rather than waiting for each country to rediscover the same names independently.

NONE OF THIS IS EXOTIC. Regional bodies elsewhere have built exactly these tools. What West Africa has lacked is not the blueprint but the political will to treat trafficking as a shared emergency rather than each nation’s private scandal.

The Region’s Future Is What Is Actually at Stake

IT WOULD BE A MISTAKE to see this only as a drug story. Every scanner that gets overridden for cash, every police escort sold for $5,000, is a small transaction that adds up to something much larger: a generation of West African institutions being hollowed out from the inside, one bribed official at a time. Money on this scale does not stop at corrupting a customs post. It buys judges, financiers elections, and arms the same criminal networks it enriches. A region that cannot secure its own ports and highways against traffickers will find it just as hard to secure them against anything else.

JOS LEIJDEKKERS WILL eventually be caught, or he will not; that is, in the end, a matter for Dutch, Sierra Leonean and Interpol investigators. But whether West Africa produces the next Leijdekkers-scale network, and whether it takes years or weeks to unravel next time, is entirely within this region’s own hands. Liberia, Ghana, Sierra Leone and their neighbors have now each been handed unmistakable proof that their ports, their patrols and their own officials are being tested for weaknesses by organized crime on an industrial scale. The only responsible answer is to close that gap together, before the next shipment — and the next bribe — finds it first. The choice in front of West Africa’s governments is not complicated. Cooperate now, or explain later why they didn’t.

World.title: Liberia: Freeman Challenges Liberia’s US$1 Billion Revenue Story, Says US$400M Is Being “Squeezed” From Economy
World.content:
Liberia’s Economist and Politician Mr. Simeon Freeman

MONROVIA — Liberia’s historic crossing of the US$1 billion domestic revenue mark is being celebrated by the government as a major fiscal achievement.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr

Liberia’s economist and politician Simeon Freeman has raised fresh questions over Liberia’s revenue system, claiming that approximately US$400 million is being squeezed out of the local economy through charges that are not reflected in the government’s budgetary revenue figures.

Freeman said the amount includes payments associated with port operations, terminal charges, shipping companies, tracking fees and other costs incurred when goods enter Liberia.

While acknowledging that international trade taxes account for a significant portion of government revenue, he argued that the broader financial burden imposed on importers and consumers extends beyond what appears in the national budget.

“If you put all of that inflow together, you’re talking about US$400 million that is squeezed out of the local economy,” Freeman stated.

Freeman argues that these additional costs ultimately find their way into the prices Liberians pay for goods and services, particularly in an economy heavily dependent on imports. “By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive,” he said, linking the alleged unbudgeted charges to rising consumer prices and declining purchasing power.

“How much money is circulating out of the pockets of Liberian consumers and businesses through charges that do not appear as direct government revenue in the national budget,” he intimated.

In a pointed economic commentary, Freeman challenged the growing celebration around government’s record revenue performance, arguing that the headline figure alone does not tell the full story of Liberia’s economic condition.

His argument is that government can increase revenue while ordinary Liberians simultaneously become poorer in real terms if the cost of raising that revenue is ultimately transferred to consumers through higher prices. “Every aspect of this budget is mopping money from the local economy,” Freeman said.

“By mopping money from the local economy, it makes the cost of goods very expensive.” The comments come days after President Joseph Nyuma Boakai announced that Liberia had raised more than US$1 billion in domestic revenue during the first nine months of 2026.

The President described the achievement as a historic milestone and said the money was mobilized through taxes, duties, fees and other lawful payments from individuals and businesses. He also said the government intends to ensure that the revenue translates into benefits that Liberians can see and feel.

But Freeman’s analysis challenges Liberians to look beyond the revenue headline.

‘The money is coming from somewhere’

Freeman’s argument rests on a basic economic principle: government revenue does not appear in isolation from the economy, he said

Taxes, duties, fees and other government charges are ultimately paid by individuals and businesses. Where businesses incur higher costs, those costs can be passed on to consumers through higher prices. That, Freeman argues, is the part of the US$1 billion story that deserves greater public scrutiny.

“The government gets the money by mopping and squeezing it from the economy,” he said “What that means is, when tuition goes up, it’s not the school that you blame.” For Freeman, the issue is therefore not whether government should collect revenue.

It is whether the country’s revenue system is increasing the productive capacity of the economy or simply extracting more money from an economy whose businesses and households are already under pressure.

Freeman focused particularly on Liberia’s import-dependent economy

He argued that the official tax figures do not necessarily capture the full range of costs associated with moving goods into Liberia.

According to his analysis, importers face customs-related taxes alongside port, terminal, shipping, tracking and other charges.

The economist contends that when those costs accumulate, they eventually become part of the price paid by consumers. “Something costs one dollar in China, very cheap. One dollar in China comes to Liberia and costs about 10, 15 dollars. Now you understand why.”

Freeman’s specific estimate that approximately US$400 million is being removed from the economy through additional charges is still subject to independent verification. But his broader economic argument is more fundamental: the price consumers pay at the end of the supply chain reflects not only the original cost of the product, but also the taxes, fees and other costs accumulated along the way.

The uncomfortable connection between revenue and prices

Freeman linked government revenue collection to the everyday economic struggles facing Liberians. He pointed to rising transportation costs, food prices, rent and education expenses as examples of the pressure households are experiencing.

“When government mop up the money, they spend it on themselves and not necessarily on us,” Freeman argued.

The IMF has reported that Liberia’s recent revenue performance has been supported by stronger income and international trade taxes, among other sources. It has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a prudent fiscal stance and improving the quality of public spending.

Freeman also turned his attention to Liberia’s debt

He argued that a significant portion of the government’s fiscal resources is already committed to servicing debt.

The FY2026 budget and subsequent fiscal planning have indeed placed substantial emphasis on debt management, while the IMF has continued to monitor Liberia’s debt position as part of its economic program.

Freeman’s concern is that Liberia could find itself in a cycle where government collects more revenue, borrows more money to finance development, and then uses an increasing amount of future revenue to service those obligations.

“You have to keep borrowing repeatedly for every major project,” Freeman said. His broader warning is that revenue growth without corresponding growth in production, investment and household incomes may not fundamentally transform the economy.

President Boakai has argued that the billion-dollar milestone must ultimately translate into tangible improvements in the lives of Liberians.

World.title: Liberia, UNDP to Host UN Side Event Linking Climate Change, Conflict and Natural Resources to the Search for Lasting Peace
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia will use the global spotlight of the United Nations General Assembly to make the case that a changing climate and a fragile peace cannot be treated as separate problems. The government, through its Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), will convene a high-level side event on the margins of the Assembly.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The event is titled “The Nexus between Climate, Conflict, and Natural Resources: Pathways to Peace, Resilience, and Sustainable Development.”

It is expected to bring together government leaders, UN officials, climate experts, development partners, civil society groups, academics, and private sector representatives. Participants will explore how climate change, natural resource management, and peacebuilding are increasingly intertwined, and why progress on one often depends on progress on the others.

The gathering comes as Liberia prepares to assume the Presidency of the UN Security Council in December 2026. The timing reflects the country’s growing voice on climate security, environmental governance, conflict prevention, and sustainable development.

At the heart of the discussion is the view that climate change acts as a “threat multiplier,” deepening existing problems such as poverty, inequality, resource scarcity, and weak governance.

In Africa and other climate-vulnerable regions, environmental pressures are intensifying competition over land, water, forests, fisheries, and other natural assets. That competition, in turn, raises the risk of tension within communities and threatens wider stability.

Liberia’s own experience illustrates both the promise and the peril. The country has made significant progress in consolidating peace and strengthening environmental governance. However, it continues to confront serious threats, including coastal erosion, illegal mining, deforestation, and the encroachment of wetlands. Organizers say these pressures show why development in Liberia and elsewhere must be both climate-resilient and sensitive to conflict.

Haoliang Xu, UNDP Associate Administrator, will deliver the keynote remarks. He will be joined by a panel of international and African leaders, policymakers, and climate experts, who will share perspectives on climate security, natural resource governance, climate finance, resilience building, and community-driven solutions.

Discussions will center on five themes: climate change as a threat multiplier; the relationship between natural resources and conflict; climate-related displacement and mobility; governance, institutions, and peacebuilding; and pathways to resilience and lasting peace.

Organizers say the event is designed to produce practical policy recommendations and to strengthen international partnerships. It also aims to attract investment and climate finance and to give local and community voices a stronger role in shaping efforts to build peace and resilience.

The forum will also give Liberia a platform to showcase its work in forest conservation, wetland protection, sustainable natural resource management, and climate policy. At the same time, the country intends to press for increased adaptation financing and stronger support for nations on the frontlines of climate change.

World.title: Kabwe DC concerned over feeder Roads
World.content:
Kabwe District Commissioner Lennox Shimwambwa has expressed concern over the failure by Kabwe Municipal Council to work on feeder roads in the district.

Mr Shimwambwa told the media in an interview that most feeder roads remain in a deplorable state despite the local authority having access to earthmoving equipment and funding for fuel.

He said the district administration was concerned about the slow pace at which the local authority was addressing the poor state of feeder roads.

“It is sad that our feeder roads in Kabwe are still in a bad state despite the Council being empowered with all the necessary earthmoving equipment. Government has gone further to provide funds for fuel for the yellow machines,” Mr Shimwambwa said.

Mr Shimwambwa urged the council to improve its performance and deliver much-needed development for the benefit of residents.

He said Government had invested heavily in earthmoving equipment through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to improve service delivery.

Mr Shimwambwa said the equipment should be used for its intended purpose of improving feeder roads in communities across the district.

Meanwhile, Mr Shimwambwa has assured the people of Kabwe of well-coordinated development initiatives over the next five years.

He said teamwork would be central to development efforts in the district, in line with Government’s devolution agenda.

World.title: Mwansabombwe urged to heighten disease preparedness
World.content:
Acting Mwansabombwe District Commissioner Katele Lengwe has urged members of the District Epidemic Preparedness Committee to remain on high alert to prevent disease outbreaks.

Speaking when he opened the district epidemic preparedness meeting at the council, Mr Lengwe said vigilance was critical following reported cholera outbreaks in some parts of the country.

Mr Lengwe said epidemic preparedness was not the responsibility of the health sector alone, but required concerted efforts from government departments, the local authority, health facilities, traditional and civic leaders, cooperating partners, communities and other stakeholders.

Mr Lengwe said the need for preparedness was heightened by the two cholera cases currently recorded in neighbouring Chiengi District.

Meanwhile, Council Secretary Felix Mwila said Mwansabombwe had not recorded a cholera outbreak in the past three years.

Mr Mwila called for concerted efforts among stakeholders to address water supply, hygiene and sanitation challenges and prevent disease outbreaks.

World.title: Four Miners still trapped 24 days after Chitambo mine collapse
World.content:
Four miners remain trapped underground, 24 days after a mine collapsed on 12 illegal miners in Lusenga Ward of Chitambo District.

Central Province Permanent Secretary Milner Mwanakampwe says efforts to rescue the four miners still trapped in the rubble are continuing.

Dr Mwanakampwe told the media in Kabwe that the Government remains committed to retrieving the miners and expressed hope that they are still alive.

He said the Bimbe Mine collapsed on 12 illegal miners, resulting in four deaths.

He said four bodies have since been recovered, while another four miners were rescued with minor injuries.

Dr Mwanakampwe said the remaining four miners are still unaccounted for, adding that rescue operations are ongoing.

He said the risk of a further collapse remains high, prompting authorities to strengthen security and prevent unauthorised access to the mine.

Dr Mwanakampwe said the mine remains closed, with security personnel continuing to monitor the situation.

World.title: U20 AFCON qualification remains priority – Mutapa
World.content:
Record 12-time champions Zambia sent a strong statement at the TotalEnergies CAF Under-20 AFCON | COSAFA Qualifier, becoming the first team to book a semi-final spot with a ruthless 3-0 win over Comoros.

The Junior Chipolopolo made it two wins from two in Group C, six points, five goals scored, none conceded – and top spot guaranteed with a game to spare.

Tumalo Mununga struck after just 5 minutes, Abel Nyirongo doubled the lead 12 minutes later, and Kayula Chinunda put the game beyond Comoros in the 64th minute.

It followed their 2-0 opening win over Malawi – the only side that could still match them on points but already beaten head-to-head.

Zambia coach Perry Mutapa says qualifying to the Africa Cup remains the main target.

“Our priority remains to qualify for the Africa Cup and then focus on winning the COSAFA qualifier. We will be very happy to qualify for the Africa Cup and to win the COSAFA qualifier,” Mutapa said.

He said winning back-to-back matches at the regional championship has not been easy.

“It has not been easy. In our first game, in the first half we did not coordinate well because for most guys this was the first test for international football. We told them to believe in themselves. This is about the development of players,” Mutapa said.

While Zambia cruised, neighbours Malawi revived their own semi-final dream with an identical 3-0 scoreline over Botswana.

Misheck Billiat (22′), Clever Kalambo (45+3′) and Grant Chibalo (90+3′) kept the Junior Flames alive on three points. They face Comoros on Wednesday while Zambia tackle Botswana.

Defending champions South Africa also stayed perfect. Amajita beat Angola 2-0 in a top-of-Group B clash through Lazola Maku (14′) and in-form Steven Mendes (41′) – his third goal of the tournament after a brace against Lesotho. South Africa have six points, five scored, none conceded.

And in the day’s thriller, Eswatini bounced back from a 4-0 hammering by Angola to edge Lesotho 3-2, captain Njabulo Gama striking a 91st-minute winner.

Gama had opened in the 13th minute, Andiswa Malaza made it 2-1 before halftime, but Lesotho twice levelled through Lekanyane Kalache and Kabelo Tuoane (90′) before Gama’s late dagger. Eswatini now have three points and face South Africa next; Lesotho remain pointless.

The 12-team tournament runs until September 27, with three group winners plus best runner-up going to the semis. The two finalists qualify for TotalEnergies CAF U-20 AFCON Ghana 2027.

World.title: Zambian Diaspora Groups To Protest At UN Over Disputed Election, Killing Of Kafwaya
World.content:
Zambians living in the United States plan to protest outside the United Nations headquarters in New York this week, timed to the UN General Assembly, over what organisers call a stolen general election, the arbitrary arrest of Opposition leaders and the killing of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya.

The demonstrations are planned for Tuesday and Wednesday, as well as the day Zambia is due to address the Assembly. Among those organising the protest is Augustine Mukoka, a Zambian governance activist and communications specialist based in the diaspora.

Speaking on Channel Africa with veteran journalist Peter Ndoro, Mukoka said the demonstrators want the restoration of what they consider a democratically elected government, alleging that the military played a role in altering the outcome of the August 13 election, in which President Hakainde Hichilema was declared winner of a second term.

The European Union’s election observation mission said polling day itself was largely calm and voters had a competitive choice, but it also raised concerns about an uneven playing field and later reported what it described as serious incidents and procedural irregularities during counting and tabulation. Regional and continental observer missions identified areas of concern and called on political actors to pursue any disputes through peaceful, established legal processes.

The activist claimed pockets of violence broke out at some polling stations immediately after voting, which he alleged the ruling party used as a pretext to suspend vote counting. At the point counting was suspended, he said, tallies from individual polling stations showed the Opposition with a wide lead.

He alleged the military was then deployed to those polling stations, after which the numbers began to change once counting resumed. The Electoral Commission of Zambia, he further claimed, did not allow observers at the national totalling centre to verify results against what had been recorded at polling stations, and the figures announced nationally differed from what had been recorded locally.

The most serious of the allegations concerns Kafwaya’s death. Soldiers under Lieutenant General Geoffrey Choongo Zyeele, the Zambia Army Commander, are alleged to have raided the private residence of Brian Mundubile, the Tonse Alliance’s presidential candidate, with Kafwaya killed during that raid.

The government initially denied any abduction or killing had taken place, according to the account given on Channel Africa. It was roughly six days later, after Kafwaya’s widow filed a habeas corpus application in court, that officials confirmed the killing. Authorities then claimed a militia had been operating from Mundubile’s residence, a claim disputed on the programme, which noted that Mundubile himself was released after being detained and questioned during the raid.

Eleven other people who were at the residence were arrested and held in different police stations without access to lawyers, their families not initially informed of their whereabouts. They were later charged with treason and have now been held for roughly 37 days.

Asked why the organisers were protesting abroad rather than relying on Zambia’s courts, Mukoka said legal avenues had been closed off. Soldiers, he alleged, were deployed to the courts on the final day for filing election petitions, the Supreme Court registrar was arrested for opening the court gates, and the court’s online filing system was also taken offline.

Civil society leader Linda Kasonde had emailed a petition directly to the Chief Justice, who referred it to the Constitutional Court, but no action was taken on it, he said. A sitting Member of Parliament and a former Constitutional Court judge had also been arrested after speaking publicly about the post-election situation, and several figures aligned with the Tonse Alliance had had their passports cancelled.

Protesters’ demands include the unconditional release of those detained, and justice for Mundubile and Makebi Zulu. They are also demanding sanctions against Lieutenant General Zyeele and Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya, commander of Zambia’s special forces, along with accountability for Kafwaya’s killing.

The group is further calling for the restoration of passports for a group of Zambians it says have been targeted, including Ambassador Emmanuel Mwamba, Hon Binwell Mpundu, Hon Emmanuel J.J. Banda, Madam Lillian Mutambo and Dr Sishuwa Sishuwa of Stellenbosch University in South Africa.

Hichilema will not travel to New York for the Assembly himself. Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe, recently appointed to the post, will represent him at the UN General Assembly instead, and it is Haimbe who will receive the protesters’ message and carry it into the Assembly on Zambia’s behalf.

World.title: Reject Scheme To Personalise Constitution, Warns Veteran Politician
World.content:
Veteran politician Dr Akashambatwa Mbikusita-Lewanika has warned of an unfolding agenda to consolidate and personalise power through selective constitutional changes. He was commenting on calls by ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) affiliates for further changes to the Constitution focused on the presidential term.

Dr Mbikusita-Lewanika urged Zambians to unite to block any partisan, personalised amendments.

“The UPND agenda is clear. They are completely set to consolidate power by making constitutional changes tilted towards consolidating personalised power,” he said.

He said such amendments were craftily designed, with the real matter of interest wrapped inside progressive-sounding clauses meant to blind unsuspecting citizens.

Dr Mbikusita-Lewanika said the purpose of the mixed-member proportional representation (PR) system was to balance governance by giving voice to less represented or marginalised groups, not to further empower a president who was already advantaged.

“So, the members of the ruling party should not benefit because they are already advantaged,” he said.

He expressed concern that PR appointees, being at the mercy of the authorities who appoint them, were vulnerable to abuse and manipulation in support of selective, personalised bills tilted towards entrenching one leader’s hold on power.

Dr Mbikusita-Lewanika accused the UPND government of turning the Zambian economy into what he termed a user-friendly economy for global capitalism, alleging that most African leaders had been bribed with shares and other business deals.

“Africa’s struggle for independence, introduction of plural politics, power sharing and freedoms have been betrayed,” he said.

He said the State had witnessed growing politicisation of key institutions. “We’ve also seen the politicisation of the police, army, Judiciary and other key institutions, and complete dominance of the local government system and the undermining of professionalism,” Dr Mbikusita-Lewanika said.

“They are creating an environment for single-party dominance and destroying the balance of power between the branches of government.”

He warned that a constitution tailored around individuals and ruling-party interests would undermine democracy and institutional independence. He urged citizens, the Church, civil society and political stakeholders to demand a people-driven, inclusive process for any further constitutional changes.

Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha has previously been quoted on radio as saying any constitutional changes would come from the people.

World.title: Civil Society Warns UPND Against Third-Term Agenda For Hichilema
World.content:
Civil rights activist Brebner Changala and governance campaigner Mulenga Kapwepwe have separately warned the United Party for National Development (UPND) government against entertaining any third-term agenda for President Hakainde Hichilema, saying Zambians will not tolerate it. Both were commenting on increasing calls by UPND members for the Constitution to be amended to give the Head of State a third term of office, or to remove the presidential term limit altogether.

Changala said Zambians would not accept the extension of the constitutional term limit, despite what he called their perceived collective docility. “If there’s something Zambians will not tolerate even in their collective docility, it is a third term. I wish to tell those calling for that to think twice before they create problems for the nation and themselves,” he said.

He warned the ruling party not to be deceived by the public’s wait-and-see reaction to the scheme, and urged citizens not to allow the Constitution to be changed to favour an individual, calling any such move catastrophic for the country’s future.

Changala pointed to the outcome of the last general election as proof that many Zambians did not want the UPND in office, noting that millions of citizens had rallied behind the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) only weeks after it emerged. He said any attempt to abolish the presidential term limit would be met with immediate backlash from Zambians that the Government might struggle to manage.

“The UPND should not take Zambians’ silence after the disputed August 13 general elections for granted,” Changala said.

He said the nation was still groaning from post-election trauma, during which the military was deployed to intimidate citizens and interfere with the management of the electoral process.

“I want to warn this administration that Zambians hate oppression and like their peace. They may not receive this machination with kindness, and that is when the giant will wake up from the slumber,” Changala said.

He added that the ruling party should not assume its numbers in Parliament gave it a free hand. “Let them not believe that they have control over Parliament and can do as they wish. Let them stop it. We now need to be talking about how to reform the compromised Electoral Commission of Zambia, police, Judiciary and the entire civil service,” Changala said.

In a separate interview, Kapwepwe said any change to the Constitution would serve an individual rather than the country, and that the Constitution was a serious document that could only be changed on the basis of facts. She questioned the rush to amend it when the nation still needed to heal from its post-election crisis.

“What is wrong with the Constitution for people to start pushing a narrative that the Constitution should be changed to allow the current Head of State, Hakainde Hichilema, to continue even after his two terms elapse?” she wondered.

“I was part of the constitution-making team, and what I learned from there was that people should not change the Constitution to favour an individual or a group of people but the country at large,” she said.

Kapwepwe dismissed remarks by nominated Member of Parliament Florence Chileshe, who had suggested Mr Hichilema must continue beyond 2031 because women in Zambia do not want democracy but development, which she framed as a personal matter. Kapwepwe said it was clear some people were testing the waters to push an agenda aimed at scrapping the third-term limit.

“It is wrong for Chileshe to say women did not want democracy just because she is in cahoots with the current regime. Chileshe should not say all of us women do not want democracy when some of us have divergent views and would want to defend the Constitution,” she said.

Other prominent UPND members have in recent days called for the removal of the two-term limit to give Mr Hichilema a third term, or for the term limit to be scrapped entirely so he could remain in office for as long as the party wished. Those calls have attracted public backlash.

World.title: Chongwe East MP’s Election Challenged Over Alleged Malpractice
World.content:
Losing United Party for National Development (UPND) parliamentary candidate Sylvia Masebo has told the Lusaka High Court that Anita Kamanga’s election as Chongwe East Member of Parliament was marred by malpractices that swayed voters against her. The claim came in her reply and skeleton arguments, filed in response to answers already submitted by Kamanga and the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). She maintains the August 13 election was not conducted in a free and fair atmosphere, and that she polled 6,798 votes against Kamanga’s 16,058.

The petition accuses Kamanga’s camp of corruption, bribery and name-calling during the campaign. It alleges that Kamanga’s agents disseminated false and defamatory statements about Ms Masebo, prejudicing her candidature and improperly influencing voters. It further claims Kamanga urged voters against her by pointing out that she had lost the UPND adoption process and had only been adopted as a candidate through her standing in the party. On that basis, Ms Masebo wants the election declared null and void and the ECZ directed to re-run the poll.

Kamanga and the ECZ have separately urged the court to dismiss the petition and let the result stand. The commission maintains the poll was free and fair, and that Kamanga was duly elected with her 16,058 votes to Ms Masebo’s 6,798.

“The elections were free and fair and the first respondent was and is the duly elected MP for Chongwe East Constituency,” the commission said.

In her own response, Kamanga denied the allegations outright, saying neither she nor her agents committed, authorised or permitted violence, intimidation, threats or harassment against Ms Masebo or her supporters. She dismissed the bribery and vote-buying claims as vague and fabricated, denying that she ever distributed gifts to induce voters. Kamanga added that she had spent more than five years before the election engaged in charitable and community welfare work in the constituency, through an NGO and with well-wishers.

Ms Masebo was not moved by that account. In her skeleton arguments, she maintained that the election was characterised by malpractices that turned voters against her, and that Kamanga’s campaign breached the Electoral Process Act and the Electoral Code of Conduct. She pointed out that some of the alleged misconduct, including remarks attributed to Kamanga and her campaign manager, Amos Malubila, had already been raised before the ECZ’s own conflict management committee.

Those earlier complaints, she argued, form part of the factual basis of her election petition. She has stood by her position that Kamanga’s election should be nullified and fresh polls held under the ECZ. The matter remains before the Lusaka High Court, one of several constituency results being contested by unsuccessful candidates since the general election, with no date yet set for a ruling.
