"Canada is continuing to remove people to the United States and subject them to detention and deportation," as a result of that agreement, she said.

"We shouldn't have it. It should be suspended in light of what's going on."

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada did not respond to a request for comment prior to publication.

WATCH | Happy to be free, Clayton Herman says after being deported to Canada: Winnipeg-born man back in Canada after months in ICE detention | Duration 1:00 Clayton Herman, a Winnipeg-born Canadian citizen, has been deported back to Canada after spending a total of nine and a half months behind bars in a California ICE detention centre, where he says he endured poor food, mouldy walls and lack of proper medical care.

While Herman is working to put his life together in Canada, he's also dedicating himself to protesting the conditions in ICE facilities.

He's started by writing a 12-page document that details the facility in Adelanto, Calif., where he was held — a for-profit ICE detention centre run by the Geo Group that Herman describes as a "hellhole."

He wants to let the world know what is going on behind its gates, he said.

"I feel sorry for what people are going through down there."

World.title: 'Father of Nunavut' has one more fight left: to live in the territory he helped create
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

John Amagoalik is widely known as the ‘Father of Nunavut,’ but after a lifetime advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination he’s now fighting to age in the territory he helped create. CBC’s Juanita Taylor shares his story and explores how it has ignited a broader conversation about Nunavut’s reliance on southern facilities for elder care.

"I'll never go back," John Amagoalik said of an assisted living facility in Ottawa, where he was sent to live by Nunavut's government in February 2025.

The territory's Department of Health transferred him to Embassy West Senior Living after an infection left no choice but to amputate part of his right leg.

"The worst part was the loneliness," Amagoalik recalled in an interview with CBC News as he sat in a wheelchair at his temporary home in Iqaluit with his wife, Evie, on Sept. 7.

"The strange surroundings. That was the worst part, being so far away from home and not ... being able to be with my many grandchildren."

Amagoalik is turning 79 in November and has multiple chronic age-related issues. He also has a difficult time talking.

He's frail, but he's still a fighter.

Amagoalik, who turns 79 in November, is shown in Iqaluit. The Nunavut government declined his request to provide adequate funding for his care and accessible housing, so he's going to court. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

After a lifetime of struggle that included being forced to attend residential schools and advocating for Inuit rights and self-determination, Amagoalik is in his last fight: to age in the territory he helped create.

"It's been my life," he said, when asked what Nunavut means to him. "And I feel fortunate in being part of it."

'Father of Nunavut'

John Amagoalik is revered as the "Father of Nunavut" for his work spanning over three decades beginning in the 1970s — earning him the Order of Nunavut and the Order of Canada.

John Amagoalik holds a photo of himself attending a meeting of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in Iqaluit in 1983. His work over three decades helped lead to the creation of Nunavut in 1999. (Graham Shishkov/CBC)

Among his many roles, he advocated for Inuit as an adviser with the Tunngavik Federation of Nunavut before it became Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. He was also on the executive council of the Inuit Circumpolar Council in the 1980s, and served as president of what was then the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, now Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami.

Amagoalik led the land claims settlement process with Nunavut Tunngavik after ratification in 1993. He also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission that designed the public government of Nunavut before the territory was created in 1999.

Amagoalik, centre, is shown with Georges Erasmus, left, who at the time was national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, and Indigenous rights advocate Louis Bruyere at a news conference in Ottawa in May 1987. (Chuck Mitchell/The Canadian Press)

It's the very government his Victoria-based lawyer and longtime friend, Steve Kelliher, said is now failing him. So he's helping Amagoalik take the Nunavut government to court.

Kelliher, who first worked with Amagoalik in the 1970s formulating Nunavut's future government, said his friend is still as much a force today as he was back then.

But when he and another friend, Mark Stiles of Ottawa — who first met Amagoalik in 1975 while working in the land claims office of the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada — visited Amagoalik at Embassy West in March, they felt he needed their help.

Victoria-based lawyer Steve Kelliher (pictured) and Mark Stiles, friends of Amagoalik, worked to bring him home to Iqaluit and are trying to secure funding from the government for his care. (Submitted by Steve Kelliher)

"I said, 'Well, how do you like it here, John?' And he said, 'I hate it,'" Kelliher said.

So he asked Amagoalik if he wanted help to return home. "He said, 'Do anything to get me out of here, to get me back to Iqaluit.'"

So they did.

First, they delivered a letter to the territory’s health minister, signed by Amagoalik and dated March 31, pleading to return home. Amagoalik claims he never agreed to the move being permanent.

A copy of Amagoalik's letter delivered to Nunavut's health minister in March. (John Amagoalik)

When the minister, Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster, didn't take any action on his request to return home, they formed the John A. Committee and brought in Iqaluit lawyer Anne Crawford.

The committee raised $30,000 for a consultant to develop Amagoalik's plan of care, buy medical equipment and supplies, and pay for eight to 10 hours of daily private home care from personal support workers.

It also secured an accessible unit at a subsidized rate of $2,000 a month that has space for his hospital bed and an elevator. The Amagoaliks' public housing unit has stairs that would be too difficult for him to use.

The committee also arranged air transportation donated by an airline to fly Amagoalik to Iqaluit. On June 12, 16 months after he arrived in Ottawa, he returned home.

Amagoalik’s public housing unit has stairs, making it difficult for him to access his home. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

An uncertain future

But despite all of the hard work to bring Amagoalik back to Nunavut, his future is still uncertain.

The funds raised by the committee were only meant to be for the short term, and Anne Crawford said the money is running out.

"Which we did tell the government at the time, this will not last forever. And therefore, can you talk to us about how and what we can do going forward to continue to support him and live in his home community?"

Anne Crawford, a longtime lawyer in Iqaluit, says Amagoalik is leading the way for Nunavut elders to be cared for in their communities. (Juanita Taylor/CBC)

The request to the territorial government for $16,000 a month to cover accommodations in the accessible unit and up to 10 hours a day of support worker care was declined. However, the government can provide a maximum of two hours per week of personal support worker care.

The committee says its research shows that Nunavut was spending about $30,000 a month for Amagoalik’s care at Embassy West.

The Health Department told CBC News that it can't comment on his care in order to protect his privacy. Brewster, the health minister, also declined to be interviewed.

But a communications manager provided a written statement saying the government has not refused to provide publicly funded health care to Amagoalik and that it continues to work in "good faith to support him."

Amagoalik and his wife, Evie, embrace. (CBC)

"So we have no alternative but to appeal to the courts to compel them to do the right thing," Kelliher said, calling the situation "despicable."

"If we've got no money, we'll go beat the bushes," he said. Amagoalik "deserves better. He's earned it. He is an exception. Who treats their leaders like that? Not the Inuit. I don't believe it."

Lack of care facilities for seniors

On Sept. 16, two notices of application for judicial review were filed in the Nunavut Court of Justice on behalf of Amagoalik.

"One for judicial review of the assistant deputy minister's letter, the decision not to fund John's care and housing," Kelliher said. "And an application for urgent relief to compel them to do so until the matter is fully heard, which could take months."

Amagoalik's care situation is emblematic of a wider problem in Nunavut. The vast territory, which covers a total area of just over two million square kilometres and is home to roughly 40,000 people, has only six seniors' facilities spread across its three regions.

The government says it's expanding two more long-term care facilities in Nunavut.

Currently, 73 elders from Nunavut are being cared for at Embassy West Senior Living, the only out-of-territory facility contracted by the government for more complex needs.

"We don't want to continue seeing our elders getting flown to Ottawa,” said Gloria Uluqsi, president of Nunavut Tunngavik. "I think they can do better. I think we as a team can do better for our elders."

World.title: This American town runs an annual festival celebrating Canada. It hit different this year
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Full interview with Channon Russette-Mondoux: As It Happens 6:06 This American town runs an annual festival celebrating Canada. It hit different this year

Channon Russette-Mondoux, grew up in Windsor, Ont., married an American and eventually made a home with her family in Kalamazoo, Mich.

But she never lost her connection to Canada — and she’s now turned that tie into an annual celebration.

On Saturday, Russette-Mondoux helped host the fourth annual Can-Am Peace Jam, a festival celebrating Canadian culture and the longstanding ties between the two countries.

That sense of cross-border friendship comes at a time when relations between Canada and the U.S. have been anything but smooth, amid an ongoing trade war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s talk of making Canada the 51st U.S. state.

In Kalamazoo, though, the focus holds onto the hope that Canadians and Americans can still come together.

This year's event featured Canadian and local bands playing hits by artists including Rush, Bryan Adams, Alanis Morissette, Avril Lavigne and Nickelback. There was also a curling demonstration, arts and crafts from local vendors, and a genealogist helping festivalgoers trace their Canadian roots.

Russette-Mondoux spoke with As It Happens host Nil Köksal about why she started the festival, what the Can-Am Peace Jam means to her community and why she believes it’s important to keep it going.

I know this is a labour of love for you but I wonder after all these years whether this year, this weekend, felt different.

Sometimes it's hard. It is hard because I love my homeland so much, which is the impetus for this really, and I think when it gets harder out there, it drives me harder to keep going.

You designed this as a celebration, but I wonder in this moment how people are reacting?

Americans, for the most part, are completely devastated over what is happening with Canada. The average person on the street is mortified to hear the things that are being said, to see the policies that are being enacted.

The festival is absolutely not about politics; it's about people. But I am also involved in my community, and I became a U.S. citizen for the sole purpose of being able to vote, and I am committed, just like I was in Canada. I was committed to my country [and] I'm committed to community here.

Channon Russette-Mondoux is the founder and director of the Can-Am Peace Jam. (Brian K. Powers/Encore Publications)

The name has changed from the Canadiana festival to the Can-Am Peace Jam. You were calling yourself a peace officer. When did you decide to make that change?

We started out as Canadianafest for the first two years, and then in 2025, when there was a lot of rhetoric starting to come out, and I knew the minute I had heard the words — 51st state coming as a joke or [Mark Carney as] the governor of Canada and all that coming out — I knew right away that we were headed for a mess of trouble.

I made a point of it [among] all this chirping going on out there [to say] ‘Let's put that away because what we do is joyful’ regardless of what anyone else says. We're gonna come together, regardless of what anybody else says.’

We called it the Can-Am Peace Jam but what we realized is that the Canadiana Fest became the organization — the celebration of Canadian culture became the organization — and the festival became the Can-Am Peace Jam, because we do things all year round.

We're doing hockey watch parties, poutine parties, Boxing Day parties. We even supported the very first street hockey program in inner-city Kalamazoo.

The festival featured plenty of Canadian favourites, including curling. (Dare'l McMillian)

The vice mayor of Kalamazoo takes part [and] was a judge at the best butter tart contest at the festival. That's one of the things that happened on the weekend. What are some of the other events?

Traditionally, we have a poutine competition called the World Champion Poutine Competition, and we've had six, seven, eight food trucks competing with various kinds of poutine. This year, unfortunately, they had to step back because we had to move the festival indoors after the realization that the storm front that was coming through on Saturday would have just shut us down.

We pivoted and reached out to a community businessman named Harvin Sandhu Singh, who happens to have ties to Canada, and he agreed to let us come into his 30,000 square foot facility in downtown Kalamazoo and use it for our festival, and so we were lucky enough to pull it off.

Do you ever have people who aren't fans of what you're doing and push back at the idea?

You're always going to hear somebody chirping about something, right? I mean, the internet is the internet. I think everybody looks for an opportunity to say something negative about something else. We're not Pollyannas, we know that there are people out there who have drank the Kool-Aid, that totally believe everything that comes out of the administration, and so they have a bee in their bonnet.

They're looking for something to be angry at. Considering the level of messaging that comes out of the White House, I'm shocked it hasn't been more.

I could tell just even from our conversation that this is emotional for you. Like a lot of people, as you said, you have two places that you call home. Does a time like this make you miss Canada more?

Yeah. It's hard sometimes and sometimes you just wanna hear the lilt of a Canadian voice, sometimes you just want to hear that more gentle approach, sometimes you wanna be standing in line and having a conversation, and you can fall into things that you grew up with, things that you're familiar with, and also just the attitude about not being so harsh, and that's what I think is a big difference between Canada and the U.S., is that Canadians are more laid back, but they're also a very fierce people. We're tenacious. We don't give up.

Oh God, I hope this will be over soon.

When this is over, and we will look back, and there've been other times, we've been through similar situations [like] during the depression, there were heavy tariffs put on Canada, [which] actually backfired like it's doing this time.

We have been through tough times in the past, and we can get back to being friends again, but I don't want to let a year go by without celebrating my homeland, and I'm not gonna hide, not gonna run.

World.title: U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.

"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."

Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.

"The United States is working on ​a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash ​from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for ​our Farmers and Ranchers."

Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.

"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.

"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"

Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.

Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.

U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.

"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.

"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”

Potash is currently exempt from U.S. tariffs. Canada exported $4.2 billion of potash to the U.S. in 2025, according to Natural Resources Canada.

Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.

The exterior of the Mosaic potash mine, located near Belle Plaine, Saskatchewan, is shown on July 16, 2025. (Alexander Quon/CBC News)

University of Regina economics professor Jason Childs said exporting potash to the U.S. from Belarus could end up costing more compared to exports from Canada.

"I'm skeptical just because you've got so much more transportation to deal with," Childs said in an interview with CBC.

"Unless you come up with some wonderful deal where Belarus is going to have way lower production costs or something like that, I don't see it being that big a boon for the American farmer."

If Trump does make a deal with Belarus, it could affect the companies in Canada by lowering the overall price of potash, Childs said.

"Right now, Belarus and Russia have not really been active in the North American market. We benefited from that," Childs said.

"If they [enter] the North American market, then we're competing against another supplier and that's going to hurt our costs. That's going to hurt the price we can get for our product."

The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.

"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.

"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."

World.title: 5 MLAs, including former leader, returning to B.C. Conservative caucus as prospect of election looms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is moving to repair ruptures in the Opposition that saw 13 legislators quit caucus or be expelled by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who stepped down on Sunday.

In a statement issued Monday afternoon, Doerkson said the Conservative Caucus of British Columbia had readmitted former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford and MLAs Scott McInnis, Linda Hepner and Claire Rattée.

Rustad says in a statement that his "time as leader is over" but not his service to the province.

The Nechako Lakes MLA also says "high level" unity talks are underway between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party, and rated the chance of success at 95 per cent.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.'s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay's resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad says there is a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were "obviously lots of people" in B.C. who don't know the Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a "quality individual" and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

WATCH | CBC's Justin McElroy looks at B.C. election speculation: Why David Eby is considering a snap election | Duration closed caption 2:37 B.C. Premier David Eby isn’t ruling out a snap election, but why is this suddenly being discussed? And what impact could it have on local elections underway across the province? The CBC's Justin McElroy takes a closer look at how speculation could turn into reality.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to "let politics go."

He said Clark and Campbell were among the "players" trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that "their time is over."

"That may mean time is over for me, too. I don't know," said Rustad. "But I'm not going to be trying to force my will or my vision in terms of what our party was … onto whoever the new leaders are going to be," he said.

"If they want me to be part of that in terms of supporting and building, I will do that. But it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside."

WATCH | Findlay resigns as leader of Conservatives: Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party | Duration closed caption 4:57

Rustad provides timeline

In a statement later Monday that confirmed he had accepted Doerkson's invitation, Rustad said talks between CentreBC and the Conservatives should succeed and the province "cannot afford two opposition parties" with an election looming.

Findlay's resignation followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, including the ejection of Rustad and two others on Friday.

He provided a timeline of the chaos the preceded that moment.

Rustad said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was "emotion and frustration around the table."

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

But on Friday he was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called, less than two years since the 2024 election, intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham won't be running for a sixth term.

B.C. NDP cabinet minister Lana Popham has announced she will not be seeking re-election in the riding of Saanich South. (CBC)

"After 17 years as the MLA for Saanich South, I have made the difficult decision not to seek re-election,” she said in a statement.

The minister of agriculture said her decision not to run again was difficult and sad.

Popham's statement came after NDP MLAs met Sunday night to discuss Findlay's departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

"I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the B.C. Conservatives," the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to "to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team," an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby's former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

WATCH | Speculation intensifies about possibility of snap election: B.C. Conservatives scramble to regroup ahead of possible snap election call | Duration closed caption 2:01 B.C. Conservatives are trying to regroup after another leadership shakeup as speculation grows that Premier David Eby could call a snap election as early as Tuesday.

The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be "election ready."

McInnis releases statement

McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay's leadership.

Unlike other colleagues dissatisfied with Findlay, McInnis did not join CentreBC under their leader Peter Milobar.

McInnis said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return "home" came at a critical time for the province.

He rejected the need for "ideological purity tests" and said the prospect of a provincial election made a united opposition more important than ever.

Scott McInnis, the MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke, is seen in the Legislature building. (Michael McArthur/CBC)

No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a "big tent party," he said.

McInnis said he never lost respect for his Conservative caucus colleagues, with whom he shared a "common belief that British Columbians deserve practical solutions, fiscal responsibility, and a government focused on delivering results."

Turmoil in the Conservative ranks, who have been divided over ideology and direction, birthed the CentreBC party which picked up eight legislators last week, including Milobar.

All are former Conservatives, including seven who quit that party's caucus in recent weeks, while Eleanor Sturko was ejected by Rustad last year.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the B.C. Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

World.title: Peter MacKay: Mark Carney must ignore Trump’s baiting and get back to the table
World.content:
Article content

Curiously no copies of the prime minister’s own book Virtues were in any of the swag bags handed out at the over 80 receptions. Perhaps some made their way to the Toronto International Film Festival that was happening simultaneously. With no ink dry on any new or substantive investment contracts the prime minister quickly jetted off to Strasbourg to address the EU parliament to bask in his Europeaness and explore ways Canada can join the club. Yet questions remain. What is the cost of “associate membership” and our closely guarded sovereignty, resources and culture, allegedly under threat from Washington, which appears to be on the table, if not the menu in Brussels? What are Canadians to make of it all ? It seems in Canada’s case talk is not cheap. Because for all the talk, the price of everything is going up, yet words flow freely.

World.title: Mr. Carney, sell gas to Europe, don’t join EU: Ben Woodfinden
World.content:
Article content

As Woodfinden notes, no one on either side seems entirely sure what it would mean to be an “associate” E.U. member, and that such an arrangement could potentially have implications for Canadian sovereignty. Instead, Woodfinden argues we should build on our existing trade deal with the E.U. and prioritize the development and infrastructure that could facilitate a boost in exports to Europe: energy, pipelines, critical minerals, and greater port capacity.
