World.title: Brugada, Mamdani swap notes on housing, care systems at U20 mayors summit in New York
World.content:
Mexico City’s public care system and Mayor Clara Brugada’s community center initiative won praise from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during the 2026 Urban 20 Mayors Summit (U20), an annual gathering of mayors from major G20 cities and other metropolises around the world.

Speaking alongside Brugada in New York on Sunday, Mamdani said that Mexico City is a city “that many of us look to for inspiration, especially in how we answer the crisis of care in our economies.”

Gracias, @NYCMayor, por reconocer las #UTOPÍAS de la Ciudad de México como un proyecto para garantizar una vida plena. Una visión de ciudad que pone a las personas y a las comunidades al centro. ¡Es un gusto que este proyecto sea inspirador en las grandes ciudades del mundo! pic.twitter.com/gvZzhVLnF2 — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 20, 2026

“When we’re talking about care blocks, we talk about these often within our own administration as an example of what it can look like to deliver for people in our own city,” he said.

Under Brugada’s leadership, the Mexico City government has set up a public care system, a central part of which is the provision of free childcare as well as services aimed at the well-being of seniors and people with disabilities.

Among the government-run centers that offer these services are Unidades de Transformación y Organización para la Inclusión y la Armonía Social (Units of Transformation and Organization for Inclusion and Social Harmony), known as Utopías. These community centers — which also offer cheap meals and a range of recreational, cultural, social and educational facilities — first opened in Iztapalapa when Bruagada was mayor of that Mexico City borough (2018-23) and are now being expanded to other parts of the capital as the city government seeks to offer greater support to primary caregivers, including working mothers.

Brugada is aiming to open 100 new Utopías during her 2024-30 mayorship, while solidifying caregiving as a “public responsibility” rather than a private one.

Mamdani said that “when we talk about Utopías, [there is] the understanding also that we have to be delivering dignity to working people … to ensure they can live lives that are full, lives that are flourishing.”

“And it is such a pleasure to have a fellow mayor here as we do with the mayors of Freetown and Rome who understand that the issues of the working class must be issues at the forefront of our politics,” he said. “And one day I will return to Mexico City, but I don’t know when that is.”

In separate remarks on Sunday, Mamdani said he would like to work with President Claudia Sheinbaum and “any other leaders from across Mexico” to address “global crises.”

“… The crises we face are global crises and that is true for Mexico City, for Rome, for Freetown, for New York City and so many others. And we’ve also watched in admiration of President Sheinbaum’s initiatives and the ways in which she is tackling the same issues of cost of living,” the mayor said.

Brugada draws inspiration from NYC

While Mamdani looks to Mexico City for inspiration, Brugada was herself inspired by New York, a city she said she visited as a young “social activist” in 1987.

In a social media post, the mayor noted that on Monday, she met with Mamdani and “repartidores paisanos” — i.e. Mexicans who work in the Big Apple as deliverymen and deliverywomen for companies such as Uber Eats and DoorDash.

“In Mexico City we will replicate some of New York’s good practices to support those who work in this activity,” Brugada wrote.

She said her government will create “spaces where [repartidores] can rest, recharge their bikes and access bathrooms.”

“We take care of our workers here and there!” Brugada wrote.

En #NuevaYork me reuní con el alcalde @NYCMayor y con repartidores paisanos. Replicaremos en la Ciudad de México algunas de las buenas prácticas de Nueva York para apoyar a quienes se dedican a esta actividad. Como espacios donde puedan descansar, recargar sus bicis y acceso a… pic.twitter.com/NBd5HeccBm — Clara Brugada Molina (@ClaraBrugadaM) September 21, 2026

On Monday morning, the mayor used the New York City Subway to get to her meeting with Mamdani.

“Hello. We’re going on the subway to City Hall where the Mayor Mamdani awaits us,” she said in a video message.

Above the video, Brugada wrote: “On the way to a meeting with the Mayor of New York. We’re continuing the exchange of ideas and experiences about the future of our cities. As in our beloved #CapitalDeLaTransformación [i.e. Mexico City] public transport is what connects and integrates major metropolises … and here we go.”

Brugada: ‘No (affordable) housing, no peace’

During an address at a U20 forum on affordable housing on Sunday, Brugada said that Mexico City would, “of course,” join a global “affordable housing coalition” proposed by Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni.

“I know that many cities present here will [also] join,” she said.

In a video posted to social media, Brugada said that Collboni had made a “very good proposal to build a coalition of cities in favor of affordable housing.”

In the same video, the mayor of Barcelona — a city with serious tourism-related housing problems — said that Mexico City is among the first cities to join “the defense of a fundamental right, as is the right to decent and affordable housing for everyone.”

“This is a fight that all the big cities of the world are in, and I’m very happy that Mexico City together with New York and Toronto … have joined the initiative in order to do big things,” Collboni said.

In her forum address on Sunday, Brugada declared that without affordable housing, there is “no peace,” and spoke about her government’s housing initiatives and the progress made during her mayorship and that of Sheinbaum, who governed Mexico City from December 2018 to June 2023.

“Between 2018 and 2025, nearly half a million people were lifted out of housing poverty in Mexico City. Despite these results, significant challenges remain. As in other cities around the world, the city continues to face a housing shortage, as well as gentrification and the displacement of communities due to speculative dynamics in the real estate market,” she said.

“To address this situation, in Mexico City we have developed the largest housing policy in our history — and one of the policies of greatest reach at an international level as well,” Brugada said.

“The three pillars of this housing policy are firstly, the large-scale construction of social housing; secondly, regulation of the real estate market; and thirdly, we carry this out in partnership with the people through a model of co-management,” she said.

“… We have the goal of building 200,000 … [affordable] homes by 2030,” the mayor said.

“I’m talking about new homes and improved homes. … This means unprecedented progress in reducing the housing shortage,” Brugada said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mass nesting event brings more than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles to Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla
World.content:
More than 100,000 olive ridley sea turtles came ashore at Oaxaca’s Playa Escobilla in a single mass nesting event last week, but the spectacle masks a fragile reproductive outlook: As few as 30% to 40% of the eggs may hatch.

According to the newspaper El Universal Oaxaca, 101,500 females emerged from the Pacific Ocean in Santa María Tonameca last Tuesday in a huge, synchronous nesting event known as an arribada.

The sixth arribada (literally “arrival” in Spanish) of the 2026-27 season lifted the season’s running total to more than 465,000 turtles as of last week, according to the paper.

The olive ridley turtle is among the smallest species of sea turtle in the world. They are found primarily in tropical regions, with a nesting season that generally runs from May through February or March.

Playa Escobilla is among the world’s leading nesting sites for the olive ridley, or Lepidochelys olivacea.

The species is listed as endangered in Mexico and faces risks from egg poaching, fishing, destruction of nesting habitat and climate-related events. Conservation efforts are abundant all over Mexico, and volunteer opportunities are many, as detailed this month in Mexico News Daily.

Despite the current large Escobilla tally, Rafael Villanueva Alcázar of the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas (Conanp) cautions that nesting totals do not guarantee a comparable increase in hatchlings.

“It sounds like a lot,” he said, “but it’s actually very low compared to other beaches that have a higher rate of hatchling production.”

Only about 30% to 40% of Escobilla nests hatch, Villanueva said. By comparison, Playa Ceuta in Sinaloa estimates an 85% hatch rate, but it has only about 500 olive ridley nests per season.

No global hatching rate for sea turtle nests could be found, but one widely cited statistic is that roughly one in every 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings worldwide survives to adulthood.

Rising sand temperatures, changes in sand composition, erosion, strong swells and low humidity are among the factors reducing hatching success. Egg theft and other human-caused damage also take a toll.

Conditions can vary sharply between seasons and sanctuaries.

At Morro Ayuta, another major olive ridley refuge on Oaxaca’s coast, a record 1.9 million olive ridley nests were protected and more than 34 million hatchlings were released into the sea during the 2025-26 season.

Guillermo González Padilla, the head of that turtle camp, said those numbers were “unprecedented” thanks to “the rains, the wetter beaches and the fact that the summer’s temperature [in 2025] was ideal for egg incubation.”

(For this season, Morro Ayuta had counted about 135,000 turtles through the start of its third arribada earlier this month, according to Conanp.)

Meanwhile, at Escobilla, conservation work over the past 35 years has helped. Officials set aside a 5-kilometer protected area for nesting during last week’s arribada, and Conanp is monitoring the nesting grounds along with other federal agencies and local communities.

Local participation is critical because available park rangers alone cannot protect the beach from poachers and other threats. Also, according to EDUCA, a Oaxacan community development NGO, locals help strategically relocate eggs — which average 100 per nest — after arribadas.

With reports from El Universal Oaxaca and MeganoticiasMx

World.title: Aeroméxico investigates possible leak of 15 million passenger records
World.content:
Aeroméxico is investigating a possible leak of customer information after the federal Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance (SABG) identified an online user offering to sell a trove of over 15 million passenger records.

However, Aeroméxico said Sunday that it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information.

🚨Detectan posible exposición de datos personales vinculada a Aeroméxico La Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno identificó indicios de una posible filtración de datos personales en un sistema que podría estar relacionado con Aeroméxico. El hallazgo surgió tras detectar,… pic.twitter.com/iSFbFpKhkx — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 20, 2026

In a statement, Aeroméxico said that “based on the information available,” it hadn’t identified any “exposure” of its customers’ “financial information,” including details of cards used to purchase flights.

The airline also said it hadn’t detected any compromise of customers’ Aeroméxico account passwords, including those used to access the Aeroméxico rewards program.

“Furthermore, this situation has not created any impact on our operations,” Aeroméxico said.

The airline released its statement after SABG said it had detected that a user of the social media and instant messaging platform Telegram was attempting to sell a 1.1 gigabyte database “supposedly attributable” to Aeroméxico and containing more than 15 million passenger records.

“Within the framework of active forensic monitoring of possible security incidents, the Ministry of Anti-Corruption and Good Governance identified signs of a possible exposure of personal data in a system that could be related to Aeroméxico,” the SABG said in a statement.

The ministry said that its monitoring allowed it to locate a Sept. 18 post on Telegram in which “a user offers a database supposedly attributable to Aeroméxico with more than 15 million records,” including — allegedly — the full names of customers of the airline, their e-mail addresses, their telephone numbers and their dates of birth.

The SABG said that it “obtained a sample of 100,092 records” and subsequently identified the names of various people, including those of public servants and public figures.

The ministry said it would “analyze the data obtained” and begin an investigation aimed at determining “the alleged responsibility for the compromised databases.”

Aeroméxico said it would cooperate with federal authorities and report on any relevant developments in a timely manner.

The airline also said it had begun its own “exhaustive investigation” in order to “verify the authenticity and veracity” of the information being offered to “third parties,” determine “its origin” and “establish the reach of any possible impact.”

While the airline said it hadn’t identified any compromise of its customers’ financial information, it advised its customers to stay alert to “unusual e-mails, messages or calls that seek personal or financial information.”

Aeroméxico didn’t say that its systems or databases had been targeted in a cyberattack.

However, hackers have previously targeted both companies and federal and state governments in Mexico. Among the victims of previous cyberattacks are the Ministry of National Defense and state oil company Pemex.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Sheinbaum pledges continued military support as Sinaloa’s cartel turf war shifts to Mazatlán
World.content:
A day after pledging Sunday to keep federal security forces in Sinaloa “as long as necessary,” President Sheinbaum on Monday repeated her conviction that U.S. interference precipitated the cartel turf war plaguing the troubled state. The violence, previously centered in Culiacán and rural areas, has spread south in recent months to the resort city of Mazatlán.

While in Culiacán, the Sinaloa state capital, on Sunday, Sheinbaum said Governor Graciela Domínguez can count on the complete support of the federal government.

Domínguez has been in office for less than a month after being appointed on Aug. 25 to replace Rubén Rocha, who was indicted by U.S. federal prosecutors for alleged links to drug trafficking.

“First and foremost, all federal forces … will remain here for as long as necessary,” she said. “We will not withdraw any element of the Army, the National Guard or the Navy; they will continue to support the governor and, above all, the people of Sinaloa.”

The state has been embroiled in a civil war between factions of the Sinaloa Cartel for two years, becoming what El País newspaper has described as “the biggest political crisis of Sheinbaum’s term.”

As the turf war spread to Mazatlán this summer, the government has deployed thousands of federal troops to the resort city, including 1,000 marines and over 800 Public Security Ministry agents last week. Despite an increase in military presence, homicides in Mazatlán outpaced killings in the larger city of Culiacán in August.

Sinaloa’s economy is facing a historic downturn, driven by severe security challenges and cartel-related violence, leading to a contraction of 4.5% in this year’s first quarter.

On Sunday, Sheinbaum blamed foreign interference for the current situation and then doubled down on that claim during her daily press conference on Monday.

“We don’t want interference from any foreign government in our territory,” she said on Sunday. “Interference generates violence, whereas cooperation for development generates peace.”

Sheinbaum said that before the U.S. “extraction” of drug kingpin Ismael Zambada, the murder rate in Sinaloa was low (“less than one homicide per day,” she claimed). Since then, violence has escalated, producing significant crime rates.

Sunday’s visit was Sheinbaum’s first to the state since the indictments against Rocha and nine other government and law enforcement officials from the state were made public in April.

To address the challenges, Sheinbaum said federal officials would travel in stages to Sinaloa; Security Cabinet officials will visit this week, followed by officials from the Agriculture Ministry.

“There will be no shortage of money to support farmers,” she said, acknowledging that agriculture is the backbone of the state’s economy.

With reports from N+, La Jornada and El País

World.title: After a shootout, authorities rescue 3 kidnapping victims and arrest 7 suspects in Puerto Peñasco
World.content:
Security forces arrested seven people and freed three kidnapping victims during an operation Friday afternoon in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, a popular seaside resort city also known as Rocky Point.

Authorities also seized an arsenal that included more than 40 long guns, approximately 4,000 rounds of ammunition, two Minimi machine guns and a Browning M2 .50 caliber gun, the federal Security Cabinet announced on Monday.

En Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, trabajos de investigación de @fgjesonora, con información del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia de @SSPCMexico @Defensamx1, @SEMAR_mx y @Amicsonora.

En una operación encabezada por @Defensamx1 y @Amicsonora permitieron ubicar un inmueble relacionado con… pic.twitter.com/dtwS2fGtft — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) September 21, 2026

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that three federal agencies and the military joined an investigation by the Sonora Attorney General’s Office (FGJES), supplying intelligence that allowed state officials to identify a property linked to the kidnappings.

As state police and soldiers approached the premises, armed civilians opened fire. The authorities returned fire, eventually outflanking the suspects and containing them.

Three Sonora Investigative Police agents were wounded in the confrontation, none seriously, and three kidnapping victims were freed. Authorities captured seven suspects, including one minor.

The suspects will face charges for attempted aggravated homicide, crimes against public servants, aggravated vehicle theft, criminal association and kidnapping.

After the shootout, the authorities obtained a search warrant and re-entered the property, confiscating the weapons. The search also turned up evidence that was sufficient to merit another warrant that led to two weekend raids on additional properties in downtown Puerto Peñasco.

The sweep of those locations resulted in the seizure of heroin, methamphetamine, loaded magazines, bullet-proof vests, tactical gear and three high-end vehicles which had been reported stolen in the United States.

“We extend special recognition to the three AMIC [the Criminal Investigation Agency] agents who were injured during the attack,” García Harfuch said in a social media post.

A FGJES press release indicated that one of its agents was shot in a lower extremity, while two female agents suffered shrapnel wounds. All three were reported to be in stable condition.

The skirmish came about after several miners reported to police that they had escaped a kidnapping attempt last week, but others hadn’t. State officials alerted federal agencies, who were able to follow the route of the captors and locate a white Chevrolet Suburban truck that had been described by the near-victims.

With reports from La Jornada, Sonora Presente and Eje Central

World.title: Hurricane Polo expected to reach Category 5 as it nears Mexico’s Pacific coast
World.content:
Listen to this article

Hurricane Polo is expected to quickly intensify after forming Monday morning in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Guerrero, with Civil Protection encouraging residents of several states to remain vigilant and follow safety recommendations.

Polo could bring heavy rain, rough surf and tropical-storm-force winds to parts of Mexico this week as it intensifies into a Category 5 hurricane near the coast of Michoacán by Wednesday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center warned.

⚠️ #Polo ahora como #Huracán categoría 1 ⚠️ ◾️Se localiza a 305 km al sur-suroeste de Zihuatanejo, #Guerrero, y a 435 km al sur-sureste de Manzanillo, #Colima

◾️Su circulación refuerza la psibabilidad de #Lluvias de distintas intensidades en Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero… pic.twitter.com/3RRiy2j0PQ — Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil (@CNPC_MX) September 21, 2026

It was centered about 410 kilometers south-southeast of Manzanillo, Mexico, and 322 kilometers southwest of Zihuatanejo at 9 a.m. CST on Monday. As of 12 p.m., it was a Category 1 storm with maximum sustained winds of 129 kph (80 mph).

Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) predicted Monday that Polo would bring heavy rainfall to Pacific coastal regions, potentially raising river and stream levels, triggering flooding and mudslides.

Intense rain is expected over the coming days in the states of Oaxaca and Guerrero (75 to 150 millimeters), very heavy rainfall (50 to 75 mm) in Michoacán, and heavy rainfall (25 to 50 mm) in coastal Jalisco and Colima.

Winds of 10 to 20 kph, with gusts of 30 to 50 kph, can also be expected along the coasts of Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Oaxaca. In addition, the storm will bring waves of 1 to 3 meters to Guerrero, Michoacán, Oaxaca, Jalisco and Colima.

Officials urged the public to remain attentive to the warnings issued by Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) and to follow the recommendations of Civil Protection.

The SMN and the U.S. National Hurricane Center established a watch zone from Tecpan de Galeana, Guerrero, to Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, warning that Polo’s trajectory will be “erratic.” It is expected to curve and move parallel to the coasts of Colima, Michoacán and Guerrero.

Farther west in the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Odalys is forecast to become a hurricane by mid-week. It was located over 2,000 kilometers west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula on Monday morning.

In September 2024, Hurricane John hit coastal Guerrero as a Category 3 storm, just one year after Category 5 Hurricane Otis devastated Acapulco, one of Mexico’s main tourist destinations with a population of over one million people, from which it is still recovering.

With reports from AP News

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Airport road update and Line 5’s environmental cost
World.content:
This week, we have an update on construction of the Guadalajara International Airport’s second entrance and how the buildout of bus rapid transit (Line 5) along the Chapala highway has affected the local environment.

Airport’s 2nd entrance road now expected to open by March 2027

The project to add a second airport entrance kicked off in earnest 13 months ago. It aimed to ease chronic traffic bottlenecks along the Chapala highway, where airport travelers, daily commuters and commercial trucks all battle for scarce road space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gobierno de Jalisco (@gobjalisco)

In summer 2025, public officials promised the work would be finished in time for the FIFA World Cup earlier this summer, but that deadline came and went. Then work was suspended to prevent construction delays around the airport during the tournament.

Now that work has resumed, we have an updated timeline for completion. Earlier this month, Jalisco Gov. Pablo Lemus Navarro declared the airport’s new 6-kilometer entrance road should be ready for its debut by March 2027.

“The Guadalajara Airport will have a second entrance; it will no longer only be possible to enter via the Chapala Highway,” he told local newspaper El Informador. “This is good news for connectivity and mobility from the airport.”

The new road will connect Adolf Horn Avenue with the airport’s south side. For southbound drivers coming from areas like Tlajomulco, Tlaquepaque and Zapopan, the road will allow them to bypass the initial segment of the Chapala highway. It will also alleviate northbound traffic congestion on the Chapala highway by diverting drivers to Adolfo Horn.

Additional airport upgrades

In addition to a second airport access road, the project includes an internal interchange and new roads to connect to the airport’s future Terminal 2.

But that is not all. The final phase of work to modernize the Chapala highway also got started this month. This project involves new pedestrian bridges, public transport stations, storm drainage, sidewalks, streetlights, bike lanes and replacement trees (more on that below).

These improvements are expected to take eight months to complete, with final delivery by May 2027.

Airport access improvements are being jointly funded by the Jalisco state government and airport operator Pacific Airport Group (GAP). Guadalajara International Airport is the third busiest in Mexico, with annual passenger traffic of nearly 18.8 million in 2025.

The high environmental cost of the city’s new Line 5 mass transit system

The extension of public transit to the Guadalajara airport was constructed in a rush ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. This new link to Guadalajara’s mass transit system was dubbed Line 5, even though it’s not a light rail system like Lines 1 through 4.

The impetus behind the new Line 5 was not visionary public planning but a FIFA requirement for all host cities, which mandated that tournament visitors have a public transport option from the airport to the soccer stadium. Chronic traffic bottlenecks along the Chapala highway, the sole access point to Guadalajara airport, also threatened to embarrass public officials on the world stage, something they were desperate to avoid.

Line 5 was completed in time for June’s World Cup matches. While some lamented the lack of rail service on this congested route, the project was widely hailed as a success.

The part that’s received far less attention is the environmental cost of this new infrastructure. Below is a look at that scorecard.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pablo Lemus Navarro (@pablolemusn)

Constructing six new BRT stations over a 22.5-kilometer stretch of the Chapala highway involved the elimination of 1,541 trees along the route, according to the Ministry of Environment and Territorial Development.

All the trees cut were located in the El Salto and Tlajomulco municipalities, with authorization granted by local officials.

Tree cover loss and its effects

An environmental impact assessment completed ahead of Line 5’s construction identified 32 tree species (97% of which were deemed healthy), 133 bird species and six reptile species inhabiting the wooded areas in its path. The trees were removed anyway, with subsequent plans to add 2,846 new trees.

How has the sudden removal of so much tree cover impacted the urban area?

Dr. Lucila Méndez Morán of the Department of Applied Ecology at Centro Universitario de Ciencias Biológicas y Agropecuarias (CUCBA) explained that deforestation on the city’s south side tied to Line 5 has intensified the “urban heat island” effect already afflicting this part of the metropolitan area.

The loss of vegetation and shade not only elevates local temperatures but also reduces the area’s ability to absorb water during the rainy season, dampen noise and flush air pollutants. The state has said that while the short-term environmental impact of Line 5 is negative, the landscape should improve over the medium term.

Despite more trees being replanted than removed, it’s not a net benefit, ecologically speaking. The amount of oxygen generated by small tree saplings is a fraction of what’s generated by mature trees. Until those trees grow to maturity over the coming decade or more, their loss will be acutely felt.

Line 5 construction compounds legacy environmental issues

Massive tree loss in Tlajomulco and El Salto is especially painful due to a well-documented environmental crisis that predates the construction of Line 5.

Uncontrolled real estate expansion on the city’s south side in recent decades has already stripped much of the forest cover, raising local temperatures by 2 degrees to 3 degrees Celsius relative to other parts of the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (GMA). Besides Tlajomulco and El Salto, this area also includes popular tourist destinations Tlaquepaque and Tonalá.

In addition, this zone suffers severe air pollution tied to chronic heavy traffic, under-regulated industrial emissions and thermal inversions in wintertime.

Going forward, this poses a risk of worse public health outcomes due to poor air quality and even hotter temperatures.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Panama Canal Investment Plan: US$8.5 Billion Pitched in New York
World.content:
Panama · Infrastructure

Key Facts — What happened President José Raúl Mulino pitched a US$8.5 billion canal plan to Citi and 26 investors in New York on 21 September 2026.

— What is in it New port terminals, a logistics corridor and the Río Indio reservoir; the canal authority’s presentation also included a gas pipeline.

— Who presented the projects Ilya Espino de Marotta, who became the canal’s first woman administrator on 7 September 2026.

— What Citi said Jane Fraser offered financing and investor links, but urged Panama to keep its investment-grade credit rating.

— The catch No breakdown of the US$8.5 billion was reported, and no concession holder has yet been chosen for the ports or the pipeline.

— Why it matters The projects aim to secure the canal’s water supply and turn it into a logistics and energy hub that earns more.

Panama’s president took the canal’s investment plan to Citi and a room of investors. The bank offered help, and a warning about the country’s credit rating.

File photograph of the Gatún locks on the Atlantic side of the Panama Canal, with ships waiting in Gatún Lake. (Photo: “Gatun Locks 03 2014 Panama Canal 7820” by Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Panama took its Panama Canal investment plan to New York’s bankers on Monday. President José Raúl Mulino presented US$8.5 billion of canal-linked projects to investors in New York on 21 September 2026.

The audience was Jane Fraser, chief executive of the American bank Citi, and 26 investors gathered by the bank. The plan covers new ports, a logistics corridor and a reservoir meant to keep ships and taps supplied.

Mulino is in New York for the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly. He is combining the diplomacy with a run of meetings with banks and multinationals.

What was on the table

The canal, Mulino told the room, remains “the backbone” of Panama’s logistics sector. He described an investment plan of US$8.5 billion “for the coming years”, according to the presidency’s account.

He named three pieces: the Río Indio reservoir, new port terminals and an intermodal logistics corridor. The presidency’s summary of the canal presentation also lists a gas pipeline.

That presentation was given by Ilya Espino de Marotta, head of the Panama Canal Authority, the state body that runs the waterway. She took office on 7 September 2026 as the first woman to lead the canal.

Espino de Marotta joined the canal in 1985 as a marine engineer and was deputy administrator from 2020. Her term runs to 2033, according to the authority.

Two ports and a pipeline

The two ports are container transhipment terminals: Corozal on the Pacific side and Telfers on the Atlantic side. The canal authority estimates their cost at 2.6 billion balboas (about US$2.6 billion).

The balboa, Panama’s official unit, is fixed at a rate of 1 to the US dollar, a parity in force since 1904. The dollar itself circulates as everyday money.

The authority says the terminals would add 5 million to 6 million TEU (twenty-foot container units) a year. Construction would take about three years once a concession holder is chosen.

The pipeline, which the authority calls an energy corridor, would run about 76 kilometres between the two oceans. It would carry propane, butane and ethane, up to 2.5 million barrels a day.

Its selling point is that the gas would cross Panama without using the locks. That saves fresh water, the canal’s scarcest resource in dry years.

Both schemes are being tendered as concessions to private operators. The authority stopped taking prequalification documents for the ports on 9 July 2026 and for the pipeline on 23 July 2026.

File photograph of Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Water first: the Río Indio lake

The main piece the authority will build itself is Río Indio, a dam and lake west of the canal. The authority says it will store 1,294 million cubic metres of water.

The canal authority says the lake would secure water for more than half of Panama’s population for 50 years. Works are expected to run from 2027 to 2031, after a design-and-build tender.

The authority’s budget for the year from October 2026 foresees the first resettlements of families in the river basin. It also schedules the tender for the dam.

In September 2025 the authority put its ten-year strategic programme at more than 8 billion balboas (about US$8 billion). The US$8.5 billion Mulino cited in New York fits within that programme.

Citi’s offer and its warning

Fraser told the Panamanian delegation, “We are here to support Panama,” according to the presidency. She offered financing capacity, access to international markets and links to institutional investors.

She also advised Panama to keep its investment-grade credit rating. Global financing programmes, she warned, will be “increasingly selective”.

Mulino, for his part, told the investors the economy grew 5.5% in the first half of 2026.

“We are going at a very good pace,” Mulino said. “We expect to exceed the IMF’s growth projections for this year of 3.8%.”

The 3.8% is the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) forecast for Panama this year.

A wider sales pitch

The Panama Canal investment plan was one item on a longer list. He also promoted a railway to David, a city in western Panama, a third metro line and a project by Petroterminal de Panamá, a pipeline operator.

He added power links with Colombia and Ecuador and a multipurpose pier at Puerto Armuelles, on the Pacific coast near Costa Rica. Wider motorways run by the state road company ENA were also on the list.

Also on Monday he addressed executives gathered by the Council of the Americas, a New York business association. Google, Apple, Intel, Ericsson, Mitsubishi, PepsiCo and Pfizer were among the companies represented, the presidency said.

“I invite American business to take part in these projects,” Mulino told them, pointing to roads, hospitals and bridges. He was joined by Felipe Chapman, the economy minister, and José Ramón Icaza, the minister for canal affairs.

What comes next

For investors, the next signal is the canal authority’s list of prequalified bidders for the ports and the pipeline. The authority has said it will publish those lists once its evaluation ends.

For Panamanians, the test is Río Indio, where resettlement and compensation must come before any concrete. The Panama Canal investment story will be judged there as much as in New York.

More: Panama coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mulino present in New York?

On 21 September 2026 President José Raúl Mulino presented a canal-linked investment plan worth US$8.5 billion. His audience was Citi’s chief executive, Jane Fraser, and 26 investors. The canal administrator, Ilya Espino de Marotta, outlined two container ports, a gas pipeline, a logistics corridor and the Río Indio reservoir. Mulino also promoted railway, metro, energy and road projects outside the canal.

Which ports are planned?

The Panama Canal Authority is tendering two container transhipment terminals: Corozal on the Pacific side and Telfers on the Atlantic side. It estimates their cost at 2.6 billion balboas (about US$2.6 billion). The authority says they would add 5 million to 6 million TEU (twenty-foot equivalent units) of annual transhipment capacity. The deadline for prequalification documents closed on 9 July 2026.

What is the Río Indio project?

It is a planned dam and lake west of the canal that would store 1,294 million cubic metres of water. The canal authority says it would supply more than half of Panama’s population and support canal operations for 50 years. Works are expected from 2027 to 2031, with resettlement of affected families starting first.

Why did Citi mention Panama’s credit rating?

Jane Fraser offered Citi’s financing and investor network for the projects. She also urged Panama to keep its investment-grade rating, warning that global financing programmes will be increasingly selective. An investment-grade rating lets a government and its agencies borrow more cheaply from large institutional investors.

World.title: Uruguay: National Party Adviser Sentenced for Laundering Drug Money
World.content:
Uruguay · Politics

Key Facts — What happened Pablo Leiva, adviser to a National Party councillor in Montevideo, was sentenced on 18 September 2026 to 30 months for money laundering.

— The drug case Police seized about 265 kilograms of cocaine and cocaine paste in Operation Trazador, valued at almost US$2 million.

— The political response The governing Frente Amplio warned on 21 September 2026 of a “permanent risk” of organised-crime money entering politics.

— What the opposition says National Party chairman Álvaro Delgado said the party’s leadership knew nothing of the adviser’s activities.

— The catch Only three people have been convicted. No charge against any politician, or against the adviser’s son, has been reported.

— What comes next Frente Amplio lawmakers and councillors will meet so the party leadership can decide its next political steps.

A paid aide to an opposition councillor in Montevideo is going to prison after a big drug seizure. Uruguay’s governing left now says organised-crime money is a standing threat to its politics.

A National Party adviser in Montevideo is going to prison for laundering drug money. The case has handed Uruguay’s governing left a fresh argument about organised crime and political funding.

Pablo Leiva, 48, was a paid aide to Gonzalo Gómez, a member of the opposition National Party on Montevideo’s departmental council, the city’s local legislature. He was sentenced on Friday 18 September 2026.

On Monday 21 September 2026, the governing Frente Amplio (Broad Front) coalition warned of a “permanent risk” of criminal money penetrating politics. It said it would weigh further action.

The seizure behind the case

The case began with Operation Trazador, a police investigation into a drug gang in Montevideo. Officers raided three properties in the Brazo Oriental and Pérez Castellanos districts.

The Interior Ministry said police seized 141.6 kilograms of cocaine paste and 124.2 kilograms of cocaine. The ministry valued the haul at almost US$2 million.

Cocaine paste, known locally as pasta base, is a cheap smokable form of the drug. Interior Minister Carlos Negro said the load was probably meant for Uruguay’s own streets.

Police also seized more than 3 million pesos (about US$74,600 at 40.20 pesos per dollar) and US$42,564 in cash. Five vehicles and two pistols were taken, and three men and a woman were detained.

Three convictions under plea deals

The Fiscalía General de la Nación, Uruguay’s national prosecution service, announced three convictions on 18 September 2026. All came through abbreviated plea agreements with its specialist narcotics prosecutor in Montevideo.

The gang’s leader received six years and six months for drug trafficking, arms trafficking, handling stolen goods and money laundering. His partner received three years for assisting drug trafficking.

The third defendant, whom the prosecutors did not name, received two years and six months. The charges were money laundering by possession and internal trafficking of ammunition.

The newspapers la diaria and Caras y Caretas identified that defendant as Pablo Leiva. Caras y Caretas reported that council records put his salary at 52,000 pesos (about US$1,290).

Avenida 18 de Julio in central Montevideo, file photograph from 2021. Photo: Intendencia de Montevideo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A councillor’s aide and his son

Gómez sits on the National Party’s governing board as a youth representative. He belongs to List 250, a faction led by Jorge Gandini.

Gandini is a former senator. He now holds the opposition’s seat on the board of the National Ports Administration (ANP), the state port authority.

Leiva’s son, Lucio, also worked for Gómez and heads the party’s Montevideo youth wing. He was detained in the raids, then released without charge.

Gómez, who was in China for a seminar, dismissed the father on social media on 18 September 2026. “Esta situación me tomó completamente por sorpresa,” he wrote, meaning the situation took him completely by surprise.

He said he accepted responsibility for not being careful enough when he hired Leiva. He apologised to the party and kept the son, whom he called a trusted friend.

Gómez said Leiva had joined his team “recently”. La diaria, citing a public records request, reported that Leiva started in December 2025.

What the Frente Amplio said

The Frente Amplio is the centre-left coalition of President Yamandú Orsi. Its executive secretariat adopted a written resolution on 21 September 2026, which the newspaper El Observador obtained.

The resolution spoke of alarms over party funding and a “permanent risk” from organised-crime money. It said the party would take steps to learn the full scope of the facts.

It also cited party-financing regulation as the kind of initiative it wants. The coalition will convene its Montevideo councillors and national legislators, and its political leadership will then decide on action.

The resolution also referred to the business used for the laundering transactions. It said the business “could” reportedly be among the declared assets of an unnamed senior figure from the same party.

Fernando Pereira, the Frente Amplio’s president, told El Observador that such cases “no longer seem isolated”. He said the party should study how to shield parties from organised-crime financing.

Gandini and the payment agency

On Monday 21 September 2026, Gandini gave a television interview about a dispute at the port of Montevideo. At the end, he was asked about the adviser’s case.

He said he could not talk about politics. “Que no tengo nada que ver, además,” he added, meaning he had nothing to do with it anyway.

Late that night, la diaria reported that police are examining a payment and exchange agency in Villa Española, a Montevideo district. Gandini’s wife, Laura Scalabrino, reportedly bought the exchange business about a year ago.

According to la diaria, Leiva lived nearby and often used the agency. He went there to pay a construction company’s contributions to the BPS, Uruguay’s state social-security agency.

Neither Gandini nor Scalabrino has been charged, and no court or prosecutor has found any wrongdoing by either. Caras y Caretas reported that their defence scheduled a press conference for Tuesday 22 September 2026.

How the National Party responded

Álvaro Delgado, chairman of the National Party’s board and its 2024 presidential candidate, told the TV news programme Telenoche the party was following the case closely. He said the case causes concern.

Delgado said the board had known nothing of the aide’s activities. He urged care in hiring political advisers.

Senator Sebastián Da Silva of the National Party called it “a serious case” in an interview. He said traffickers “slip in” to parties now and then, and that Gómez’s trust had been abused.

Why the left is pressing the point

The National Party, also called the Blancos, is Uruguay’s largest opposition party. Frente Amplio senators have seized on the case.

Senator Sebastián Sabini asked Blanco leaders for a “mea culpa”. He recalled that National Party senator Sergio Botana had called the Frente Amplio a “narco party”.

Senator Eduardo Brenta urged the Jutep, Uruguay’s public ethics and transparency board, to open its own inquiry. No review by the board has been reported.

For now, the only people found guilty are the three defendants in the drug case. What the National Party adviser’s conviction means for party funding rules is a question for Parliament.

More: Uruguay coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the National Party adviser convicted in Uruguay?

Local newspapers identified him as Pablo Leiva, 48, a paid aide to Montevideo councillor Gonzalo Gómez of the National Party. On 18 September 2026 prosecutors announced his sentence: two years and six months for money laundering and ammunition trafficking. Gómez dismissed him the same day.

What is Operation Trazador?

It is a police and prosecution investigation into a drug gang in Montevideo. Police seized about 265 kilograms of cocaine and cocaine paste, cash, vehicles and weapons. Three people, including the gang’s leader, were convicted under plea agreements.

What did the Frente Amplio decide?

Its executive secretariat warned on 21 September 2026 of a “permanent risk” of organised-crime money entering politics. It will meet its councillors and legislators, and its leadership will then decide what political action to take. It has cited party-financing rules as one area for initiatives.

Has any politician been charged?

No charge against any politician has been reported. The councillor’s other aide, the convicted man’s son, was released without charge. National Party chairman Álvaro Delgado said the party’s leadership had known nothing of the aide’s activities.

World.title: Guyana Deportee Deal With US: Ex-President Ramotar Wants It Published
World.content:
Guyana · Migration

Key Facts — What happened Former president Donald Ramotar said on 20 September 2026 that Guyana’s third-country deportee agreement with the United States should be published.

— The money A US official told Kaieteur News that Washington provided US$7,740,215 for the programme, run by the UN migration agency.

— Who has come so far Six people, four Cubans and two Afghans, landed on 4 September 2026. The government says none has a criminal record.

— What Georgetown says President Irfaan Ali says Guyana vets every case and can refuse anyone Washington proposes.

— The catch The deal’s text is unpublished, the US$7.7 million figure comes from an unnamed US official, and no cost breakdown is public.

— The bigger picture Forbidden Stories counts at least 25,447 people sent by the US to third countries through 31 August 2026.

Guyana’s government says it keeps a veto over every person the United States sends. Its critics, among them a former head of state, want to read the agreement.

Guyana Deportee Deal With US: Ex-President Ramotar Wants It Published

A former president wants the Guyana deportee deal published, the pact under which Guyana takes people expelled by the United States. Donald Ramotar made the call on the SOURCES talk show on Sunday 20 September 2026, News Source Guyana reported.

His demand follows the first price tag attached to the arrangement. A US official told Kaieteur News, a Georgetown daily, that Washington had provided US$7,740,215 for it.

Guyana is a country of about 800,000 people on South America’s northern coast, now growing fast on offshore energy revenue. Opposition parties, a rights group and Ramotar himself have criticised its hosting of other nations’ deportees.

What Ramotar said

Ramotar led Guyana from 2011 to 2015 for the People’s Progressive Party/Civic, the party that governs today. He called the arrangement an attempt to “re-colonize” Latin American and Caribbean countries.

He said he was sure the deal was “forced on all the countries” that accepted it, not only on Guyana. “Despite what Governments might say,” he added.

He had already criticised the programme in a letter earlier in September, Kaieteur News reported.

He also rejected the official argument that Guyana might gain skilled people. He pointed instead to Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state.

“Rubio is telling us the types of skills he is sending,” Ramotar said, listing “pedophiles, rapists, child molesters”. Rubio has said Washington wants to send “some of the most despicable human beings” abroad, as quoted by Kaieteur News.

Ramotar said Guyana should refuse anyone Washington rejects, “except if they are Guyanese nationals”. Robert Persaud, the foreign ministry’s top civil servant, has said all six people sent so far had no criminal histories.

The US$7.7 million

Kaieteur News reported the figure on 18 September 2026, citing a US official. The State Department money covers financial and technical support over two years.

It is handled directly by the International Organization for Migration, the United Nations agency that runs the scheme on the ground. The agency offers counselling on returning home.

Those who choose to return receive temporary accommodation, food, clothing and household items. No member of the government has published a detailed breakdown of costs, the newspaper reported.

A government statement on 5 September 2026 said Guyana would not bear the programme’s cost. The United States would bear the full cost of relocation, it said.

The sum puts the Guyana deportee deal in line with other small-state agreements. Palau agreed in December 2025 to take up to 75 people for US$7.5 million, according to Forbidden Stories, a Paris-based journalism nonprofit.

What the government says it signed

President Irfaan Ali told a news conference on Monday 14 September 2026 that Guyana’s participation depends on US financial and technical support. “It must be a joint effort,” he said.

Ali said only third-country nationals, citizens of neither Guyana nor the US, qualify. They need expedited or final removal orders and US medical clearance. Unaccompanied children, Guyanese nationals, pending US asylum seekers and people with known violent records are excluded.

“The government of Guyana retains complete discretion to approve or deny individuals proposed for removal,” Ali said. The United States must supply criminal and health histories, and Guyana then runs its own checks.

Official statements on 5 September 2026 described a temporary one-year framework, not permanent resettlement. A source told the outlet Demerara Waves that up to 12 people could arrive each month.

Six people have come so far, four Cubans and two Afghans, who landed on Friday 4 September 2026. Persaud said Washington had made no further requests.

Who else wants the text

The Guyana Human Rights Association says the arrangement may breach Article 141(1) of the constitution, which bans inhuman or degrading treatment. It argues that protection covers every person in Guyana, not only citizens.

Amanza Walton, an MP who leads the opposition Forward Guyana Movement, said the government negotiated for months without telling parliament. She noted that Guyana has no national asylum law and has not joined the 1951 Refugee Convention.

Christopher Ram, a chartered accountant and frequent government critic, asked what Guyana gains. He wondered whether it was “goodwill, strategic credit or insurance against Venezuela”, which claims about two-thirds of Guyana’s territory.

No court has ruled on the rights group’s constitutional argument. No release of the agreement’s text has been reported.

A much bigger American programme

Guyana’s share is small next to the global numbers. Forbidden Stories counts at least 25,447 people the United States sent to third countries through 31 August 2026.

About 20,000 of them went to Mexico, The Tico Times reported from the investigation. At least 35 countries have agreed to take such deportees, and at least 28 have received some.

The investigation, published on 21 September 2026 with partners including The Washington Post and The Guardian, examined a State Department office. Internal documents showed its Office of Remigration planned to spend at least US$410 million on the deals.

Of that sum, about US$81 million was meant for governments and more than US$178 million for the International Organization for Migration. The rest was largely earmarked for the UN refugee agency.

As with most of the money Forbidden Stories tracked, Guyana’s funds go through the migration agency rather than directly to the government.

More: Guyana coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Guyana deportee deal?

It is a migration cooperation framework between Guyana and the United States, announced on 5 September 2026. Guyana temporarily hosts people the United States is removing who are citizens of other countries. They wait in Guyana while their immigration status is resolved, then return home or move elsewhere. The International Organization for Migration runs the programme on the ground.

How much is the United States paying?

A US official told Kaieteur News that the State Department provided US$7,740,215 for financial and technical support over two years. The money is handled by the International Organization for Migration, not paid as a lump sum to the government. The Guyanese government says it bears none of the cost.

Who has been sent to Guyana so far?

Six people, four Cubans and two Afghans, arrived on 4 September 2026. Robert Persaud, the foreign ministry’s top civil servant, said background checks showed none had a criminal history. He said Washington had made no further requests for transfers.

Why do critics want the agreement published?

Opposition politicians, the Guyana Human Rights Association and former president Donald Ramotar say the public and parliament have not seen the terms. They question the legal basis, the costs and Guyana’s capacity to manage the arrivals. The government says it keeps full discretion to reject anyone proposed.

World.title: Mexico’s G20 Growth Ranks Second, but US Rate Hike and Diesel Cap Weigh
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts — What happened Mexico’s G20 growth ranking: second-fastest in the second quarter of 2026, behind only India, says the OECD.

— The numbers Output rose 1.4% on the previous quarter after a 0.3% contraction in the first quarter, the OECD said.

— Why it matters now Banxico, the central bank, decides on interest rates on Thursday 24 September 2026, eight days after a US rate hike.

— What Barclays expects The British bank expects Banxico to hold its rate at 6.50% at each remaining meeting of 2026.

— The catch Keeping diesel at 27 pesos a litre (about US$1.57) costs 163 million pesos a day (about US$9.5 million), one analyst estimates.

— The official view President Claudia Sheinbaum said on 21 September 2026 that growth would improve in the third and fourth quarters.

Mexico’s economy bounced back between April and June faster than almost any big economy. The harder part starts now, with higher US interest rates and an expensive fuel price cap.

Office and hotel towers along Avenida de la República in central Mexico City, file photograph. (Photo: Carlos Valenzuela, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Mexico’s G20 growth ranking has gone from contraction to near the top in three months. Between April and June, only India grew faster among the Group of 20 (G20), the forum of the world’s major economies.

The ranking comes from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the Paris-based club of mostly rich economies. Mexico’s output rose 1.4% on the previous quarter, twice the G20 average of 0.7%.

The good news lands in an awkward week. Mexico’s central bank sets interest rates on Thursday, days after the United States raised its own.

From contraction to second place

The OECD published the provisional figures behind Mexico’s G20 growth ranking on Monday 14 September 2026. It said G20 growth slowed slightly, from 0.8% in the first quarter to 0.7% in the second.

India led with 1.8%. Mexico followed at 1.4%, ahead of Indonesia at 1.3%, Turkey at 1.1% and China at 0.9%.

The United States grew 0.4% and Canada 0.8%, making Mexico the fastest of the three North American trade partners. Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, grew 0.5%.

The jump follows a weak start to the year. The OECD records a 0.3% contraction for Mexico in the first three months of 2026.

Saudi Arabia dragged the group down. Its output shrank 4.8% in the quarter, which El Financiero, a Mexican business daily, linked to lower oil activity.

The president highlights the ranking

President Claudia Sheinbaum highlighted the ranking at her morning press conference on Monday 21 September 2026. “Second place in economic growth in the second quarter of 2026,” she said, according to Animal Político, a Mexican news site.

She added that the economy would do better in the third and fourth quarters.

The underlying data come from INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics institute. In August 2026 it revised quarterly growth down to 1.4%, from an early estimate of 1.5%.

That made it the best quarter since early 2022, according to El CEO, a business news site. Services, more than 60% of output, got a lift from World Cup spending.

Year on year, the economy grew 1.9% in the second quarter. In the first half it grew 1.2%.

The finance ministry cut its 2026 growth forecast on 8 September 2026. It now expects 1% to 2%, down from 1.8% to 2.8% in April.

Private analysts and international bodies expect growth of 1.1% to 1.5% this year, El CEO reported, near the middle of that range.

The Bank of Mexico headquarters in central Mexico City, beside the Palacio de Bellas Artes, file photograph.

A Fed hike tests Banxico

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point on Wednesday 16 September 2026. The new range is 3.75% to 4%.

It was the first Fed increase since July 2023, Bloomberg reported. Most Fed officials projected another hike before the end of the year.

That matters for Mexico because investors compare returns on Mexican and US bonds. A narrower gap can weaken the peso and push up import prices.

The Bank of Mexico, known as Banxico, has held its rate at 6.50% since May. Its next decisions fall on 24 September, 5 November and 17 December 2026.

Barclays, the British bank, expects Banxico to hold at all three meetings. El Economista, a Mexican business daily, reported the forecast on 22 September 2026.

Latin American central banks now follow the Fed less closely than before the pandemic, Barclays argues.

The bank still names a limit: Banxico would have to follow if Fed hikes topped half a point within 18 months. Barclays does not expect that.

Barclays also forecasts that Mexican inflation will rise to 4% by the end of 2026, from 3.26% in August. It sees 4.5% by mid-2027, mainly from the effect of El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern, on food prices.

The diesel cap bill

The second pressure is fiscal. Mexico caps diesel at 27 pesos a litre (about US$1.57) through a voluntary pact between the government and fuel retailers.

To hold that line, the finance ministry waived the whole excise tax on diesel for 19 to 25 September 2026. That tax, called IEPS, is 7.36 pesos a litre (about US$0.43).

The ministry added a further stimulus of 1.83 pesos a litre (about US$0.11), the business magazine Expansión reported.

Energy specialist Ramsés Pech puts the current cost of the cap at 163 million pesos a day (about US$9.5 million). He was quoted by El Economista on 21 September 2026.

His worst case assumes supply disruption in the Middle East and Ukraine. The cost would then reach 308 million pesos a day (about US$17.9 million).

Pech calls the frozen price “a silent fiscal bomb”.

His central scenario, assuming today’s market holds, puts the daily cost at 236 million pesos (about US$13.7 million). The government has not published an official daily total.

Dollar conversions in this article use a rate of 17.2 to the US dollar, near Banxico’s reference rate on 21 September 2026.

What it means for outsiders

For foreign investors, Mexico’s G20 growth ranking is a useful rebound signal, not yet a trend. One strong quarter followed a contraction.

For companies and visitors, the practical questions are the peso and prices. Thursday’s Banxico decision will show how much room the central bank believes it still has.

More: Mexico coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was Mexico really the second-fastest-growing G20 economy?

Yes, on a quarter-on-quarter basis in the second quarter of 2026. The OECD’s provisional figures, published on 14 September 2026, show Mexico’s output rising 1.4% from the first quarter. Only India grew faster, at 1.8%. On a year-on-year basis Mexico’s growth was a more modest 1.9%, according to INEGI, the national statistics institute.

Why does a US rate hike matter to Mexico?

Investors weigh returns on Mexican assets against US ones. When the Federal Reserve raises rates, the gap narrows unless the Bank of Mexico follows. A narrower gap can weaken the peso and raise import prices. Barclays expects Banxico to keep its rate at 6.50% for the rest of 2026. It would follow only if the Fed raised rates by more than half a point.

How much does Mexico’s diesel price cap cost?

The finance ministry publishes the per-litre tax relief each week. Energy specialist Ramsés Pech, quoted by El Economista, estimates the current daily cost at 163 million pesos (about US$9.5 million). In his worst-case scenario it would rise to 308 million pesos a day (about US$17.9 million). The finance ministry has waived the whole excise tax on diesel for 19 to 25 September 2026.

When is the next Banxico decision?

The Bank of Mexico announces its next interest rate decision on Thursday 24 September 2026. Its remaining 2026 decisions are scheduled for 5 November and 17 December. The benchmark rate has been 6.50% since May.

World.title: Guatemala M4 Rifles Arrive as the Army Buys American Weapons Again
World.content:
Guatemala · Defense

Key Facts — What happened About 2,000 Colt M4A1 rifles bought from the United States landed in Guatemala City on Monday 21 September 2026.

— What was bought 2,699 rifles, 59 machine guns, 57 grenade launchers and 11,220 magazines, about US$5.03 million in total, according to state news agency AGN.

— How it was paid A sale through the US Foreign Military Sales programme, funded by Guatemala’s own budget, not an American grant.

— Where they go A new jungle operations brigade in Petén, the northern region bordering Mexico, to fight drug trafficking.

— Why it matters Washington restricted arms for Guatemala’s army from 1977 over civil-war abuses; Guatemala announced the restriction lifted in March 2026.

— The catch The headline figure of 14,000 is mostly magazines; the rifles number 2,699, arriving in lots.

About 2,000 American carbines landed in Guatemala City on Monday. The army paid for them itself, after Washington lifted a restriction that dates back to the civil war.

US Air National Guard aircrew talk with Guatemalan army officers during a delivery of donated US equipment to Guatemala; file photograph. (Photo: U.S. Air National Guard photo by Tech. Sgt. Christopher Sherlock, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

A batch of Guatemala M4 rifles bought from the United States landed in Guatemala City on Monday 21 September 2026. About 2,000 Colt M4A1 carbines arrived on an American military aircraft.

The US embassy’s top diplomat called it the first purchase of its kind in about five decades. Washington had restricted arms for Guatemala’s army since 1977 over civil-war atrocities.

The plane landed on the military ramp of the Guatemalan Air Force at La Aurora International Airport. President Bernardo Arévalo and Defence Minister Henry Sáenz, a major general, received the shipment.

What Guatemala actually bought

The purchase was made through Foreign Military Sales, the US government programme that sells American weapons to foreign governments. Guatemala paid with its own money; it is not a grant.

The total is US$5,033,645, according to the state news agency AGN. Its itemised breakdown lists 2,699 M4A1 rifles, 59 M240 machine guns and 57 grenade launchers.

It also lists 11,220 magazines holding 30 cartridges each. Together the four items make 14,035 pieces, the figure of more than 14,000 cited by officials.

Most of those pieces are magazines, not guns. Arévalo himself described the order as more than 14,000 “units” of modern armament.

Monday’s aircraft carried about 2,000 rifles, according to Jorgan Andrews, the chargé d’affaires who runs the US embassy. Sáenz said the grenade launchers had arrived in an earlier lot, and the machine guns come next.

Nor was Monday the first delivery: the defence ministry told the newspaper Prensa Libre that a first lot had arrived on 30 June.

Arévalo said deliveries would continue over the coming months. Prensa Libre, citing the sales documentation, reported that the rifle order is scheduled for full delivery by the third quarter of 2027.

Where the Guatemala M4 rifles will go

The weapons are destined for a new Special Jungle Operations Brigade in Petén, Sáenz said. Petén is the vast northern lowland region bordering Mexico, used by drug traffickers.

The brigade’s base is in the final stage of construction, according to the newspaper La Hora. Its tasks include fighting drug trafficking, guarding the Mexican border and protecting natural resources.

Asked how the army would stop the rifles reaching criminals, Sáenz said control protocols had been reviewed. He cited an earlier incident that exposed failures in supervision, which led to criminal complaints.

Bernardo Arévalo in Guatemala City on 26 June 2023, as a presidential candidate; file photograph. (Photo by Luis Acosta / AFP via Getty Images)

A restriction older than most soldiers

Guatemalan officials describe the ban as a 47-year embargo. The history began with a refusal by Guatemala itself.

In March 1977 the new Carter administration sent Guatemala a State Department report on its human rights record. On 11 March 1977, Guatemala’s foreign ministry replied in a diplomatic note.

It declined “in advance any aid or sale of military equipment” conditioned on foreign judgments of its internal affairs. That is recorded in a US embassy telegram published by the State Department’s Office of the Historian.

Congress then acted. The foreign aid appropriations law President Jimmy Carter signed on 31 October 1977 prohibited military credit sales to Guatemala.

The measure targeted the army rather than the country. The UN-backed truth commission later attributed 93% of documented violations in the 1960 to 1996 conflict to state forces.

The ban was never airtight. DW, Germany’s international broadcaster, reported that Washington kept donating equipment to Guatemala’s armed forces for counter-narcotics work.

Cut off from American sales, the army turned elsewhere. Israel supplied Galil assault rifles, La Hora recalled, and DW reports that Israel and Colombia remain its main suppliers.

How the door reopened

Sáenz announced on Monday 9 March 2026 that the United States had lifted the restriction. He said no document formalised the change, which followed Guatemala meeting a series of conditions.

Those included keeping the army under a democratic president and focused on borders, drug trafficking and transnational threats. Sáenz said at the time that the army had about US$50 million to spend on arms in 2026.

On Monday, Arévalo argued the conditions behind the ban were gone. “The army of today is fundamentally different from the army of 1978,” he told reporters, as quoted by AP.

Why Washington wants this sale

Andrews called the purchase “historic”. He said Guatemala was investing its own resources and taking on more responsibility.

He linked the rifles to a wider effort to equip 16 Guatemalan battalions with nearly 8,000 additional rifles. He also promoted the Coalition of the Americas against cartels, a US-led regional security initiative.

Critics see a cost. The Mutual Support Group (GAM) represents relatives of people who disappeared during the war.

In a column for the Guatemalan news site Agencia Ocote, GAM argued that lifting the ban removes pressure over wartime archives.

The archives remain a current issue. In August, a United Nations working group on enforced disappearances urged the army to open those archives, AP reported.

For now, the Guatemala M4 rifles deal is small in money but large in symbolism. It turns decades of distant military ties into an ordinary customer relationship.

More: Guatemala coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Guatemala receive 14,000 rifles from the United States?

No. The order covers 2,699 Colt M4A1 rifles, 59 M240 machine guns, 57 grenade launchers and 11,220 magazines. Together those make 14,035 items, which is where the 14,000 figure comes from. About 2,000 of the rifles arrived on 21 September 2026, and the rest are being delivered in lots.

Was this American military aid?

No. Guatemala bought the equipment through the US Foreign Military Sales programme and paid about US$5.03 million from its own budget. The American chargé d’affaires, Jorgan Andrews, stressed that Guatemala was investing its own resources.

Was there really a 47-year US arms embargo on Guatemala?

Not in a single clean form. In March 1977 Guatemala rejected US military aid tied to human rights reports. In October 1977 Congress barred military credit sales to it. Washington still donated some counter-narcotics equipment in later years. Guatemala announced on 9 March 2026 that the restriction had been lifted.

What will the rifles be used for?

Defence Minister Henry Sáenz said they will equip a new Special Jungle Operations Brigade in Petén, the northern region bordering Mexico. Its missions include fighting drug trafficking, guarding the border and protecting natural resources.

Sources: AGN on the itemised US$5.03 million purchase, Prensa Libre on the US chargé d’affaires’ remarks, Soy502 on the arrival at La Aurora, La Hora on the Petén jungle brigade, AP on the purchase and the civil-war background, US State Department historical documents on the 1977 break, DW on the March 2026 announcement, Prensa Libre on the contract and delivery schedule

World.title: Venezuela IMF Office to Open in Caracas in 2027, Fund Chief Says
World.content:
Venezuela · Politics

Key Facts — What happened IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said on 21 September 2026 that a Venezuela IMF office will open in Caracas next year.

— Who she met Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, who also saw the heads of the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the UN.

— Why it matters Venezuela wants to restructure debts that most analysts put at US$150 billion to US$200 billion, Reuters reported.

— The catch Brazil’s president, Lula, says Washington acts as if it governs Venezuela, and urged Rodríguez to call elections.

— What the polls say A poll promoted by state media shows 91% back US dialogue; another finds 91% oppose her Trump meeting.

— What comes next Rodríguez is due to meet Trump on Tuesday and to address the UN General Assembly on Wednesday.

The International Monetary Fund will open an office in Caracas next year, its chief said after meeting Venezuela’s acting president. Delcy Rodríguez is due to meet Donald Trump on Tuesday.

Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, speaking at a government press conference, in a file photograph (Photo: Rio Times media library)
