World.title: A Cuban zoo, and its animals, in epic battle for survival
World.content:
Two Bengal tiger cubs (Panthera tigris) rest at the National Zoo of Havana in Havana on September 15, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

HAVANA, Cuba (AFP) — Every day, veterinarians and zookeepers make their way to Cuba’s National Zoo by whatever means they can, determined to not abandon the nearly 1,000 animals in their care and help save species at risk of extinction.

Their dedication and food donations are vital to keeping alive an array of rhinos, jaguars and tigers — including an extremely rare white tiger — in the midst of a severe crisis that has left many Cubans struggling to feed themselves.

Just getting to the reserve situated 20 kilometres (12 miles) from central Havana is a headache for staff, as public transportation has come to a near standstill nine months into a US fuel blockade.

“The workers come by bicycle, pedal scooter or electric motorbike to ensure the animals have food and water every day,” said Yoel Machado, the zoo’s animal welfare manager.

Their efforts are about more than keeping the animals fed.

The 345-hectare (850-acre) park serves as a genetic reserve of international conservation importance, housing breeding populations of vulnerable or endangered species, including black and white rhinos, hippos and jaguars.

Yet the same crisis that has left workers scrambling to source meat, medicine and water has forced the zoo to curb reproduction programs and increasingly rely on handouts to sustain its animals.

During a recent visit by AFP, two Bengal tiger cubs, one an extremely rare white specimen, frolicked in their enclosure beneath the watchful gaze of their mother, oblivious to the strenuous efforts made to keep them alive.

AFP did not see any animals that appeared malnourished or ill, but Angel Cordero, the veterinarian in charge of big cats, said the tiger cubs “could be in better shape.”

He revealed he needed to ration their food to prevent it from running out.

“It’s no use giving them plenty if it only lasts three days,” he said.

Big cats need about seven kilograms (15 pounds) of meat per day per adult, but such quantities are hard to come by.

Even when it is available, recurring blackouts of up to 30 hours at a stretch make it difficult to preserve.

With fuel extremely scarce, there’s also the issue of how to distribute food in a nature reserve the size of New York’s Central Park.

For now, private donors have come to the rescue for the zoo’s various needs.

Every Monday, Ana Fernandez, a Cuban-American woman born in Tennessee who has been living in Cuba for nine years, donates meat.

“The animals shouldn’t have to suffer,” the 50-year-old said, though she added that “some days it’s not enough for all of them.”

Recently, the reserve went 23 days without electricity, which meant it also lacked running water.

The staff “didn’t just sit around waiting for things to fall from the sky,” the zoo’s director Juan Carlos Corella said.

“We looked for solutions, water trucks were brought in, and we found food for the animals almost daily,” he said, while admitting that keeping the park open has become “very difficult.”

An exodus of vets has added to the zoo’s woes.

More than a third have left for better-paying jobs elsewhere, mostly in Cuba’s burgeoning private sector.

Some wait tables in cafes while others work for private veterinary clinics.

The zoo is home to the only breeding group of black rhinos outside of Africa, as well as a large population of white rhinos, the largest herd of Grant’s zebras in the Americas and hippos that regularly bear calves.

“Here we have a high genetic value, and one of immense international importance,” Machado, the animal welfare manager, explained.

However, the crisis has forced the park to slow down its breeding programs.

The reason is simple: each new offspring requires more food, medicine, and staff.

“We can’t keep increasing the number of animals,” Machado said, adding that he preferred to ensure the current population was “as well cared for as possible.”

And yet life keeps renewing itself, regardless.

In recent months, the zoo has welcomed baby tigers, hyenas, jackals, and a black dromedary named Esperanza (Spanish for “Hope”), the first of its kind born in Cuba in three decades.

World.title: Golding makes fresh bid to overhaul Crown lands law
World.content:
A screen grab of PNP President Mark Golding addressing the public session of the party's 88th Annual Conference on Sunday.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Following two failed attempts to introduce a private member’s bill that would reduce the qualifying period for Jamaicans illegally occupying Crown lands from 60 to 25 years, People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding announced that another attempt will be made to have the bill accepted by Parliament.

Golding stated this will take place as soon as Parliament returns from its summer break which is slated for Tuesday.

“And I will seek the support of both sides of the House of Representatives to pass it into law. We want justice when it comes to land in Jamaica,” stated Golding as he delivered the main addressing the PNP’s 88th Annual Conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar on Sunday.

​According to Golding, he took the bill to Parliament in July, where two attempts were made to have it tabled before the summer recess.

“I was blocked from doing so by the Speaker of the House.”

Currently, the qualifying period to acquire ownership of Government land through adverse possession — the legal principle allowing individuals to claim ownership of land through unauthorised, continuous, and open occupation for a specific period — is 60 years.

This contrasts with the 12 years it takes for persons occupying private property to be able to make a claim.

Golding pointed out that this duration was legislated in the 1830s around the time of emancipation, when life expectancy in Jamaica was less than 60 years.

“The formerly enslaved people of Jamaica were not given any land at emancipation, and that 60-year rule was plainly intended to ensure that the people did not acquire ownership of land by possession when they left those plantations,” argued Golding.

“That is why I have prepared the legislation entitled The Crown Lands Reform Act 2026, which seeks Parliament to reduce 60 years to 25 years, subject to a fair legal process.

Golding said the proposed bill would also enable an area impacted by a disaster such as Hurricane Melissa last October, to be declared a Disaster Adjudication Area so that legitimate claims for ownership by possession or otherwise can be settled quickly and titles issued to those who can establish their entitlement.

The Opposition Leader had first made the proposal for the change in the law while on the campaign trail in the lead up to the September 2025 General Election.

At that time Golding had told a party meeting in Spanish Town, St Catherine: “When I think of all the thousands of Jamaicans who live on land, and have occupied that land for years but don’t have security of tenure, and they can’t use their investment in the property to further themselves with education, or in business or to deal with any emergency, I say time come to reform that 1833 law that says you have to be on land of government for 60 years before you can become an owner.

“And we going to drop it substantially so that the people who have been there for at least 25 years will be entitled to their titles. It’s not one or two, but tens of thousands, possibly hundreds of thousands of Jamaicans who will benefit from becoming owners of the rock because of that one piece of emancipatory legislation that we will be bringing forward”.

World.title: EU-Cyberbehörde: Chinesische Hacker haben 2025 die Schifffahrt in mindestens sieben EU-Staaten angegriffen
World.content:
Die Schifffahrt ist eine besonders anfällige Branche, in der schwerwiegende Cyberangriffe erhebliche Folgewirkungen auf den Handel haben können. | Morris MacMatzen/Getty Images

Eine chinesische Hackergruppe habe im Laufe des Jahres 2025 immer wieder Cyberangriffe auf europäische maritime Organisationen verübt, warnte die Cyberagentur der EU am Dienstag.

„Mustang Panda“, eine in China ansässige Spionagegruppe, habe Organisationen aus der Schifffahrtsbranche mit „anhaltenden Kampagnen angegriffen, von denen mindestens sieben EU-Mitgliedstaaten betroffen waren“, so die EU-Agentur ENISA in ihrem Jahresbericht, in dem sie die Cyberbedrohungen für die Union darlegt. Das US-Justizministerium wirft der Gruppe vor, von der chinesischen Regierung unterstützt zu werden,

Zu den Hackerangriffen gehörten Spionage und die Beschaffung strategischer Informationen, so die ENISA. Sie fügte hinzu, dass „Mustang Panda“ eine „erhebliche Bedrohung“ für EU-Organisationen darstelle, da die Gruppe über fortschrittliche Fähigkeiten verfüge und in der Lage sei, wiederholte Angriffe auf den maritimen Sektor und Organisationen der öffentlichen Verwaltung durchzuführen.

World.title: In blow to Meloni, Italy misses early exit from EU fiscal watch
World.content:
The state of the economy will be top of voters’ minds in the 2027 elections.

BRUSSELS — Italy's government has failed to rein in its public spending enough to shake off EU fiscal oversight in a blow to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of next year's general election.

The Italian National Institute of Statistics today confirmed that the gap between the country’s public expenditure and revenues last year was 3.1%, above the EU's budget deficit cap of 3% under the bloc's rules for public spending. The deficit breach keeps it in the European Commission's "excessive deficit procedure," a red flag that Brussels slaps on governments that need to improve the health of their public finances.

Italy's been subject to the EDP and, as a result, the Commission's fiscal oversight since 2024, forcing Rome to pursue stricter caps to bring its spending under control.

World.title: Macron pushes for energy truce between Ukraine and Russia
World.content:
France's President Emmanuel Macron meets with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York City on September 21, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

The French president met with Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy before the U.N. General Assembly in New York.

French President Emmanuel Macron has called for a moratorium on energy sector strikes between Ukraine and Russia on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday.

Following a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York, the French president said on X they had discussed pooling efforts “to secure a moratorium on strikes against energy infrastructure.”

Macron also discussed “the prospect of an energy truce” with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later on Monday evening.

World.title: Chinese hackers targeted shipping in at least seven EU countries, cyber agency reports
World.content:
Shipping is a particularly vulnerable industry where disruptive cyberattacks could have major knock-on effects on trade. | Morris MacMatzen/Getty Images

The China-based Mustang Panda group represents a “significant threat” to EU organizations, the ENISA said.

A notorious Chinese hacking group carried out cyberattacks against European maritime organizations at a “sustained tempo” throughout 2025, the EU’s cyber agency said on Tuesday.

Mustang Panda, a China-based cyber-espionage group that U.S. justice department officials accuse of being sponsored by the Chinese government, hit shipping-related organizations with “continuous campaigns impacting at least seven EU member states,” EU agency ENISA said in its annual report outlining the cyber threats facing the bloc.

The hacks included spying and strategic intelligence collection, ENISA said, adding that Mustang Panda is a "significant threat” to EU organizations as it is equipped with advanced capabilities and capable of carrying out repeated attacks against the maritime sector and public administration organizations.

World.title: Germany says Costa losing touch ‘with reality’ on EU budget
World.content:
However, Germany and allies from Northern Europe — whose contributions to the budget exceed their EU payouts — are pushing in the opposite direction, insisting that the EU slash its cashpot by hundreds of billions of euros. They argue that introducing new EU taxes is not an alternative to major cuts.

“One has to wonder whether Mr. Costa has completely lost touch with reality by now,” Krichbaum told reporters.

He added that “national budgets are under enormous pressure ... and everyone knows that the sky isn’t the limit.”

EU governments are lobbying the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU — which is steering the budget talks — to reflect their preferences in a new budget negotiating document, also known as a negobox, that is set to be presented in early October.

Ireland has urged ministers to outline on Tuesday where they are ready to compromise on the most sensitive issues in the negotiations, including spending cuts and own resources.

Costa will take over the negotiations after an October European Council, when EU leaders will react to Ireland's proposal. Over the past month, Costa toured 25 EU capitals to sound out leaders on the most difficult topics in the negotiations.

World.title: Pour atténuer les prix des carburants, Emmanuel Macron demande des assouplissements à l’UE
World.content:
Emmanuel Macron a notamment demandé à la Commission de reporter d'un an l’entrée en vigueur des nouvelles règles européennes qui prévoient des amendes pour les entreprises pétrolières et gazières qui ne déclarent pas leurs émissions de méthane. | Pool photo par Laurent Cipriani via AFP/Getty

PARIS — Le président français Emmanuel Macron a demandé à la présidente de la Commission européenne, Ursula von der Leyen, d’assouplir les règles de l’Union européenne relatives à la composition des carburants et aux obligations de déclaration des émissions de méthane, dans le but de maîtriser la flambée des prix de l'énergie, dans un courrier consulté par POLITICO, révélé par Les Echos et BFM.

Emmanuel Macron a notamment demandé à la Commission de reporter d'un an l’entrée en vigueur des nouvelles règles européennes qui prévoient des amendes pour les entreprises pétrolières et gazières qui ne déclarent pas leurs émissions de méthane.

Cette réglementation, destinée à réduire les émissions de l'un des gaz à effet de serre les plus puissants, a été vivement critiquée par le gouvernement américain et le secteur des énergies fossiles, qui affirment qu'elle fera fuir les importateurs de pétrole et de gaz et mettra en péril la sécurité énergétique de l'Europe.

World.title: UK seeks to broker global AI agreement at G20
World.content:
“I think we can really do something in this space [that is] very significant,” Burnham said.

Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump for the first time as prime minister on Tuesday, and said he will assure the U.S. president that the U.K. will take a balanced approach on AI.

“I think you have to be clear-eyed about the huge benefits it can bring as well as recognizing where we do need to be careful,” Burnham said — noting that Trump has warned of risks from AI. The U.S. president has also branded existential warnings around the tech as a “HOAX.”

Burnham said warnings from AI company insiders have “made me pause” but said that he is determined to find a “sweet spot” on balancing the tech's benefits against its risks, and not turn into a “doom-monger about AI.”

The U.K.’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has traveled with Burnham to New York, where No. 10 said AI would dominate diplomatic engagements.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday evening, Burnham is expected to call on countries to work together to harness AI for good and promise U.K. leadership on the issue.

World.title: Macron asks EU to relax energy and climate rules to ease soaring fuel prices
World.content:
He asked the European Commission to delay by one year new EU rules that will impose fines on oil and gas companies which fail to report their methane emissions.

The methane regulation is designed to reduce emissions of one of the most potent planet-warming gases which are often released during the production and transport of coal, oil and natural gas. But it has been heavily criticized by the U.S. government and fossil fuel sector, who say it will frighten off oil and gas importers and endanger Europe’s energy security.

The Commission had already recommended member countries hold off fining offenders until the end of 2029. But, to provide more legal certainty to fossil fuel importers, the French President asked Brussels to explicitly delay those rules by one year.

Macron also proposed temporarily softening EU rules on the quality of fuels, which regulate parameters such as density and vaporization limits, and to allow the use of more biofuels in diesel.

“I believe it is useful to draw your attention to several points which, if addressed and implemented at the European level, could collectively strengthen our import and production capacities in the short term,” Macron wrote in a letter sent to von der Leyen last Friday and seen by POLITICO. The letter was first reported by French media.

For months, the government has been paying fuel subsidies to most-affected sectors and, later on Tuesday, it is expected to present more measures.

World.title: Exclusive: EU countries sound alarm over weapons brought back from Ukraine front line
World.content:
Soldiers returning from the front line in Ukraine are bringing back weapons and military equipment, raising concerns that battlefield components could start circulating within the European Union, according to a confidential EU document seen by Euronews.

 

The risk of firearms being diverted from the battlefield will be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, as European authorities step up efforts to track weapons entering the bloc.

"Member states have reported weapon components and military equipment in the possession of returning combatants," reads the EU Council document, which focuses on the war in Ukraine's impact on EU internal security.

"While not necessarily connecting these individuals to organised smuggling activities, these detections demonstrate a potential risk of military components or other battlefield equipment being transported from Ukraine into the EU," the document continues.

In recent months, several EU countries have pushed to bar former and current Russian combatants from entering the bloc over potential security risks, namely their involvement in sabotage and hybrid attacks on European soil.

The ban was included in the 21st sanctions package but was eventually watered down following opposition from France and Italy.

However, at an informal meeting of foreign ministers earlier this month, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said there was "broad support" to move forward with the visa ban, following an attempted drone attack in Leipzig in which one of the suspects reportedly entered the Schengen area on a tourist visa issued by Italy.

Meanwhile, Estonia has launched an intelligence-sharing operation with other countries on the so-called eastern flank to pool entry-refusal decisions against identified Russian combatants based on a judicial or administrative ruling.

"Foreign fighters, either volunteers or mercenaries, continue to pose a risk, as they acquire military skills and experience that could be further exploited once they withdraw from the conflict zone to engage in criminal activities or terrorism," the document adds.

But the concern is not limited to Russian combatants. It also extends to Ukrainians returning from the frontline, particularly in member states hosting large numbers of Ukrainian refugees, such as Germany, Poland and Czechia.

At the same time, authorities in these countries point out that the security issue relates to the EU as a whole, since they are part of Schengen, and that soldiers reuniting with their families are unlikely to sell those weapons legally, Euronews understands.

According to a report published in March by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, there is currently no substantial weapon inflow from Ukraine to neighbouring countries, but weapon circulation remains a "structural risk."

Kyiv, for its part, has already established a National Firearms Focal Point that supplies Europol with lists of seized, stolen or lost firearms.

Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, is directly involved and is due to establish a dedicated Firearms Hub by the first quarter of 2027 to improve the analysis and exchange of data on seized weapons.

Ukraine is also expected to adopt a dedicated roadmap on firearms trafficking by the end of this year, following the model of one already undertaken in the Western Balkans. Specific benchmarks on the issue have even been written into Ukraine's accession negotiations.

Frontex, the EU's border agency, has also issued specific instructions for border guards and customs authorities on firearm diversion, with a focus on Ukraine.

"One of the most significant long-term concerns in the context of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is the proliferation and diversion of firearms and other SALW [Small Arms and Light Weapons]. So far, few weapons have been seized and few arrests made," the document says.

World.title: Iraq to collect 6 million weapons despite pushback from Iran-backed militias
World.content:
Iraq's government is pressing ahead with a plan to collect an estimated 6 million weapons held outside official institutions, the Interior Ministry said, even as Baghdad quietly retreated from a September 30 deadline that had been set for armed factions to surrender their arsenals.

 

Iraqi Deputy Interior Minister Hussein al-Awadi said the government was treating 30 September — originally set as a hard deadline for factions to hand over weapons, timed to coincide with the final withdrawal of US-led coalition forces — as the start of a regulatory process rather than a completion point.

A four-member committee including Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and former Premier Mohammed Shia al-Sudani is working on a revised mechanism.

Al-Awadi was speaking during a visit to Salah al-Din province, where he said the government had shifted focus from combating terrorism to tackling organised crime, and that security files would be handed to provinces one by one in coming months.

He said the ministry had made measurable progress in roughly 100 days since al-Zaidi took office.

The disarmament push is being conducted through negotiation rather than force. Al-Zaidi said in August his government had no intention of using military means against the factions, and that some had already handed over weapons while talks continued with others.

In recent days he said the US troop withdrawal would leave "no justification or need for any resistance in Iraq" and that he would not accept "a state within the state".

Tehran-backed militias at the centre

The campaign is running under significant US pressure. Washington asked Baghdad in June for a clear timetable for bringing weapons under state control, and the Trump administration has linked compliance to Iraq's access to dollar flows critical to its economy.

The factions at the centre of the standoff are mostly Shia militias that formed under Iranian guidance and operate with Tehran's backing.

They are loosely grouped under the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an umbrella organisation established in 2014 after Iraq's most senior Shia cleric, Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, issued an order calling on volunteers to fight the so-called Islamic State group.

Some factions within the PMF have been formally incorporated into Iraq's state security structure, while others have maintained independent command chains and continued to receive weapons, funding and direction from Iran's IRGC.

Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba — two of the most hardline Tehran-aligned groups, both of which have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and launched attacks on Gulf states during the ongoing Iran war — have refused to hand over what they describe as "resistance weapons".

By contrast, Saraya al-Salam, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali have reached an understanding with the government to surrender weapons or regularise their status.

Saraya al-Salam formally separated from cleric Muqtada al-Sadr's movement and was integrated into the Iraqi security forces in a ceremony in Samarra in June.

Al-Zaidi, a 40-year-old billionaire businessman with no prior political or government experience, was approved as prime minister by parliament on 14 May as a compromise candidate following months of deadlock within the Shiite Coordination Framework.

Restricting weapons to state control was a central commitment of his government programme.

World.title: Head of Spain's RTVE backs ongoing Eurovision boycott over Israel's participation
World.content:
The head of Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE says he supports Spain continuing to boycott this year's Eurovision contest over Israel’s participation.

 

RTVE president José Pablo López said it was “deeply painful” that Israel’s public broadcaster remained eligible to compete while the humanitarian crisis in Gaza continued.

López said he would ask the board of RTVE to uphold Spain’s departure from Eurovision, with a final decision expected by mid-October.

López told a Senate committee on Tuesday that it was "deeply painful" that Israel's public broadcaster would continue to participate in Eurovision "despite everything, and given this situation that is still being experienced in Gaza."

Spain’s withdrawal would be more significant as one of Eurovision’s “Big Five”, the group of countries that make the largest financial contributions to the European Broadcasting Union and therefore automatically qualify for the final.

The announcement was reported and televised by the corporation's news outlet, RTVE Noticias

The Spanish government has been a vocal supporter of Palestine and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been one of Israel's most virulent critics, labelling its actions in Gaza a genocide.

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, Gaza's health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israel's retaliatory military operation.

Additionally, since an October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli strikes have killed more than 1,300 people in the devastated Palestinian territory, according to the Gaza health ministry, whose figures are considered generally reliable by the United Nations.

Two countries have already announced boycotts

Ireland and the Netherlands have already confirmed they will boycott Eurovision 2027, which is due to be held in Bulgaria.

The Irish broadcaster RTÉ said in a statement: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the ⁠appalling and ongoing loss ⁠of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to ‌put the lives of so many civilians at risk."

Performers on stage as voting results are collected during the Grand Final of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna, 16 May, 2026 AP Photo

Eurovision director Martin Green said he "regretted" RTÉ 's stance, but "fully respect their decision."

It followed the announcement from Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who are also boycotting next year's show as it is no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity."

Both Ireland and the Netherlands were among the five countries who decided to opt out of the 2026 competition, along with Spain, Iceland and Slovenia.

World.title: France warns of fresh oil shock, urges EU to free up refinery capacity
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron asked Brussels to take emergency steps to boost Europe’s diesel and jet fuel supply as the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East threaten to further tighten global oil markets, according to a letter seen by Euronews.

 

Macron said that the oil market has so far been kept supplied largely through higher refinery output, weaker Asian demand and the drawdown of existing stocks. However, he warned that this cushion is rapidly eroding, with France already having 14% of gas stations suffering with shortages or near-shortages on 22 September at 9 am, according to the French government.

"In recent weeks, international supply has deteriorated once again, driven by the combined impact of the targeting of energy infrastructure — in Russia and the Middle East — and the recovery of consumption in Asia," reads the letter addressed to the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and sent on 18 September.

Macron said that if Hormuz remains effectively closed and Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline does not return to operation, the depletion of Saudi stocks could remove at least another 4 million barrels a day from global crude supply, potentially triggering another sharp price increase. Global oil inventories have fallen by more than 500 million barrels, according to Macron's letter.

The French president said European dependence on Middle Eastern imports is particularly significant for jet fuel, where 36% of imports come from the region, and diesel, at 18%.

Unlock refinery capacity

The bloc cannot quickly replace the crude oil it has lost, but Macron argued that it could maximize fuel output from the crude and refinery capacity that remain available.

He urged the Commission to temporarily relax some EU fuel-quality specifications to allow refineries to produce more jet fuel and diesel, as oil-logistics companies struggle to confirm deliveries.

"France-based players in the oil logistics sector report increasing difficulties in confirming deliveries for the coming weeks. Furthermore, several member states are seeing gas storage fill levels that are lower than those recorded in recent years," Macron wrote.

He added that changes to parameters including density, volatility and desulphurisation could increase refinery output by around 5% to 20%, depending on the plant.

The proposal would require the Commission to work with carmakers to determine which standards could safely be relaxed without damaging vehicles or infrastructure, while maintaining health and safety requirements. France points to the precedent set during the Covid-19 crisis, when the Commission temporarily eased some fuel specifications.

Macron also asked the EU to allow greater use of B10 diesel, containing up to 10% biodiesel, instead of the standard B7 diesel. Temporary limits could be agreed with vehicle manufacturers to determine which engines can safely use the higher biofuel blend.

Taken together, the measures would seek to increase Europe’s effective fuel supply without having to wait for the geopolitical crisis around the Strait of Hormuz to subside, Macron argued.

Delay methane-import rules

Macron's letter also takes aim at another potential constraint on fossil-fuel imports — the EU's methane law.

"It is also important not to weaken European production capacities while preparing for long-term supply difficulties," reads the letter.

EU member states adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing the bloc’s first framework for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions in the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases.

Facing soaring prices and fuel shortages, France wants Brussels to postpone by one year, until 1 January 2028, the obligation for importers of crude oil and natural gas to transmit information under the bloc's methane rules.

Related Brussels proposes easing methane penalties after heavy lobbying from industry

The Commission has already recommended delaying financial penalties by three years, until the end of 2029, but Paris argues that the underlying reporting obligation itself could expose importers to additional legal uncertainty while supply conditions are deteriorating.

Paris also wants the Commission to reassess the EU's joint-gas purchasing mechanism, created following the war in Ukraine and the sudden decoupling from Russian gas.

Macron suggested examining whether the approach could be extended to diesel and jet fuel, potentially giving the EU greater collective leverage in securing oil and refined products.

Reacting to the French letter, the Commission said on Tuesday the potential supply shortages across member states are "extremely high on the agenda and on our radar" and the topic will be discussed soon at a high-level meeting with the industry, EU countries and the Commission.

World.title: New book by Princess Diana's brother prompts war of words with King Charles
World.content:
A new book published on Tuesday by the brother of the late Princess Diana has made headlines around the world with its damning allegations about her ex-husband, now King Charles III, and reopened decades-old wounds within Britain's royal family.

 

In “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” Charles Spencer alleges that he argued with the then-Prince Charles over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession.

Spencer says he told Charles that Diana, who was killed in a car crash in Paris at the age of 36, would not have wanted her boys to undergo the ordeal.

He claims the prince “went ballistic” during the argument, and told him: "Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough."

Spencer also accuses Charles of having “contempt” for his ex-wife and of sounding “elated” after her death.

After excerpts of the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace responded with a strongly-worded statement that's rare by the measured standards of the royal household.

Britain's Prince Harry speaks with his uncle Earl Spencer at Kensington Palace, 1 July, 2021 AP Photo

“His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” it said.

Spencer has stood by his claims, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. On the royal rebuttal, he asked: “Is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?”

War of words

Charles, then 32, married 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer in a lavish ceremony at St. Paul’s Cathedral in 1981. The couple divorced in 1996, and a decade later Charles married Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla.

Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, has long clashed with the royals over their treatment of his older sister.

Tensions between the palace and the Spencer family following her death were dramatised in the film “The Queen” and the Netflix series "The Crown."

In a searing eulogy at his sister’s funeral, Spencer vowed that her “blood family” would carry on her “imaginative and loving” legacy in raising her two sons. The speech was widely considered a swipe at the royal family.

At the time, many in Britain and beyond felt Queen Elizabeth II and the royals were too slow to acknowledge the global outpouring of grief over Diana's death and that the monarchy was deeply out of touch with the public mood.

Britain's Prince Charles kisses his bride, the former Diana Spencer, on the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London, 29 July, 1981 AP Photo

Press treatment of Prince Harry

The royals have spent decades putting that period of crisis behind them. The warmer, more personable approach of William and Harry, and in recent years the king, is a legacy of that time.

In his book, Spencer also criticised the royals for what he described as a “lack of obvious care” for the then 12-year-old Harry.

He recounted how “tiny, and slight and bereft” his nephew looked after the funeral.

“He needed Diana’s hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him,” he wrote. “But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control.”

King Charles and Queen Camilla in Ottawa, 27 May, 2025 AP Photo

Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma 30 years on.

The aristocrat said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, “once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths.”

Asked if the relationship between the press and Harry and his wife, Meghan, mirrors the way the media treated his sister, Spencer told the BBC: “(Diana) was really brought low by all that criticism. I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now.”

Penguin Press said the book will be published globally and translated into 12 languages.

World.title: The EU spent billions on a cyberattack shield — nobody checked if it worked
World.content:
Brussels has allocated €1.4 billion to defending Europe from cyberattacks. Its own auditors found that when that funding is passed on to third parties, nobody independently checks whether it could be reaching organisations exposed to influence from hostile states.

 

The warning comes from a report published on Monday by the European Court of Auditors (ECA), which examined how well the EU detects and responds to major cybersecurity incidents between 2022 and 2025.

Grant beneficiaries are responsible for assessing the ownership and control of any third parties receiving EU cybersecurity funding. But the European Cybersecurity Competence Centre, the body overseeing these grants, does not verify those assessments itself, the auditors found.

As a result, sensitive infrastructure, operational data and security-critical technologies could be exposed to security risks.

The funding falls under the Digital Europe Programme, the EU's main channel for cybersecurity spending as part of its 2021-2027 budget.

An alarm system still lagging

The audit also found that the EU's early-warning network for major cyberattacks is not yet operational.

Two hubs meant to anchor the European Cybersecurity Alert System, known as ATHENA and ENSOC, still lack the tools to detect threats and share information after repeated procurement delays.

The cooperation agreements, common classification system and technical standards needed to get the alert system running were also still missing, auditors said.

"The EU has made progress in building a cybersecurity cooperation framework, but it is not yet working as effectively as it should," said George-Marius Hyzler, the ECA member in charge of the audit.

"When a serious cyber incident occurs, timely and actionable information is essential. Without it, networks and mechanisms lose much of their added value."

Information-sharing as the 'Achilles heel'

Auditors identified poor information-sharing as the central weakness in the EU's cyber defences, describing it as the "Achilles heel of the entire system".

The scale of the problem was laid bare last September, when a ransomware attack on Collins Aerospace, a major aviation technology provider, forced airports including London Heathrow, Brussels, Berlin Brandenburg and Dublin to revert to manual operations, causing widespread delays and cancellations.

Under the EU's own rules, an incident of that scale should have qualified as significant or large-scale, triggering formal notification. None of the affected states reported it as either.

It is not an isolated lapse. No member state has classified a single cybersecurity incident as "large-scale" since 2016 — not even WannaCry, NotPetya, or the global IT outage triggered by a faulty CrowdStrike update in 2024.

As a result, the EU's crisis-escalation procedure for major cyberattacks has never once been fully activated.

Member states formally notified just 14 cross-border incidents in 2025, submitted by only seven countries or a fraction of the 322 incidents affecting two or more member states that ENISA had separately identified the year before.

Gaps in the system

The Cyber Blueprint, adopted in 2025, largely clarifies roles and responsibilities during major cybersecurity crises.

However, how the EU's two main cyber networks work together has still not been formally defined, the report found. That has hampered cooperation between the CSIRTs network, which brings together national incident-response teams, and EU-CyCLONe, the bloc's crisis cooperation network.

All but two member states missed the deadline to transpose the EU's updated cybersecurity rules, including the NIS 2 Directive.

Together, auditors said, these gaps mean EU networks may struggle to detect threats early and mount an effective joint response.

Overlapping mandates

The report also flagged duplication between EU bodies tasked with monitoring cyber threats.

The European Commission's cyber situation centre, set up in 2022 and largely supported by external providers, was found to be doing work that overlaps with the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), which already monitors threats and builds situational awareness across the bloc.

The auditors' recommendations include improving information-sharing between EU networks, clarifying how bodies with overlapping mandates should work together, integrating the alert system into the wider cybersecurity landscape through clear cooperation agreements and interoperability standards, and strengthening security checks on funding recipients.

Responsibility for responding to cybersecurity incidents lies mainly with individual member states, but the EU also plays an important role when incidents cause major disruption, significant financial losses or affect several countries at once, beyond what any single state can handle alone.

The alert system was established under the EU Cyber Solidarity Act in February 2025 to act as a unified network for real-time monitoring, early threat detection and cross-border intelligence-sharing on large-scale cyberattacks against Europe.

Earlier this year, the European Commission proposed a new cybersecurity package to revise the Cybersecurity Act, including a strict, risk-based supply chain security framework to prevent high-risk third countries from accessing critical EU infrastructure.

The package also proposes drastically increasing ENISA's budget and revising existing EU and national laws to streamline the administration and implementation of Union-wide cybersecurity rules.

As of this September, under the Cyber Resilience Act, hardware and software manufacturers must report any exploited vulnerability or severe security incident within 24 hours to national CSIRTs and ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, with fines reaching up to €15 million or 2.5% of global turnover for serious breaches.

World.title: France’s budget: Oxfam targets ‘super-inheritances’ in tax plan
World.content:
At a time when every euro spent and saved is being scrutinised in the search for ways to reduce France's deficit, Oxfam is targeting a tax break for inherited family businesses that it says disproportionately benefits the wealthiest heirs.

 

In a report published on Tuesday, the NGO called for tighter limits on the Dutreil pact, which exempts 75% of a qualifying company’s value when gift or inheritance tax is calculated.

Oxfam estimates that reforming the scheme could raise more than €3bn a year, as France searches for savings and additional revenue ahead of its 2027 budget.

As the French public deficit and public debt worsen between 2025 and 2026 — with the deficit expected to rise from 5.1% to 5.4% of GDP and debt from 115.7% to 119.3% — the government says significant fiscal measures will be needed in the coming years. In this context, Oxfam argues that the budgetary effort could also involve a thorough review of certain tax breaks.

What is the Dutreil pact?

Introduced in 2003 and named after the then Minister for Trade and Crafts, Renaud Dutreil, the Dutreil pact is designed to make it easier to pass a family business from one generation to the next.

Under the scheme, only 25% of a qualifying company’s value is taken into account when gift or inheritance tax is calculated. The aim is to prevent heirs from having to sell the business to pay the tax.

In return, beneficiaries must keep the company shares for a set period and meet rules on how the business is run. France tightened the scheme in 2026 by extending the minimum holding period from four to six years and excluding assets not used for the business, such as homes, works of art and jewellery.

According to Oxfam, the Dutreil pact has cost the French state almost €3bn a year on average over the past four years, with a peak of more than €5.5bn in 2024, according to the French Court of Auditors.

Oxfam believes that maintaining the current rules could mean an even bigger shortfall in future. According to its calculations, passing on the wealth of French billionaires over the age of 70 via the Dutreil pact could deprive the public finances of more than €111bn over the next 30 years.

This figure is a projection rather than an amount that the state would automatically recover if the scheme were scrapped. But for Oxfam, it illustrates the budgetary potential of reforming the scheme.

Various euro banknotes - Illustration AP Photo

Oxfam targets France's largest fortunes

For the organisation, the main problem is the concentration of this tax advantage. Oxfam argues that the wealthiest beneficiaries gain far more from the scheme than others.

According to its calculations, the 110 most advantaged beneficiaries, or around 1% of the total, each saved an average of €30 million in tax between 2023 and 2024. By contrast, the least advantaged half of beneficiaries each saved less than €40,000 on average.

Oxfam uses the term “super-inheritances” to refer to the estates received by the top 0.1% of heirs. The organisation estimates that these inheritances average €13m and that their effective tax rate is around 10%, even though the theoretical marginal rate can reach 45% for the largest transfers.

Oxfam therefore proposes capping the tax advantage available under the Dutreil pact at one million euros per beneficiary. It estimates that this reform would leave 90% of current beneficiaries unaffected by the cap, while allowing the state to recover more than €3bn a year.

The organisation also recommends reducing the exemption rate from 75% to 50%, restricting it more closely to strictly business-related assets and introducing a requirement to preserve jobs.

The debate on the Dutreil pact could therefore feature in discussions on France’s 2027 draft budget. The key question will be how far this tax advantage can be curtailed without undermining its original aim: to make it easier to pass on businesses and avoid families being forced to sell them to pay inheritance tax.

But according to Layla Abdelke Yakoub, advocacy manager for tax justice and inequality at Oxfam France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu “was keen to stress that the government would not touch the Dutreil pact” when presenting his initial budget plans.

“This refusal to touch such an unfair tax loophole does not meet French people’s wish to see the largest fortunes contribute more,” she said. “Oxfam hopes the prime minister will have a change of heart; the ball is in his court.”

Behind the technical debate over the Dutreil pact lies a much more political question: in a France desperately searching for billions to get its public finances back on track, how much of the effort should be borne by the very largest fortunes and the biggest inheritances?

World.title: After floods, Nepal minister demands 'climate justice'
World.content:
With Nepal still reeling from the devastating floods in August, Kathmandu is calling for climate justice and seeking compensation from the UN-backed Loss and Damage Fund, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary told DW.

Nepal is seeking $20 million (just under €17.5 million) from the international Loss and Damage Fund, the UN-backed mechanism designed to support countries suffering irreversible climate-related losses, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary said in an exclusive DW interview.

The move comes after floods and landslides killed more than 1,400 people in August and left thousands missing.

"We have already issued the official letter for the fund for the loss and damage," Chaudhary told DW. "Most of the countries have sent us a positive response."

The flash flooding caused widespread destruction across large swathes of Nepal, damaging homes, agricultural land and infrastructure. Rescue and recovery efforts are still ongoing in several areas, while authorities continue to assess the full scale of the losses.

In the Himalayan nation, the tragedy has become a powerful symbol of what developing countries describe as the unfair climate burden of contributing little to global emissions while facing disproportionate consequences.

'Sympathy alone will not work for us'

Talking to DW, Chaudhary repeatedly framed Nepal's response through the lens of climate justice, a concept that has become increasingly prominent in global climate negotiations.

"Sympathy alone will not work for us," she said. "We don't need sympathy. We need justice. It's high time. If you're not able to give us justice, then we also don't need the words."

"Those countries who are emitting the most and are able to contribute the funds, they need to pay for the climatic disasters like what we are facing," she said.

Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Its geography, however, makes it extremely vulnerable to climate-related risks. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas have accelerated glacial retreat and increased concerns about glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and extreme weather events across the region.

Alps warming fast: Europe's water lifeline is running dry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the wake of the most recent disaster, the government has intensified calls for more adaptation financing, direct access to climate funds and stronger international commitments to fight consequences of climate change.

'The world is watching'

Chaudhary pointed to melting glaciers, warming temperatures and changes in mountain environments as factors behind the deadly floods.

"Our evidence is showing that this catastrophic event is because of climate change," Chaudhary said.

While many scientists agree that climate change increases the likelihood and severity of such events, establishing a causal relationship between a specific disaster and global warming typically requires detailed attribution studies.

Researchers are more likely to point to a combination of factors, including glacier and permafrost degradation, extreme weather conditions and geological vulnerabilities.

The Nepali government, however, insists that the connection is clear.

"We are the real example and the world is watching us," Chaudhary told DW.

Building support ahead of COP31

The minister's comments come as Nepal seeks to build momentum for COP31, the UN's annual climate conference set to be held in Turkey this November.

When asked about her government's plans for the conference, Chaudhary said "Nepal will no longer negotiate on vague promises or slow-moving traditional and development aid."

According to the minister, Nepal intends to push for greater recognition of the specific challenges facing mountainous countries, arguing that global climate discussions often overlook the risks confronting Himalayan regions.

"Mountain issues need to be addressed," she said. "The world needs to see us, that we are victimized countries. We are paying the price."

Chaudhary also pointed out that Nepal received strong backing from fellow vulnerable nations at the recent gathering of Least Developed Countries (LDCs) in Timor-Leste.

"All the LDCs stood with us," she said. "They are very concerned."

The government plans to bring climate concerns to the UN General Assembly, highlighting the recent disaster and calling for concrete support from the international community.

Nepal to improve its early warning systems

The scale of the disaster has also prompted scrutiny inside Nepal, particularly of the country's warning systems and its disaster response.

Residents in some affected areas have complained that warnings came too late or did not adequately reflect the scale of the danger.

After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chaudhary defended the government's response but conceded that existing systems were overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the event.

"We had sent them messages and information," she said. "But the situation was beyond imagination."

She acknowledged that Nepal's early warning systems must improve and said authorities are now reviewing and strengthening existing monitoring mechanisms.

"Our hydrology and meteorology departments are working on that," she said.

The floods also highlighted the importance of cooperation between Nepal and its neighbors, particularly China, in monitoring river systems and glacial hazards that cut through national borders.

"We are working closely," Chaudhary said, adding that technical teams from both countries are sharing information and examining future risks.

Himalayan catastrophe as a warning for the world

For Chaudhary, the disaster is not only a national tragedy but a warning about the future.

"Our snow is melting, our lakes are in danger," the minister said.

She warned that, unless global warming is limited in line with the Paris climate agreement of 2015, vulnerable countries could face increasingly severe disasters.

Asked whether the world is acting fast enough, the minister responded: "I don't think so."

World.title: Could we see MMA at the Olympics?
World.content:
Mixed martial arts has made its debut at the Asian Games this week. It takes the sport closer to the Olympics but there are doubts about the next step, and the influence of the popular and lucrative UFC.

The form of mixed martial arts (MMA) making its debut at the Asian Games looks almost completely distinct from the visceral brawls of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), which have come to define combat sports in recent years.

In order to get a version of the sport into the Games, currently taking place in Nagoya in Japan, adaptations had to be made. The fights take place without the familiar cage, on an open mat and with small boxing-style gloves. While MMA's presence in the Asian Games is significant in itself, it's also a clear effort to get close to Olympic recognition.

"We think without the cage we will have a better alignment with the Olympic values and hopefully recognition from the IOC," Galastein Tan, the director general of Federation of International Mixed Martial Arts (FIMMA), told press agency AP . "It takes time to change a perception. We hope to be able to share that there is a new form of MMA, and this form is more aligned with the Olympics."

FIMMA is not the only body purporting to represent the sport, with the International Mixed Martial Arts (IMMAF) also staking a claim. But Tan, a Chinese billionaire property mogul, is a vice president of the Olympic Council of Asia. This could potentially open doors in a movement which has so far kept MMA at arm's length, with violence levels among its concerns. DW contacted both FIMMA and the IMMAF for comment but received no response.

UFC has outstripped MMA

In the past the UFC, a lucrative MMA-based competition, has also pushed for Olympic recognition. But the growth of that arm of the sport, highlighted by it staging an event on the South Lawn of the White House at the 250th anniversary celebrations of US independence earlier this year, has meant that the aims of a sport that was marginal two decades ago have shifted according to Karim Zidan.

UFC hosted matches at the White House earlier this year Image: Kent Nishimura/AP Photo/picture alliance

"I don't necessarily think it's that important to MMA. The sport has already found its success on a professional level, which is what the fan base demanded of it," said Zidan, who has written an upcoming book 'The Ultimate Strongmen: MMA and the Rise of the New Authoritarian Right' on the subject.

"The UFC is bigger than it's ever been in terms of the amount of money it's making" added Zidan. "The UFC's growth mainstreamed MMA as a sport, but it also cannibalized it. So there's really not much remaining. Olympic recognition might seem like a badge of honor, but it doesn't amount to much else."

With events for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles already set, the earliest MMA could make its bow would be 2032 in Brisbane. But the IOC told AP that "mixed martial arts does not meet ... eligibility criteria" at this point. DW has sought clarification from the IOC on this.

Does MMA have enough appeal for Olympics?

Tan appears to be trying to find a way to change that, citing the sport's popularity. "MMA is popular globally, able to engage fans at a gut level and attract fans at a youth level," he said.

But Zidan argues that its popularity is through the UFC, rather than any grassroots popularity.

"There isn't much of an MMA ecosystem outside of the UFC for me to say there's an entirely different worldview existing in the sport that's demanding this. There are pockets within the sport that enjoy amateur MMA and are operating within it, but I don't think it's a significant part of the fan base at all," Zidan said.

"I'm not particularly convinced that this is a turning point or a significant moment for mixed martial arts, honestly. I think the sport has suffered tremendously under the burden and the weight of the UFC over the past decade."

Senegal gears up for Youth Olympic Games To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UFC's links with the Trump administration are deep and clear, with UFC president Dana White also speaking at the Republican convention in 2024.

But Zidan also pointed to the IMMAF's link up with Brave Combat Federation, a Bahraini organization headed by Khalid bin Hamad Al Khalifa, a son of King of Bahrain, Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa. A 2025 Amnesty International Report said Bahrain continued to "to suppress the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including through arbitrary detention and prosecutions."

Authoritarian links remain for MMA

Such links with authoritarian governments have become, Zidan added, fairly commonplace in the sport.

"They've already had associations with authoritarian regimes in the past and it's very likely that relationship will build. If this [the Asian Games and potential Olympic acceptance] means that we will now have more amateur MMA events being hosted around the world in youth championships, it's very likely that authoritarian regimes will jump on that."

The challenge for FIMMA, who appear to want to take MMA in the Olympic direction and away from UFC and its associations, is to make the sport more "normal" and less about spectacle, FIMMA's vice president Alex Engelhardt told AP.

"It's very challenging in the sense that the whole mindset in the sport is so focused on promotions," he said.

Even if that can change, and sport's debut at the Asian Games adds some legitimacy, the Olympics still seem some way off.

World.title: Iran war spreads through region as Trump seeks way out
World.content:
Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue different objectives while searching for a way to end the Iran war.

Nearly seven months into the Iran war, negotiations between Washington and Tehran have led nowhere, and the conflict has spread from the Strait of Hormuz to another strategically important shipping route.

In September, Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen took over critical positions on the Yemeni coast and are threatening Red Sea trade routes while launching attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia. This compounds a global energy crunch brought on by the Strait of Hormuz blockade.

Earlier in September, Saudi officials blamed Iran-backed militias in Iraq for blowing up the critical East-West oil pipeline.

According to The New York Times, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called US President Donald Trump on Sunday to once again urge him to intervene and stop the Houthi's rapid advance.

Trump is reported to have considered airstrikes against the Houthis at one point, but later abandoned the plans. This weekend, Fox News reported that Trump said the Houthi rebels had agreed not to attack US targets. The US news outlet Axios also reported that Trump had rejected a Saudi request for strikes against the Houthis the previous week.

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump seeks a way out

Against the backdrop of record high gasoline and diesel prices coming down hard on voters ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump is under pressure to show results in the Iran war.

"President Trump wants to end the Iran war from a position that allows him to claim that Iran's nuclear and military capabilities have been significantly weakened, freedom of navigation has been restored, and Tehran has been forced back to the negotiating table," Iran expert Fatemeh Aman told DW.

Aman, who has worked with organizations including the Middle East Institute, the Atlantic Council, RFE/RL and Voice of America, however, added that a coherent strategy for achieving these objectives remains difficult to discern.

The US has imposed high military and economic costs on Iran and appears to have made progress in weakening the country's military capabilities. But Tehran has not capitulated and there is no lasting ceasefire agreement.

Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week. China is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil and an important political partner of Tehran. The US president is likely to bring up China's economic and financial ties with Iran and hope that Beijing will use its influence over Tehran — particularly when it comes to the security of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, Trump has signaled that he is open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is traveling to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Senior representatives from the Gulf states are also expected in the US over the coming days.

According to Axios, Trump plans to discuss the Iran war with representatives of several Gulf states on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gulf nations want regional stability

There is still no common position emerging between Iran and its Arab neighbors in the Gulf. A planned meeting involving Iran, the Gulf states and Iraq was canceled last week. The cancellation may be linked to the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

"At first glance, there appears to be little common ground between Iran and the Gulf states," Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told DW. "But behind the scenes, there is at least a shared interest in preventing further military escalation."

The Gulf states recognize that they would be unlikely to prevail in a direct military confrontation with Iran, and generally favor de-escalation and a pragmatic easing of tensions with Tehran.

An agreement, however, is not currently in sight. In particular, Iran's demands for greater control over the Strait of Hormuz go too far from the perspective of the Gulf states.

The war in Yemen further limits the scope for rapprochement. Saudi Arabia, for example, is unlikely to make concessions while it remains under pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis.

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran's two-track strategy

A permanently hostile, US-backed coalition of Gulf states would be strategically costly for Tehran, Aman said.

She added Iran could pursue a two-track strategy: This would involve resisting a US-led regional containment architecture, while simultaneously offering the Gulf states an alternative model of regional security based on accommodation and dialogue.

"After all, the Gulf states are not only Iran's rivals but also its neighbors — and neither side can change that geographic reality," Aman said.

According to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei, Tehran is demanding that the US end the fighting on all fronts.

Tehran is also calling for the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets and the lifting of the naval blockade in the strait. Talks with Qatar and Oman are reportedly continuing. The Iranian regime is now waiting for a response from Trump. Whether these diplomatic signals can translate into a broader political process remains uncertain.

For now, the main obstacle is that Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue very different roadmaps for ending the months-long conflict.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Turkey: Several pupils injured in shooting outside school
World.content:
The shooter, a pupil, allegedly took a rifle and shot indiscriminately at his schoolmates in front of their high school. Turkey was shocked by two back-to-back school shootings earlier this year.

A shooting near a high school in Turkey's Manisa province resulted in at least 11 injured pupils, two of whom were in critical condition on Tuesday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.

The shooter, a pupil at the school, was arrested together with both of his parents and his grandfather.

What do we know about the shooting incident?

The suspect is said to have taken the weapon from his grandparents' house, with his grandfather believed to have had a licence for it.

Local authorities said the attack took place at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district at about 08:00am local time (07:00 CET).

The motive for the shooting is also under investigation. Some reports suggest the student had suffered from bullying.

Two back-to-back school shootings in April left around 10 killed and dozens more injured Image: Ensar Ozdemir/REUTERS

"When the ​security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any ​negligence, any irresponsibility to be overlooked," the minister posted on his X account.

"The ‌circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon's storage, the parents' obligations regarding care ‌and supervision, and allegations of bullying prior to the incident ‌are ​being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles," Gurlek added.

Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the school, while police told families to stay away from the area.

Gun control tightened after school shootings

School shootings are rare in Turkey, but this year alone saw two back-to-back shootings that shocked the nation.

Two school shootings that took place in April resulted in the tightening of gun controls and the increase of security measures at educational facilities as the academic year started last week.

Several students and their teacher were killed in one of the attacks, with the other resulting in 16 people being injured.

According to Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, 31,000 school supervisors and police officers on duty were assigned to school seen as being at risk, as per a new measure introduced only on Monday.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan responded to the latest shooting attack by promising even tighter gun controls.

"When we look at similar attacks around the world, especially in the United States, we see one of the perpetrators' aims is to terrorise society," the Turkish leader said.

World.title: Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes as Zelenskyy attends UNGA
World.content:
The Russian army targeted economic infrastructure in Ukraine, while Ukraine struck an oil refinery. This comes ahead of the UN General Assembly, where President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is due to meet Trump on the sidelines.

Russia and Ukraine traded strikes targeting infrastructure overnight, ahead of a United Nations General Assembly where the war in Ukraine is due to be widely discussed.

Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight into Tuesday killed four people, Ukrainian officials said, while also cutting the electricity supply to thousands.

The strikes took place in the cities Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram. The barrage included anti-ship and ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 212 drones.

DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The region of Dnipropetrovsk is the country's industrial heartland, where major production industries are located, including steel-making and machine building.

In the city of Dnipro, four people were killed and six were injured. According to Hanzha, the strike also damaged a local business and a warehouse.

Ukraine strikes Russian oil refinery; 1 killed

In Russia, Ukrainian drones killed one person and injured four in the Samara region, local authorities said. The region is home to important facilities, including oil refineries.

Moscow's Defense Ministry said it had intercepted 297 drones over various regions in Russia overnight.

Samara is located some 1,000 kilometers southeast of Russian capital Moscow.

Zelenskyy attends UN General Assembly

Russia and Ukraine have both stepped up attacks recently, as the war has dragged on for four and a half years with no end in sight.

Both parties deny targeting civilians, while also blaming each other for civilian casualties.

The latest attacks come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is planning to meet US counterpart Donald Trump in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not expected at the UN General Assembly.

World.title: Male infertility is 'grossly underreported'
World.content:
It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm. Spoiler: It doesn't.

Sperm counts have fallen globally by more than 51% since 1973, and the decline is accelerating. That's according to a 2026 review of studies published in the journal Antioxidants . But men are less likely to get tested than women for infertility.

"Male infertility is understated. It is so huge a problem," said Edidiong Akang, a reproductive biologist at the University of Lagos, Nigeria.

In a study led by Akang and published in the journal Scientific Reports in 2023, he and his colleagues analyzed semen samples from more than 17,000 men and found that the quality of sperm shape and size (known as sperm morphology) had deteriorated by about 50% between 2010 and 2019.

Sperm motility (how well it swims to the female egg) had also dropped significantly — in Nigeria, for example, by 87% in that same period.

And yet, as Akang told DW, the male share of infertility is "grossly underreported" and, as a result, misunderstood.

What affects a man's fertility?

Male fertility depends on a healthy sperm shape, size, motility, and its concentration and count. The latter is often used as an indication of male fertility because many millions try to reach the egg but only one or few make it. They need to be strong swimmers.

Why do some healthy embryos fail to implant in the uterus? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

These factors depend on other, underlying health conditions: Male infertility can be caused by weight gain, stress, poor sleep, smoking, microplastics and cannabis use.

Weight gain in particular effects the testes (also: testicles), which produce sperm and hormones like testosterone.

The testes function best at two degrees centigrade cooler than the rest of the body. Fat raises the temperature, and that can affect the sperm — its concentration, count and motility.

Why male infertility often goes undiagnosed

Male sexual health is often overlooked, possibly because men under the age of 40 don't generally have a regular reason to get checked — if you're older than 40, you may get your prostate checked annually. But even a urologist won't check your sperm count unless you ask them.

Women, on the other hand, get a monthly signal — their menstrual cycle — and may be able to infer from that that something is wrong.

A man gets no such natural signals about his fertility until he tries to conceive with a woman. And by then he may be 30 or 40, when some health outcomes are hard to reverse.

Riffat Bibi, a clinical embryologist who has led an IVF laboratory in Pakistan for 17 years, described what men often say on arrival: "Okay, check my wife first."

Sometimes a mother-in-law brings the daughter-in-law, which also suggests that the mother-in-law thinks: It can't be my son's fault.

And some patients "feel sexual activity is equivalent to fertility, which it is not," said Bibi.

Roughly 80% of Bibi's cases now involve a male factor, far above the 50-50 split long assumed, and her laboratory has had to adapt, she said.

They are also seeing this development in IVF (in vitro fertilization) treatment. Sperm has become so poor that nearly all her clients need an embryologist to pick a single sperm and inject it directly into the egg.

But there is another factor than many men don't talk about much: synthetic testosterone — or steroids.

IVF explained: Process, costs & risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Testosterone shuts down sperm production

Some men, keen on a muscley body, suppress their own sperm production unknowingly by taking anabolic steroids, a synthetic form of testosterone.

The appeal of anabolic steroids is straightforward, said Harrison Pope, a Harvard Medical School researcher: Steroids enhance athletic performance. A steroid user, who drinks, smokes and skips half of his workouts can outperform a dedicated, clean athlete.

Pope, who has studied steroids for three decades, said "they are highly effective."

But what you gain in athletic performance, you lose in fertility, because an over-supply of testosterone can shut down sperm production.

A healthy body will keep testosterone levels in balance. Too little testosterone can also impede sperm production.

Sperm production can restart if you stop taking testosterone supplements, but Pope said it depends on your age, and much you were taking and for how long.

Occasional steroid users usually regain a "normal" sperm count. The World Health Organization considers a normal sperm count to be about 16 million sperm per milliliter of semen (or higher).

Heavy, long-term steroid users, meanwhile, often do not recover or return to normal sperm production.

Users typically take steroids in cycles – weeks on the drug, followed by a a break to let the body recover. But when Dutch researchers followed 100 men through one cycle of steroids and for a year after, they found two-thirds still had very low sperm counts, some had no sperm at all, and a year later, their counts had still not returned to normal.

Not everyone takes steroids, and yet falling sperm counts still occur. Take India, for example, where Chirag Bhandari, runs the Institute of Andrology and Sexual Health in Jaipur. Bhandari estimates that steroids account for less than 0.1% of the country's falling sperm counts. Overweight, heat-stress and smoking are usually the cause.

If a man is tested early, his sperm count will often return to normal within six to twelve months, both Bhandari and Bibi said. But the longer the problem goes undetected, the less likely that becomes.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: UNGA: Leaders gather as General Assembly kicks off
World.content:
Skip next section World leaders gather in New York for 81st UNGA session

09/22/2026 September 22, 2026 World leaders gather in New York for 81st UNGA session

United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres and Assembly President Khalilur Rahman

will open the UN's 81st General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday morning as world leaders gather for their annual six-day confab.

As Guterres puts it, "In a world marked by turbulence, division and uncertainty, the United Nations is more necessary than ever."

This year's session comes as war — mainly in Ukraine and Iran — climate catastrophe, and the specter of artificial intelligence overshadow the world's myriad other problems.

The session offers an opportunity for leaders to politick in person with numerous bilateral meetings expected to take place on the main stage's sidelines.

The event will likely get off to a rousing start when US President Donald Trump — who has delivered belligerent and fantastical addresses in the past — takes the stage after Brazilian President Inacio Lula Da Silva in the morning session and before Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Further speakers will include leaders from Africa, Central Asia, Europe, Scandinavia, South America and the Middle East.
