World.title: Poland’s Catholic church recruits priests from Africa and Asia to stave off vocations crisis
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Marcin Choduń (published in cooperation with Tygodnik Powszechny) With the number of Poles training to be priests falling steadily, Catholic parishes are increasingly looking beyond Europe to fill the gaps. Father Fransiskus Laka will never forget his first day in Poland. When he stepped out of the arrivals hall at Warsaw’s Okęcie (now Chopin) airport in October 1999, he thought he would not last long. Why? The bitter chill in the air. “It was only seven degrees,” he laughs. It is not surprising that the young man from Indonesia was having second thoughts. At home, a cool day meant 25°C. Now, though, having spent 27 years in Poland, no weather fazes him. In the middle of winter, he will sometimes even go out in just a T-shirt to shovel snow or bring wood for the stove. Father Fransiskus has settled in the village of Brzegi, near Zakopane in southern Poland, where he has been parish priest for the last two years. And the mountainous Podhale region it is part of still has long, cold and snowy winters. Father Fransiskus, a Verbite, is not the only foreign Roman Catholic priest working in Poland, where around 70% of the population is Catholic. Their numbers are growing every year in response to the rising shortage of Polish priests. Polish dioceses are increasingly keen to invite young foreigners to study at their seminaries. Poland’s shortage of priests Most of those invited are from Africa. In Kielce, for example, there are currently two seminarians from the Central African Republic and seven from Angola. The Tarnów seminary also trained a priest from the Central African Republic in recent years (ordained as a deacon in the nearby village of Szynwałd in 2024). In the diocese of Ełk, Bishop Jerzy Mazur announced in a letter read out in churches in 2023 that he would be combating the shortage of priests by inviting clergy from Africa to the diocesan seminary. In return for receiving training in Poland, the newly ordained priests were to spend at least a few years working in the region. Previously, the support of retired priests had been sufficient. But, as the shortage grew, the curia even considered reducing the number of services or merging parishes. That was when the idea of seeking help from abroad came about. Just one new priest was ordained in Łódź, Poland's fourth largest city, this year – the lowest figure ever recorded One church figure admits there has been a “dramatic decline” in interest in the priesthood while the head of a seminary calls it a “crisis” https://t.co/QuwKsoPSg3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2023 “Priests from Poland increasingly work for as long as their health permits,” says Andrzej Kobyliński, a priest and ethicist from Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University in Warsaw. “However, that doesn’t change the fact that, in a few years’ time, we’ll have a staffing shortfall, because Polish seminaries are more and more deserted.” In recent years, a lack of recruits has led to several seminaries merging or closing down. The Wrocław, Legnica and Świdnica seminaries have been combined into one institution – which in reality means the two smaller schools being transferred to the big city. Clerical students in Kalisz have met a similar fate, having to go to Częstochowa to study, while seminarians from Elbląg have been sent to Olsztyn. The seminaries in Łowicz and Bydgoszcz have closed, and education in Drohiczyn and Sandomierz has been suspended. “The changes are happening at such an alarming rate that at present over a dozen seminaries will need to be closed,” says Kobyliński. “Let’s take the Płock diocese. You could say that the students in the seminary there are being put through a mental ordeal.” “Since there are currently 13 seminarians studying in seven year groups, that means that some years are empty or only have one or two people. That causes terrible loneliness. Because how can you survive seven years on your own?” For Kobyliński, the Ełk diocese is a symbol of the changes that are coming. This year, it only ordained one deacon – from Togo, West Africa. A new home in Poland The deacon’s name is Roger and he arrived in Poland a few years ago, along with another prospective priest from Togo who decided to return home for personal reasons. “There are currently seven people studying in our seminary, three of them from Africa. Apart from Roger, we have two more, from Ghana,” says Marcin Maczan, chancellor of the Ełk curia. According to him, however, the presence of African seminarians in Ełk is not only a response to the shortage of priests. “Bishop Jerzy Mazur, who himself spent several years working in Ghana and in the past was the head of the missions committee of the Polish Episcopal Conference, is familiar with the realities of mission dioceses. He knows very well that they can always use help in training priests.” “So these two ideas were combined: training a priest for his home diocese in Africa and his ministry in Poland for eight to ten years after ordination. All in line with the terms of the agreements that the bishop of Ełk made with bishops in Africa,” Maczan says. These agreements vary. Some priests return to their home dioceses shortly after ordination – seminarians from Kielce, for instance. Others remain for many years, such as Father Fransiskus Laka, whose stay in Poland is prolonged by the congregation’s provincial superior every three years. Poland was not his first choice. Shortly before being ordained, each of the clerical students in Fransiskus’s seminary, the Divine Word Missionaries in Pieniężno, northeastern Poland, was supposed to name three countries where they wished to serve. He chose Ecuador, Nicaragua and, in last place, Poland. Usually, one of the first two options is selected, but the provincial superior suggested otherwise. A surprised Fransiskus agreed, and he has never regretted his decision. After spending the first four years in the parish in Pieniężno, he returned to the seminary to become a prefect, responsible for keeping order. In this period, he travelled the length and breadth of Poland to lead retreats in parishes. He then spent seven years as a curate in Chludów, near Poznań, before in 2024 becoming the priest of the parish of St Anthony in Brzegi in the Podhale region. “I arrived on 8 December – so almost immediately I had Christmas pastoral visits to make to parishioners’ homes,” says Father Fransiskus. “They really welcomed me very warmly. They often help me – show me how to light the stove, or leave food outside my door. I learn hard work, humility, patience and faith from them. The mountains are tough terrain – you really need grit to survive.” Poland became home. Fransiskus feels safe here – despite growing hostility towards foreigners, which is particularly visible in the public and online space (foreign ministry statistics confirm that in 2024-2025 the total number of hate crimes reported in Poland increased by more than 50% – from 760 to almost 1,200 cases). “I’ve never yet encountered any hostile behaviour towards me,” says Fransiskus. Although he regularly visits his home island of Lembata, there are many things in Indonesia that he can no longer accept. The organisation of mass, for example: if it is supposed to begin, say, at 7 a.m., worshippers turn up just before 9. They don’t understand why Fransiskus sees this as a problem. Or a bus journey – when the driver passes his house, he’ll usually take a break to have lunch and play with his children. “The passengers wait patiently and no one thinks anything of it,” laughs Fransiskus. The Togolese footballing priest Father Romuald Mawakina Tchilabalo Mozou, from Togo (pictured top), is a newer arrival in Poland. His stay in the country is on the same basis as Fransiskus – an interdiocesan agreement extended every three years. Romuald has only been here seven years, but already speaks impeccable Polish, with barely a trace of a foreign accent. Upon arriving in Poland, he learned the language intensively – for seven months, from Monday to Saturday, seven hours a day. “I knew from the outset that if I couldn’t communicate well with the faithful, I wouldn’t build any relationship with them,” he says. Romuald was born in the village of Kaza, near Sotouboua. His father was a French teacher in the local primary school. And so his first language was French – he only learned Kabije, the ethnic language in northern Togo, in later years. His family is Catholic. And their neighbours? A mixture, just like everywhere else in Togo: the majority are Muslims, but there are also some Catholics and followers of traditional faiths. The proportion of people in Poland who are religious non-believers has risen to a record 14% while those who attend Sunday mass have fallen to a low of 34%. But a large majority of Poles still identify as believers and Catholics https://t.co/2yqrLePAsw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 23, 2024 The Mozou family are very religious. As a young boy, Romuald and his family would pray together daily, and this was what first brought him into indirect contact with Poland: every evening, along with his parents, two sisters and two brothers, he recited Saint Faustina Kowalska’s Chaplet of the Divine Mercy. He also associated Poland with John Paul II – to date the only pope to have visited Togo. Romuald’s great passion has always been football. His dream of a professional career led him to neglect his studies, until his father made things clear: first school, then football. While at high school, however, Romuald started to consider the priesthood. After taking his exams, he began studying in a seminary in Lomé, the Togolese capital. Three years in, the bishop proposed that he go to Poland to study at the seminary in Opole. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 As a dean, Father Romuald gained hands-on experience in Krapkowice. After his ordination in May 2024, he became a curate in Opole (and from August this year he will be based in nearby Ujazd). I ask him how the new parishioners responded to him. “Well, to be honest, they were a little surprised at first,” he laughed. “But that’s hardly surprising – after all, I’m the first priest from Africa to serve in the Opole diocese. They gave me a very warm welcome, though – I’ve never encountered any unfriendly gestures or words from them.” In Poland, Romuald’s childhood passion has been rekindled: he’s playing football again. First for Maciowakrze, a club playing in Klasa B (the eighth tier of the Polish league system), then in Żywocice, in Klasa A. He now plays as a striker for GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory. “I don’t know if I’ll return to my homeland – everything is possible,” Romuald says. “I feel good in both Poland and Togo.” Polish dioceses recruiting in Africa In 2026, 196 priests are to be ordained in Poland – 12 fewer than last year and some 205 down on the figure from 2013. The number of dioceses in which no ordinations took place because of a lack of candidates is growing – seven this year, compared to six in 2025. “We actually have a vocations crisis everywhere in Europe, so we will be looking for priests in other parts of the world,” says Andrzej Kobyliński. “Essentially, we have two areas where we can recruit candidates for the priesthood. Mainly Africa, and possibly India, but the experiences of German and Italian dioceses show that priests from India find it harder to settle in Europe.” “Latin America is not an option, as the Catholic church there is facing its own crisis of a mass exodus to Pentecostal churches,” he adds. “So in the future we will definitely be working intensively with African dioceses. This is an enormous historical change, because it was once Poland and Europe that sent missionaries to Africa.” One of the lads Przywory, a village near Opole, the GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory home pitch. Seven p.m. Training has started. Father Romuald Mozou is a little late, so he rushes into the dressing room. “Romek, you’re doing push-ups as punishment,” laugh his teammates when he appears on the pitch. Everyone calls him by this Polish diminutive – Romek. The team’s coach, Marcin Chudala, admits that the players like to have a laugh at the footballing priest’s expense. “Sometimes we joke when he’s sitting on the bench staring at his phone: ‘What are you doing, Romek – confessing?’ The banter can be cruel,” says the coach. But he also admits that Romek’s presence has left its mark on the team. Less swearing, for example. Even if there is nothing to suggest that Romek is a priest. “We treat him just like one of the lads from the playground,” Chudala says. The original version of this interview can be seen here. Translated by Ben Koschalka. Marcin Choduń is a journalist and translator of German and English. He publishes his articles mainly in Tygodnik Powszechny and Duży Format, a supplement of Gazeta Wyborcza. In 2012, he was nominated for the Grand Press Award in the reportage category for his article “The Blood of a Skinhead, the Blood of a Jew”. World.title: Poland to expand warning siren network along Ukraine border amid Russian attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland plans to have more than 1,000 warning sirens in the eastern Lublin province by the end of the year in response to increased Russian attacks in Ukraine near the Polish border, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński has announced. The Polish government is also working on an application that would use Cell Broadcast technology to turn mobile phones into warning devices, allowing them to function like sirens in a crisis, the minister added. Minister @MKierwinski w Lublinie:💬Budujemy system ochrony ludności niemal od podstaw. W województwie lubelskim na początku 2024 roku było około 30 syren, które można było uruchomić zdalnie. Dziś jest ich prawie 350, a do końca tego roku będzie ich ponad tysiąc. To pokazuje, jak… pic.twitter.com/6uWAgcNrJh — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 19, 2026 Speaking in Lublin on Saturday, Kierwiński said that the region now has almost 350 automatic sirens, compared to just 30 at the start of 2024. The number is expected to triple to over 1,000 by the end of this year. “Jet-powered drones and missiles are increasingly flying near the Polish border” and Poland is therefore “turning to tools designed to counter the associated threats,” Kierwiński said, quoted by news website OKO Press, adding that the government had to build Poland’s civil protection system “almost from scratch”. As part of these efforts, Poland’s fire service, working with the Lublin governor, is now rolling out a project to identify and mark the province’s nearly 3,500 shelters. Last year, Poland launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in the case of an emergency. By the end of the year, Poland also wants to introduce an application that would allow it to “take over” residents’ phones “to function like a siren”, Kierwiński added, without providing any further details. Residents in areas close to the Ukrainian border have heard warning sirens during Russian attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks and received alerts through the state warning system. The opposition has criticised the alerts for not giving residents clear instructions on what to do when the sirens sound. In response, the ministry has stepped up its public information campaign, including a television and social media campaign on emergency preparedness. Additionally, more than 500 fire stations in the eastern Lublin and Subcarpathian provinces held training over the weekend on how to respond to emergency alerts. The sessions were part of a wider campaign that has already involved 630,000 people across Poland. Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats https://t.co/MS0APufAmq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Poland has stepped up preparations along its eastern border following a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation follows a number of incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski described the attacks in the border area as “another escalation” by Russia, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. During his visit to Ukraine last week, Tusk announced that Poland had joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries working together to develop an integrated air defence system for the continent. World.title: Moody’s cuts Poland’s credit rating to lowest level since 2002
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. World.title: Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
World.content:
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.

Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.



Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.

Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.

If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.

Last winter was colder than average

The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.

According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.

The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.

Heating costs could increase next year

Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.

The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.

Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Where to See Prague’s Best Autumn Colors Without Leaving the City
World.content:
Autumn in Prague does not have to mean a crowded walk across Petřín or a stroll through Stromovka.

Beyond the city’s best-known parks, forests, valleys and protected natural areas offer quieter routes where the changing season can be enjoyed without leaving Prague.

Many of these places are also surprisingly easy to reach. A tram, bus or train can take you close to the starting point, making it possible to plan a two- or three-hour walk without a car or a full-day trip.



Vinoř Park and the Satalice Pheasantry

In northeastern Prague, a marked trail links Vinoř Park with the Satalice Pheasantry through a narrow wooded valley.

The landscape is shaped by the Vinořský Stream, sandstone formations and small springs. Along the route, walkers can also come across traces of the area’s history, including rock carvings, the remains of an old hillfort and the entrance to a water cave.

The area is especially attractive in autumn, when old oaks and other trees turn yellow and brown. A long avenue between Vinoř and Satalice adds another distinctive feature to the route.

The official educational trail is about 3.5 kilometers long and takes roughly two hours. It starts near the Malá Obůrka pond and finishes close to the Chapel of St. Anne in Satalice. From there, buses and trains provide connections back into Prague.

Hvězda offers more than its main avenue

Hvězda Game Reserve is one of Prague’s better-known green spaces, but many visitors stay on the central avenue leading from Vypich to the white Renaissance summer palace.

The quieter parts begin once you leave the main route and head into the surrounding woodland.

Oaks, beeches and hornbeams dominate the reserve. According to Prague’s records, more than half of its forest stands are over 150 years old. Several notable beech trees date from plantings carried out after 1763, including a tree recognized as the oldest and largest beech in Prague.

A loop through the reserve can lead from the summer palace toward the pond and Světlička wetland meadow before returning along one of the smaller paths.

Dalejské Valley offers a different side of Prague

Prokopské Valley is familiar to many Prague residents, but the landscape continues west toward Řeporyje in the quieter Dalejské Valley.

Here, limestone cliffs, former quarries, open slopes and the Dalejský Stream create a landscape that changes frequently along the trail.

One option is to follow the green-marked hiking route from Řeporyje toward Hlubočepy. Rather than forming one continuous wall of autumn foliage, the valley combines yellow trees with exposed rock and brownish grass-covered slopes.

The area forms part of the northeastern section of the Bohemian Karst and is recognized for its geological features. Prague’s Nature Portal recommends following the valley along the stream.

Hostivař Forest Park changes after summer

Hostivař is closely associated with its reservoir and summer swimming, but the area takes on a different character once the bathing season ends.

The woods surrounding the water offer numerous walking routes, with more than 35 kilometers of paths and trails running through the forest park.

A shorter walk can follow the reservoir, while longer routes continue through woodland and meadows and pass the animal enclosure near the gamekeeper’s lodge. The Botič Stream Basin educational trail also crosses the area.

Autumn brings changing colors to the oak and larch trees, while the reservoir provides views that are particularly noticeable on cooler mornings.

World.title: New Dog Playground Opens in Central Prague with Agility Course
World.content:
Prague 1 now has its first public dog playground, giving dog owners in the city center a dedicated space for exercise and training.

The new facility is located on Ludvík Svobody Embankment, next to the Ministry of Transport’s traffic playground and close to Lannov Park. It has been open to the public since September 16.



At the center of the site is an approximately 92-meter-long agility course. It includes a tunnel, slalom poles, an A-frame and several jumping obstacles. The playground is freely accessible and does not require prior booking.

“Space in the center of Prague is very limited, so we want to use every suitable location to serve local residents,” said Kateřina Klasnová, Prague 1’s deputy mayor responsible for the environment.

The playground is currently unfenced, meaning dogs can enter and leave the area freely.

Some dog owners raised concerns about the lack of a fence during the opening, and Prague 1 said it would consider adding one.

An information board at the site explains the operating rules and provides instructions for using the agility equipment. The playground also has a waste bin and two dispensers containing bags for dog owners to clean up after their pets.

Responsibility for the site lies with the Prague 1 Department of the Environment. Visitors can report damaged equipment or other defects directly to the municipal district.

World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket. The offer is valid from 14 to 21 September 2026 for tickets in sectors 102-109, subject to availability.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Péter Magyar and Ukraine clash over new Carpathian Eight initiative
World.content:
Péter Magyar and Ukraine have become embroiled in a public diplomatic dispute after Budapest rejected claims that Hungary had joined the newly launched Carpathian Eight regional initiative. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the Hungarian government’s position as unnecessarily confrontational, while Magyar insisted that no sovereign country could be declared part of an international cooperation format without its consent.

The exchange unfolded on social media after Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in parliament on Monday that Hungary was not a member of the Carpathian Eight, or C8, launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy days earlier.

Sybiha described Budapest’s reaction as surprising and unnecessarily confrontational. He argued that the initiative was designed to strengthen regional development, cross-border relations and mutually beneficial investment.

Sybiha also criticised Budapest’s reaction to a separate cooperation agreement between Ukrainian and Hungarian energy companies.

Péter Magyar and Ukraine disagree over Hungary’s C8 status

The dispute centres on a fundamental question: whether Hungary ever actually joined the new regional format.

Zelenskyy announced the Carpathian Eight at its inaugural summit in western Ukraine on 18 September. Ukrainian officials described the initiative as bringing together Ukraine, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Czechia, Austria and Serbia. Its proposed areas of cooperation include security, energy, logistics, investment and cross-border economic development.

However, the Hungarian government says Budapest never agreed to become a member.

Hungary was represented at the meeting by Ádám Ceglédi, chargé d’affaires at the Hungarian Embassy in Kyiv, but the Foreign Ministry said his presence did not amount to Hungary joining the initiative.

Hungary also did not sign the declaration adopted at the summit. According to the ministry, the document was endorsed by Ukraine, Austria, Romania, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia. Czechia also did not sign.

Magyar told parliament that Hungary had received an invitation but had decided not to join.

In his response to Sybiha, he argued that declaring Hungary a member without prior agreement was unacceptable. He illustrated his point with a football analogy, saying it would be like someone forming a team in a neighbouring village and then informing another person that they were already a member and expected to bring the ball.

If you missed yesterday: Russia election 2026: What Putin’s strengthened majority means for Hungary

Ukrainian foreign minister invokes the Orbán era

Sybiha went further in his criticism, linking the current dispute to Hungary’s foreign policy under former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

He suggested that although Orbán was no longer in office, what he described as a policy of “obstruction and isolation” remained visible in Budapest’s approach.

The Ukrainian foreign minister also referred critically to “Orbánism”, while stressing that Kyiv remained open to pragmatic and mutually beneficial cooperation with Hungary.

The remarks are notable because Magyar’s government has sought to distinguish its foreign policy from that of its predecessor, although the C8 dispute shows that significant disagreements between Péter Magyar and Ukraine remain.

MOL–Naftogaz deal adds another layer to dispute

The diplomatic argument has also become entangled with a planned energy project involving Hungarian oil and gas group MOL and Ukraine’s state-owned Naftogaz. Details: Ukraine could store fuel in Hungary as MOL and Naftogaz strike deal amid Russian attacks

Naftogaz announced on 20 September that the companies had signed a memorandum during the first C8 summit concerning the development of facilities in Hungary, close to the Ukrainian border, that could store petroleum products for the Ukrainian market.

The Hungarian government reacted cautiously.

Magyar said in parliament that no such oil storage facility would be built near the Ukrainian-Hungarian border under his government. Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány also said MOL had not informed the cabinet before signing the memorandum. According to the Hungarian side, the agreement begins a longer preparatory process rather than immediately authorising construction.

Sybiha, however, characterised the arrangement as direct and pragmatic cooperation between companies from the two countries and argued against political interference in such commercial relations.

What is the Carpathian Eight?

The C8 is intended as a new regional framework rather than a military alliance or a supranational organisation.

Its organisers say the initiative should connect governments, regional authorities, businesses and investors across the wider Carpathian region, with cooperation focusing on energy, security, transport, logistics and cross-border development.

The inaugural summit took place in Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region from 18 to 20 September. Zelenskyy presented the initiative as a way of creating a stronger framework for regional cooperation and closer coordination at European Union level.

Whether Hungary will eventually participate remains unresolved. Budapest says it will continue to follow the development of the initiative, but for now insists that attendance at the inaugural summit should not be interpreted as membership.

The public exchange between Magyar and Sybiha therefore goes beyond terminology: it highlights unresolved questions over how Budapest and Kyiv intend to manage regional cooperation, energy projects and bilateral relations under Hungary’s new government.

World.title: Hungarian food industry urges government to scrap price margin cap
World.content:
Hungary’s food producers and retailers are jointly calling on the government to abolish the country’s price margin cap immediately, arguing that the measure has outlived its original anti-inflation purpose and is now distorting the market. The debate puts Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s new government in a difficult position: while inflation has fallen sharply and both businesses and the central bank see room for an exit, consumers have become accustomed to direct state intervention keeping some supermarket prices down.

What is Hungary’s price margin cap?

The Hungary price margin cap is not technically a traditional price freeze. Instead of fixing the final shelf price of a product, the state limits the difference between the price at which a retailer buys a product and the price at which it sells it.

The measure was introduced by Viktor Orbán’s government in March 2025 as food inflation was accelerating again. For the food categories covered by the regulation, retailers generally cannot apply a margin above 10%, while a lower average margin used in January 2025 must also be respected where applicable.

This distinction matters. A retailer can still increase the shelf price if its purchase price rises, but it cannot freely determine its mark-up. Moreover, the retail margin is not the same thing as a company’s net profit: wages, rents, logistics, energy bills, taxes and other operating costs must also be paid from the difference between purchase and retail prices. The European Commission has specifically criticised Hungary for treating the margin as if it were equivalent to profit.

The intervention was originally presented as temporary. However, successive extensions followed, and shortly before leaving office in April 2026, the Orbán government removed its automatic expiry. The new parliament subsequently incorporated the restrictions into statutory law, meaning that they remain in force until the legislation is changed.

If you missed it: Hungary reveals new diesel subsidy details: Who gets EUR 55 and when will payments begin?

Food industry calls for immediate abolition

In a joint statement on Tuesday, organisations representing Hungarian food manufacturers, agricultural producers and retailers said the time had come for the price margin cap to be removed.

They pointed to months of improving inflation data.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), consumer prices were only 1.3% higher year on year in August 2026. Food prices actually fell by 1.4% compared with August 2025, or by 4.8% when catering services are excluded.

The organisations argue that maintaining the restriction under these circumstances is no longer justified.

They also claim that the Hungary price margin cap interferes with normal market pricing, prevents real production costs from being fully reflected in retail prices and weakens suppliers’ negotiating position.

Another concern is imports. According to the industry organisations, when retailers cannot achieve viable margins on domestically produced goods, they may have a stronger incentive to replace them with cheaper imported alternatives, potentially hurting Hungarian farmers and food processors.

Among those calling for the immediate withdrawal are the Federation of Responsible Food Manufacturers, the Hungarian mineral water and soft drinks industry association, confectionery, meat, refrigeration and canning industry organisations, the National Federation of Agricultural Cooperators and Producers, the Hungarian Chamber of Agriculture and the Milk Interprofessional Organisation and Product Board.

The Hungarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry separately reached a similar conclusion last week, saying the measure had become a distortion of competition rather than an effective long-term tool against inflation.

Central bank sees limited inflation risk from removing the cap

The strongest argument for an exit may come from the National Bank of Hungary (MNB).

In its June Inflation Report, the central bank estimated that abolishing the margin restrictions would cause only a limited rebound in prices because much of the adjustment following their introduction had already worked its way through the supply chain.

The MNB estimated that only around one-quarter of the original 1.4-percentage-point technical price-reducing effect would return. Its modelling suggested an inflationary impact of up to roughly 0.4 percentage points, with inflation remaining below the central bank’s 3% target even after an immediate withdrawal of the measure.

This does not mean that every affected product would remain at its present price. Some could become more expensive once retailers regain freedom to set margins. However, the central bank also expects competition between supermarket chains to limit the extent of such increases.

Why has Péter Magyar’s government kept the policy?

This is where economics and politics collide.

The measure was inherited from the Orbán government, but Péter Magyar’s administration did not dismantle it upon taking office. Before the transfer of power, TISZA had indicated that it would initially retain the system because there was not enough time for an abrupt withdrawal. In August, Magyar said the government had not yet discussed ending the measure, while acknowledging that inflation had fallen to levels not seen for years.

By 18 September, his position had moved further: the prime minister said the government was examining either abolishing or transforming the scheme because of the damage it could cause to Hungarian agricultural producers, particularly dairy farmers. He also said the decline in inflation meant an exit might no longer produce a major jump in supermarket prices.

The government therefore faces a policy-exit problem familiar from other forms of administered pricing. Once consumers become accustomed to a lower regulated shelf price, removing the intervention can look and feel like a government-induced price rise, even when the underlying inflation rate is low.

That creates a political incentive to postpone reform.

Yet maintaining the scheme carries costs of its own. Producers and retailers warn of distorted supply chains and greater import pressure, the MNB says the inflationary justification for maintaining it has weakened, and the European Commission argues that the restrictions breach EU single-market rules.

In July, Brussels referred Hungary to the Court of Justice of the European Union over both the food and drugstore price margin restrictions. The Commission argues that the system disproportionately affects non-Hungarian companies and can force retailers to sell products at levels insufficient to cover their wider operating costs.

If you missed it – Hungary new home VAT 2027: developers and buyers brace for a costly shift

What can the government do next?

The government has several possible routes without necessarily moving from full regulation to complete deregulation overnight.

It could abolish the margin cap immediately, relying on supermarket competition and falling producer prices to limit the resulting price increases. The MNB’s estimates suggest that this is considerably less inflationary today than it would have appeared when the policy was introduced.

A second possibility would be a phased withdrawal, for example by gradually increasing the permitted margin or removing individual product groups from the regulation. Such an approach could limit sudden changes in shelf prices while giving producers and retailers time to renegotiate contracts.

A third route would be to replace broad price intervention with targeted assistance for lower-income households if food affordability remains a concern. That would separate social policy from retail price-setting, although any such programme would have its own fiscal cost.

The government could also rely more heavily on competition enforcement, price transparency and measures aimed at reducing costs along the supply chain rather than determining commercial margins directly.

For the Magyar government, the decision is therefore broader than whether a litre of milk or a kilogram of meat becomes slightly more expensive after the cap disappears. It is an early test of how quickly the new administration is prepared to unwind direct market interventions inherited from its predecessor when the original emergency conditions have eased.

With food prices now falling year on year, businesses demanding an exit, the central bank seeing manageable inflation risks and an EU court case pending, the pressure for a decision is becoming increasingly difficult to postpone.

World.title: CATL launches trial operations at Debrecen battery factory
World.content:
CATL Debrecen began trial production at its newly built battery cell factory on 22 September 2026 after completing the regulatory and technical requirements needed to launch operations. The trial phase will be used to set up, optimise and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins.

The Chinese battery manufacturer announced plans for its second European production site in Debrecen in August 2022, aiming to strengthen its presence in the European automotive and e-mobility supply chain and serve major carmakers operating across the continent.

Construction of the first battery cell building started in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the facility had been equipped with production technology, while an occupancy permit was granted in August.

Trial production begins on two battery cell lines

Following the approval of the necessary permits and completion of the conditions required under its integrated pollution prevention and control permit, CATL Debrecen launched trial operations on the first two production lines of its cell manufacturing facility on 22 September.

According to the company, the main purpose of the trial phase is to configure, optimise and validate both the equipment and the manufacturing processes ahead of full-scale series production.

The trial period will also allow engineers to monitor production performance and make adjustments before commercial output begins.

Earlier regulatory concerns addressed before launch

Before issuing the occupancy permit, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out a series of on-site inspections at CATL’s facilities.

The checks followed earlier deficiencies and issues that had raised concerns among some local residents during the permitting and construction process.

According to CATL, representatives of the authority confirmed that the company had remedied all deficiencies identified earlier in the procedure before trial production was allowed to begin.

The company said it would continue cooperating closely with the Hungarian government and competent authorities, particularly on environmental protection as well as employee health and workplace safety.

CATL added that environmental, occupational health and safety indicators would also be closely monitored throughout the trial phase, with the results proactively submitted to the authorities.

If you missed it: Exclusive interview – Chinese Ambassador: Hungary-China ties on a ‘steady track’ as Budapest emerges as a potential robotics hub

CATL Debrecen targets 100 GWh production capacity

Once all parts of the project are completed, the Debrecen plant is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing base outside China.

The planned annual production capacity is 100 GWh, making the investment one of the largest battery manufacturing projects in Hungary and a major component of the country’s rapidly expanding electric vehicle supply chain.

CATL says its Debrecen facility will supply leading European car manufacturers, several of which have already developed significant electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary and the wider region.

The plant has been designed with flexible production lines intended to adapt to the requirements of different automotive customers.

More than half a million battery modules already produced

Battery cell production is not CATL’s first manufacturing activity in Debrecen.

The company has been producing battery modules at the site since autumn 2024 and says it has manufactured approximately 537,000 modules since production began.

The start of trial cell production therefore marks another major step towards the full operation of the Debrecen complex.

Environmental and workplace safety remain under scrutiny

CATL said it would continue working with authorities during the trial period and reiterated its commitment to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety.

The company also said it supports regulatory transparency and remains open to inspections by the relevant authorities.

The Debrecen investment is significant not only for the city and the surrounding region, but also for Hungary’s industrial strategy and Europe’s electric mobility supply chain. Once series production begins and the entire facility reaches its planned capacity, the factory is expected to become one of CATL’s most important production centres outside China.
