World.title: Azerbaijan's Astara Terminal scales up cargo handling by 30% in 8M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Cargo handling at the Astara Terminal of Azerbaijan Railways CJSC, located in Iran, rose by approximately 30% from January through August 2026 compared to the same period last year.

This was reported by the press service of Azerbaijan Railways CJSC (ADY).

According to the information, over 537,000 tons of cargo were handled at the terminal during the reporting period, while in the same period of the previous year, this figure stood at 415,000 tons.

In August of this year, 76,000 tons of cargo were handled at the terminal, representing an increase of approximately 50% compared to the same month last year.

In August 2025, 51,000 tons of cargo were handled at the terminal.

The Astara Terminal, located in Iran, facilitates cargo transportation along the International North–South Transport Corridor. Construction of the terminal began in 2017 under an agreement between Azerbaijan and Iran, and cargo handling operations have been underway there since 2018.

World.title: Kazakhstan appoints Yerzhan Yertaev as vice minister of energy
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 22. Yerzhan Yertaev was appointed vice minister of energy of Kazakhstan today by a government resolution, the press service of the Kazakh government said.

Yertaev was born in 1985 in Kazakhstan’s Pavlodar region. He graduated from Innovative Eurasian University and Anhalt University of Applied Sciences in Germany.

He began his career in 2009 as an electromechanic at a private company.

From 2009 to 2013, Yertaev worked as a leading and chief specialist in the energy department of the Pavlodar region’s Energy and Housing and Utilities Department.

From 2013 to 2014, he served as chief expert and head of a department at the Committee for State Energy Supervision and Control of the Ministry of Industry and New Technologies.

From 2015 to 2018, Yertaev headed territorial departments of the Ministry of Energy in the Akmola and Karaganda regions.

From 2018 to 2020, he served as Deputy Chairman of a committee at the Ministry of Energy.

In 2020-2021, Yertaev headed the Energy and Housing and Utilities Department of Pavlodar region.

From 2021 to 2022, he was Head of the Office of the Chairman of the Management Board of Samruk-Energy.

From 2022 to 2023, he served as General Director of the Bulat Nurzhanov Ekibastuz GRES-1 power plant.

From 2023 to 2024, Yertaev was Deputy Chairman of the Committee for Atomic and Energy Supervision and Control of the Ministry of Energy.

Since July 2024, he has served as Chairman of the Committee for State Energy Supervision and Control of the Ministry of Energy.

World.title: Vulnerable residents feeling 'distress' as Mildura power outage drags on
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A power outage in the north-west Victorian city of Mildura is set to enter a third day, raising concerns for the elderly, residents reliant on medical devices and domestic violence survivors.

Power has been out for almost 3,000 residents and businesses since a ute crashed into a critical power pole at nearby Birdwoodton about 6.30am on Monday.

Just before 7pm Tuesday, electricity distributor Powercor said the expected timeframe for "the majority of the network" to be restored had been extended from Wednesday afternoon to midday Friday.

Among those without electricity are 24 supported accommodation homes run by Sunraysia Residential Services (SRS).

SRS CEO Marian Luehman said many affected were elderly or living with a disability, who relied on electricity to power equipment and undertake everyday tasks.

Marian Luehman says outages cause anxiety for the elderly. (Supplied: Sunraysia Residential Services)

"Prolonged periods without power can be distressing and isolating," she said.

"Uncertainty around restoration timeframes can add further anxiety, particularly for those already facing health or personal challenges."

Ms Luehman said the situation highlighted a need to strengthen emergency response arrangements for vulnerable residents, who needed support accessing generators, alternative accommodation, transport assistance and targeted welfare checks.

An anxious wait for victim-survivor

Sarah, a victim-survivor of domestic violence whose name has been changed to protect her privacy, said the outage had caused anxiety, because it meant her home security cameras were not operating.

"[Previously, the perpetrator] would park across the road. Some nights he would be standing in the shadows of a tree watching my house," Sarah said.

"[The cameras] alert me to any activity around the boundaries of my property and they give me a feeling of safety.

"I spent quite some time not being able to shower or sleep in the dark unless I had someone there to ensure I was safe. The cameras helped me a great deal."

Victoria Police said it was sorry to hear about the impact on a victim of domestic violence, and told "anyone who feels threatened by the presence of someone at their home, or anywhere else for that matter, to call Triple Zero immediately".

Police will not respond to alarms

Mildura police Acting Inspector Daron Hulls urged residents to "remain calm" and "check on [your] neighbours".

Acting Inspector Hulls said Victoria Police had increased patrols around the impacted area, but would not be responding to alarms until power was restored.

"For security, we encourage [residents] to obviously manually lock their doors and their windows, especially if they've got automatic systems in place there," Acting Inspector Hulls said.

"[People] need to be aware of alarms because we won't respond to an alarm or a security system that's been triggered by power failures."

In the case of a break-in, Acting Inspector Hulls said victims would need to contact police and may be required to submit extra evidence.

"We'll have to rely on some other supporting information, such as phone calls or observations," he said.

Outage extended to Friday

Powercor spokesperson Jodan Oliver said crews were prioritising regular welfare checks for about 130 residents living with life support apparatuses.

He said the outage was an "unusual one".

Many Mildura shops are closed as the power outage continues. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

"The different circuits on that pole, one was very high voltage and we have low voltage as well, which connects people's homes," he said.

"We're checking with customers' properties whether [that high voltage] has entered into people's wiring, switchboards … and potentially caused damage.

"So we're really keen on people to make any reports to us of any damage they notice at their homes and their switchboards, appliances not working."

Powercor has set up an information station outside the Alfred Deakin Centre in Mildura. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

A relief centre has been set up at the Benetook Room of the Alfred Deakin Centre at the corner of Deakin Avenue and Twelfth Street.

Chargers are available for residents' devices, as well as information from Powercor, Mildura Rural City Council and local police.

World.title: US attacks Australia's 'opt-out' algorithm law in rare intervention
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Trump administration has made an extraordinary public intervention into Australia's debate about its proposed digital duty of care, warning the Albanese government that the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".

It called for the Australian government to exclude US social media companies from its plans to give users the option to opt into algorithmic recommendation feeds — a decision that would effectively neuter the law, removing the biggest platforms from its application.

The rare public rebuke took the form of a response to a consultation on the draft digital duty of care bill, which would force platforms to take actions to mitigate and respond to harms caused by digital platforms.

The submission, published by the US Embassy today, said Washington had "serious concerns" about how Australia would decide what counts as "foreseeable harm".

This comes with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese currently in the middle of a United States trip to promote his government's tech policy agenda at the United Nations General Assembly.

His support for international AI regulation and his government's teen social media ban have increasingly earned the ire of the Trump administration.

Washington objects to harm rules and feed mandates

In the submission, the US government said it was concerned by what it described as rigid, one-size-fits-all design requirements.

Such mandates, it argued, would push platforms to demote sensitive or controversial topics to comply, reducing the reach of independent journalists and other voices.

"The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship," the submission said.

Communications Minister Anika Wells and the federal government are developing digital duty of care laws. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

It put a number of questions to the Australian government, including how Australia would define "harm" and "risks", how they would be adjudicated, by whom, and whether platforms or users could appeal. It also asked about the role of the eSafety Commissioner and impacts on privacy.

While it is common for governments to express their views on other countries' policies, those views are usually communicated through private channels.

It is exceedingly rare for a foreign government to make a direct, public intervention into a domestic debate like this.

The US government's hostility toward the digital duty of care was signposted earlier this month in a statement from White House spokesperson Kush Desai to the Guardian Australia.

He said President Donald Trump had warned other nations against imposing "digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America's leading technology sector".

Warning Australia's tech policies could spread elsewhere

The submission argued forced changes to mitigate Australia-specific risks could change how users everywhere, including Americans, experienced the platforms.

If other jurisdictions adopted conflicting duty-of-care mandates, platforms could face incompatible design requirements not technically or commercially scalable in parallel, it said.

Australia's teen social media ban inspired a number of other countries to introduce, or pledge to introduce, similar restrictions.

Earlier today, it was reported by Politico Australia that the American industry body representing American tech companies had joined in a High Court challenge to Australia's teen social media ban.

The group, NetChoice, described it as "the most extensive prohibition on youth access to social media in force in any liberal democracy".

The digital duty of care draft shows how the government plans to create a legal obligation for online services, including social media, gaming and other platforms, to create a safe experience for users through its design.

The Albanese government said it would use this law, if passed, to force platforms like Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to send users a pop-up offering a choice between a personalised algorithmic feed and a feed limited to accounts they follow.

Communications Minister Anika Wells last week downplayed the White House's warning as "broad" and said she had not directly received such a warning from a US representative.

When asked about the US government's intervention, Ms Wells's office and the US Embassy both declined to comment.

World.title: Teen tells court of 'painfully real' impacts of explicit deepfake images
World.content:
A teenage girl who had sexually explicit deepfake images of her shared online has told a court that, although fake, the images have had a "painfully real" impact on her.

William Hamish Yeates, of Netherby, appeared in South Australia's District Court today for a pre-sentence hearing after he pleaded guilty to two counts of creating or altering sexual material without consent earlier this year.

The 20-year-old was the first person in Australia to be charged under federal laws introduced in 2024 to combat the rise of deepfake pornography.

The offending, which occurred between October 2024 and February 2025, involved the creation of sexually explicit deepfake images and videos of his victim that he shared online.

The now-19-year-old woman was supported by more than a dozen family members and friends as she delivered her victim impact statement to the court.

"For a long time, I've carried the shame of something that was never my fault. Today, I'm here to give that shame back to the person it belongs to," she told him.

"I want to make it very clear, these images of me were fake but the impact they had is painfully real."

William Yeates has previously pleaded guilty to two counts of creating or altering sexual material without consent earlier this year. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

In her statement, the teenager said the first time she saw her graduation picture was on a pornography website.

"Knowing that my graduation photo was taken and used with such a corrupt context has been one of the hardest things for me to process," she said.

"The first time I saw my actual graduation picture was on a pornography website beside altered videos of me with my full name and school attached to it.

"Every time I now see that photo, I feel sick.

"You took a memory that was supposed to represent achievement, friendship and happiness and turned it into something so painful."

The 19-year-old said the discovery of Yeates's offending resulted in the "darkest period" of her life but said she would not let it define her.

"Despite everything I will refuse to let what you did to me define me forever," she said.

"I am not your victim, Will. I am a survivor.

" You tried to reduce me to an image on a screen, but I am so much more than that. "

Yeates read an apology to his victim in which he said the harm he caused the girl was "unintended".

"My actions were repulsive and will continue to plague my mind for as long as I breathe," he said.

Exposure to explicit online content

Yeates's defence barrister, Jane Powell SC, told the court that a psychologist had diagnosed the 20-year-old with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and that a report mentioned a diagnosis of compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (CSBD).

She said he developed "a sense of an obsession" with the victim.

The victim made her impact statement in South Australia's District Court today. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Powell also told the court that in the lead-up to his offending, Yeates began engaging in "communities" on the social media platform X, formerly Twitter, "where everyone was in the same mindset".

"It was very common to post nude images of women in such communities," she said.

" His exposure to that content made him think that sharing photos of women in a sexually derogatory manner was OK. "

Ms Powell also told the court that Yeates had been introduced to Andrew Tate online, who she referred to as a "hateful, misogynistic individual".

Tate is a well-known social media influencer, self-described misogynist and alleged rapist.

"Mr Yeates found himself conflicted in some ways but still attracted to that platform … in the months and year leading up to the offending," Ms Powell said.

She asked the court not to sentence Yeates to time behind bars as it would "weigh heavily" on his mental health.

However, a prosecutor from the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (CDPP) opposed Ms Powell's submission and said a term of imprisonment would be the only appropriate sentence due to the "extremely insidious" nature of the "serious conduct".

William Yeates, right, did not comment as he left the Adelaide Magistrates Court alongside his lawyer, Tim McGrath. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

"One might be able to accept, on the one hand, that there was a desire to belong in this deplorable community of the Andrew Tate manosphere but that is not an exclusive motivation for this offending when one looks at the content that he was posting," she said.

"Two things can be true, which is: he wanted to belong, but he also wanted to degrade and humiliate the victim online."

The prosecutor said a sentence of imprisonment would work to deter others from committing similar offences.

"The nature of this offending is significant, it is prolific and it is online and it is growing," she said.

"A sentence in this matter has to deter particularly young men from engaging in this type of behaviour."

Yeates faces a maximum penalty of seven years behind bars and will be sentenced next month.

World.title: Teen jailed over home invasion that traumatised Melbourne family
World.content:
Last August, Kai Li and his family were jolted awake just before 4am.

Intruders had jumped the fence and were using garden shears to smash a downstairs window.

Seconds later, Mr Li was face-to-face with five of the masked group.

Some were armed with machetes, and the Children's Court later heard they had no hesitation in using them.

During the aggravated home invasion, Mr Li fought desperately to protect two children, his wife, his grandparents and a nanny inside.

Mr Li's wife and grandparents were assaulted but Mr Li's injuries were the most severe.

He was stabbed 11 times in the face and upper body before the intruders allegedly stole the family car and fled the Kew home.

Mr Li was left with permanent damage to his eyesight and his family remains traumatised.

Today, one of Mr Li's attackers was jailed for two years and nine months after pleading guilty to aggravated home invasion, assault charges and a raft of other car theft crimes.

Victims' lives changed 'forever'

"What happened to my family has changed our lives forever," Mr Li told the ABC this afternoon.

"I never imagined that something like this could happen in our own home."

Mr Li said his case was emblematic of "weaknesses" in the legal system and called for stricter bail laws and tougher sentences for violent crime.

"I hope both the Australian government and the Victorian government will introduce policies that genuinely improve community safety, so that families like mine do not have to experience this again," he said.

In sentencing the 17-year-old attacker, Judge Jack Vandersteen said the home invasion was a "grave violation".

Not only had the judge considered the police report and Mr Li's victim impact statement, he also viewed footage of the incident which was captured on a baby monitor in the home.

"The screams, the threats, are evident. The fear of the occupants was palpable," he said.

"A home should be a place of safety."

A teenager will spend nearly three years in jail for his role in the violent Kew home invasion. (ABC News)

Prosecutors did not allege the 17-year-old directly caused Mr Li's injuries but argued he was part of the broader plot to storm the home.

The teenager said he had taken drugs and alcohol before the attack and said the incident remained "a bit of a blur".

He had written an apology letter, committed himself to reform while in youth detention and had the support of his family and church community, the court heard.

Invasion occurred before new laws passed

The aggravated home invasion occurred before Victoria's "Adult time for Violent Crime" laws were passed.

It meant the case was not automatically transferred to the County Court, where judges have the power to impose the same sentences on children as they do for adults.

Under the new regime, a child guilty of aggravated home invasion could be sentenced to life in prison by the County Court, however the judges have not yet come close to imposing such a devastating sentence.

The maximum penalty the Children's Court can set is four years in youth detention.

Mr Li said he was grateful to the local police officers who handled his case, and said politicians needed to tackle the issue of repeat violent youth offenders.

"What families need is not symbolic measures, but policies that actually address the problem and give ordinary residents a greater sense of safety in their own communities," he said.

Two others charged with breaking into Mr Li's home remain before the courts.

Police are continuing to hunt for two more people.

World.title: 'Sophistication' spat over foot traffic decline in Adelaide CBD
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A sharp decline in foot traffic in Adelaide's CBD has prompted a prominent property industry lobbyist to take a swipe at the city council, which he has accused of lacking "sophistication".

But the lord mayor has staunchly defended the council's approach to CBD visits, and hit back at those she said "don't understand the city is a complex beast".

According to Adelaide City Council documents citing Kepler Analytics data, there were 138.8 million foot traffic visitors in 2023, before the figure dropped to 130.6 million in 2024 and 122 million in 2025.

A month-by-month dashboard, published by the Adelaide Economic Development Agency, shows 13.9 million visits were recorded citywide in the month of July 2023, before the figure fell to 10.9 million in July 2024.

In July 2025, there were 10.2 million visits and, in July of this year, 9.6 million visits.

Rundle Mall is the city's main shopping strip. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Executive director of the state's Property Council, Bruce Djite, blamed factors including car parking, which he said was having a deterrent effect on visitors.

"This is what happens when you have — with all due respect — Adelaide city councillors who are very nice people but unfortunately lack the sophistication required to attract people into the city on a regular basis," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"We have a council that is at war with car parking without an alternative solution.

" When you're ripping out car parks and putting in bike lanes, you make it increasingly difficult for anyone who needs to travel into the CBD to get there, do their shopping and get home. It's too inconvenient. "

Bruce Djite said parking and a lack of housing were deterrents to visitors. (ABC News: Dan Taylor)

Mr Djite said a more significant factor than parking was housing, and he accused the council of failing to make best use of its building stock, more of which, he said, should be converted for residential use.

"What they need to do is have more residential in the city," he said.

"They could put some of their underutilised buildings to the development sector, so they could have professionals come in and deliver the residential supply that's required in the CBD."

Adelaide Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith rejected Mr Djite's criticisms, but said she did not wish to "have a discussion about people's character".

"I'm not into criticising him for his sophistication — that's not my style," she said.

Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith says Adelaide has a strong record on affordable parking. (ABC News)

Cr Lomax-Smith said foot traffic figures were partly reflective of demographic changes.

"More people are working from home now than there were five years ago, and it's taken a while for the foot traffic to recover after COVID. There's been a bounce back," she said.

" Clearly people don't understand the city is a complex beast — we have retail, we have nightlife, we have all sorts of professional services and we've had a growth in business activity in the city. [There are] more businesses now than ever before. "

Cr Lomax-Smith said CBD parking in Adelaide compared favourably with other Australian capital cities, and added that the council's housing strategy was paying dividends.

"We've had an increase of 3.5 per cent in our residential population in the last year, and that's the largest increase of any council area in South Australia," she said.

Foot traffic has decreased in Adelaide's CBD. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Rundle Mall tailor Joseph Uzumcu said he had not noticed a decline in passers-by, and said his business was "doing incredibly well".

"People point fingers at other outside effects of why people are not coming into the city," he said.

"We've got to realise the population of Adelaide is [smaller than elsewhere].

"We're not Sydney, we're not Brisbane."

World.title: Grand jury declines to indict anyone in death of Black teen in Mississippi
World.content:
A grand jury in Mississippi has unanimously declined to indict anyone in the death of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old Black man whose body was found on an island after a trip with friends.

Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath's office released the grand jury's report on Monday, local time.

"The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 on the Triton, the Palm Beach, or the Tideline engaged in any criminal conduct related to the death of Mr Wells," the report said.

Alleged 'threats' amid Nolan Wells probe Three people have been charged for allegedly threatening a US authorities and witnesses connected to the investigation of Nolan Wells's death.

US civil rights advocates and prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump had sought a comprehensive ​investigation and transparency from authorities on Mr Wells's death.

Mr Crump, who is representing the Wells family, said on X after the grand jury report was released that Mr Wells's death still demanded answers and that the grand jury's decision to not indict anyone does not resolve how he died.

Mr Wells's body was found on July 6 on the north-west end of ‌Horn Island, ⁠a barrier island off the Mississippi Gulf Coast, after he went missing during a Fourth of July weekend trip with friends from nearby Ocean Springs, Mississippi.

Nolan Wells went missing on July 4, 2026, after going on a trip with friends off the coast of Mississippi. (Supplied: Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

His death evolved from a local investigation into a case drawing scrutiny from across the United States.

Although authorities had not alleged foul play, questions were raised in the weeks after Mr Wells's death by family members, civil rights leaders and others about transparency, accountability and disparities in attention to cases involving Black victims.

The grand jury found that "the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells' body is consistent with drowning".

"Both the State of Mississippi Chief Medical Examiner and Dr [name redacted] opined that the cause and manner of Mr Wells' death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion," the report said.

The report said the grand jury understood that neither forensic expert had ruled out accidental drowning as a cause of death.

"Jackson County, after a thorough and exhaustive investigation, your grand jury met last week concerning the death investigation of Nolan Wells and unanimously returned a no true bill," Ms McIlrath said in a Facebook video.

Ms McIlrath said there was no evidence to support the allegations that Mr Wells's disappearance and death were racially motivated.

Reuters

World.title: CEO seeking legal advice after given immediate termination notice
World.content:
Three West Australian councillors have resigned after the shire chief executive was sacked without warning.

Mia Maxfield confirmed to the ABC her contract was terminated at a council meeting after six years as Shire of Coorow chief executive officer.

Ms Maxfield said her contract was due to expire next year, but she was told her services were no longer required and immediately had her work laptop taken and building access revoked.

She said she had no warning of the termination and was seeking legal advice.

Ms Maxfield said she was handed a document citing "non-performance" as the reason for her dismissal.

Mia Maxfield says she was sacked without warning. (Supplied: LinkedIn / Mia Maxfield)

The document has not been seen by the ABC due to confidentiality restrictions.

The meeting minutes and recordings remain unpublished, but it is understood councillors voted 4-2 to terminate her contract.

Newly-appointed shire president Colin Hassell has declined to comment.

Do you know more? Contact Brianna Melville on encrypted email here Melville.brianna@proton.me Please note - you will need your own encrypted email account - such as Protonmail - to ensure end-to-end encryption

Issues raised earlier this year

Earlier this year, the council's former deputy CEO Sam Currulli was charged with nine offences including fraud, corruption, stealing and perjury related to his time working at the shire.

He has not yet entered a plea to those charges and is due in court again in October.

Ms Maxfield referred some of the allegations to police on behalf of the shire.

Last year Ms Maxfield was nominated in the National Awards for Local Government in the Women in Local Government category by her staff.

She is also on the board of of Local Government Professionals WA.

Loss of confidence

Former shire president Guy Sims, deputy shire president Giulia Censi and councillor Luhan Van Den Heever resigned in the wake of Ms Maxfield's sacking, citing a "loss of confidence" in the remaining council.

Giulia Censi, Guy Sims and Luhan Van Den Heever resigned following Wednesday's council meeting. (Shire of Coorow)

"I have grave concerns about what has happened in the process of the termination of the CEO," Mr Sims said.

He stepped down as president days before the meeting for reasons he could not disclose publicly, but said the council was aware of.

Mr Sims had an approved leave of absence on the day of the meeting.

"It's actually the first meeting I've missed in nine years," he said.

"I only found out what happened afterwards.

"I was appalled at what happened.

"There remain four councillors, all of which have less than a year's experience."

The meeting was closed to the public and Ms Maxfield left the room as council considered the CEO annual performance review, in line with confidentiality measures for staff employment discussions.

Guy Sims resigned as Coorow shire president last week and left the council altogether after the CEO's ouster. (ABC News: Piper Duffy)

The details of what happened during the meeting are confidential but the councillors who resigned said "proper processes" were not followed and all three of them were blindsided.

Mr Van Den Heever, who was in his first term as a councillor, said he could not stay on the council following the decision.

"For some councillors to be excluded and then just find out at the trigger point is concerning," he said.

"I did not feel that that is how a council should behave.

"It was not right."

Remaining councillors (clockwise from top left) Gene Hannington, Durwin Melbin, Colin Hassell and Dirk Gericke. (Shire of Coorow)

A state government spokesperson said Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley was aware of the situation.

"The Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety have been in contact with and is providing assistance to the Shire," they said.

"The Local Government Inspector also has oversight of the situation and has been contact with the Shire."

Local Government Inspector Tony Brown said complaints made to his office were confidential.

"We closely monitor the affairs of all local governments in Western Australia and can intervene if there is a suspected breach of the Local Government Act 1995," he said.

The four remaining elected officials include President Colin Hassell and councillors Gene Hannington, Dirk Gericke and Durwin Melbin.

World.title: Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman finds
World.content:
The ABC's Four Corners program had insufficient verification and fact-checking and a culture of "limiting knowledge" about anonymous sources, its independent ombudsman has found, identifying breaches of editorial standards in two stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal .

The ombudsman's report, released this afternoon, found two episodes failed to meet editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing, and independence.

"Audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims," the report said.

The ombudsman made seven recommendations, which include amending the ABC's editorial standard on anonymity, further legal and editorial training for the Four Corners team and more support for less experienced reporters.

The ABC says it accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them.

ABC News had already removed the two episodes covered by the ombudsman's review — Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway — after its own investigation into the anonymous interviewees.

In total, three episodes of Four Corners and two of Background Briefing by Fazal have already been withdrawn by the ABC, with a short segment edited out of another Four Corners episode.

Last month, the ABC said its own review found verification policies on anonymous interviewees were "not followed to a level that meets our editorial standards".

"The ABC is committed to journalism of the highest standard. Maintaining the trust of Australians depends on upholding those standards and we take any concerns about our journalism seriously," it said.

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, had his employment terminated in May after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year.

He had launched an unfair dismissal claim in the Fair Work Commission, but his hearing was removed from the schedule. The ABC said it was aware Fazal was no longer pursuing his claim.

In a social media video post last month, Fazal said he felt like the ABC was "trying everything in their power to stop me from ever working again".

"Even though all my work was approved across different teams and departments, cross-checked and met the standards before broadcast, they've decided there's now different standards that are retrospectively being applied to all of my stories," he said.

"They want to make me a scapegoat? Don't give a s***. I won't stop."

He has previously said he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, but that proximity had then been used against him.

Previously, Fazal's reporting appeared in VICE, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

Last month, the ABC announced its head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, was leaving the public broadcaster after a 25-year career.

She had oversight of Four Corners and Background Briefing.

Other senior managers at the ABC at the time of Fazal's reporting, , including news director Justin Stevens, have already left the broadcaster. The ABC's incoming news director Simon Robinson started in the role on September 14.

Last week, ABC managing director Hugh Marks rejected an Australian Communications and Media Authority finding that the public broadcaster breached impartiality obligations in an unrelated Four Corners program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial.

ACMA said on Thursday it had found the program's March 2025 episode, Sacrifice, had "unduly favoured one perspective".

The ABC says it "stands behind the team" that created the episode.

"If this interpretation of the code is applied, including more widely across the industry, it could have a chilling effect on the body of investigative journalism that delivers the important stories that serve the public interest," Marks said in a statement.

World.title: Lachie Neale banned for grand final in sensational tribunal ruling
World.content:
Lachie Neale’s one-match ban will stand. And he will be ineligible for the grand final.

In a comprehensive ruling, the AFL tribunal has upheld Neale’s one-match ban for striking Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in Saturday’s thrilling preliminary final at the MCG.

The AFL tribunal was critical of the veteran Lion, who hadn’t been suspended in 320 AFL matches.

Lachie Neale a training on Tuesday. Getty Images

“Neale jogged towards Ginnivan and formed the immediate intention to swing his arm forcefully at Ginnivan, and that is what he did,” said tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson.

“We have listened carefully to Neale’s evidence.

“But we find that it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video, and to what extent we do not accept it.

“There is no doubt in our minds that this should be graded as medium impact.

“While Ginnivan was not injured and did not appear to suffer any significant pain or discomfort, the blow was forceful and knocked him off his feet.

“As we have said, he immediately doubled over in a manner more consistent with a more than negligible blow having landed.

“It is relevant that this strike occurred nowhere near the ball, was not affected in or around the play, and because Ginnivan did not see Neale coming from behind or the side until the very last moment, he had no expectation of being struck until it was too late to meaningfully defend himself.”

The tribunal also dismissed any arguments that there were “compelling and exceptional circumstances” for Neale to avoid suspension and be eligible to play.

In a compelling case that both tested the AFL’s crackdown on “gut punches” and whether a player such as Neale should be granted leniency after more than 300 matches without suspension, Neale and the Lions can take the case to the AFL appeal board.

MORE TO COME

World.title: Albanese signs AI declaration with world leaders calling for international safeguards
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAI Albanese signs AI declaration with world leaders calling for international safeguards Rob Harris Updated September 22, 2026 — 9:58pm ,first published September 22, 2026 — 2:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will issue a rallying cry for world leaders to unite on efforts to protect people from the risks of artificial intelligence, warning no country can manage the technology’s growing risks alone. Australia was among a group of 22 signatories to call for new international safeguards on AI at the United Nations on Monday, amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the opening Ceremony of New York Climate Week on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer The prime minister joined colleagues, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to call for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. The declaration warned that capable AI systems have already been seen circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems.



Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it “Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks,” the statement said, which was also co-signed by Ireland, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. It called for a UN-style international organisation that would set standards and oversee AI use. The leaders stopped short of calling for a halt to development, instead arguing that AI’s potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen economies should be preserved while stronger controls are imposed. “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control,” they said, insisting that it must be developed and used in accordance with international law.



Its release comes ahead of Thursday’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI expected to be a major topic of discussion. Trump said following the declaration that US law enforcement agencies like the Department of Justice would regulate artificial intelligence risks if necessary, but emphasised his primary goal was to encourage its development. Downplaying potential dangers, Trump argued against stifling AI growth, comparing its future impact to the Industrial Revolution and the internet. He maintained the US must protect its edge over China while fostering both AI and superintelligence. Loading “We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way!” Trump wrote on social media.



Related Article Opinion

AI Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Albanese has cited Australia’s role in shaping international rules for AI as a key plank of its bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. He said he hoped for a positive meeting between Trump and Xi. Addressing the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI, Albanese will say the risks posed by increasingly capable systems will cross borders and require countries to work together on common standards. “And no country can manage these risks alone,” he will say. “We must come together.” Albanese will argue countries can seize and share the opportunities created by AI while developing common standards to protect children and communities.



“We can develop clear shared expectations and common guardrails,” he will say. The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, while Washington and Beijing have resisted calls from industry figures including Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the development of frontier models amid warnings that humans could lose control. Neither the US nor China are part of the new declaration. The declaration calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory testing before systems are deployed and independent assessments by qualified evaluators given sufficient access to identify risks. Governments and regional organisations are also urged to develop common standards, strengthen transparency and share reports of serious AI safety incidents. Albanese said AI had the potential to improve lives, strengthen the economy and productivity, and advance science and medical breakthroughs, but “humans need to be in control of it”.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates He said he had played a central role in the statement through conversations with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the declaration along with Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. The leaders want countries across all regions to have access to the scientific expertise, technical capacity and trusted evaluation needed to assess advanced AI systems. The declaration also calls on UN member states to explore creating an international institution that could set standards, enable verification and convene governments when AI systems cross agreed capability thresholds. The group warned that efforts to control frontier AI should not widen the gap between countries with access to the technology and those unable to benefit from its advances.



At a separate business event with Macquarie, Albanese will argue Australia is being recognised internationally for moving early on emerging challenges. “I think the world is seeing Australia as a smart, adaptable and successful middle power, succeeding because we’re not afraid to get ahead of the curve on the issues that matter to the future,” he will say. World.title: The opinion piece at the end of the world
World.content:
Peter Riley of Penrith writes: “We keep hearing that AI is going to make humanity extinct, so I asked AI if C8 is also doomed. It replied ‘Nothing is truly permanent, but Column 8 is as close to immortal as Australian journalism gets. Getting a snippet published by Granny is a major life milestone. It creates an intensely loyal micro-community within the SMH Opinion section. The newspaper would face open revolt from its core subscriber base if they ever tried to axe it.’ So there. AI wouldn’t fib, would it?”

While it’s time to move on from encounters with the Bee Gees (C8), there are other celebrities stepping up, and for Jeff Stewart of Huskisson, the encounter might’ve altered the course of popular music: “On a flight from Hong Kong to Colombo I was seated behind a woolly-headed individual who had his feet on the bulkhead and was jiggling and dancing around in a most disturbing fashion. My tray table was attached to his seat, and I was trying to work. I gave him a decent go but couldn’t manage any longer so tapped him on the shoulder and firmly but politely requested he stop. This he did and with apologies. It was only then that I noticed Yoko Ono seated across the aisle. And, yes, the ‘woolly-headed’ one was John Lennon. Who knows what new Beatles song I may have disturbed!” If it’s the track Flying, you’re off the hook.

Tom Meakin of Port Macquarie’s experience was a historic affair: “My mother once shared a cupboard with John Profumo while playing hide and seek.”

For Sue Hoad of Merewether, high school German (C8) “came in handy 30 years later on a 36-hour bus ride with Turkish guest workers returning to their jobs in Germany. Not a word of English - ‘Is this stop 10 minutes for the loo?’ ‘An hour for dinner?’ ‘Crossing the border to Greece?’ Saved!”

“The German experience matches my Japanese efforts,” admits Brian Byrne of Flinders. “After a tortuous term at Wagga Wagga TAFE, my only remaining scrap of this language allows me to tell any Japanese visitor that ‘My hotel is red’.”

World.title: A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void? Nick Wright September 22, 2026 — 8:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jamayne Isaako has revealed he never wanted to leave the club he helped build from the ground up, and that proved responsible for resurrecting a career he contemplated walking away from. In three of his four seasons in Dolphins colours, the Kiwi flyer has topped the NRL scoreboard – his 1043 points coming as he featured in all 97 games of the club’s history. “It’s hard not to be reminded of when you’re watching footy games, someone’s taking the goal kick and your name pops up on the TV,” Isaako laughed. Eyes on the tries: Jamayne Isaako of the Dolphins scores in the corner. Getty “But it’s something I’m certainly proud of.”



Friday night’s preliminary final showdown with the Roosters will be the last time Isaako calls Suncorp Stadium home before he departs for the Storm, with Redcliffe unable to match the offer for his services to retain their growing contingent of rising stars and off-contract marquee men. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow “It is a bit of a bittersweet moment. I would have loved to have stayed here, being a foundation member and player,” Isaako admitted. “I didn’t want to leave, but at the end of the day, everyone in the game understands how the salary cap works, and we couldn’t come to an agreement. “Being in this finals campaign, I want to give it a red-hot crack. I’m certainly coming to the back end of my career and probably won’t get too many of these opportunities.”



Much like Dolphins hooker Jeremy Marshall-King, who conceded the Bulldogs’ decision to re-sign Reed Mahoney prompted him to explore a move from Belmore, Isaako’s career was uncertain until he received a lifeline from then-coach Wayne Bennett, having been released by the Broncos and not re-signed by the Titans in the same 2022 season. “When I came here I was at a bit of a crossroads with my career, and I wasn’t too sure whether or not I still wanted to play footy,” Isaako said. “I saw the quality of players, the foundation players they had signed here – the Bromwich brothers [Jesse and Kenny], Mark Nicholls, Felise Kaufusi, who were at the top of their game at the time – and I saw an opportunity to be part of a winning team. “To be here now is certainly a great achievement.”



In a backline blessed with the flair of Herbie Farnworth, Selwyn Cobbo, Jack Bostock and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Isaako has been a calming, unflappable influence. One of the rising stars he has mentored is part of the reason he could not be retained. Loading Plucked from New Zealand rugby union, Tevita Naufahu recalled his brief conversation with Bennett before securing his first NRL deal, laughing at how the super coach – known for his distaste for handshakes – grimaced when the rookie extended his hand, before labelling him “a presentable kid”. “That’s all he told me – I look like I have good manners. The next time I came back, I had a watch on trying to look more presentable for him and prove my point,” the 20-year-old laughed.



But he takes a more serious tone when asked to reflect on what Isaako has done for him, as he vowed to continue his legacy beyond this year and “repay” the Dolphins for backing him to fill the void. Dolphins squad movements Losses Jamayne Isaako (Storm), Oryn Keeley (Storm, mid-season), Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers), Ray Stone (retirement), Daniel Saifiti (medical retirement, mid-season) Gains George Williams Key retentions Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (2029), Tevita Naufahu (2029), Brad Schneider (2028), Kurt Donoghoe (2028), Francis Molo (2028) Off contract (at the end of 2027) Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Thomas Flegler, Connelly Lemuelu, Morgan Knowles, Trai Fuller, Felise Kaufusi, LJ Nonu, Sebastian Su’a, Elijah Rasmussen, John Fineanganofo “When I moved over, I told myself it was an opportunity to become a sponge and soak up all the knowledge I get from these older blokes,” Naufahu said. “Under pressure, Jamayne is really good. He’s taught us young boys that if you’re committed to whatever you’re going to do, stay calm and you’ll come out the right end.” Isaako will be joined by fellow inaugural Dolphins Kodi Nikorima, Jake Averillo and Ray Stone in the departing class, and each have been pivotal in the club’s ascent.



It is the loss of Nikorima – another former Bronco – that could prove most telling, with the five-eighth forging one of the code’s most dominant halves pairings alongside halfback Isaiya Katoa. Katoa’s kicking game has laid the foundations for the Dolphins, booting for more metres across the past three seasons than any player (30,918), while his willingness to dig deep into the defensive line and pass late for Nikorima has allowed the latter to exploit the backline. Kodi Nikorima will leave a huge void at the Dolphins. Getty Images Nikorima was also eager to remain at Redcliffe, but the recruitment of England halfback George Williams and a compelling two-year offer from the Dragons triggered his looming exit. Katoa, however, was adamant that the Dolphins would remain a premiership threat, and felt he and Williams – who will likely vie for Isaako’s goal-kicking duties – would “definitely” strike a balance, despite both typically being dominant No.7s.



“I’m not the type to want all the glory. He’s a quality player, and a very experienced player, so I know for me, it actually helps my game,” Katoa said. “I feel like it will take a little bit of pressure off me as well, which allows me to free up a little bit. But at the moment, I’m just building on the connection me and Kodi have. “It’s going really well, but we know as a halves pairing, we can be better.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Australians are at risk of being ‘priced out’ of parenthood, expert warns
World.content:
Exclusive NationalCost of living Australians are at risk of being ‘priced out’ of parenthood, expert warns Wendy Tuohy September 22, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost of raising children has become so high that parents and those hoping to become them are being forced to shrink their intended family size, Australia’s leading parenting advocate says. New data from national advocacy organisation The Parenthood shows the cost of raising one child per year now sits at around $17,800 a year, and two or more costs more than $36,500. Francesca Steele and her elder chidlren, Banjo and Jeanie, with dog Snoop. Justin McManus Georgie Dent, a mother of three and chief executive of The Parenthood, will address the National Press Club on Wednesday warning that Australians are at risk of being priced out of parenthood. It comes two days after Treasury released its latest intergenerational report, which forecasts the nation’s steep birth rate decline will reshape the economy in coming decades. “The birth rate has plummeted and a significant part of that drop is not in desire, it’s in affordability,” Dent told this masthead. “Parents are genuinely beside themselves; so many families are very genuinely squeezed.”



The intergenerational report predicts that the national fertility rate will drop to 1.34 by 2065-66 (a fertility rate of 2.1 is needed for the population to be replaced from one generation to the next without migration), meaning deaths would outnumber births. This compares with the stated wish of Australian men and women to have more children: “Men want exactly two kids, and for women it’s 2.1 – but that’s not what’s happening,” Dent said. Related Article Parenting Are the parents all right? Why raising children feels harder than ever Australia is already wrestling with rock bottom birth rates, which fell by 25 per cent to a record low of 1.48 in 2024 from a peak of 2.02 in 2008. Dent says that without better access to childcare, a big increase in paid parental leave and more support from workplaces, this will only worsen. The Parenthood’s research, commissioned analysis from consultancy ConnellGriffin, found that over the last two decades, the cost of running a family has risen 32 per cent higher than family incomes grew over the same period.



“What it actually takes to run a family has risen 134 per cent, but the money that lands in the bank each week has risen only 102 per cent [in the last two decades],” Dent will say in her Press Club address. “Childcare has climbed from 27 to 33 per cent of the cost of raising a child.” Previous research commissioned by The Parenthood also found the struggle for parents in regional, rural and remote areas to access childcare is so great that 86 per cent “are experiencing financial stress as a result”. The costs measured by ConnellGriffin are higher than those released by the Australian National University’s Centre for Social Policy in June, which estimated one child costs roughly $13,000 per year, and two costs $23,000 – a figure that equates to about $391,000 over 17 years. Public policy changes such as increasing the minimum paid parental leave scheme from the current six months to the OECD average of one year, and providing “genuinely universal” affordable, accessible, quality childcare delivered by a professionally paid and supported workforce would free parents both to work the hours they need and afford subsequent children, Dent said.



“In 2020, only 12.5 per cent of centre-based [childcare] services had average fees above the fee cap. Today, it is about 43 per cent.” Dent has campaigned for 18 months for a national Early Childhood Education and Care Commission to oversee delivery of quality, accessible universal childcare. The Parenthood chief executive Georgie Dent will address the National Press Club on Wednesday about the urgent need for reforms to help support Australians afford the family sizes they wished for. Alex Ellinghausen Given one-third of Australia’s current workforce has dependant children, and Treasury’s Centre for Population estimates that if people’s fertility intentions had been realised between 2001 and 2022, Australia could have had an additional 881,000 births, Dent will argue that doubling parental leave and boosting childcare will have a meaningful impact. “Remove the childcare subsidy and fund it like schools,” she told this masthead on the eve of her speech. “These changes would enable people to afford the number of children they could really like.”



Related Article Motherhood ‘Thanks, Mum, but I don’t want your life’ – is the load that buckled their mothers putting off Gen Z? Mother of three, Francesca Steele, who recently wrote to Dent about the incompatibility of federal and state childcare subsidies, will observe the speech from the home she shares in Jan Juc on Victoria’s surf coast with her husband and three children aged 11, eight and two-and-a-half. Steele, an associate director of human rights and social impact at KPMG, and her husband, Simon, a winemaker, say that although they consider their family to be financially comfortable, the rocketing cost of living has forced them to cut back on holidays and children’s extracurriculars, among other expenses. Of cost of living increases recently, Steele says, “it feels exponential”. “I feel very privileged, [but] when we look at our monthly income, costs and outgoings, we’re actually going backwards,” she said.



Many parents also need to help support elder relatives as their children are entering their teen years, because of failures or gaps in the aged care system and costs associated with specialist dementia care, she said. Related Article Parenting ‘They are much better parents than us’: How modern mums and dads rise to the challenge Families like Steele’s, who are navigating this and the fact that mothers’ incomes and job promotion opportunities have historically been curtailed by the need to cover childcare, are pushed to find the extra money to also support their parents’ needs. “We don’t go out to eat or get takeaway food, we’re not spending money on extravagant things like clothes; we live a pretty simple life,” Steele said. “I have no idea how other people are surviving.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How Brownlow win will make Daicos richer; Dockers star slams flight price gouging; AFL green-lights rookie rule change
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing: Brownlow win will line Daicos’ pockets

Fremantle star slams airlines for price gouging.

AFL Commission adds extra First Nations list spot. Daicos cashes in on medal win Zoey Duchene, Hannah Kennelly and Jake Niall Nick Daicos will receive a financial windfall worth hundreds of thousands of dollars from his Brownlow win, including a bonus that was written into his Collingwood playing contract and proceeds from a marketing campaign that kicked off before the medal was even around his neck. Brownlow medallist Nick Daicos on Monday morning. Zoey Duchene



A box of Nike T-shirts commemorating Daicos’ triumph arrived at Crown Palladium while the count was still in progress, while towering billboards went up around Melbourne. Nike, a Collingwood partner with whom the 23-year-old also has an independent deal, launched the campaign branded “inevitable” on the morning of the Brownlow count. A sign commemorating NIck Daicos’ Brownlow win in Richmond. Luis Enrique Escui Daicos is one of the small handful of AFL players who command such independent deals, earning more than $500,000 a year from commercial partnerships alongside his Magpies contract, which this masthead reported was worth $1.2-1.3 million last season and runs to 2029. That earning power will only increase with his Brownlow win, which came from a record number of votes (47).



Nike, which lost French soccer superstar Kylian Mbappe to rival shoe manufacturer On this week, leant into Daicos’ $1.01 favouritism before the Brownlow Medal count. Nick Atkinson, the senior marketing director at Nike Pacific, said Daicos was “an athlete at the top of his game,” and was bound to be awarded the medal at some stage. Loading “We wanted a piece that felt authentic to Nick and mirrored the confidence at the heart of the idea, showing him in a moment of success,” Atkinson said. This masthead reported in 2023 that a Brownlow would trigger a $100,000 bonus in Daicos’ contract, before his contract was extended.



He can also receive proceeds from any signed Brownlow memorabilia, which he spruiked on his Instagram story on Monday. The morning after celebrating with his family – including parents Peter and Colleen – friends, and teammates, Daicos said he was determined not to become consumed by his growing profile and platform. Nick Daicos (right) with his parents Peter and Colleen. AFL Photos “I’m trying to stay as present as I can, and I know that there’s still many holes in my game. I need to keep improving,” said Daicos, who is desperate to win a second premiership and is already a four-time All-Australian. “From an on-field point of view, that’s what I’m focusing on now.” “I probably become a little bit numb to [the fame and commercial opportunities]. I don’t know if that’s a good or a bad thing, but I just find to try and focus on my daily processes and what works for me.”



Related Article CBD Shoulder pain or a broken heart: The mystery of Bailey Smith’s Brownlow sideshow He did appreciate the special delivery of “inevitable” Daicos T-shirts, though. “It [such bold marketing] happens a bit clearly overseas, and not much in Australia I don’t think, but hopefully I think we’re starting to see a shift in that,” Daicos said. “It was a really nice initiative from Nike, and really nice to include my family,” Daicos said. “I’ll definitely keep those shirts for the rest of my life.”



Dockers star Young damns flight price gouging Marc McGowan Fremantle match-winner Hayden Young has called out airlines’ price gouging in AFL grand final week as many Dockers fans pay thousands of dollars for a return flight to potentially witness their team make history. Hayden Young’s goal on the three-quarter-time siren inspired Fremantle’s preliminary final win. via Getty Images Young inspired Fremantle’s dramatic preliminary final comeback victory over Sydney from 28 points down with a best-on-ground performance that included a brilliant goal from the boundary after the three-quarter-time siren.



The Dockers will contest the second grand final in their 32-year history at the MCG on Saturday against the Brisbane Lions, who are chasing a flag three-peat and league immortality. Fremantle lost the 2013 decider by 15 points to Hawthorn, so Young and co. could be part of the club’s maiden AFL premiership, which is why he is so disappointed that exorbitant flights from Perth to Melbourne might mean the average fan cannot afford to be there. View post on X The cheapest tickets on Qantas travelling on Thursday – the day before the grand final parade – and returning this weekend are north of $2000, not to mention the costs of a grand final ticket and accommodation. “I find it ridiculous. It’s frustrating, and it annoys me,” Young told this masthead.



“Even for us as players, we’re having to fork out a fair bit of money to get our families over as well, and obviously the fans have to do that, too, so we’re all in the same boat. I don’t get why they do that, but it’s above my pay grade. “Hopefully, we can win and bring the cup back to our fans in Perth and Freo, and we can share it with them.” Young grew up in Victoria and played for Somerville and the Dandenong Stingrays, so his family won’t have to absorb the soaring flight costs this time around. His younger brother, Josh, lives in Perth and plays for South Fremantle, but managed to get to Melbourne before the price hike. Josh was in Sydney to watch the Dockers’ preliminary final victory, along with another sibling – ex-AFL player Lachie – and other relatives.



Young said he would relish the opportunity to realise his childhood dream and play in an AFL grand final in front of family and friends. However, he is not wearing the weight of expectation of tortured Dockers supporters desperate for their first flag. Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 Bombers seeking first-round pick if Ridley leaves to Cats or Roos, as AFL reveals their assistance package “I think maybe if you grew up in Fremantle and barracked for them your whole life, maybe you would understand that [feeling],” Young said. “But I’ve been here for seven years. I can appreciate the passion of our fans, but I’ll probably never understand what it’s been like to be in their shoes. “So, in a way, I don’t carry that pressure with me of the fans, but I certainly acknowledge the privilege that I have to represent them and what it could mean and the influence that we have. Since I’ve been here, our fans have been incredible, and it would be pretty special to do it for them.”



List spots added to foster Indigenous talent Jake Niall The AFL will allow clubs an extra list spot for First Nations players – including senior players who have been delisted – as part of the league’s push to arrest the decline of its Indigenous playing ranks. The AFL has approved additional list spots for AFL and AFLW teams in 2027. Paul Rovere The AFL Commission has agreed to the change, which gives clubs the option – it is entirely voluntary – of adding an additional category B rookie spot for the AFL and a rookie list spot for AFLW if the player is designated as First Nations. The list spot is available for the 2027 season.



The extra spot for First Nations players will allow clubs to draft players who have been delisted, such as Carlton’s Zac Williams, who can act as mentors to younger Indigenous players on the list and bolster depth. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 ‘More harm than good’: The flaw in the AFL’s plan that has Indigenous icons worried Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Clubs have been informed of the rule change, which is a response to the critical decline of First Nations players over the past five years, as numbers have dwindled from the high-water mark of more than 11 per cent of the AFL in the early 2010s. Critics of the rule within the game have argued that bolstering numbers through the extra list spot does not necessarily prolong careers or create more sustainable pathways for First Nations players. The AFL had identified that First Nations players’ careers were, on average, one year shorter than non-Indigenous players in both the men’s and women’s competitions.



But the AFL, with the backing of the AFL Players’ Association, has pushed on with what is the most radical step yet to arrest the decline, which has coincided with cuts to football department budgets post-COVID and a reluctance of clubs to take risks with limited list spots. Richmond and West Coast were among the clubs that warned during the COVID-19 period that the cuts to football budgets would impact adversely on First Nations players’ participation. One caveat to the rule is that clubs cannot delist a First Nations player and then immediately re-draft them as a rookie, or what clubs call “re-rookie” the player. Indigenous representation dropped to a 20-year low this season. There are 66 First Nations players on AFL club lists – about 8 per cent of the total playing group – and 22 First Nations players across the AFLW.



As reported by this masthead in March, the AFL set a target to reach 81 Indigenous players in the AFL and 29 in the AFLW (representing just under 10 per cent of the competitions) by 2030. “First Nations representation across the game is a key focus area for the AFL, and the introduction of this mechanism will go a significant way to providing opportunity for more First Nations players to play at the highest level,” said AFL executive general manager football performance Greg Swann. Indigenous dancers perform at the Dreamtime at the G game in May, the centrepiece of the AFL’s rounds celebrating First Nations culture. Getty Images “Our game as we know it has been shaped by First Nations players, and we want to ensure we continue to provide the best opportunity for First Nations players of the future to thrive.” General manager of First Nations engagement and inclusion, Taryn Lee, said increasing the number of First Nations players in the game was one of three priorities for the AFL.
