World.title: Your GP is probably already using AI. Now it could talk to you about your medicines
World.content:
TechnologyAI Your GP is probably already using AI. Now it could talk to you about your medicines David Swan September 22, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In consulting rooms across Australia, millions of patients this year have been asked whether they mind artificial intelligence transcribing the appointment. About 40 per cent of GPs were using a tool of that kind late last year, according to a Royal Australian College of General Practitioners poll, up from 22 per cent in 2024. None of those products are approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration. They don’t need to be. The biggest of them is Heidi, built in Melbourne by a former vascular surgery resident, and it runs in about 2.8 million patient visits a week worldwide. It is exempt for a single reason: as it works today, it only writes things down. Heidi co-founders Waleed Mussa, Thomas Kelly and Yu Liu. That’s about to change. On Tuesday night the company announced it had raised $US340 million ($476 million) to roll out AI agents that will help tackle a global healthcare worker shortage. The capital raise, led by Australian venture capital firm Blackbird, values the company at $1.26 billion, making it Australia’s latest “unicorn”, or billion-dollar tech start-up. American venture capital firm General Catalyst has separately provided a $US240 million loan to be repaid from revenue Heidi makes from investing that money into its business. Blackbird, its first backer, has repeatedly called Heidi the fastest-growing company in its portfolio, ahead of Canva.



In Australia, Heidi says its software has been rolled out at the Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne, Children’s Health Queensland and Metro South Health in Brisbane, and that its annual recurring revenue grew from $US1 million to $US50 million in the two years to April. “From the day I started Heidi, the ambition was always bigger than writing doctors’ notes,” chief executive Thomas Kelly said in announcing the raise. “I imagined that AI would sit alongside clinicians and complete real work under their supervision.” In the near term, Kelly told this masthead, Heidi’s agents will take on work such as clinical coding, follow-up and checking on patients over time, with the doctor approving each task. The company will provide more detail on how this would work in practice in a larger product release within a month. Tatiana Lowe, an emergency physician and medical director of telehealth service My Emergency Doctor, which uses Heidi, said she would hand off workers’ compensation certificates, the wording of death certificates and writing up medication charts to the app, though she would still sign the documents. Lowe, whom Heidi made available for interview, would not hand over complex diagnostic decisions, or a conversation with a family at the end of a patient’s life. “It’s something that I might do twice a day, but this is the only time they’re ever going to hear it,” she said. “They will reference their life by that discussion.”



Further out, Kelly has described Heidi handling clinical tasks such as repeat prescriptions and drug-dose calculations, which he acknowledged may mean his software becomes a regulated medical device. Related Article Cybersecurity Doctors are relying more on AI, but some tools may be open to manipulation Heidi’s coming capabilities will not be released in Britain or the European Union, a decision that Kelly attributed to differing regulatory regimes. Sean Stevens, who chairs the RACGP’s digital health and innovation specific interest group and is a clinical adviser to rival scribe company Lyrebird Health, said that the new functionality would probably require TGA oversight. “When it steps into that territory, then I think it becomes software as a medical device and needs regulation,” Stevens said.



A Therapeutic Goods Administration spokesman said the regulator did not have a view on vendors’ commercial decisions, such as when products are released in other markets. But clinical AI features that meet the definition of a medical device must comply with its requirements before they are supplied in Australia, the spokesman said, with devices regulated according to their intended purpose and risk. “The TGA’s 2024 AI review found the existing regulatory framework remains fit for purpose and sufficiently flexible to accommodate emerging technologies,” the spokesman said. Tom Sulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, said Australians should be concerned that they have fewer protections than patients in Britain or Europe. “It’s not OK for us to be treated like guinea pigs for tech companies to test out their incomplete products, especially when the data being used is our most sensitive and private information,” he said. Heidi was built in Melbourne by a former vascular surgery resident and now runs in about 2.8 million patient visits a week across 190 countries and 110 languages. Australia’s health regulator has spent the past year conducting a review of AI scribes that is now complete.



In Sydney on August 3, the regulator’s product quality division head, Tracey Duffy, told a conference that the review had found scope creep, “inclusion of AI that’s influencing decisions of clinicians”, and a lack of transparency about how vendors manage their systems. She said that action could follow over the next 12 months. The TGA told this masthead that it would publish the review’s outcomes and updated guidance shortly, and that any compliance matters would be handled under its compliance framework. It did not say whether any action involved Heidi. The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, which regulates doctors, said questions about the line between administrative tools and those that influence clinical decisions “are receiving significant attention across the regulatory system”, and it would update its guidance as needed. Up to June 30, the practitioner regulation agency had received 19 notifications about practitioners using AI scribes. Most concerned privacy breaches, patients who had not consented to the consultation being scribed, and practitioners refusing to release scribed notes. Heidi co-founder Waleed Mussa said that the company had a good relationship with regulators, wanted pragmatic regulation and told authorities in advance what it planned to build.



Heidi in operation. Clinical errors across the sector remain a risk. Lowe said she proofreads every consult and the errors are now rare, but she still finds them. Her favourite: a patient allergic to the antibiotic Keflex, recorded by Heidi as allergic to “Catholics”. The ABC earlier this year reported a case in which a scribe wrongly recorded that a patient used illicit drugs. Elizabeth Deveny, chief executive of the Consumers Health Forum of Australia, said research shows that people check automated work less as they get used to it. With a scribe, an unchecked error may enter a record; with an agent, it may result in something happening. Research by the forum last year found only about half of people surveyed thought AI scribes acceptable, and fewer than one in 10 were comfortable with AI deciding treatment options. She said productivity alone should not be the test. “Some friction is waste,” Deveny said. “But some friction is the point where someone notices something is wrong.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Lachie Neale banned for grand final in sensational tribunal ruling
World.content:
Lachie Neale’s one-match ban will stand. And he will be ineligible for the grand final.

In a comprehensive ruling, the AFL tribunal has upheld Neale’s one-match ban for striking Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in Saturday’s thrilling preliminary final at the MCG.

The AFL tribunal was critical of the veteran Lion, who hadn’t been suspended in 320 AFL matches.

Lachie Neale a training on Tuesday. Getty Images

“Neale jogged towards Ginnivan and formed the immediate intention to swing his arm forcefully at Ginnivan, and that is what he did,” said tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson.

“We have listened carefully to Neale’s evidence.

“But we find that it was inconsistent in key respects with what we saw on the video, and to what extent we do not accept it.

“There is no doubt in our minds that this should be graded as medium impact.

“While Ginnivan was not injured and did not appear to suffer any significant pain or discomfort, the blow was forceful and knocked him off his feet.

“As we have said, he immediately doubled over in a manner more consistent with a more than negligible blow having landed.

“It is relevant that this strike occurred nowhere near the ball, was not affected in or around the play, and because Ginnivan did not see Neale coming from behind or the side until the very last moment, he had no expectation of being struck until it was too late to meaningfully defend himself.”

The tribunal also dismissed any arguments that there were “compelling and exceptional circumstances” for Neale to avoid suspension and be eligible to play.

In a compelling case that both tested the AFL’s crackdown on “gut punches” and whether a player such as Neale should be granted leniency after more than 300 matches without suspension, Neale and the Lions can take the case to the AFL appeal board.

MORE TO COME

World.title: Albanese signs AI declaration with world leaders calling for international safeguards
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalAI Albanese signs AI declaration with world leaders calling for international safeguards Rob Harris Updated September 22, 2026 — 9:58pm ,first published September 22, 2026 — 2:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will issue a rallying cry for world leaders to unite on efforts to protect people from the risks of artificial intelligence, warning no country can manage the technology’s growing risks alone. Australia was among a group of 22 signatories to call for new international safeguards on AI at the United Nations on Monday, amid warnings from scientists and industry executives that the rapid development of powerful systems could outpace governments’ ability to control emerging risks. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the opening Ceremony of New York Climate Week on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer The prime minister joined colleagues, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to call for mandatory safety testing, independent evaluations and greater international oversight of so-called frontier AI models. The declaration warned that capable AI systems have already been seen circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems.



Related Article Data centres This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it “Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks,” the statement said, which was also co-signed by Ireland, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. It called for a UN-style international organisation that would set standards and oversee AI use. The leaders stopped short of calling for a halt to development, instead arguing that AI’s potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen economies should be preserved while stronger controls are imposed. “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control,” they said, insisting that it must be developed and used in accordance with international law.



Its release comes ahead of Thursday’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI expected to be a major topic of discussion. Trump said following the declaration that US law enforcement agencies like the Department of Justice would regulate artificial intelligence risks if necessary, but emphasised his primary goal was to encourage its development. Downplaying potential dangers, Trump argued against stifling AI growth, comparing its future impact to the Industrial Revolution and the internet. He maintained the US must protect its edge over China while fostering both AI and superintelligence. Loading “We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way!” Trump wrote on social media.



Related Article Opinion

AI Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Albanese has cited Australia’s role in shaping international rules for AI as a key plank of its bid for a seat on the UN Security Council. He said he hoped for a positive meeting between Trump and Xi. Addressing the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI, Albanese will say the risks posed by increasingly capable systems will cross borders and require countries to work together on common standards. “And no country can manage these risks alone,” he will say. “We must come together.” Albanese will argue countries can seize and share the opportunities created by AI while developing common standards to protect children and communities.



“We can develop clear shared expectations and common guardrails,” he will say. The US and China are locked in a race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, while Washington and Beijing have resisted calls from industry figures including Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the development of frontier models amid warnings that humans could lose control. Neither the US nor China are part of the new declaration. The declaration calls on AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory testing before systems are deployed and independent assessments by qualified evaluators given sufficient access to identify risks. Governments and regional organisations are also urged to develop common standards, strengthen transparency and share reports of serious AI safety incidents. Albanese said AI had the potential to improve lives, strengthen the economy and productivity, and advance science and medical breakthroughs, but “humans need to be in control of it”.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates He said he had played a central role in the statement through conversations with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the declaration along with Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. The leaders want countries across all regions to have access to the scientific expertise, technical capacity and trusted evaluation needed to assess advanced AI systems. The declaration also calls on UN member states to explore creating an international institution that could set standards, enable verification and convene governments when AI systems cross agreed capability thresholds. The group warned that efforts to control frontier AI should not widen the gap between countries with access to the technology and those unable to benefit from its advances.



At a separate business event with Macquarie, Albanese will argue Australia is being recognised internationally for moving early on emerging challenges. “I think the world is seeing Australia as a smart, adaptable and successful middle power, succeeding because we’re not afraid to get ahead of the curve on the issues that matter to the future,” he will say. World.title: The opinion piece at the end of the world
World.content:
Peter Riley of Penrith writes: “We keep hearing that AI is going to make humanity extinct, so I asked AI if C8 is also doomed. It replied ‘Nothing is truly permanent, but Column 8 is as close to immortal as Australian journalism gets. Getting a snippet published by Granny is a major life milestone. It creates an intensely loyal micro-community within the SMH Opinion section. The newspaper would face open revolt from its core subscriber base if they ever tried to axe it.’ So there. AI wouldn’t fib, would it?”

While it’s time to move on from encounters with the Bee Gees (C8), there are other celebrities stepping up, and for Jeff Stewart of Huskisson, the encounter might’ve altered the course of popular music: “On a flight from Hong Kong to Colombo I was seated behind a woolly-headed individual who had his feet on the bulkhead and was jiggling and dancing around in a most disturbing fashion. My tray table was attached to his seat, and I was trying to work. I gave him a decent go but couldn’t manage any longer so tapped him on the shoulder and firmly but politely requested he stop. This he did and with apologies. It was only then that I noticed Yoko Ono seated across the aisle. And, yes, the ‘woolly-headed’ one was John Lennon. Who knows what new Beatles song I may have disturbed!” If it’s the track Flying, you’re off the hook.

Tom Meakin of Port Macquarie’s experience was a historic affair: “My mother once shared a cupboard with John Profumo while playing hide and seek.”

For Sue Hoad of Merewether, high school German (C8) “came in handy 30 years later on a 36-hour bus ride with Turkish guest workers returning to their jobs in Germany. Not a word of English - ‘Is this stop 10 minutes for the loo?’ ‘An hour for dinner?’ ‘Crossing the border to Greece?’ Saved!”

“The German experience matches my Japanese efforts,” admits Brian Byrne of Flinders. “After a tortuous term at Wagga Wagga TAFE, my only remaining scrap of this language allows me to tell any Japanese visitor that ‘My hotel is red’.”

World.title: A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 A creative genius and a point-scoring whizz make a last stand. Can the Dolphins fill the void? Nick Wright September 22, 2026 — 8:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jamayne Isaako has revealed he never wanted to leave the club he helped build from the ground up, and that proved responsible for resurrecting a career he contemplated walking away from. In three of his four seasons in Dolphins colours, the Kiwi flyer has topped the NRL scoreboard – his 1043 points coming as he featured in all 97 games of the club’s history. “It’s hard not to be reminded of when you’re watching footy games, someone’s taking the goal kick and your name pops up on the TV,” Isaako laughed. Eyes on the tries: Jamayne Isaako of the Dolphins scores in the corner. Getty “But it’s something I’m certainly proud of.”



Friday night’s preliminary final showdown with the Roosters will be the last time Isaako calls Suncorp Stadium home before he departs for the Storm, with Redcliffe unable to match the offer for his services to retain their growing contingent of rising stars and off-contract marquee men. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow “It is a bit of a bittersweet moment. I would have loved to have stayed here, being a foundation member and player,” Isaako admitted. “I didn’t want to leave, but at the end of the day, everyone in the game understands how the salary cap works, and we couldn’t come to an agreement. “Being in this finals campaign, I want to give it a red-hot crack. I’m certainly coming to the back end of my career and probably won’t get too many of these opportunities.”



Much like Dolphins hooker Jeremy Marshall-King, who conceded the Bulldogs’ decision to re-sign Reed Mahoney prompted him to explore a move from Belmore, Isaako’s career was uncertain until he received a lifeline from then-coach Wayne Bennett, having been released by the Broncos and not re-signed by the Titans in the same 2022 season. “When I came here I was at a bit of a crossroads with my career, and I wasn’t too sure whether or not I still wanted to play footy,” Isaako said. “I saw the quality of players, the foundation players they had signed here – the Bromwich brothers [Jesse and Kenny], Mark Nicholls, Felise Kaufusi, who were at the top of their game at the time – and I saw an opportunity to be part of a winning team. “To be here now is certainly a great achievement.”



In a backline blessed with the flair of Herbie Farnworth, Selwyn Cobbo, Jack Bostock and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Isaako has been a calming, unflappable influence. One of the rising stars he has mentored is part of the reason he could not be retained. Loading Plucked from New Zealand rugby union, Tevita Naufahu recalled his brief conversation with Bennett before securing his first NRL deal, laughing at how the super coach – known for his distaste for handshakes – grimaced when the rookie extended his hand, before labelling him “a presentable kid”. “That’s all he told me – I look like I have good manners. The next time I came back, I had a watch on trying to look more presentable for him and prove my point,” the 20-year-old laughed.



But he takes a more serious tone when asked to reflect on what Isaako has done for him, as he vowed to continue his legacy beyond this year and “repay” the Dolphins for backing him to fill the void. Dolphins squad movements Losses Jamayne Isaako (Storm), Oryn Keeley (Storm, mid-season), Kodi Nikorima (Dragons), Jake Averillo (Tigers), Ray Stone (retirement), Daniel Saifiti (medical retirement, mid-season) Gains George Williams Key retentions Selwyn Cobbo (2031), Kulikefu Finefeuiaki (2029), Tevita Naufahu (2029), Brad Schneider (2028), Kurt Donoghoe (2028), Francis Molo (2028) Off contract (at the end of 2027) Herbie Farnworth, Jack Bostock, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Thomas Flegler, Connelly Lemuelu, Morgan Knowles, Trai Fuller, Felise Kaufusi, LJ Nonu, Sebastian Su’a, Elijah Rasmussen, John Fineanganofo “When I moved over, I told myself it was an opportunity to become a sponge and soak up all the knowledge I get from these older blokes,” Naufahu said. “Under pressure, Jamayne is really good. He’s taught us young boys that if you’re committed to whatever you’re going to do, stay calm and you’ll come out the right end.” Isaako will be joined by fellow inaugural Dolphins Kodi Nikorima, Jake Averillo and Ray Stone in the departing class, and each have been pivotal in the club’s ascent.



It is the loss of Nikorima – another former Bronco – that could prove most telling, with the five-eighth forging one of the code’s most dominant halves pairings alongside halfback Isaiya Katoa. Katoa’s kicking game has laid the foundations for the Dolphins, booting for more metres across the past three seasons than any player (30,918), while his willingness to dig deep into the defensive line and pass late for Nikorima has allowed the latter to exploit the backline. Kodi Nikorima will leave a huge void at the Dolphins. Getty Images Nikorima was also eager to remain at Redcliffe, but the recruitment of England halfback George Williams and a compelling two-year offer from the Dragons triggered his looming exit. Katoa, however, was adamant that the Dolphins would remain a premiership threat, and felt he and Williams – who will likely vie for Isaako’s goal-kicking duties – would “definitely” strike a balance, despite both typically being dominant No.7s.



“I’m not the type to want all the glory. He’s a quality player, and a very experienced player, so I know for me, it actually helps my game,” Katoa said. “I feel like it will take a little bit of pressure off me as well, which allows me to free up a little bit. But at the moment, I’m just building on the connection me and Kodi have. “It’s going really well, but we know as a halves pairing, we can be better.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Like its institutions, America is crumbling
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Like its institutions, America is crumbling September 22, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. WORLD ORDER The Age’s North America correspondent, Michael Koziol, writes Washington “is a grand city of monuments to American endeavour and excellence” being turned by Trump “into monuments to his own ego” (“In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way”, 22/9). The president’s heritage vandalism epitomised by the overblown White House ballroom, similarly monstrous triumphal arch, botched reflecting pool renovation and threatened demolition of the Kennedy Centre, pales into insignificance though alongside his other outrages.

These include dismantling American democracy and the country’s machinery of government, incompetently and lethally enforcing immigration, imposing illegal and economically damaging tariffs worldwide, making war on Iran and exploiting the presidency to increase his personal wealth by more than $1.2 billion so far.

Trump’s solipsistic ego, unleashed by his second presidency, seems on the way to destroying America’s credibility as a nation: politically, socially, economically and militarily.

His egotistical tinkering with buildings and monuments in Washington, is superficial by comparison.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills



Histrionics instead of leadership

I am convinced that history repeats itself in many different ways over time if one has ever read any history and compared events. I refer to the falling of two empires in recent times, the fading hegemons of Britain and France, both of which have all but disappeared before my eyes since I was born as a ‘Baby Boomer’.

Now, in such a short space of time, we have the passing of the American empire, crashing down like the last of those tripods in H.G. Wells’ War of the Worlds.

The last teetering tripod is steered by a transactional Donald J. Trump, seemingly determined to wreck the world economy before he leaves with histrionics reminiscent of the now reviled Benito Mussolini, who once strutted the world stage.

Derek Costello, Belmont Some light amid the gloom

Given the current state of the world, it is tempting to succumb to despair. Yet, this week in Washington and Jerusalem, two uplifting, positive events occurred. When Trump banned a number of left-wing news outlets from the president’s public events because he disliked their coverage, the rest of the news corp stood with them in solidarity – including right-wing organisations like Fox News.

In Jerusalem, orthodox hooligans attacked a progressive synagogue and harassed the congregants. In the aftermath, several orthodox rabbis reached out in support of this synagogue.

The proverbial glass is never completely empty.

Sue Fisher, Coburg Do as US media has done

Finally, we see some solid action. The US media – ABC, NBC, CBS and Fox – (“Networks refuse to cover Trump, 22/9) have stood up to Trump’s bullying of the press, and censorship of reporting that he doesn’t like.

We have a similar situation. Pauline Hanson is following Trump’s every move and has blocked The Guardian and the ABC from her press conferences. The Age and Sydney Morning Herald, along with The Australian, the Australian Financial Review and the Herald Sun, must follow the US media’s lead and boycott Hanson and the rest of the One Nation MPs and candidates in support of those media outlets so Australians get the full range of news.

Amy Bachrach, McKinnon Race to bottom on immigration

No matter how low Labor goes with its immigration policy, Pauline Hanson and One Nation will go lower. How low do we have to go in this ugly debate full of misinformation to set our migration policy?

Anne Maki, Alphington THE FORUM



What limitless resources?

Re ″⁣More power to the redheads″⁣, 22/9. Exclusive Brethren’s Bruce Hales, who says he is “so close to the Lord Jesus that he can feel his heartbeat”, advocates – like Gina Rinehart and ‘the redhead’ – digging up our “limitless resources”. On what planet are resources limitless? In what universe is our planet not burning up?

Bearing arms is against Brethren doctrine, but by all means pray for it and advocate for it, via God, in the political sphere.

Hales’ support for Hanson is now on the record. One Nation national director Ashby will not comment. The Coalition continues to defend the Brethren. Will the “intense scrutiny” now being applied to examine their activities – including ties with neo-Nazis – curtail their actions at polling booths next time around?

Fiona Colin, Malvern East Intergenerational report

It is ironic that Australia’s net migration is being cut just as the Intergenerational Report (IGR) finds that in coming decades the nation will “rely more heavily on migration as fertility rates drop” (“Future living standards at stake in numbers game”, 22/9). The Pauline Hanson effect will have a lot to answer for.

As political editor Peter Hartcher notes, another Hanson effect is a 60 per cent decline in Labor MPs’ mentions of “climate change” (“Labor’s enemy ... with benefits”, 19/9). But using the term is not the same as enacting policy. When the Coalition and One Nation use “climate change”, “emissions” and “net zero”, it is largely as criticism.

At least the government’s IGR acknowledges “overwhelming evidence that human-induced climate change is occurring” and its potentially increasing negative economic effects. Its Energy Transition section is able to point to Treasury’s Net Zero Plan modelling, the 2025 National Climate Risk Assessment and the Climate Change Authority’s 2025 Annual Progress Report. This contrasts with the 2015 and 2021 IGRs under the Abbott and Morrison governments, when climate change received far less attention.

But approving new fossil-fuel projects undermines that message. If climate change is an intergenerational threat, 37 new fossil-fuel approvals is an odd response.

Ray Peck, Hawthorn Albanese out of step

Anthony Albanese certainly has a credibility problem on climate change (“PM warns on climate ahead of UN summit”, The Age, 22/9).

Speaking about global cooperation on climate at New York Climate Week while leading one of the world’s largest fossil fuel-exporting nations, and while on the verge of approving another carbon bomb in Woodside’s Browse gas project, smacks of hypocrisy.

Australians are already showing the way forward through strong support for a gas export tax, countless objections to new gas projects (Letters, “Gas, coal and petrol? No, we don’t need it”, 22/9), and the rapid uptake of solar panels and home batteries. The public is ready for a clean energy future. The government needs to catch up.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Some chutzpah

Prime Minister Albanese warning the United Nations about climate impacts while his government refuses to release a commissioned report on the security risks to Australia from climate impacts is one thing. To then lament ″⁣escalating climate catastrophes″⁣ (″⁣PM warns on climate ahead of UN summit″⁣, 22/9) while spruiking gas– well that really takes some chutzpah.

Brenda Tait, Northcote Superannuation fantastic

If the past few decades of Intergenerational Reports from Treasury have taught us anything, it’s that superannuation is fantastic. It gives us a well-funded retirement.

It also, for most people, relegates the pension to something more like a safety net for our ‘very, very old age’, should we live that long and need it.

The other lesson the IR teaches, each and every time, is that the Liberal Party deeply resents the middle-class having a comfortable retirement, and they’ll never give up their mission to undermine and dismantle the superannuation system, at every opportunity they get.

Geoffrey McNaughton, Glen Huntly



Hands off super

Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg seems determined to undermine the integrity of Australia’s superannuation system, to encourage first home buyers to stretch themselves even further in pursuit of the great Australian dream, and to boost the fortunes of property vendors and related enterprises at the same time.

Looking back 30 years, when the property market was last enduring an extended soft patch, it was property industry luminaries who stepped up and called for home buyers to gain access to their superannuation funds. Politicians usually only popped up with these kinds of proposals during property market peaks.

While respecting his work ethic and commitment to advancing the coalition’s prospects, I can only conclude that Andrew Bragg represents a bold new strain of politician who combines the slightly questionable instincts of both property spruikers and vote chasers.

Fraser Faithfull, Caulfield South Noisy neighbours

I heard the CEO of data centres Australia on ABC radio (22/9) explaining that the new rules around their establishment in Victoria will discourage investment in Victoria. Good. Who really wants a giant, noisy, energy greedy, monolith in their backyard? And to what end?

All of this “investment: is for the advancement of AI. Again, to what end?

We must all question why tens of billions of dollars are being spent by the “Tech Bros” in this race for power. Anyone who has carefully considered their motivation for this race should be scared of the possible outcomes. I know I am.

Bill Proctor, Launching Place Death, taxes, premierships

Trying to predict where Australia will be in 40 years’ time is rather pointless. About all we can be certain about is that our population will be larger and St Kilda will still be looking for their second premiership.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne

Yobbos all over

Not just at the MCG. The bottle throwing at the end of the NRL semi-final in Auckland on Sunday night, when the referee and colleagues were subjected to the same spectator abuse, should be equally condemned.

Brian Kidd, Mt Waverley Decent blokes all

The AFL has rules, and according to the letter of these rules, free kicks were awarded against three Hawthorn players (decent blokes all) in the last two minutes of that spectacular preliminary final, turning the tide in the game. Lachie Neale intentionally punched an opponent in the chest behind play, knocking him down. The rules say he should not play this week. Decent bloke or not.

Lynn Corcoran, Carlton Don’t shut your mouth

I agree with the letter about the content and presentation of the national anthem (21/9), but when will the czars of football realise the very bad look of AFL footballers standing side by side when it is sung before a game, with few opening their mouths?

Margaret O’Connor, Balwyn



Croydon report

I quite agree with writer Angus Delaney that Croydon’s very ordinariness is its strength. I also thank him for adding a new word to my vocabulary, namely the term ″⁣eshay″⁣ for a certain kind of local lad (″⁣My suburb lacks an appeal to young adults. But moving back gives fresh perspective″⁣, 21/9).

It must be obvious that I do not follow social media and had not heard of the Audie Hillman song about Christmas time in Croydon.

I think Angus has a lively writing style, but I also found a couple of grammatical mistakes which jarred.

For instance, in the fifth paragraph he writes: ″⁣Growing up, Croydon station had a reputation″⁣. Croydon station was not growing up, Angus was; and so the sentence could start like this: ″⁣While I was growing up, Croydon station had a reputation...″⁣.

He begins his lament about housing affordability: ″⁣Like many Melbourne suburbs, rising house prices...″⁣.

House prices are not like suburbs. This sentence can only make sense if recast to read: ″⁣As in many Melbourne suburbs, rising house prices have resulted...″⁣.

Janna McCurdy, Northcote Trams to cuddle

Your correspondent (Letters, 22/9) says the European Tram Driver Championship shows Melbourne’s tram network is not world-class.

In response, I draw my fellow Victorians’ attention to the grand old town of Bendigo, where lovingly restored heritage trams ply their trade among tourist destinations, 19th-century architecture and the graceful Rosalind Park.

Theirs is a stable that has brought us the meticulously painted Sistine Tram, the Blues Tram that hosts live bands, a 1920s machine so heavily yarn-bombed as to be the only 20-tonne vehicle you can actually cuddle, the restaurant trams of course, the tram café where a pre-world war one tram car parked in a leafy side street serves coffee and toasties to all comers, and, my favourite, the Friday Night Drinks Tram.

Yes, Bendigo is the only place that truly puts the “pub” back in public transport.

Bendigo’s trams might not dominate the championships’ official events, but they could certainly be judged the most fun.

Peter Bear, Mitcham AND ANOTHER THING Political bedfellows

Exclusive Brethren continue to lobby politically. Now they’re backing ″⁣the redheaded lady″⁣ (″⁣More power to the redheads″⁣ 22/9). I’m alert and alarmed, and I’d like someone to create an appropriate fridge magnet.

Jane Ross, San Remo Religious sect leaders seem to have missed the point when Jesus said, “In my Father’s house are many mansions”, going by the massive compounds they live in.

Mark Kennedy, Sebastopol



Bruce Hales may be called the Exclusive Brethren’s “Elect Vessel” but the only vessel he emulates is a submarine where all his activities are below the surface.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Pauline Hanson’s views that domestic crime “is a two-way street″⁣, speaks loudly to the fact that she has made no public comment on what has happened in NSW over the last short while. Not a leader in any way, shape or form.

Philip West, Jan Juc In years to come, when One Nation and Pauline Hanson are long forgotten, our falling birthrate and shortage of workers will see Australia competing with other countries for migrants.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood If Angus Taylor’s obfuscation that ″⁣union officials determine how superannuation is invested″⁣ were true (it’s not), a cursory look at comparative returns between industry super funds and those in the retail sector, might encourage circumspect investors to applaud that endeavour.

John Dickson, Glen Waverley AFL

Congratulations Nick, you represent what’s good in young men. Humble, kind, family values and you are pro-feminist. Good on you, Peter and Colleen Daicos for raising wonderful young men who have not allowed the spotlight to tarnish them.

Irene Alexandrou, Williamstown



What would Digger from the “Coodabeen Champions” say about the umpires’ decisions from last Saturday’s preliminary final?

Kerry McInerney, Mornington The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Australians are at risk of being ‘priced out’ of parenthood, expert warns
World.content:
Exclusive NationalCost of living Australians are at risk of being ‘priced out’ of parenthood, expert warns Wendy Tuohy September 22, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost of raising children has become so high that parents and those hoping to become them are being forced to shrink their intended family size, Australia’s leading parenting advocate says. New data from national advocacy organisation The Parenthood shows the cost of raising one child per year now sits at around $17,800 a year, and two or more costs more than $36,500. Francesca Steele and her elder chidlren, Banjo and Jeanie, with dog Snoop. Justin McManus Georgie Dent, a mother of three and chief executive of The Parenthood, will address the National Press Club on Wednesday warning that Australians are at risk of being priced out of parenthood. It comes two days after Treasury released its latest intergenerational report, which forecasts the nation’s steep birth rate decline will reshape the economy in coming decades. “The birth rate has plummeted and a significant part of that drop is not in desire, it’s in affordability,” Dent told this masthead. “Parents are genuinely beside themselves; so many families are very genuinely squeezed.”



The intergenerational report predicts that the national fertility rate will drop to 1.34 by 2065-66 (a fertility rate of 2.1 is needed for the population to be replaced from one generation to the next without migration), meaning deaths would outnumber births. This compares with the stated wish of Australian men and women to have more children: “Men want exactly two kids, and for women it’s 2.1 – but that’s not what’s happening,” Dent said. Related Article Parenting Are the parents all right? Why raising children feels harder than ever Australia is already wrestling with rock bottom birth rates, which fell by 25 per cent to a record low of 1.48 in 2024 from a peak of 2.02 in 2008. Dent says that without better access to childcare, a big increase in paid parental leave and more support from workplaces, this will only worsen. The Parenthood’s research, commissioned analysis from consultancy ConnellGriffin, found that over the last two decades, the cost of running a family has risen 32 per cent higher than family incomes grew over the same period.



“What it actually takes to run a family has risen 134 per cent, but the money that lands in the bank each week has risen only 102 per cent [in the last two decades],” Dent will say in her Press Club address. “Childcare has climbed from 27 to 33 per cent of the cost of raising a child.” Previous research commissioned by The Parenthood also found the struggle for parents in regional, rural and remote areas to access childcare is so great that 86 per cent “are experiencing financial stress as a result”. The costs measured by ConnellGriffin are higher than those released by the Australian National University’s Centre for Social Policy in June, which estimated one child costs roughly $13,000 per year, and two costs $23,000 – a figure that equates to about $391,000 over 17 years. Public policy changes such as increasing the minimum paid parental leave scheme from the current six months to the OECD average of one year, and providing “genuinely universal” affordable, accessible, quality childcare delivered by a professionally paid and supported workforce would free parents both to work the hours they need and afford subsequent children, Dent said.



“In 2020, only 12.5 per cent of centre-based [childcare] services had average fees above the fee cap. Today, it is about 43 per cent.” Dent has campaigned for 18 months for a national Early Childhood Education and Care Commission to oversee delivery of quality, accessible universal childcare. The Parenthood chief executive Georgie Dent will address the National Press Club on Wednesday about the urgent need for reforms to help support Australians afford the family sizes they wished for. Alex Ellinghausen Given one-third of Australia’s current workforce has dependant children, and Treasury’s Centre for Population estimates that if people’s fertility intentions had been realised between 2001 and 2022, Australia could have had an additional 881,000 births, Dent will argue that doubling parental leave and boosting childcare will have a meaningful impact. “Remove the childcare subsidy and fund it like schools,” she told this masthead on the eve of her speech. “These changes would enable people to afford the number of children they could really like.”



Related Article Motherhood ‘Thanks, Mum, but I don’t want your life’ – is the load that buckled their mothers putting off Gen Z? Mother of three, Francesca Steele, who recently wrote to Dent about the incompatibility of federal and state childcare subsidies, will observe the speech from the home she shares in Jan Juc on Victoria’s surf coast with her husband and three children aged 11, eight and two-and-a-half. Steele, an associate director of human rights and social impact at KPMG, and her husband, Simon, a winemaker, say that although they consider their family to be financially comfortable, the rocketing cost of living has forced them to cut back on holidays and children’s extracurriculars, among other expenses. Of cost of living increases recently, Steele says, “it feels exponential”. “I feel very privileged, [but] when we look at our monthly income, costs and outgoings, we’re actually going backwards,” she said.



Many parents also need to help support elder relatives as their children are entering their teen years, because of failures or gaps in the aged care system and costs associated with specialist dementia care, she said. Related Article Parenting ‘They are much better parents than us’: How modern mums and dads rise to the challenge Families like Steele’s, who are navigating this and the fact that mothers’ incomes and job promotion opportunities have historically been curtailed by the need to cover childcare, are pushed to find the extra money to also support their parents’ needs. “We don’t go out to eat or get takeaway food, we’re not spending money on extravagant things like clothes; we live a pretty simple life,” Steele said. “I have no idea how other people are surviving.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: RMA replacement laws pass in Parliament
World.content:
The two laws replacing the Resource Management Act (RMA) have passed their third reading in Parliament.

The RMA is being superseded by the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill.

The government said the reforms were "the most significant overhaul" of New Zealand's planning system in more than three decades, and would make building infrastructure easier, faster and more affordable.

But opposition parties have warned the changes could make the system more unworkable, and dilute environmental protections.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said scrapping the RMA was breaking free from a system that had stifled economic growth.

"We are restoring the freedom for New Zealanders to shape their own futures by using property as they choose, a once in a generation shift towards growth, choice and prosperity," he said.

At the heart of the reforms were enjoyment and use of people's own land, he said, labelling that "the Kiwi dream".

Bishop said the Opposition had painted property rights as "some evil, right wing plan".

Labour's Rachael Brooking said the inclusion of regulatory relief scheme (that would see landowners compensated by councils for changes that affect them) would either cause chaos and great expense for ratepayers, or see councils give up on environmental protections.

"This [reform] will lead to a big, muddy mess ... it will not improve efficiencies, and it will not improve the cost burden on the public," Brooking said.

A Labour government would not flip-flop on the reform - rather, make amendments, she said.

The Greens' environment spokesperson Lan Pham said the laws would allow untold harm to human health and the environment.

"With the passing of these bills, Aotearoa is in a new era of environmental exploitation at the hands of polluting industries," she said.

Pham said the government had ignored official advice, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment and 75 percent of submitters.

The ACT party is claiming victory, saying National had in the past been against RMA reform but ACT had never run from the massive job of replacing it.

Infrastructure spokesperson Simon Court said the old system "let every Tom, Dick and Harry say no" to building projects.

World.title: Alleged kidnappers accused of impersonating police officers
World.content:
Two Bay of Plenty youths were detained by three people allegedly pretending to be police officers and driving a former police car.

The three people have been charged with multiple offences, including kidnapping, indecent assault and impersonating police after the "traumatic" incident last Sunday.

Acting Detective Senior Sergeant Ash Clements said the two youths were detained on Sunday 13 September by two men and a woman who had presented themselves as police officers and appeared to be driving in an unmarked police car.

Clements said one of the men had a 2017 black Holden Commodore, which had been a police vehicle and had been stripped of all police equipment and markings before being sold at auction.

He said parts of the car had been allegedly re-fitted with off-market lights to make it look an unmarked police car.

"The occupants of the vehicle were in plain clothes - not police uniform, were not wearing police body armour, and were portraying themselves as detectives. This, paired with the imitation police vehicle, is more than enough to trick an unsuspecting person."

A 34-year-old man was arrested yesterday over this incident and prior reports of impersonating police. He has been remanded in custody, and faces charges of impersonating personnel, indecent assault, intimidation, two counts of kidnapping, and five counts of impersonating police.

A 19-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman were also arrested today. The 19-year-old has been charged with indecent assault, two counts of kidnapping, and two counts of impersonating police, while the woman faces kidnapping charges.

"Detaining a person under false pretences and without the proper authority amounts to kidnapping, which is an extremely serious offence in addition to impersonating police, and we take this offending seriously," said Clements.

"This was a traumatic incident for the victims involved.

"Anyone who doubts that they are speaking with a real police officer is urged to ask for their police issued ID, and if you still have concerns, call 111 immediately and a police communicator can identify the officer for you."

World.title: Man dies after fight in Lower Hutt last month
World.content:
A man critically injured in a fight in Lower Hutt last month has died in hospital.

Police were called to Waterloo Road on Sunday 30 August, after reports of a brawl in which a number of people were hurt.

A 45-year-old man was arrested after he handed himself in at the Wellington Central Police Station.

He was charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and striking with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

World.title: Senior official appearing to try hide information being taken 'very seriously'
World.content:
This story has been updated to clarify the Public Service Commissioner is not investigating the matter

The secondary teachers union fears a video that shows an education official seemingly trying to "subvert" the Official Information Act is part of a wider problem with secrecy around the government's curriculum rewrite.

The head of the Education Ministry is investigating the case after leaked footage given to the NZ Herald showed senior Ministry of Education official Catherine Law telling staff not to put information shared with the minister's office in writing and reminding them it was "OIA-able" - referencing the Official Information Act.

"What we do not need is anything in response in writing that shows that this stuff has gone backwards and forwards between them and us," she said.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405403556112

"It's just really important.

"As far as anyone's concerned it's just feedback from me."

Law was seconded from her role as principal of Avonside Girls' High School to lead work on the secondary school curriculum.

Post Primary Teachers Association president Chris Abercrombie told RNZ the video raised significant concerns and the union believed there was a widespread problem.

"It confirms rumours we've been hearing that there's this real push to not have things written down, to be really opaque about what's occurring in the curriculum," he said.

"I don't think this one individual just decided off their own bat that this was something they were going to talk about. I think this is really clearly a government trying to work in secret on the curriculum and you tie this in with the heavy use of non-disclosure agreements, the significant sort of pushing out of individual voices - this is a real concern."

Abercrombie said the development of a school curriculum should be transparent .

"If there's anything in this country that should be done publicly, it's our national curriculum," he said.

"There should be no secrets about this and it should be clear who's involved, why they're involved, and the process behind it."

Abercrombie said knowing the debates and thinking that shaped curriculums was vital.

"Curriculums just don't appear out of thin air. It's a process, it's an understanding. What was left out? What was not put in? What was the discussion about?" he said.

"Those discussions are just as important as the finished document... Every single thing in a curriculum is that someone made a decision. So who made that decision? Was it teachers? Was it ministry officials? Or was it someone in the minister's office that has no accountability?"

Abercrombie said the union would raise the issue at its next meeting with the ministry.

The government's curriculum rewrite has been dogged by criticism and controversy.

Groups representing teachers of various school subjects repeatedly criticised the process for writing the curriculums and the resulting documents

The Waitangi Tribunal said last week the rewrite was ideological, aided by people hostile to Māori knowledge, and breached multiple Treaty principles.

'Not a surprise'

The primary teachers union, NZEI Te Riu Roa said it had asked Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche to investigate.

The union's national secretary Stephanie Mills said the video reinforced ongoing concerns from the education sector about the closed and unnecessarily secret development of curriculum documents over the past two years.

"The Minister of Education stands to benefit from this attempt by ministry staff and her office to breach transparency because it reduces public scrutiny of her decision-making," Mills said.

"It is implausible in our view that she had no knowledge of the approach they were taking."

A former Education Ministry curriculum writer, Claire Coleman, said the video was the type of behaviour she and other ministry staff had encountered.

"It's not a surprise to me in the slightest," she said.

"It's exactly the kind of thing going on - don't write it down, instructions coming through verbally so that there is no record. Yeah, it's not a surprise at all," she said.

Coleman said there were a lot of questions about who had input to the curriculum and it was clear the minister's office had a lot of influence.

She said some of the content was not supported by evidence or appeared to be ideological.

"If you're trying to create a curriculum where you want to suggest that it's been written by experts and it's been properly done through a process, you don't people to know that's not the case," she said.

Coleman said there should be an independent inquiry into the way the curriculum was rewritten.

She made similar allegations earlier this year.

'We take our obligations extremely seriously' - Stanford

Speaking to media earlier, Erica Stanford said she was confident her Secretary of Education had the situation "in hand".

"She's already talked to the Public Service Commission, she's already talked to the Ombudsman, and she's already looking into the matter and taking it very seriously, as I expect that she would do."

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Stanford denied instructing officials to subvert the OIA process.

"We take our obligations extremely seriously, and as I said, this is a matter for the Secretary of Education and her staff.

"My political staff and I have not seen the documents that she was talking about."

Asked if there was a culture where officials were trying to hide information so they did not embarrass her, Stanford said she hoped "that's not the case".

"I've always made sure that the Secretary of Education understands that we are abiding by the Official Information Act, and I've made that clear again yesterday."

Labour leader and former education minister Chris Hipkins said circumventing transparency laws was "inexcusable".

"Ultimately, ministers sign off the curriculum so there's there's nothing that should be secret here.

"There should be a transparent process around that, and trying to circumvent that so that you can make edits to the curriculum without anybody knowing that's what you're doing seems bizarre, secretive, and just inexcusable." he said.

World.title: Decision to send 12-year-old home with 'safety plan' shortly before her death questioned
World.content:
Warning: This story discusses details of a suspected suicide.

A coroner has questioned whether it was appropriate to send a 12-year-old New Plymouth girl home with a "safety plan" shortly before her suspected suicide in 2017.

An inquest into the girl's death is being held at the New Plymouth District Court.

Coroner Heather McKenzie asked the Oranga Tamariki supervisor, who managed the social worker dealing with the case, how a child could be responsible for their own safety.

"I'm challenged by what seems a pretty big thing to put on a 12-year-old's shoulders. Do you have any comment on that?"

The supervisor, who cannot be named for legal reasons, said it could be appropriate for a young person of that age.

"A child of an age who has a certain ability to run away, to call somebody for help as opposed to an infant who has not got that ability... she had the ability to what we call 'self-protect' to a degree, to let people know that stuff was happening."

The safety plan involved teachers, wider whānau members - including an aunt who lived in the home - neighbours and calling 111 if the girl felt unsafe.

Two years after her death, a drug-addicted Taranaki woman was jailed for four years and three months for the physical and psychological abuse of three children.

The Oranga Tamariki supervisor gave evidence for most of Tuesday, outlining the ministry's interactions with the child's family and those with other agencies dating back to the mid 2000s.

The coroner asked the supervisor, if she had a "magic wand" what would she wish for that could've made a difference in the girl's case.

"I wish that we had a centralised point by which some key agencies and ministries - so we're talking Ministry of Education, Ministry of Health, police and Oranga Tamariki - had a centralised place to record things.

"If there was a database and it had a particular criteria where we could all... just instantaneously access that information, we would be a lot further ahead."

The supervisor said the social worker who had allowed the girl to return home with a "safety plan" and was managing the situation via a "whānau family agreement" didn't have all the information available at the time because of the way it was being reported and sometimes filed.

She said workload was also an issue, with the social worker concerned dealing with 42 clients when "the ideal was no more than 17".

The supervisor pushed back on previous witnesses assertions that Oranga Tamariki didn't act quickly enough in the girl's case.

"I consider that incorrect. We actually did give it urgency. We gave it more urgency than even our own contact centre believed we should."

Asked by McKenzie if the agency had done anything wrong up until the time the child died, the supervisor said she didn't believe so.

"I think everybody did everything they could with what they had at the time, and so from Oranga Tamariki's perspective, every practice guidance that we had at the time, and every policy that we had at the time, was met."

Counsel assisting the inquest Rebekah Jordan had earlier asked the supervisor about the 12-year-old's well-being and suicide risk assessment.

The child had scored 4 out of 25, when 12-plus was considered high-risk and would result in a referral to the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services.

This was despite her admitting to having thoughts about "ending it all" and having self-harmed.

The Oranga Tamariki supervisor said her risk was considered low.

"It seems crazy to say that now, doesn't it? Now, given what we know now. But from the Kessler screening, her risk was considered low. She certainly had need in that space, but it wasn't considered urgent that day.

"So, at the assessment at that time, she said she wasn't suicidal, she didn't have a plan ... and she was [considered] in very low psychological distress."

Earlier, Detective Sergeant David Beattie, who had oversight of New Plymouth police family harm unit at the time, gave evidence.

After the child died, he carried out an internal review of the family harm unit's involvement in the case.

Beattie said the review found there was a high degree of collaboration between the unit and the agencies dealing with the family, but there was inconsistent recording of outcomes, a reliance on partner agencies to do follow ups, and difficulty responding to a high volume of cases.

He was sad the girl had found herself at a "crossroads".

Beattie feared a serious allegation made by the 12-year-old in May 2017 could've been a tipping point.

"She's either acting out and behaving badly, and there's been some behavioural stuff going on at school, or she's being completely honest, and she's let that secret out, and she's shared it with the school about what's really going on at home."

Police questioned the mother about the allegation but she denied it.

Beattie said if allegation was true, then the girl "would have felt extremely alone that the one person who was supposed to have her back, didn't".

"I say that with a lot of caution, but if she was telling the truth, then she would have felt extremely betrayed by her own mother."

He said the case had affected a lot of staff and was "just a tragedy".

Coroner McKenzie asked the detective what challenges still existed working with families in similar situations.

He pointed the finger firmly in one direction.

"I think alcohol plays a big part part in in our communities. I've seen mothers give up their children because the desire for the bottle is stronger than the love for their child. I think it gets underestimated, the impact of alcohol in our community.

"When it's just alcohol abuse or alcoholism, I think it gets lost. Like there almost needs to be blood on the floor to really get people to see it for what it is."

The inquest continues Wednesday.

World.title: Tarakihi catch limits reduce to 10 per person nationwide
World.content:
Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says tarakihi catch limits will be reduced, with a nationwide recreational fishing limit of 10 per person.

Commercial limits for the eastern fishery are being reduced by 20 percent, and the western fishery by 55 percent.

Jones said he has considered the latest science and catch information, uncertainty about future stocks of young fish, and the effects of use of the fishery in making the decision.

"These measures will immediately reduce fishing pressure on these tarakihi stocks and put them on more positive trajectories, while allowing a lower level of fishing to continue.

Limits have been increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast, leatherjacket on the South Island's east and south coast, and frostfish and blue mackerel in deep water.

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Butterfish catch limits have also been reduced, with a five-per-person recreational limit.

Seafood NZ chief executive Lisa Futschek said the quota management system was working as intended.

"This process matters. Sustainable fisheries management isn't about catch limits remaining static; it is about making changes when the evidence shows they are needed."

The company's general manager for inshore fisheries Tiff Bock said they supported decisions to ensure tarakihi stocks continued to rebuild.

"Industry has been actively rebuilding east coast tarakihi since 2018 through catch reductions, avoidance measures, gear changes, improved monitoring and significant investment in research. We remain committed to rebuilding the stocks."

Reduction 'does not cut it'

Benn Winlove, a spokesperson for the LegaSea non-profit marine life advocacy group, said a 20 percent reduction on the east coast "does not cut it" and the government should expect further court cases.

"We have watched the stock fall dramatically, with little intervention from officials or successive fishery ministers. Court cases by Forest and Bird and the Environmental Law Initiative have made the government make bigger reductions, but it's not working.

"On the east coast, tarakihi is at 7.7 percent of its estimated original biomass. This is well below the 10 percent hard limit where closure is an option, and the rebuild plan is clearly not working."

The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) said tarakihi fared better on the West Coast at 29 percent of its unfished biomass - but it was in rapid decline.

Policy director Raewyn Peart said EDS sought a total closure of the fishery, until the stocks recovered. Seafood New Zealand and other commercial fishing interests sought the 20 percent reduction in the harvest that was adopted by the minister.

"Given how depleted tarakihi stocks are, and how important this fish is for New Zealanders, the minister's decision is extremely disappointing," said Peart.

"EDS called for a complete closure of the fishery given its perilous state. But the minister's decision doesn't even mention closure as an option. This is despite the eastern stock being below the hard limit, which is when closure needs to be considered under the Harvest Strategy Standard," she said.

Fisheries New Zealand's analysis indicated that the harvest reductions adopted by the minister would mean the stocks would continue to be overfished, Peart said.

"It is also clear the western stock will continue to decline and the eastern stock will remain at very low biomass levels for an extended period. This brings the risk that any adverse event, such as a marine heatwave, could tip it over the edge so it never recovers."

"EDS is now investigating legal options to challenge the decision," Peart said.

Catch limit changes:

Inshore

Snapper, increase - SNA 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Trevally, increase - TRE 2 - East Cape, Hawke's Bay, and Wellington

Leatherjacket, increase - LEA 3 - east coast South Island, Southland

East Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1E, 2, 3, 7E - east coasts North and South Island

West Coast tarakihi, decrease - TAR 1W, 7W, 8 - West coasts North and South Island

Stargazer, decrease - STA 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Butterfish, decrease - BUT 7 - West Coast and top of the South Island

Shortfin eel, decrease - SFE 13 - Te Waihora (Lake Ellesmere)

Pāua, decrease - PAU 7 - Marlborough

Elephant fish, decrease - ELE 3 and 5 - east coast South Island, Southland, and Sub-Antarctic

Ling, decrease - LIN 1 - Northland, Auckland, Waikato, and Bay of Plenty

Pāua, decrease - PAU 5D - Southland and Otago

Deepwater

Blue mackerel, increase - EMA 7 - west coast North Island, West Coast South Island

Gemfish, increase - SKI 3 - east coast South Island, Chatham Islands

Frostfish, increase - FRO 3 - east coast South Island

Scampi, increase - SCI 3 - east coast South Island, western Chatham Rise

Ling, decrease - LIN 7 - West Coast and Top of the South Island

World.title: Nicky Hager's new book Dirty Work 'exposé' of Taxpayers' Union
World.content:
Investigative journalist and author Nicky Hager has released a new book called Dirty Work, an "exposé"of the Taxpayers' Union (TU), "the latest front for New Zealand's radical right," he says.

Hager argues the Taxpayers' Union used anti-Māori rhetoric as a political tool - especially during its Stop Three Waters campaign - and shifted the 2023 election campaign to the right.

He claims both Act leader David Seymour and National leader Christopher Luxon pivoted toward this rhetoric to gain votes.

Hager called Dirty Work the third part of a trilogy which began with The Hollow Men. The third part of the trilogy focused on the TU.

He argued the TU arranged a "multi-million-dollar" campaign that helped move New Zealand's 2023 election "to the right".

The key characters were the co-founders, Jordan Williams and David Farrar, and a sister organisation called Hobson's Pledge, set up by Don Brash, he wrote.

Nicky Hager at the launch of his book Dirty Work. RNZ / Melanie Phipps

Hager said the book was the story of how a "campaign of racist politics unfolded," alongside the "continual attacking, mocking and smearing of their political opponents".

Hager said the story was about democracy. He said the book (and its predecessors) show "how easy it is to spin and manipulate" and how "our defences as a society (news media, electoral laws and so on) are inadequate to protect the public".

He said the "rise of unregulated social media and dramatic collapse of traditional media have only made this problem worse."

RNZ has gone to those featured in the book for comment.

Taxpayers' Union says it is under attack

Shortly after the book's announcement, Williams sent supporters an email saying the book was "full frontal attack" on the Taxpayers' Union, himself, and Farrar.

"Hager calls himself a journalist. But yet again he has ignored the most basic principles of fair journalism: put serious allegations to the people accused and give them a reasonable opportunity to respond," Williams said.

He said Hager did not put the allegations in the book to the Taxpayers' Union, nor did he seek an interview or give the TU the opportunity to "correct errors or provide missing context" before publication.

"Instead, he released his accusations at a carefully choreographed media event, in the middle of an election campaign, knowing that the headlines would be written before we could even obtain a copy of the book - let alone check its claims."

World.title: Search to continue for missing 1978 plane after inconclusive object found in Lake Moeraki
World.content:
Search crews scouring a South Westland lake for a plane that disappeared in 1978 say an object sighted on Tuesday does not appear to be an aircraft.

The renewed search for flight ZK-EBU has brought relatives of its pilot and six passengers to the shores of Lake Moeraki north of Haast.

Coastguard, police and navy teams used sonar equipment to scan the lakebed on Tuesday, before divers took a closer look at a shape they had detected.

Senior Sergeant Mark Kirkwood, who was in charge of the operation, said it was worth looking at closely, but the divers were not confident it was an aircraft.

"After 47 years, we understand the significance of this moment for the families of the seven people who disappeared, some of whom are here today, and for everyone who has worked to find answers about what happened to them," he said.

"We will take time tomorrow to have a closer look."

Crews would undertake further analysis of sonar imaging on Wednesday and also search further into the lake, he said.

The renewed search followed decades of efforts by volunteer aviation investigators to find the plane, a Piper Cherokee 6.

Using his own sonar equipment, Hastings resident Gavin Grimmer detected an object in the lake earlier this year.

Westland mayor Helen Lash, who was also watching the search on Tuesday, said it was an emotional day for relatives of the people who vanished.

"They're hopeful, but it's a restrained hope because the worst fear is that it's not what we're hoping it might be," she said.

On Tuesday the search team deployed sonar equipment from a Coastguard boat, Katie Todd/RNZ

"If this means finding something that's been missing for some time and giving those families closure, that's amazing."

The plane had 28-year-old pilot Edward "Ned" Morrison, five members of the Dunedin-based Stuart family and 20-year-old David Hogg on board.

In the days after it disappeared, search crews scoured 2.1 million hectares of land but found no trace of the plane.

Fiordland's John von Tunzelman, who was involved in the search, told RNZ it was "most disappointing" to come up empty handed.

World.title: NRL's hardest job a family affair for Rob Toia
World.content:
Marking Herbie Farnworth is just about the hardest job any centre can have in rugby league, but Roosters flyer Robert Toia will not have to do it alone.

Friday night's preliminary final will be a family affair for the 22-year-old in more ways than one.

As a Redcliffe junior and one of 10 siblings, Toia cannot even begin to count how many friends and family he will have in the stands at a sold-out Lang Park, but he is sure to have some kin close at hand for his battle with Farnworth.

"Me, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong, we're all related," Toia said.

"We're cousins through our grandparents. Me and Salesi have always known since we were young, but Siua we only found out last year.

"[Redcliffe] is home. It's always felt like home, and every time I play at Lang Park, it's the stadium with the best atmosphere."

Toia and Wong discovered they were related last year. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Wong will line up at second row alongside Toia on the Tricolours right edge, against Farnworth and Toia's State of Origin teammate Max Plath, and both know what to expect from the fires of "The Cauldron".

Toia made his Queensland debut there after just 10 NRL games last year, while Wong is in the midst of his fourth finals campaign in as many years.

Foketi has been a later starter, only securing a place in the run-on side in recent weeks, but the three have been close ever since they lived together in the Roosters academy house as boys.

Around that same time, the trio played in a junior grand final against a Penrith side containing future Dolphins kingpin Isaiya Katoa, who will be a target for Foketi on Friday night.

The miracle wins that made Isaiya Katoa Isaiya Katoa prepares for his NRL semifinal debut as the prince of the game's playmakers and four years ago it was a series of brilliant finals performances that birthed his budding legend.

A bustling run from the 20-year-old knocked Cronulla halfback Nicho Hynes out of last week's semifinal after just 75 seconds and proved why he is a danger man even among a team with as much strike as the Roosters.

"I'm so proud of him. Everything is God's timing, because he was battling and playing Cup in the beginning of the year, but he got an opportunity and took it with both hands," Toia said.

"He's one of the best backrowers in the comp."

But as big a job as the Dolphins face with containing Foketi, Toia has an even more difficult one on his hands as he tries to put a saddle on Farnworth.

The Englishman has proven he is the best centre in the world several times over, if not one of the best players overall.

Farnworth leads the NRL in tackle breaks with 161, a full 44 ahead of the next best centre, and is first among all players for offloads with 75.

Farnworth is the best centre in the world and enters the prelim in terrific form. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

He is first among centres for runs, run metres and post-contact metres and is fresh off a magnificent showing in the Dolphins' 26-16 win over the Warriors that has them one win away from their first-ever grand final.

Toia has the size and athleticism to hold his own in any battle — in that star-making Origin debut last year, he held his own against no less than Latrell Mitchell — but Farnworth still shapes as a challenge that will go a long way towards deciding whether the Roosters can progress to their first grand final since 2019.

"You see the tackle-busting ability he has, but his work rate is underrated. He's always involved, on the offensive side and the defensive side," Toia said.

"I think pressuring him, shutting him down, getting my D movements right and hopefully, I can stop him from doing what he does best."

Toia comes into the match in imperious form of his own. He has scored in both the Roosters' finals matches and, along with Mark Nawaqanitawase, was the club's chief destroyer in last week's win over Cronulla.

The highlight was a massive fend on KL Iro that sent the rugged Sharks centre, who normally defends like someone taught a bicep muscle how to tackle, fully airborne.

It is a measure of how much Toia has continued to improve this season after claiming rookie of the year honours last year and a reminder that the best is yet to come, something the Tongan international believes is just as true for his team.

"I got a bit lucky there," Toia said.

"The boys just put me in the right spots and I was just moving for them.

"It's the best feeling [winning]. It's been frustrating for a lot of the year, we haven't been able to produce our brand of game, so it was good to show a glimpse of that.

"I feel like we still haven't played 80 minutes of Roosters footy."

World.title: Chimney colours unveiled for Norwood SANFL victors amid TV ratings boost
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Norwood Football Club's colours have been unveiled atop the Brickworks chimney to celebrate its SANFL Grand Final win in what was the most-viewed game since a modern rating system began.

The total national television audience on Sunday was up 16 per cent on 2025 numbers to 109,700, which included 93,500 broadcast TV viewers.

It also included 16,100 viewers from broadcaster video on demand (BVOD), which was up 52 per cent.

The VOZ ratings, which started in 2022 and combine both broadcast TV and BVOD, found that 87,500 viewers of broadcast TV viewers were from Adelaide, along with 12,800 of those streaming online.

The Norwood and Sturt colours will stay atop the Hoffman Kiln until the end of season 2027. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The broadcast ratings were exceptional, broke every record for the last five years," SANFL executive Darren Chandler said.

"And when you compare those to what's happening in Western Australia and Victoria, we've absolutely blown it off the charts."

SANFL kicking TV goals SANFL crowds are continuing to climb each year after COVID-19 restrictions put a dent in numbers

Football commentator Mark Soderstrom said 71 per cent of South Australian televisions switched on were tuned into the decider between Sturt and Norwood, which drew 38,250 spectators to Adelaide Oval.

The WAFL Grand Final, on the other hand, drew 19,210 people to Perth Stadium, continuing a four-year decline in crowds, while the VFL Grand Final drew just 12,941, the first time the league had attracted more than 8,000 fans in seven years.

A time-honoured tradition

The annual winners and runners-up of the SANFL grand final have been displaying their colours atop the 1913 Hoffman-designed kiln at Thebarton since the start of the decade.

The much-loved ceremony of nearly 70 years had to be moved from its previous home chimney at the West End Brewery after the facility was closed by its owners, Lion, in 2021.

Redlegs supporters came out to celebrate their team's 2026 premiership win. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Redlegs coach Jade Sheedy, who was a premiership player for Sturt in 2002 when he won the Magarey Medal with teammate Tim Weatherald, also coached Woodville-West Torrens in back-to-back premierships in 2020-21.
