He told the crowd of Redleg supporters at Thebarton that when the siren blew on Sunday and Norwood beat Sturt 87 points to 73 after a final-quarter comeback, he thought he was "still in a dream for 15 minutes".

"I guess it was two years of building something pretty special, and to come together in the last 30 minutes and to believe in that, and to kick five goals three to one point in the last quarter showed how much the group had grown and that's what I'm most proud of," Sheedy said.

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and coach Jade Sheedy were still celebrating on Tuesday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said the team had not changed "too much structurally" since they lost the preliminary final by two points in 2025 but had "increased the belief in how we play".

"We just fell short in 2025, but we took a lot of learnings from that and a lot of confidence reviewing how we were playing our footy," he said.

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle payed tribute to the Redlegs at the chimney ceremony. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt football manager Geoff Riddle attended the ceremony on behalf of the runners-up.

"I think we can all agree that Sunday was a great spectacle, and it was a great  for the competition and the league across the country," he said.

He said Norwood were "deserved winners" as the "most consistent team all year".

World.title: NRL grand final loses headline act for pre-match entertainment
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL says it is prepared to have no pre-match entertainment at its grand final this year after talks broke down with Australian artist Tones And I.

Instead the league is offering to increase funding to grassroots competitions with the money set aside for a pre-game performance.

Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC the money spent on pre-match entertainment could be put to better use.

"I'd prefer to see 20,000 underprivileged kids who can't afford to play rugby league play rugby league, rather than spend a million dollars on 11 minutes of a musical performance," he said.

The move would be a stunning break from tradition — the grand final has regularly featured pre-match entertainment, including international pop-star Teddy Swims last year.

Teddy Swims performed at last year's NRL grand final. (Supplied: NRL)

Billy Idol and Tina Turner are among other acts to have taken the stage for the event.

V'Landys said the total cost of such performances ran close to $1 million and that the plan for grassroots funding was one he had been mulling for sometime.

V'Landys was unconcerned as to whether the event could be underwhelming without pre-match entertainment.

"Our game sells itself," he said.

"People come to watch rugby league — they don't come to watch a pop concert."

V'Landys did not provide details on the record of why or how the negotiations with Tones and I broke down.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the issue centred the NRL's insistence that Tones and I perform the song Dance Monkey, which she had refused to do.

"You spend money to get outcomes and I think it's a better outcome to get kids that can't afford to play with their mates, gear etc, to play rugby league," V'Landys said.

"I'm a fan of Tones and I. She is a great performer, no doubt about that, and she's got some great songs, but as I said, we both decided to go to a different direction.

"We consider a lot of artists over a period of time, but as I said, I've been toying with this idea for a couple of years now, about giving the money to kids to play rugby league rather than a musical act."

Peter V’landys (right) says the league has decided it would prefer to spend its money elsewhere. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The grand final hosting rights are bid for by state governments across the country. New South Wales holds the rights now, but it is not clear if the minister for sport or the premier were consulted over the matter.

Neither office has replied to requests for comment.

NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said he had "a short conversation" with V'Landys about the prospect of funds being directed towards grassroots footy.

"I applaud his decision to use the funds to support grassroots rugby league, and particularly those children who may have financial constraints on their ability to participate in such a wonderful community sport," Trodden said.

"Rugby league has a unique ability to provide community support to those who need it the most."

World.title: Lachie Neale to miss grand final after AFL tribunal decision
World.content:
Brisbane Lions star Lachie Neale has failed in his attempt to overturn a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan at the AFL tribunal and will miss Saturday's grand final against the Fremantle Dockers.

Neale's "gut-punch" on Ginnivan means the former Brisbane co-captain has played his last game for the Lions, as the team seeks a second premiership three-peat in club history.

The appeal, held remotely with Neale watching from Queensland, took more than two hours, with deliberations going for close to two and a half hours.

Neale's counsel, Adrian Anderson, argued that the dual-Brownlow-winner's case was not a strike, rather a bump or body-check. He said if it was ruled a strike, that it was of "negligible impact" and if the Tribunal disagreed then there were "exceptional and compelling circumstances" to justify a ban being overturned.

Neale gave evidence that he had watched Ginnivan come together with Brisbane's Eric Hipwood, ending up lying on the tall forward and giving him several jumper punches.

He said he went over to "express his disappointment", and collided with him shoulder-first.

But the Tribunal did not accept his version of events.

AFL counsel, Andrew Woods KC, told the Tribunal that Neale was running away from the direction of the ball to confront Ginnivan.

"Neale is running ... he has time to decide what he is going to do," Woods said.

"It's not a football act. It's a forceful arm, you really see this with respect to the vision, that swinging towards the opposition player."

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC, told Anderson the incident was "well off the ball, not in play" and not a strike that happened during a grapple of scuffle.

Anderson argued that Neale's long and honoured career (320 games) without suspension was worthy of making an exception to the ban.

"The primary (argument for exceptional and compelling circumstances) is he is one of the best and one of the fairest to have ever played the game," he says.

However, the Tribunal disagreed.

"Having carefully reviewed the evidence and listened to Neale’s explanation, we find that this was a forceful blow, delivered with a swinging arm and an open hand," Gleeson said delivering the verdict.

" When played at normal speed, it appears clear to us that this was, to use the common vernacular, a strike to the guts. We are comfortably satisfied that this is what occurred. "

Gleeson said that after consideration, the panel did not feel there were exceptional circumstances to overturn the ban.

"The purpose of the [gut-punch] guideline is to stamp out this very sort of conduct. Neale ignored it, and he knew the consequences,' he said.

"Even Neale's outstanding record does not render a one-match suspension for that act inappropriate or unreasonable."

Look back at how Tuesday night's proceedings unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Diamonds name Klau for Constellation Cup squad
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Diamonds netballer Sarah Klau has retained her spot in Australia's Constellation Cup squad after pleading guilty to assault.

Klau was included in the 14-player squad named on Tuesday, less than a week after the goalkeeper was sanctioned by Netball Australia (NA).

The 31-year-old was handed a $5,000 fine and a two-match ban — suspended for 12 months — by the sport's national governing body.

Klau fined after unprecedented assault charge Diamonds defender Sarah Klau is handed a $5,000 fine and a suspended two-game ban after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the incident prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Klau had fronted Downing Centre Court earlier this month, facing a common assault charge.

She had allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub in Sydney's eastern suburbs when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

The NSW Swifts player had reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match a day after an ongoing leg injury ruled her out of the remainder of the Super Netball season.

Klau, who has represented Australia on 67 occasions since her Diamonds debut in 2019, failed to disclose the matter to NA before the Commonwealth Games in July, resulting in the sanctions.

Sophie Dwyer also retained her spot in the Diamonds squad, looking for a chance to find redemption after missing an after-the-siren shot in the Commonwealth Games semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Constellation Cup First Test: October 18 (Auckland)

Second Test: October 21 (Christchurch)

Third Test: October 25 (Sydney)

Fourth Test: October 28 (Melbourne)

Dwyer was left on the bench in Australia's bronze-medal win over England in Glasgow.

The core of coach Stacey Marinkovich's squad remains the same from the Games, with Jo Weston unavailable for selection.

Jessie Grenvold, Amy Parmenter and Donnell Wallam return to the side after travelling to Glasgow as reserves.

Grenvold is yet to make her Diamonds debut after earning her maiden call-up in May following a breakout season in defence for the Melbourne Mavericks.

The Constellation Cup begins on October 18, with the Diamonds travelling to Auckland to take on the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds squad: Kiera Austin, Courtney Bruce, Sophie Dwyer, Sophie Garbin, Matilda Garrett, Jessie Grenvold, Georgie Horjus, Sarah Klau, Cara Koenen, Kate Moloney, Amy Parmenter, Jamie-Lee Price, Donnell Wallam, Liz Watson

AAP

World.title: More votes than three entire clubs: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

World.title: Formula 1 agrees to shorter races in 2027
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Formula 1 has approved a 15 kilometre reduction in official race distances starting next season.

The change means the total distance will be cut from 305 to 290 kilometres.

The Formula 1 Commission finalised the decision in London.

"In line with the refinements to the power unit regulations to be introduced in 2027 on fuel flow, a reduction in the total race distance from 305km to 290km was approved, corresponding to a reduction of two or three laps," a statement read.

Aussie F1 GP loses season-opening honour Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

The power unit regulations favour increased engine power over hybrid electrical output.

To better handle rain delays and red flags, the commission has also abolished the strict three-hour overall event cap.

While the two-hour maximum of active racing time remains, the change gives organisers flexibility to complete full race distances.

Another objective ‌is to give spectators the best possible chance ‌to enjoy a full race when disruptions occur.

Practice sessions will also gain added flexibility to extend following stoppages.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Lions 'praying' Neale gets off but confident they will cope if ban stands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Lions players are confident they can cover the potential absence of Lachie Neale in the grand final, with the two-time Brownlow medallist facing a one-match ban.

Neale and the Lions will challenge the suspension at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday evening.

The 33-year-old has been charged with striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

If the suspension is upheld, Neale will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

Lions teammate Jarrod Berry said it would be a blow to lose Neale.

But he said the Lions were equipped to overcome any adversity.

"One of our best traits is being able to deal with that [adversity]," Berry said.

"We do it well and there's no point putting energy into it until we know the result.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact by match review officer Michael Christian.

There is damning vision showing Neale guilty of the behind-play strike and numerous precedents this season of other players being banned for one match for similar incidents.

But the Lions are set to argue the suspension should be downgraded to a fine.

They will cite a fresh clause that allowed Collingwood great Scott Pendlebury to avoid a suspension in March.

Clause that could save Neale The Brisbane Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Pendlebury was given a one-match ban for rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

He was found guilty by the tribunal but the sanction was downgraded to a $3,000 fine due to "compelling and exceptional circumstances", a clause open to the tribunal that will be central to Neale's case.

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record.

"However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances."

The Magpies successfully argued the clause applied to Pendlebury, who had never previously faced the tribunal in his storied 21-year career.

Neale also has not previously appeared before the tribunal in his 320-match career.

He is also a dual Brownlow medallist and premiership captain, plus a four-time All Australian.

Geelong coach Chris Scott does not agree with the provision.

"Seriously, when we're starting to say, 'There's a rule for you because you've done good things for the game,' it's almost implying that other people haven't done a good job," Scott said on Fox Footy.

But Scott added: "I know his record is exceptional, but aside from that, I just like to see them play.

"I actually think that's going to be hard to defend personally, but my hope is that he does play."

AAP

Tech.title: Oppo’s new phone is the first with three 200-megapixel cameras
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Oppo’s new Find X10 Pro Max flagship phone, launched today in China, is the first anywhere to use 200-megapixel sensors on all three of its rear cameras. A 17-stop dynamic range for the main camera, delivered thanks to what Oppo calls “DeepPix sensor technology,” suggests megapixel count won’t be the only thing this camera has going for it — a good thing, since raw resolution hasn’t been the main driver of smartphone image quality for some time.

The triple rear camera is built into a square, raised camera island, with a separate bar to one side holding the flash and an additional sensor. An orange accent line nods to Oppo’s ongoing camera partnership with Hasselblad. The regular Find X10 (there’s no sign of a simple Pro, oddly enough) has a similar design but without that extra lens element, and drops to a 50-megapixel ultrawide shooter.

The test for the Pro Max will be whether the cameras’ other specs deliver; resolution alone doesn’t mean much. Image: Oppo The regular Find X10 is a little smaller, with some reduced camera specs. Image: Oppo

The Pro Max is powered by MediaTek’s new Dimensity 9600 Pro, with the 9600M in the base Find X10. Both phones have big 8,000mAh batteries, IP69 ratings, and customizable photography color profiles and film looks.

Oppo’s Find X10 launch comes hot on the heels of yesterday’s X500 series launch from Vivo (with the same 17-stop dynamic range), while tomorrow sees Xiaomi reveal its 18 Pro flagships, as China’s biggest Android manufacturers get their flagships out in time for holiday sales seasons. Oppo has already confirmed that the Find X10 Pro Max will eventually get an international launch too.

Tech.title: Peloton is back with a ‘cheaper’ folding treadmill
Tech.content:
Last year, Peloton did a sweeping refresh of its hardware that added cameras, fans, and AI-powered software called Peloton IQ. This year, it’s zeroing in on its treadmill lineup — refreshing its two existing Treads and adding the new, more affordable Tread Flex into the fold.

At a New York City launch event, Peloton chief product officer Nick Caldwell told the press the $2,195 Flex — which can be folded upright to save 50 percent more floor space — was meant to address user feedback for a more easily stowed machine. When folded, the Flex purportedly has a smaller overall footprint than the Bike Plus. It also has caster wheels so it can be maneuvered more easily. For safety, the wheels can be locked in place, it has the existing Tread Lock passcode, and it has a slow-opening mechanism using a two-cylinder release. In person, it took about 25 seconds for the deck to lower fully. You don’t have to do anything or push the deck, and there’s no ka-thunk — it just sort of gently falls. That said, Peloton confirmed at the event that there are no sensor-based safety features.

There’s a two-cylinder release system that takes about 25 seconds to fully lower the deck.

While running, the Flex has a relatively quiet motor at 70 decibels. It’s hard to gauge exactly how quiet it is in a demo space, but it was notably quieter than other treadmills I’ve run on. I don’t think most people will have an issue running on the Flex’s shorter deck, but it might be a concern if you have particularly long legs. Like Peloton’s other treadmills, it has a swivel screen so you can do other types of workouts, but no camera, precluding it from some of the new Peloton IQ features (more on that below).

Meanwhile, its existing two treadmills have been rebranded as the $3,495 Tread Vision and $6,695 Tread Plus Vision. (The former is a $200 price increase, while the latter is the same price.) Here, the upgrades are more refinements. The Vision has a new deck that’s got better cushioning, redesigned jump buttons that let you go up and down for speed / incline, plus a redesigned tray for holding tablets, phones, and water bottles. The Tread Plus Vision also has the new jump buttons, plus a new “sled” mode that may appeal to Hyrox or Crossfit athletes. Both still have a swivel screen and motion tracking cameras that enable some new treadmill-related Peloton IQ features.

As far as software goes, all the treadmills are getting personalized pace. After about 10 running workouts, you’ll get a recommended pace targets that automatically populate within a workout. They may adjust over time as fitness improves. Peloton is also launching a new feature called ReRun, which lets you upload outdoor run course data recorded in the Peloton app or from a smartwatch into the treadmill so you can “re-run” them. That includes automatic incline adjustments based on outdoor elevation on a route. Peloton is partnering with NYRR so that users can “re-run” segments of the New York City Marathon course. At the event, press were told that the company is exploring partnerships for other famous races as well.

For the camera-enabled treadmills, Peloton is adding a running analysis feature. There’s a one-time calibration and then afterward, the movement-tracking camera will run in the background of subsequent workouts. Based on steps, cadence, vertical oscillation, and stride length, users will get a running efficiency score and tips on how to improve their form.

Previous Next















1 / 9 The Tread Plus Vision now has a sled and free mode that lets you have up to 300 pounds of resistance to mimic pushing exercises.

So far, Peloton’s big bet on refreshed hardware and AI hasn’t translated into earnings. At least, not with its existing user base. That may be why at the event, it seemed Peloton was keen to emphasize who it was hoping to reach with each treadmill. The Flex, for example, was repeatedly referred to as the ideal treadmill for walkers, hikers, and folks living in cramped New York City apartments. Its “cheaper” $2,195 price is also more in line with its bikes, though that’s relative considering you can buy other walking pads and treadmills for much less. On the other end of the spectrum, the Tread Plus Vision was described as the treadmill of choice for performance athletes. The Tread Vision was envisioned for multi-member households who might have people at varying fitness levels. (Various Peloton reps and instructors also pointed out the new redesigned tray as a great option for people who want an alternative to a walking pad — though it’s not possible to hook your laptop up to the display as a second monitor.)

Peloton has repeatedly identified the treadmill space as one it views as ripe for growth in earnings calls. Altogether, it’s clear that Peloton is hoping these new treadmills — but particularly the Flex — might attract new membership signups.

Tech.title: It’s time for the Mac Neo
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The Mac Mini is a great little desktop computer, and back when it cost $599, it was easy to recommend to anyone who wanted something speedy, simple, and cheap. The new M6 model is even better, but it starts at $899, and its 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU might actually be overkill for someone who just wants macOS and mostly does web stuff.

That’s why we need a Mac Neo. The MacBook Neo proves Apple can get good-enough laptop performance from an iPhone chip for $699. And you get a great screen, keyboard, trackpad, and battery with that money. Throwing a smartphone chip, a power supply, some basic speakers, and a few ports in a small box shouldn’t cost all that much if a whole-ass laptop version is $699. I mean, it’s a screenless phone with a couple of USB ports, Michael. What could it cost? $499?

And while the current Mac Mini chassis is incredibly small for what it can accomplish, a stripped-down model with a phone chip and no fan could be even tinier. Apple could go super small or just repurpose something that exists, like the chassis it uses for the Apple TV 4K. Add some ports — maybe not quite enough, knowing Apple — give it a couple fun colors, and you’ve got a Mac Neo. Or, dare I say, a Mac Nano?

As Apple’s M-series chips keep getting more powerful and more expensive, there’s a segment of people it’s leaving behind. RAMageddon is making everything cost more, even the MacBook Neo, but the Neo showed that a lower-cost MacBook wasn’t just viable — it could be great. There’s no reason a Mac Neo can’t do the same.

Tech.title: Meta patches Muse exploit that let attackers control the AI agent
Tech.content:
Meta has issued a patch for its Muse macOS app following the discovery of a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of the AI agent. The bug found by security researcher Patrick Wardle utilized an undocumented Muse setting that enabled potential attackers running local code to redirect transcription processing from Meta’s servers to their own endpoint, Ars Technica reports, giving the attacker access to the Muse account.

Several design decisions reportedly enabled this flaw, including having Muse dictation occur in the cloud instead of on-device, and allowing any app to control all of Muse’s undocumented settings. Proof-of-concept attacks developed by Wardle to test the exploit enabled him to take pictures and write malicious files to disk via Muse, which did not alert the user in many cases.

“We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want. So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself,” Wardle told Ars Technica. “At the very least, they should be thinking about security from the very start, and they are just not.”

That stands in contrast with the emphasis that Meta placed on Muse’s privacy and security features when it announced the AI agent earlier this month. Meta patched the vulnerability in the hours following the Ars report being published, and asserts that real-world security concerns were minimal because the exploit required local access to the user’s device.

“This was a local privilege escalation attack, not a remote exploit. Using it to do harm therefore requires malicious code already running on the user’s machine under their user account and the practical risk to users of the Muse Mac app was therefore quite low,” David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs said on X. “Nonetheless, we have issued a hotfix to the app to address the issue.”

While quickly addressed, the Muse exploit comes at a time when Meta’s AI agent is already being scrutinized as the company tries to claw back ground from rival AI providers. Amazon recently blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce platform and claims Meta never obtained its permission to do so. Still, the launch has been successful for Meta — during its first 12 days, estimated downloads of the Muse mobile app have reportedly outpaced ChatGPT’s own 12-day debut in the US and Canada, with Meta stock climbing by 11 percent on Monday.

Tech.title: Can you forget how you feel about Meta?
Tech.content:
In 2021, as a whistleblower emerged with dramatic allegations that Facebook was harming children, CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted a rebuttal on Facebook. âWe care deeply about issues like safety, well-being and mental health. Itâs difficult to see coverage that misrepresents our work and our motives,â he wrote in a note to Meta staff, which he reposted publicly. âAt the most basic level, I think most of us just donât recognize the false picture of the company that is being painted.â

Away from the stream of often inane public replies, one reader didnât like what they saw. Zuckerberg spoke with the unidentified person privately on WhatsApp, according to exhibits later released as part of a series of lawsuits, and the figure urged Zuckerberg â a parent himself â to make child safety even more central in his messaging. âi am not saying facebook is duplicitous and evil,â they wrote. âi am saying the opposite, you have heard the chorus and will PERSONALLY make this issue over adolescents your issue.â

In the privacy of the conversation, Zuckerberg was candid. âI care deeply about this and weâll continue focusing on being industry-leading with young people,â he responded, âbut Iâm not going to say itâs my personal main focus when I have a number of other areas Iâm more focused on like building the metaverse.â

Zuckerberg later reiterated that âI personally care about this.â But he appeared ambivalent, nudging his conversation partner away from older concerns and toward his vision for the future. âHow do you think this fits with our focus on promoting building the metaverse as the next major opportunity?â he asked. âThatâs not at odds with safety, but itâs a much different and more innovation-focused message.â Weeks later, Zuckerberg made a huge announcement: The company was changing its name to Meta in honor of its newest, most important priority.

Years after that conversation, online child safety concerns have ballooned â while if anybodyâs talking about the Metaverse, itâs likely as a multibillion-dollar money sink where nobody has legs. But the exchange is a microcosm of how Zuckerberg has run Meta, a sprawling online empire worth well over a trillion dollars: by always chasing the next big opportunity. Facebookâs motto was once, famously, âMove fast and break things.â Its new one might be closer to Move fast, break things, move on.

For two decades, Metaâs products have been at the center of what people do online. But Meta now finds itself besieged on all sides. Lawsuits have piled up as regulators turn on social media. A push into smart glasses has triggered a mountain of negative press and backlash â including the pejorative moniker âpervert glasses.â The company remains firmly behind in the AI race. Public perception of Zuckerberg himself has curdled.

Yet Meta is far from finished. It maintains a growing, highly profitable social media business. Itâs dominant in AI-powered smart glasses, what many tech leaders consider the next mobile computing platform. Itâs defused potential regulatory threats. And its latest platform, a âpersonal AI agentâ dubbed Muse, was released in early September, giving Zuckerberg his next metaverse-like project.

Muse is Zuckerbergâs latest bid to reinvent the company. Early numbers for Muse are promising; an Apptopia estimate this week indicates itâs got over 600,000 daily active users in the US, shooting it to the top of the iOS App Store charts. Yet the question remains: Can a company synonymous with safety and privacy debacles become the AI-powered voice in everyoneâs ear?

When Zuckerberg took the stage at Facebook Connect to announce that one of the most recognizable names in tech was getting a new identity, he was planting a flag. Facebook, the social media company known for its âbig blue appâ? That was the past. The future of the internet was the metaverse, an immersive 3D space where digital avatars could socialize, work, and collaborate, built on a virtual reality headset the company acquired in 2014. And after the covid pandemicâs mass shutdowns of physical space, Facebook believed in the metaverse so much that it would rebuild its entire identity around the niche world of virtual and augmented reality.

But to call Metaâs investment an abandoned boondoggle isnât quite accurate either. Meta dominates the nascent but growing smart glasses market, perhaps its biggest success story in recent years. The metaverse may not be the future of computing, but its augmented reality ambitions could still pay off.

Few expected the Ray-Ban Meta glasses to take off when they launched in 2023. After all, Metaâs first attempt, the Ray-Ban Stories in 2021, was a bona fide flop. Ninety percent of owners left the glasses to rot in their drawers. But improvements to cameras in the next-generation hardware helped Meta to sell roughly 2 million units â surprising even Zuckerberg. By the end of 2025, EssilorLuxottica â Metaâs partner in building these devices â had sold an additional 7 million units. All told, Meta and EssilorLuxottica reported that smart glasses sales doubled in Q2 of 2026.

Few expected the Ray-Ban Meta glasses to take off â but their success has surprised even Zuckerberg

Most importantly, Zuckerberg and Meta leadership view this tech as the perfect vehicle for the companyâs latest, shiniest interest: its AI investments. So much so that Meta is aggressively trying to brand these as AI glasses.

âI think in the future, if you donât have glasses that have AI â or some way to interact with AI â I think youâre probably [going to] be at a pretty significant cognitive disadvantage compared to other people and who youâre working with or competing against,â Zuckerberg said in a 2025 earnings call.

Meta is still funneling billions into the AR space without profit, but thatâs not necessarily disastrous. âThereâs no true way to tell if [Meta] is successful or not. You could measure market share, and they absolutely have that, but that still doesnât speak to profitability or if the spending to date is justified,â says Jitesh Ubrani, research director at IDC, noting that the runway for XR â the umbrella term for virtual, augmented, and mixed reality â is a notoriously long one.

VR and the metaverse also had long runways that never paid off. But right now, the smart glasses market is building momentum, making it far too early to say whether itâs doomed to the same fate.

Looking at what numbers do exist, Meta is the undisputed king. According to IDC, Meta commands 69.2 percent of the smart glasses and headset market as of Q2 2026. That number jumps up to 76 percent of AI glasses without displays. That said, Ubrani argues that itâs unlikely that any company will see a return on investment in the next five years. Itâs possible, he says, that could take as long as 25 years. Absent profit, the next best measure of success is often determined by who can afford to stay in the game long enough â while ignoring demanding investors â to influence the next chapter.

âIn the XR market, Iâd say that [Meta] is the leader in every segment they play in,â says Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. That can be a double-edged sword, though. âTheyâve both been a steward of the XR and AR space, but theyâve also limited its potential because they control the platform, the spending, and they decided who were the winners and the losers by investing with their dollars.â

Both Sag and Ubrani also agree that Meta wouldnât currently be the leader in smart glasses or a major player in AI if not for its early, if flawed, investments in VR.

Metaâs success on this front has kicked off a race among tech companies. Google is pushing its Android XR platform, working with Samsung to launch several âintelligent eyewearâ products later this year. Bloomberg has reported that Apple is also working on a pair. Outside the major players, there are dozens of Ray-Ban dupes from smaller companies. Again, Ubrani says itâs difficult to put hard numbers on how much tech companies are pouring into this space â but whatever the cost, the prize is winning what Silicon Valley sees as the next big mobile computing platform.

Ubrani points to the smart glasses supply chain, where âone player whoâs willing to invest no matter where the market is goingâ has massively changed the game. He contrasts that approach with Google, which retreated after criticism of its own glasses over a decade ago. âWhen people didnât like [Google Glass], they scaled back significantly, and that in a sense, hurt the entire industry. Now with Meta, weâre seeing that even if Metaâs not making money, the industry is still moving forward.â

âEven if Metaâs not making money, the industry is still moving forward.â

On paper, it might seem Metaâs already won the battle for the next mobile computing platform. At least, if Meta werenât Meta. While the company gained serious momentum in 2024 and 2025, itâs attracted a public backlash largely of its own making. Meta pushed its glasses as a way to make content for Instagram and other platforms, but failed to account for how bad actors might misuse its products. Online pickup artists and pranksters have started using the devices to harass women and retail workers, resulting in the âpervert glassesâ label. The resulting videos are pushed to social media, where they effectively publicize the techâs most troubling aspects. All this stokes roughly a decadeâs worth of privacy concerns stemming from indiscriminate data collection, breaches, and advertising practices. Itâs not just that Meta perhaps underestimated how its products could be misused. It already built a reputation for not taking privacy seriously.

In recent months, activists have launched guerrilla campaigns in major cities by âremixingâ Metaâs own marketing, painting smart glasses users as privacy threats.

Meta has tried to demonstrate that it cares about privacy. âIf people arenât comfortable with you wearing the glasses, not only do we personally think thatâs bad, but we wouldnât have a business anymore,â Alex Himel, Metaâs VP of wearables, recently told The Verge ahead of a mandatory update that makes it harder to disable the LED light that alerts people that the headset is recording. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has also recently said Meta will take down prank videos captured with the Ray-Ban glasses.

But these have been largely reactive policies. For the public, they look more like attempts to distract from unflattering news that feeds into Metaâs notorious privacy reputation. The New York Times reported that Meta intended to launch facial recognition software during political unrest to throw off privacy advocates. That was soon followed by a Wired report that said Meta had shipped â but not activated â this facial recognition tech to millions of glasses. Rounding out the trifecta was a Financial Times report that Meta is working on âsuper sensing glassesâ that will be able to see what youâre doing 24/7. Andrew Nazdin, director of Glasgow Actions Team, one of the groups behind the guerrilla campaigns, says it would be âfoolish for us to let them police themselves instead of calling on society to reject this [tech].â

Itâs too soon to say if this backlash has hurt Metaâs smart glasses ambitions. Ubrani says we likely wonât see any impact on sales â if there is one â until the holiday season. Even so, analysts arenât convinced Metaâs bad reputation is enough to derail its hopes for smart glasses.

âMetaâs done a very poor job of talking about privacy and setting the right tone,â acknowledges Sag. âBut itâs funny because if you go [politically] far left or far right, people care more about privacy. In the middle, people care less and just want to have a good experience.â

âIf you go [politically] far left or far right, people care more about privacy. In the middle, people care less and just want to have a good experience.â

As for public distrust of Zuckerberg, Sag says his thorny reputation may not sit well with the public, but itâs considered part of Metaâs strength in a niche space like XR.

âMeta would not be where it is today if it werenât for Mark Zuckerberg â¦ Even if people disagree with him, ultimately what he wants is what gets done,â Sag says. âI think his fear of losing the AI race is what sparked the whole Superintelligence Lab, and now theyâre back in the competition. He has blind spots, but heâs able to correct much more quickly than any other CEO founder â¦ every time people have counted him out or questioned his leadership, heâs been able to claw the company back.â

That unilateral doggedness is why Meta seems hell-bent on barreling forward with AI glasses, privacy qualms be damned. A few months ago, it released Meta Glasses, a newer and cheaper version of the Ray-Ban glasses sans Ray-Ban branding. At a launch event, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth told the press that Meta was contemplating audio-only glasses without cameras. It will likely launch even more new styles, collaborations, and potentially new hardware and privacy protections at Meta Connect 2026 this week.

âMeta missed mobile, they missed VR when it first came out. The metaverse didnât pan out the way they thought it would. Thatâs one of the reasons why weâre seeing them so determined and willing to spend to make AI glasses happen,â says Ubrani.

Itâs unclear whether Meta can maintain its lead in the XR space. AI wearables are only just beginning to heat up, with players big and small eager to throw their hat in the ring across multiple form factors ranging from pendants to smartwatches. Meta only has glasses â and itâs tying the glassesâ success to the overall success of the companyâs AI bets. And on that side of the business, things are looking like a hot mess.

Last summer, Zuckerberg attempted to lure top AI talent to supercharge his companyâs lagging AI division. He offered a series of staggering pay packages, running up to $1 billion, to join Metaâs Superintelligence Labs. But more than a year later, the company doesnât have much to show for it besides two manifestos published by Zuckerberg and the recently released Muse.

Zuckerberg may have inspired confidence among investors and analysts, but sources at or close to the company told The Verge that morale is down, AI initiatives are scattered at best, and the companyâs AI strategy is running largely on vibes alone.

âItâs a shitshow,â says one longtime Meta employee, who works on Reality Labs and requested anonymity for fear of retaliation.

Meta dipped its toes into AI around its metaverse restructuring and released a small group of models. But focused on Zuckâs VR ambitions, it missed its competitors investing in upstarts that would soon become AI giants. Its first frontier models were released in 2023 to lukewarm reception, and it wasnât until the tepid response to Llama 4 in 2025 that the company jumped into the AI race with both feet.

Thatâs when Zuckerberg kicked off his AI hiring strategy in earnest, even hand-delivering soup to researchers and engineers he wanted to recruit from rivals and other industry heavyweights. In June 2025, Meta invested $14.3 billion in data-labeling company Scale AI and poached its CEO, Alexandr Wang, to lead Metaâs AI efforts. But many AI engineers turned down Zuckerbergâs advances. Meta AI underwent wave after wave of reorganizations, and its superintelligence sub-team, TBD Lab, has reportedly clashed with Meta executives over opposing goals.

TBD Lab has reportedly sought to think longer-term and build best-in-class models to secure the companyâs place among its competitors. But executives have reportedly remained focused on more platform-specific ways to drive revenue, like companion chatbots and social media features. Some attempts to integrate AI into platforms like Instagram have drawn backlash â it briefly launched and then suspended a controversial Instagram deepfakes generator, and said it âmissed the markâ on an AI tool that provided creepily detailed information about a userâs children.

âEvery time a new technology comes that could potentially augment the companyâs revenue stream beyond ads, the company kind of goes manic.â

Metaâs most prestigious AI team is a âtotal mess,â according to Wired reports that describe internal chaos and ever-changing strategy. Zuckerberg reportedly admitted to employees during an internal town hall this summer that progress on AI agents was slower than expected. On a recent Meta earnings call, an analyst told executives he had been fielding questions from investors about Metaâs amount of debt compared to capital, as the company ramped up its spending to try to get ahead in the AI race. Zuckerberg has also been criticized for slashing team sizes to reportedly replace a significant number of employees with AI systems, per Reuters.

The current employee says Meta has a bad habit of jumping from hype cycle to hype cycle: âEvery time a new technology comes that could potentially augment the companyâs revenue stream beyond ads, the company kind of goes manic in order to invest and to change and to grow, to incorporate this new technology. It happened with crypto. It happened with VR and the metaverse. Itâs happening now with AI. I think it stems from a lack of maturity of our founder [and] a lack of maturity of our leadership.â

A former Meta employee, who also requested anonymity, echoes those thoughts: âLike most big tech, thereâs just been such a big push to AI-ify everything ... but itâs basically a laughingstock internally.â

In a May podcast interview, Wang denied that he and Zuckerberg had been fighting a lot, saying leaders at the company know frontier model development and product integration are both important. But, he added, âlike any company â¦ we debate the points deeply.â

But the current employee says Metaâs AI strategy simply isnât based in the reality of the business or what its customers actually want. âThereâs a whole different planet between what the C-suite is talking about and whatâs happening on the ground,â they say, later adding, âThat tension is literally at the core of the problem at Meta â¦ building AI for the sake of having the biggest building or the biggest fucking dildo versus building a useful product.â

Meta has spent an extraordinary amount on AI, but itâs made few waves in the industry

Zuckerbergâs latest manifesto â in which he lays out his vision of superintelligence that people use âto create and discover extraordinary new things, build new businesses, express new ideas, learn new concepts, and advance our health and quality of lifeâ â didnât make many waves in the broader AI industry. And so far, the features Meta has added to smart glasses and the products itâs rolled out havenât broken through compared to the companyâs biggest rivals. Given the early usage statistics, Muse could break this pattern â but itâs too early to know.

Noah Smith, senior director of NLP research at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (Ai2), says the manifesto âreads to me a bit like PR â¦ I also didnât find anything particularly surprising there, or new.â Instead, Smith found himself asking what is going on behind the scenes to make Zuckerberg publicly state all this now.

Zuckerbergâs manifesto also wasnât received well internally, according to the current and former Meta employees The Verge spoke with. In particular, the current employee says itâs a typical example of putting the cart before the horse.

âThe manifesto did not articulate the biggest question,â he says. âWhat will AI do for our business as an advertising business? What is the benefit in terms of return on investment on the hundreds of billions of dollars that weâre spending? We donât even have a product play.â He adds that even after Metaâs massive investments, he wouldnât rank his own company in the top three of AI players â and that thatâs reflected by the fact that engineers at the company donât typically prioritize using Metaâs own AI models, instead using models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Chinese AI companies.

He says that after Meta announces a new AI model internally, people will try it out for a little bit and then typically go back to using Anthropicâs Claude models; he compares employees using MetaAI to children goaded into eating their vegetables.

âI think if we actually cared about developing AI well, we would have everyone just use [our] AI and constantly give feedback,â he says. âThat would be monumental. But likely we would take a productivity hit in other ways.â

Overall, âmorale is in the gutter,â the current employee says. âPeople do not trust leadership. I get a strong sense that leadership doesnât even trust Mark in his direction.â They add that employees feel the company is spying on them and forcing AI into everything, and amid restructuring and layoffs, workers are âtired of the pizza partiesâ and havenât seen any movement on top internal complaints, like problematic incentive structures, misuse of tokens, and pace of work.

The former employee says that colleagues at the company feel that itâs âlike the Metaverse 2.0,â and though Zuckerberg bought some of the best AI talent in the world, âstill, they donât have a thing that anybody wants.â

A lot of people at Meta, the employee says, think itâs an inevitability that the company will drop its AI efforts the same way it sidelined its metaverse ones.

Meta is betting on giving users free, easily packaged access to agentic AI, but its position in the industry is tenuous

âItâs not going to be framed [as him] abandoning anything,â the current employee says. âThey were going to turn off Horizon Worlds, and Zuck got wind of it and he said they need to keep it on even though itâs a money-suck â¦ Zuckerberg does not want to admit defeat. But there will be a strategic pivot â¦ away from this manic AI spending to whatever is next, maybe a derivative of AI, maybe more wearable stuff.â

Muse is the next step in Zuckerbergâs plans: a move from straightforward language and image models toward more practically useful agentic AI. Itâs betting on giving users free, easily packaged access to the kinds of tools that might previously have required dedicated hosting machines or cost hundreds of dollars a year. But itâs too early to tell if users will trust Meta with the keys to their digital lives. Meanwhile, Metaâs position in the industryâs top tier appears as tenuous as ever.

In response to questions from The Verge, Meta spokesperson Alex Dziedzan said that âat Meta, our philosophy is simple: let our teams deliver. We encourage you to check out Connect to learn more.â

Meta is still trying to convince investors â and the tech industry more broadly â that its relatively nascent AI business has legs. In the meantime, the company is fighting to retain control of its true money machines and the original business proposition: pumping usersâ social media feeds, particularly on its flagship Instagram, with whatever keeps them engaged.

Four years ago, Instagram teased what would become perhaps its most reviled change to date: an âimmersiveâ experience where photos and videos took up a userâs full screen and filled it with content from accounts a user didnât follow. The feature was blatantly ripped from TikTok, its newer, more ruthless competitor, and to many users, the update represented a betrayal of Instagramâs core social elements.

Tati Bruening saw something worth saving in Instagramâs earlier, actually social, peer-to-peer communication platform. The photographer and creative tapped into widespread resentment and frustration, posting a graphic that was simple and to the point: âMAKE INSTAGRAM INSTAGRAM AGAIN,â it read. âStop trying to be tiktok i just want to see cute photos of my friends. Sincerely, everyone.â Kim Kardashian and Kylie Jenner, titans of attention-based online economy, reposted Brueningâs graphic. An online petition racked up hundreds of thousands of signatures. Eventually, the heat became too much to bear, and Instagram rolled back the changes. But it was only kicking the can down the road; this was the beginning of the end of an era.

Several years on, watching vertical videos of strangers is a cornerstone of social media, including Instagram. And Bruening has a new perspective, having seen platforms rise and fall and upend her job.

âThis is going to be the most shocking thing to hear coming out of my mouth, but I think in terms of all of the creator platforms, [Instagram] is going to be the one that makes it out of this era,â Bruening says.

âI think in terms of all of the creator platforms, Meta is going to be the one that makes it out of this era.â

Meta (as Facebook) acquired Instagram in 2012 for approximately $1 billion, and it eclipsed the companyâs then-eponymous blue app in relevance years ago. Central to the creator industry, celebrity culture, and lifestyle content, Instagram is a cash cow for Meta: eMarketer estimates it will pull in $52 billion in US ad revenue this year, compared to Facebookâs $48 billion. For the last few years, itâs been playing catch-up not only to TikTok but to a whole internet where people spend less time connecting with friends and relatives and more on an algorithmically sorted recommendation feed.

Yet along with its rival YouTube, Bruening says, Instagram remains one of the few social media platforms thatâs been somewhat stable. Snapchat no longer serves creators, and TikTok is too filled with slop and TikTok Shop content. Meta may have turned its photo app into a vertical video slot machine, but at least it rewards the creators who obey â if you make shortform videos, Instagram will show them to someone.

Creators and brands still see Instagram as the prestige, more polished platform where most advertising spend goes, says Lia Haberman, an influencer marketing expert who writes ICYMI, a social media newsletter. Whatever lead TikTok had in shortform content a few years ago has narrowed or even closed. The threat of TikTok disappearing from the US made advertisers nervous, Haberman says; creators started to think about backup plans and diversifying their platforms and online presence. When brands ask creators for deliverables â the assets and content that they want an influencer to post â Instagram Reels and Stories are typically first on the list, in Habermanâs experience.

Instagram is Metaâs cultural crown jewel, but the company is trying to diversify its revenue through other apps, too. Meta has tried to pull more creators onto Facebook with cash incentives. The companyâs massive messaging platform WhatsApp remains popular, especially outside the US; executives said subscriptions and paid messaging drove record non-advertising revenue. Threads, the X competitor, reached 500 million monthly users this summer, but it still feels a bit like the black sheep â in earnings reports, Metaâs âfamily of appsâ is defined as âFacebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp, and other services.â

The company has introduced a slew of other apps, like standalone platforms for Facebook groups and Marketplace, with leadership saying AI is speeding up development.

âSocial media is saturated in many ways. The hyper growth days for Meta are over.â

But despite Zuckerbergâs soliloquies on an AI-powered future, Meta is at its core in the business of serving ads, and that business is still booming: The company reported in July that its revenue from advertising grew 27 percent year over year. Some projections show Metaâs ads business surpassing Googleâs by the end of 2026.

The bigger problem is the people it shows those ads to, and the content it puts those ads in between. The average social media user is less interested than they once were in posting, and Metaâs access to a new generation of users is under threat.

âThere is sort of a tension brewing where weâre seeing this double-digit growth in their ad spend, but we are not seeing double-digit growth when it comes to overall usage [in the US],â Minda Smiley, senior analyst at eMarketer, says of advertisersâ spending patterns. âI think that just really speaks to the fact that social media is saturated in many ways. The hyper growth days for Meta are over.â

People in general are now using social media to consume content rather than share it; a Morning Consult poll found that a third of respondents say they post less on social media compared to last year. Whatâs more, entire generations of young people are logging off or forcibly being logged off.

The past few years have seen bipartisan, multinational, and cross-generational support for either limiting minorsâ access to social media or banning them altogether. When kids can get online, Gen Z and Gen Alpha donât want to express themselves fully on the social media sites their parents or relatives are on, and whatâs more, they want in-person experiences, Haberman says. They want to touch grass.

Katie Harbath, a former Meta public policy director who now runs tech policy consultancy Anchor Change, says that thereâs a small point of relief for Meta here, though: Kids arenât how theyâre making their money. Data compiled by research platform BusinessStats primarily from Facebookâs Ads Manager found that about 3.2 percent of Facebookâs global audience was between the ages of 13 and 17. On Instagram, using a similar dataset, that share was slightly higher, but still just 5.8 percent of the appâs global audience, according to BusinessStats.

âIf all of a sudden they canât have kids under 18 on, itâs not great, but itâs also not the vast majority of the people that are on the platform,â Harbath says.

But Meta will eventually need those users â it canât dine off the social media habits of older generations forever. What happens to Meta if its user base peters out, and advertisers follow? A reckoning could be coming in two to three years, Haberman says, if these trends continue as Gen Alpha comes of age.

Teen users are a tiny part of Metaâs business â but losing the next generation is something it canât afford

âIâm not sure that weâve really fully grasped yet how much of a big deal that this could be once audiences stop showing up or audiences age out,â Haberman says. âEssentially, itâs going to become kind of a graveyard for millennials, Gen X, and boomers.â The implications are manifold â for the social platforms themselves, naturally, but also for the advertisers, brands, and influencers whoâve taken for granted that social media is an effective way to reach people.

The elephant in the room is AI â Metaâs costly buildouts and investments, of course, but also the question of how to handle AI content on the platform, and how much of it users actually want. On its second quarter earnings call, Zuckerberg said the company would soon be able to provide a ânearly infinite universe of personalized contentâ to users through its image and video generation tools, to supplement content from influencers, creators, and usersâ friends and family. AI content is cheap, fast, and replaceable, made to be chewed up and spit out as long as the algorithms will allow it to be served up. This is what creatives like Bruening are competing against.

âYou would have to become an AI robot in order to keep up with a lot of the metrics and standards for what [Metaâs] best practices are,â Bruening says. âA human artist is not going to have the same level of output as an AI machine thatâs going to appease the algorithm.â How far can Meta push the human creators before they decide they no longer want to compete with their automated counterparts?

Much like Meta, creators are constantly chasing the next big thing, trying to weather shifting societal expectations and tastes. For individual creators, a failure to adapt can be career-ending; Meta now finds itself in similar precarious footing. But concerns about how people use social media arenât just a matter of business. Theyâre the object of serious inquiry for lawmakers across the world â all bent on reining in what they see as one of the tech industryâs most dangerous players.

Over the past decade, Meta has become one of the biggest punching bags in politics â and its CEO the face of a callous, out-of-touch, and exploitative âBig Tech.â Zuckerberg, Mosseri, and other executives have been dragged before congressional committees and juries and berated for a perceived carelessness toward kidsâ safety and disinformation, a ruthless crushing of competition, and even complicity in lynching and genocide. But through each PR crisis, Meta has somehow still found its footing, and in many cases, dodged the worst-case outcomes.

Meta grew to massive scale and influence in part through two key acquisitions: its purchases of Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014. But by 2020, those deals became the focal point of a major antitrust lawsuit seeking to break up the company. Since then, Metaâs acquisitions and competitive actions have faced intense scrutiny in the US and around the world, and its dealmaking leveled off. In 2020, it closed 10 acquisitions worth a total of $1.37 billion, according to data compiled by PitchBook; as it fought monopolization claims, its deal count and value dropped each year through 2024.

Through political crisis after political crisis, Meta has dodged the worst-case outcomes

Long-standing fears about Metaâs data collection efforts also reached a boiling point in 2018, when reporters uncovered evidence that London elections consultancy Cambridge Analytica had harvested millions of Facebook profiles to analyze and target users with pro-Trump messaging in 2016. That led to a flood of calls among users to #DeleteFacebook, even from Brian Acton, cofounder of WhatsApp.

But Zuckerberg later told The New York Times that the movement hadnât resulted in any âmeaningfulâ defection from the platform. In Europe, Meta was ordered to make changes impacting its ad-targeting practices after a $1.3 billion fine, but in the US lawmakers are still unable to agree on an industry-wide data privacy law.

Most recently, Metaâs most pressing policy challenge has been child safety. For the first half of the year, it appeared to be caught on its back foot. Two juries issued decisive blows to the company, resulting in close to a billion dollars in fines across an individual plaintiffâs case in Los Angeles and a case brought by New Mexicoâs attorney general. But the New Mexico judge later declined to impose the most disruptive structural changes the AG had asked for.

On the surface, a landmark settlement with 47 other state AGs in August looked even worse for Meta. The settlement included significant changes: new age assurance benchmarks, a two-hour daily usage limit (with exceptions for messaging and longform content), and default restrictions on nighttime and school hour notifications for teens.

But it also presented Meta an opportunity to turn attention onto its rivals. The company called on TikTok, YouTube, and Snap to adopt similar limits, and it tied part of its settlement payout to their actions. This helped Meta twice over: It could put a target on its competitorsâ backs while mitigating the potential negative business impact of its own deal.

New child safety regulations could end up helping Meta as well. eMarketer forecasts that Snap and TikTok would feel more of a hit than Meta if a nationwide classroom cellphone ban, another popular proposal, went into effect. TikTok would lose out on more than $1.25 billion in ad revenue this year, the firm estimates, and Snapâs ad revenue would be especially vulnerable because of the high concentration of teens on the platform who use the app throughout the day. A hit on Metaâs revenue, meanwhile, would âhardly register,â eMarketer says, thanks to its scale.

Meta could lose out under child safety regulations â but its competitors might lose more

Even so, Metaâs legal battles over kidsâ safety arenât over. Meta and other tech companies still face thousands of lawsuits from individual plaintiffs and school districts, likely culminating in a blanket settlement. The scope of cases and potential penalties is so large that itâs difficult to understand exactly how much risk they carry. It would take quite a lot for Meta to feel the sting, but the billions in settlements and court orders are beginning to add up.

Meta has already invested huge sums into fighting these cases. In the second quarter alone, it took a $2.4 billion charge over litigation expenses. Prior to Metaâs recent settlement with state AGs, Peter Chapman, deputy director of the Knight-Georgetown Institute, said that âsuggests to me that theyâre playing a long gameâ around the First Amendment and online liability shield Section 230.

Following the settlement news, Chapman says he still sees it as early days amid the mountain of litigation before Meta and other tech companies, but âthe long game certainly has changed.â Now it seems to include targeting industry competitors to get on board with the terms Meta already accepted, while a fight to preserve its protections under Section 230 will likely continue through appeals of the earlier cases Meta lost.

Metaâs settlement may bring some solace to investors who were unsure how to price in its legal risk. After the news of the deal, its stock price shot up. âThe state AGs got an okay deal. I donât think they knocked it out of the park,â says Paul Gallant, a tech policy analyst at investment bank TD Cowen. As a result, Meta shareholders should have âconfidence that the company knows how to manage the government.â

The $17 billion settlement represents an âimmaterialâ amount for Meta, Gallant says. In the last quarterly earnings report, Meta said it made more than $60 billion. But additional cases still present some risk, and large fines may be more of a problem today than when the European Union levied them in the past. âThe companies are spending so much on AI infrastructure that cashflow is a bigger focus of Metaâs stockholders, especially if the damage awards get into the tens of billions or more,â Gallant says. And unlike the tactics at its disposal to fight off impending legislation, Gallant adds, âof all of the features of the US governmental system, the least controllable by Meta is juries.â

âThese massive trials are happening against this company, and then what is Mark Zuckerberg doing? Putting out an AI manifesto.â

State and local governments also appear ready to take on tech while federal efforts stall, including in Metaâs latest area of focus, AI. Many are looking at how they can rein in AI and deal with the energy demands it creates on their electrical grids. Data centers have become a flashpoint across the country, and a nationwide push for a slowdown could be particularly meaningful for Meta and other businesses in the AI race. âThatâs the thing that could really not just slow them, but slow everybody down â having enough compute,â says Harbath. âWe talk so much about what happens at the federal level, but I actually think the biggest risk to Meta and these tech companies right now is at the hyper-local level.â

Zuckerberg has become the face of many of these battles, testifying for hours before policymakers and juries, and even standing up in Congress to apologize to parents who lost children after battles with online harms. The public testimonies have largely not seemed to endear him any further to his critics.

âItâs almost like this bizarre disconnect where these massive trials are happening against this company, and then what is Mark Zuckerberg doing? Putting out an AI manifesto,â Smiley, the analyst at eMarketer, says. âItâs sort of like, âWhat planet are you on?â It just feels like thereâs just this big disconnect.â

Whether it will matter is another unresolved question.

Despite the litany of PR problems, user frustrations, legal troubles, and internal personnel conflict, Meta still feels like an immovable force. It has managed to sidestep, acquire, and pivot its way out of scandals and blowups that would have sunk most other companies. Itâs spending lavishly on its new, AI-powered future.

But that future remains far from certain. Smart glasses are unproven, its AI labs are behind newer upstarts, the legal landscape is hostile, and it may be hitting its ceiling in finding new users.

Tech.title: Apple’s first live music venue is opening beneath its UK headquarters
Tech.content:
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is preparing to open a new “state-of-the-art” live music venue in the UK, a 600-capacity space for hosting performances, recording sessions, and video broadcasts. The venue, called Apple Music Hall, is located underneath Apple’s European headquarters in London’s iconic Battersea Power Station, and is set to open next week on September 28th. Details about the opening show have yet to be announced.

“Apple’s deep love for music dates all the way back to the very beginning, from the launch of the iPod to the long-running iTunes Music Festival to the debut of Apple Music,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vice president of Apple Music and International Content. “Today, with the opening of Apple Music Hall, we are once again taking an unprecedented step further in our commitment to artists and fans by supporting live music in ways only Apple can do.”

Previous Next



1 / 3 The staging area is a pit-like space that can be reconfigured for traditional front-facing sets or more in-the-round experiences. Image: Apple

The limited capacity and layout is “designed intentionally to close the gap between intimacy and production value,” according to Apple’s announcement, with seating that feels close to the performer while providing artists with a 38-foot-wide stage that can be reconfigured to their needs. Apple Music Hall has a 48-speaker spatial sound system positioned around the audience, is hardwired for 16 or more broadcast cameras, and includes two dedicated recording and mixing studios behind the stage that allow it to operate as a full production facility.

Previous Next





1 / 4 Here you can see some shots of the new Apple Music radio studio. Image: Apple

The performance space is opening alongside new Apple Music radio studios in Battersea, with Apple announcing that all of its London-based hosts and shows will now broadcast from the facility. “We’re always looking for new opportunities to connect the artists and the fans because we are fans,” said Apple Music’s global creative director, Zane Lowe. “Great music and memories will be made at Apple Music Hall.”

Apple Music Hall marks the company’s return to London’s music scene, having previously run the iTunes Music Festival in England’s capital city for a decade — hosting acts like One Direction, Lady Gaga, Elton John, and Adele at intimate local venues — before its cancellation in 2017. Battersea Power Station, a decommissioned Art Deco facility that reopened in 2022, also has its own roots in music history, having appeared on the cover of Pink Floyd’s Animals album.

Tech.title: A cut cable disrupted hundreds of flights across the US
Tech.content:
is a senior editor who has obsessed over headlines and internet speeds since 2011. He previously worked as an advocate for the National Park System.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Hundreds of flights were cancelled or delayed on Monday after construction crews in New Jersey accidentally cut a Verizon fiber cable used for air traffic control.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a circuit failure led to the discovery of the severed fiber cable, ABC News reports. The outage hammered airports across the Northeast, causing ground stops at all three major New York City airports.

In a statement to CNBC, Verizon said that it bore “no responsibility for this incident,” putting the blame on “construction contractors working in the area” that “dug up and cut our cable.”

Ironically, it looks like trains make have taken out the planes, but fingers are still being pointed. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an Amtrak crew accidentally cut the line, but AP reports that Amtrak blames a New Jersey Transit crew for the disruption. “This incident occurred on New Jersey Transit property and involved a New Jersey Transit contractor,” an Amtrak spokesperson told NBC4.

As of Monday evening, Duffy said that “the telecom lines have been repaired, and all airport operations in the Northeast are resuming,” but cautioned that it will take “some time to clear all existing delays.” According to FlightAware, there were over 1,000 canceled flights today in the US

Tech.title: Amazon wants to help the Colorado River, but we still don’t know how much water the company uses
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon plans to spend $20 million on water conservation projects along the Colorado River, a crucial but dwindling water supply for 40 million people in the Western US.

The initiative comes as Amazon and other tech companies face mounting scrutiny over how much water their data centers use. Amazon has a goal of becoming water positive — replenishing more water than it uses — by the end of the decade. It recently disclosed some information about its water use, but we still have an incomplete picture of the company’s impact as a whole.

Amazon announced the launch of a Colorado River Basin Collaborative today, with a mission to “create one of the biggest corporate water conservation efforts for a single U.S. watershed.” It expects to raise $100 million over two years — including the $20 million investment from its own coffers — for water conservation efforts.

The Colorado River brings water to 40 million people

Stretching 1,400 miles, the Colorado River brings water to 40 million people across seven states in the Western US and and two states in Mexico. The waterway has faced “unprecedented” drought over the last 26 years, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Decades of overuse on top of human-caused climate change have exacerbated the problem. To cope, the US Department of the Interior finalized a plan in August imposing steep water cuts on Arizona, Nevada, and California.

As the first stop for most goods the US imports from Asia, California is home to more Amazon warehouses than any other state.
